## No. 36. RESOLUTION OF PAUL I ON THE SENATE REPORT CONCERNING THE SURVEYING OF LAND FOR THE CHERNIGOV COLONISTS (1800)

19,523. — August 21. Highest resolution on a Senate report. — On surveying the requisite quantity of land for the Little Russian colonists.

Report. The Expedition of State Economy and Guardianship of Foreigners presents to the Senate that, having received notification from the Little Russian Provincial Board concerning the colonists settled in that governorate on the Belovezh steppe, it observed that with respect to husbandry only a few of them are in moderate circumstances, while the greater part are in a poor state, the cause of which was the crop failures of past years, the loss of livestock, and the misfortunes suffered during the epidemic. The Treasury Chamber, under whose jurisdiction the colonists were placed, taking this as its basis, and knowing their genuine exhaustion, represented to the Senate the impossibility of collecting the money expended on them by the Treasury. This matter, as pertained to it, came before the Expedition of State Economy for consideration, which, having noted certain contradictions and deficiencies therein, corresponded with the Provincial Board and the Treasury Chamber. But since even so the information received could not fully satisfy the Expedition's need to determine an accurate resolution regarding those colonists, it instructed Collegiate Councillor Konteniuz — who by Your Imperial Majesty's Highest pleasure had been sent to inspect the foreign colonies settled in New Russia Governorate — to stop on his return journey from there to St. Petersburg at the Belovezh colony, and, having examined the colonists' condition in detail in every respect, to present a report on how most reliably and without undue burden to recover from them the money expended by the Crown, improve their condition, and establish economic administration over them. From the description he compiled, as well as from all the papers previously submitted to the Expedition, it appears that these colonists departed in 1765 and 1766 from places lying near Frankfurt am Main, and in 1768 from the environs of Danzig and Elbing; their number at that time consisted of 742 souls of both sexes. In the early years of their settlement many died, but in 1785 the Director of Economy found 469 males alone; according to the 1795 census there were 565 of them, and now there are reckoned to be 639 male and 588 female souls. They were of two kinds: farmers and craftsmen. Upon their departure from St. Petersburg for the place of settlement they concluded contracts with the Treasury, in which, among other things, it was stated: 1. That each family be given in kind a dwelling house with a barn and stable, grain for sowing and subsistence for the first year, the requisite number of livestock and poultry, and everything necessary for husbandry. 2. That churches be built for Catholics and Lutherans with all their appurtenances, and houses for the clergy, with their maintenance at Treasury expense for two years. 3. That they have the freedom, upon repayment of the money expended on them by the Treasury, to leave Russia. 4. That until they repay it, neither they themselves nor their heirs may abandon their dwelling and household, but must in all things act according to the contract without further recourse to the issued Manifesto. 5. That they not be charged for what was required for their travel and maintenance from St. Petersburg all the way to the place of settlement. 6. That of the sum expended in aid of their settlement, the farmers, apart from the first two years, pay in subsequent years six percent annually until the capital is fully repaid, and for fields and meadows, apart from the first year, according to their assessed value, 5 percent, or 25 percent of profit annually; while the craftsmen were to pay everything, after the ten years of exemption had passed, within three years, with the stipulation that thereafter they pay taxes on an equal footing with other subjects. As a result of this the colonists were provided for in full, except that no church was built for the Lutherans, nor houses for the craftsmen. The entire sum expended on them amounts to 71,219 rubles 83½ kopecks, the deadline for repayment of which, under their contracts, though it has passed — for the farmers in 1769, and for the craftsmen in 1777 — nevertheless, owing to the insolvency and poverty of all of them, it has to this day been possible to collect no more than 8,437 rubles 35¾ kopecks; after this collection there remains owing from them 62,782 rubles 48¾ kopecks, which sum, however, includes 20,708 rubles 57½ kopecks expended on their travel costs, from payment of which, by force of the contracts, they ought to be exempt. The craftsmen, among whom were various manufacturers, while awaiting the construction of the small town which was intended to be built on the site designated for their settlement, not having received the houses promised them under the contract, built themselves huts at their own expense, in which they still live in a state of hardship. The manufacturers, over the course of 30 years, have for the most part died out; the survivors, as well as the children of the deceased, for lack of means to practice their trade, have become tillers of the soil; but having only a very small quantity of land, some are compelled to rent plowland and hayfields from their neighbors, while others seek subsistence through wage labor. The farmers, meanwhile, are settled on the Belovezh steppe in five villages, built well and properly by the Treasury. The land held by both groups together is reckoned at 2,985 desyatinas, a quantity that was sufficient for them at the time of their initial settlement; but now, when their numbers have considerably increased, this quantity is quite insufficient, for it comes to no more than four and a half desyatinas per soul. Reckoning 4 souls per family, according to the number of souls presently on hand there would be a total of 160 families, and allotting to each 30 desyatinas, as designated by the former Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, 4,800 desyatinas of land would be required; but since they now have only 2,985, and of this, moreover, 47 desyatinas, under the name of the Kilchinovsky and Smolovoy hamlets, situated in the very midst of their allotments, are being taken from them by state peasants who formerly served the overseers previously placed over this colony and who were settled there by them, they are thus short 1,815 desyatinas. On this account the Expedition applied to the Little Russian Treasury Chamber as to whether such a quantity of land might be found in that governorate to satisfy the colonists, and also whether it might be possible to allot to that amount the state hamlet lying near the colony, called Chernechy, consisting, according to the statement of Collegiate Councillor Konteniuz, of 250 desyatinas held under quitrent, and to grant 50 desyatinas of state land lying near the village of Khvastovtsy, and further requested that the Chamber remove the peasants from the Kilchinovsky and Smolovoy hamlets, which belong solely to the colony, to another location. To which the Treasury Chamber replied that, since there is a very considerable shortage of land needed to satisfy the 15-desyatina allotment for the state department's peasants, it could not, without a special order, either resettle the peasants from the Kilchinovsky and Smolovoy hamlets, or assign to the satisfaction of the colonists the quitrent land situated at the Buromsky hamlet and the village of Khvastovtsy; but since those colonists are listed in the register sent to the Senate as among the state peasants, then upon receipt of a final determination on the division of the quitrent lands, they too would not be left unsatisfied. These colonists, the thirty-year exemption granted by the Highest Manifesto of July 22, 1763, having expired, were registered by the Treasury Chamber as state peasants, and accordingly for the year 1799 each colonist soul was assessed taxes of 3 rubles 40 kopecks, and, following the example of other state settlers, the sale of spirits was established in the colony, from which the colonists themselves had previously benefited, deriving profit from it. According to the testimony of Collegiate Councillor Konteniuz, these colonists, through their industry and diligence in farming and household management generally, deserve regard; but owing to the lack of pastureland and hayfields, they cannot expand their husbandry as they would wish; for however much attention they devote to livestock breeding, they do not succeed at it for want of fodder. Their income, judging by the small amount of land and the low prices of their produce, must be modest; for although in fruitful years they sell various surplus household products and livestock, on the other hand they are compelled to purchase hay, firewood, and timber for house repairs, and after such necessary household expenses little profit remains to them from their labors; and so Collegiate Councillor Konteniuz found in the whole colony only 12 households of good means, 80 of moderate means, 116 with a sufficient livelihood, and 13 poor through their own negligence. To recover the money expended on them by the Treasury, according to the aforementioned Collegiate Councillor's report, cannot be done without hardship except by improving their condition through an increase of land; whereas if it were collected under their present circumstances, many would become destitute. The colonists themselves have declared that if enough land is added to what they already have so that every family receives 30 desyatinas, they will be able to pay annually to the Treasury 20 rubles for it, provided they are thereby freed from all other taxes.

The Senate, having examined in detail the Expedition of State Economy's proposals for improving the condition of the Little Russian colonists, and noting that, having suffered crop failures and losses of livestock from the very time of their settlement, they fell from the first years into an inability to fulfill their obligation to the Treasury; that thereafter, however many measures were undertaken to improve their situation, these were never put into effect, so that neither the taxes due from them nor the repayment of the money expended on their establishment could be collected by the appointed deadlines; and that now, given the changed circumstances and the considerable increase of families, those measures can no longer be usefully applied, for although the said colonists are more in a moderate than in a poor state, the shortage of land is the chief reason it is impossible to collect, without utterly exhausting them, the debt to the Treasury reckoned against them — the Senate, in accordance with the Expedition's conclusion, in order to reconcile the Treasury's interest with the genuine welfare of the colonists, ventures most humbly to submit for Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical consideration the following opinion: 1. Since the craftsmen, upon their arrival in Russia, finding no opportunity at their place of settlement to practice their trade or craft, abandoned it and for the most part turned to farming, they should be placed on the same footing as the farmers and all provided with land at 30 desyatinas per family, reckoning 4 male souls per family. By this reckoning, for 160 families there ought to be allotted 4,800 desyatinas; but since they hold only 2,985 desyatinas, it is necessary to survey and allot to them an additional 1,815 desyatinas of suitable land. Into this number should be included the nearby Chernechy hamlet, consisting of 250 desyatinas, and the state land near the village of Khvastovtsy amounting to 50 desyatinas, while the remaining quantity should be allotted to them, as far as possible, not at any great distance, so that it may be convenient and without great expense to transfer a certain number of families there. And although it is evident from the statement of the Little Russian Treasury Chamber that there is a considerable shortage of land for satisfying the fifteen-desyatina allotment for state settlers, pursuant to Your Imperial Majesty's Highest decree of November 11 (27), 1797, nevertheless, in view of the fact that it is proposed to grant the said colonists, according to the arrangement of the former Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, 30 desyatinas per family, that is, half again more than the allotment set for state settlers, the Senate proposes to satisfy them in preference to the state peasants. 2. That the peasants settled in the Kilchinovsky and Smolovoy hamlets, situated within the plan of the Belovezh colony, placed there through the actions of the former overseers of the colony, be removed to other locations, in order to prevent disorders and disputes that might arise from joint ownership. 3. That of the 62,782 rubles 48¾ kopecks reckoned as the state debt owed by the colonists, 20,708 rubles 5½ kopecks expended on travel costs be excluded, since, both under the terms of point 3 of the Highest Manifesto of July 22, 1763, and by force of the conditions specially concluded with these settlers, this amount ought to be written off; after which the actual debt owed by them will be reckoned at 42,074 rubles 42¾ kopecks. 4. Under the contracts concluded with the Treasury, these colonists undertook to repay the loaned money, after the expiration of the known period of exemption, by an annual payment of 6 percent, and to pay as tax 25 percent of the profit they earn; but since they are unable to pay the former, and the payment of the latter is very difficult to determine, requiring a new calculation to be made every year, and since, moreover, the payment deadlines have passed, then, in order to avoid misunderstanding and further difficulties in calculation, the Senate deems it most convenient, rescinding the former arrangement, to substitute for it, with the colonists' own consent, having surveyed for them the above-mentioned quantity of land, to collect thereafter from each 30 desyatinas allotted per family 20 rubles annually, with the stipulation that 10 rubles of this be paid in as a land tax to the District Treasury and credited to the general State revenues, while the other 10 rubles be applied to the repayment of the debt reckoned against them, at the disposal of the Expedition of State Economy, for the restoration of the colonists' own condition, pursuant to the Highest Personal decree of Your Imperial Majesty given to the Senate on April 21, 1798, until such time as the entire aforesaid debt sum of 42,074 rubles 42¾ kopecks shall have been repaid, after which the full 20-ruble assessment will be collected from them as land tax into the general State revenue, on the same basis as has been established with regard to the Ostrogozhsk colonists; this will amount to 66⅔ kopecks of land tax per desyatina, which, in comparison with the tax paid by the St. Petersburg colonists, is deemed quite sufficient. 5. Having set an annual tax for the Little Russian colonists commensurate with their circumstances and therefore reliably payable to the Treasury, they should be freed from any other tax and excluded from the poll-tax assessment. 6. For the maintenance of proper order in this colony, the Senate deems it necessary to entrust it to the care and administration of the Office of Guardianship of the New Russian Foreign Settlers, established by Your Imperial Majesty's Highest command following the Senate's most humble report of April 6 of this year 1800, which, owing to the colony's not being far distant from Novorossiysk [Yekaterinoslav], may conveniently take charge of all arrangements concerning these colonists according to the instructions and directives of the Expedition of State Economy.

For the rest, the Senate, submitting all of this to Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical pleasure, requests Your Majesty's Highest decree.

Resolution. Begin by surveying the necessary quantity of land, as is done in the German lands; then sort this land into three kinds, and then, according to their custom there, establish the labor and form of tax, exactly as is customary in their lands.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVI. P. 268-272.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 36.

As this act shows, the situation in the Belovezh colonies at that time was quite typical of the early German colonies in general: problems with land allotment that worsened as the population grew, a shortage of pastures and hayfields, the unsettled state of artisans, and, as a result, low incomes and an inability to repay treasury debts on time. The measures proposed to remedy the situation are likewise fairly standard. One of them, however — placing the colonists under the newly established Office of Trusteeship of Novorossiya's Foreign Settlers — proved clearly unsuccessful, since the Belovezh colonies were too far from Novorossiya, and in 1809 this decision was rescinded (see doc. No. 56).

Ostrogozhsk colonists — inhabitants of the Voronezh colony of Riebensdorf, located in Ostrogozhsk uyezd.

Manifesto of July 22, 1763 — doc. No. 11; decree of April 21, 1798 — doc. No. 32; report of April 6, 1800 — doc. No. 34.

## No. 39. INSTRUCTION ON THE INTERNAL ORDER AND ADMINISTRATION OF THE NEW RUSSIA COLONIES (1801)

19,873. — May 16. Instruction for the internal order and administration of the New Russia foreign colonies.

Article I. On the obedience of settlers to the church; on the maintenance of Pastors

and the duties of the latter both toward parishioners and toward the authorities.

§ 1. The foremost duty of all settlers is to obey the law of their church: for this purpose each of them must, on Sundays and holy days appointed by the Priests, come to the church, pray with all reverence, listen attentively to the Word of God, and, when deemed worthy, partake of the Holy Sacraments. If someone absents himself not for lawful reasons but solely out of laziness and negligence, he is to be admonished the first and second time, then a fine of 10 kopecks is to be taken from him; and if this is exacted three times in one year and the guilty party does not desist, then in addition the monetary fine is to be doubled each time, and he is to be employed for a whole day in public labor, the money collected being placed into the common fund.

Note. Public works may consist of the repair of bridges and roads, the digging of ditches, the planting, clearing, and preservation of forests and mulberry trees, the establishment of vineyards, the improvement of meadows, and so forth, as may arise according to the local situation of the colony and the economic establishments therein. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 117

§ 2. Colonists of the Lutheran and Catholic confessions, after the expiration of the years of exemption, when payment of salary from the treasury to their Pastors ceases, must maintain both them and the Schoolmasters at public expense, for which the necessary sum of money is to be levied from them according to the number of souls composing their parish, apportioning this levy not by souls or families, but by the number of workers, counting those from 16 to 60 years of age. This collection must take place three times a year: in the months of January, May, and September; for this purpose special church elders are to be elected annually from among the settlers, who, collecting the money assessed by common consent of the community, must hand it over each third of the year to the District Head, and receive receipts from him. The Schulzen, for their part, are obliged to render every assistance to such church elder, so that nothing may fall into arrears; and whoever fails to pay his assessed sum by the appointed date shall, the first time, be charged in addition, instead of a fine, 10 kopecks, the second time 15 kopecks, and the third time shall be kept at public labor until he pays, and shall be reported concerning him through the District Head to the Office, with an account of his circumstances and the reasons that led him to such disobedience.

§ 3. The spiritual teachers of the Mennonites carry out the duty of their calling according to the rules of their confession, and the Pastors of the colonists according to the instructions and prescriptions given them by their Spiritual Authority: in secular matters and other affairs unbefitting the priestly rank they must in no way interfere.

§ 4. Since the Lutheran Pastor must have his actual residence in the Josephstal colony, and travel only temporarily to the Elisavetgrad and Swedish colonies, which are not situated at a close distance; it is therefore arranged that those colonies shall pay him travel money for his journey, in the amount required according to the number of versts and the apportionment of the Office, or, should the colonists so wish, send their own carts for him and drive him back, on the understanding that, having received travel money or carts, the Pastor may no longer demand from the colonists any further compensation for such journeys beyond his salary, as stated in § 2. In winter, once a year (and if the colonists are willing and able to pay travel money, or to send carts, then twice a year), he must without fail visit those colonies, and stay in each one not less than a month, both to confirm the colonists in the rules of the faith and to teach the children the elements of Christian doctrine.

§ 5. The Lutheran Pastor, during his presence in the Elisavetgrad and Swedish colonies, oversees the Schoolmasters, so that they perform their duty with due exactness, for which purpose he must give them full instruction from himself; in the Josephstal colony, however, he has continual oversight of the Schoolmaster. The Catholic Priest and the spiritual teachers of the Mennonites are likewise obliged to exercise the same oversight over their Schoolmasters.

§ 6. The clergy of all colonies must keep accurate records or parish registers of those married, newborn, and deceased, and after the passage of each half-year must without fail submit copies of them to the Office.

§ 7. If any offense should be committed against the named clergy by their parishioners, this must be reported immediately to the Office. But if the Pastor or church teacher agrees to forgive such a person, they are then exempted from the report and the fine; parishioners likewise have the right to complain to the Office, through their Head or Schulz, of dissatisfaction with their clergyman.

Article II. — On the establishment of Administrative Offices and the election of Heads, Schulzen,

Assessors, and other officials, and on their duties.

§ 8. Special Administrative Offices are to be established in the colonies, and in every Office there must be an elected administrative official, or Head, assisted by two Assessors and one clerk; for the Office in the settlement where the Head resides, one of the inhabitants' houses shall be designated annually in rotation, or it shall be established in one permanent location by voluntary consent and monetary contribution from all the settlements composing that Office; and there, in a chest and coffer under the lock and seal of the Head together with the Assessors, are to be kept the receipt and expenditure ledgers, the money collected by the Office for various public needs, all written papers, and the orders sent by the authorities. In each settlement belonging to an Office, there must specifically be a Schulz, two Assessors, and one tithingman for every ten households.

§ 9. The Head, Schulzen, Assessors, and holders of other special posts are to be elected by each settlement by majority vote from among adults who have their own household, who are prudent, just, of good behavior, diligent and exemplary in their farming, and especially skilled in agriculture, gardening, and animal husbandry, so that they may serve as an example to others, each casting his vote in turn for whomever he chooses for whatever post, without any servility, and following neither friendship nor enmity; and whoever receives the greater number of votes shall be confirmed by the signed agreement of all, these elections being submitted for the approval of the Office.

§ 10. Administrative elected officials, or Heads, and clerks are to be elected for three years, and administrative Assessors for two years, from all the villages of the colony assigned to the Office, with the proviso, however, that one of the Assessors retires after the first year following the initial election; while the one who takes his place remains in office for a full two years thereafter. Village elected officials, or Schulzen, and village Assessors are to be elected for two years under the special supervision of the Heads and with the consent of each settlement; but with the proviso that at the first election the Assessors shall be elected for only one year, while at the subsequent election the following Assessors shall already be elected for two years. This arrangement concerning administrative and village Assessors is necessary so that it may not happen that all posts are suddenly filled with new people at once. These village Assessors gather for judicial proceedings once or twice a week, as needed and at the summons of the Schulz. Confirmation of both administrative and village officials is to be reported to the Office. Tithingmen are replaced monthly.

§ 11. Those settlements which, owing to their distance from one another, are unsuitable for assignment to any Office, shall elect a Schulz for three years, and two Assessors for two years, on exactly the same basis as stated for administrative Heads; hence such a Schulz thereby performs all the duties assigned to a Head as well.

§ 12. When an elected Head or Schulz has been confirmed by the Office, he must then demand of his predecessors a proper accounting both of public affairs and of the sums of money, and after receiving all of it, record it in a ledger with attestation from the predecessors that it has indeed been handed over, and that the new Head or Schulz has entered upon his administration. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 119

§ 13. The Head, administrative Assessors, clerks, and Schulzen, in consideration that they must devote their time to the public good, are to receive salaries: the District Head 20 rubles, the administrative Assessors and the clerk 15 rubles each from the whole Office, and the Schulz 10 rubles a year from the settlement; moreover they are personally exempted from all levies and labor duties, but are not excused from the monetary payment of state taxes; the village Assessors and tithingmen, however, since the former are not always assigned to be continually in office, and the latter are chosen monthly and in rotation, are to perform their duties without pay, and without any exemption from taxes or other obligations.

§ 14. Heads, clerks, Schulzen, and Assessors are to be honored by subordinate settlers of every rank. In case of disobedience or verbal insult, the offender pays a fine — one ruble to the Head, and half a ruble to all the others. But should anyone dare to raise a hand, a triple fine is exacted from him and he is sent for a time to prison, or set to various labors.

§ 15. All village Schulzen are subordinate to the Head of the Office to which they belong, and he must therefore diligently observe that each of them carries out what has been entrusted to him and conscientiously fulfills his duty.

§ 16. The Head in every Office, and the Schulz in every village, must at the communal assembly:

1. Publicly announce enacted laws pertaining to the knowledge of the settlers, and, for the edification of the inhabitants, read both these and the present instruction given by the Office, after Divine service, at the churches or prayer houses, and at gatherings that occur, in installments.

2. Explain, instruct, and teach matters pertaining to good morals and the welfare of communal life among the settlers, so that the young may be respectful and obedient to their parents and elders, while the latter, by their own example, teach them diligence, honesty, temperance, and peaceful cohabitation in the settlements and families.

3. Instruct concerning church decorum, the duty of each to devote Sundays, holy days, and solemn festivals to divine service; and also, according to the traditions of each Religion, concerning confession and, when deemed worthy, partaking of the Holy Sacraments.

4. Take precautions against contagious diseases, cattle plague, and fire, and see that weights and measures are everywhere of the prescribed standard, and that nowhere, under any pretext, may harmful unlicensed liquor trading occur.

§ 17. Heads, Schulzen, and Assessors, being distinguished and honored above all other settlers, are obliged in return to further the settlers' welfare in every way, and to warn everyone against harm; in the discharge of their office they must exact compliance strictly, but with due order, and otherwise treat the settlers indulgently and amicably, patiently receive all their petitions and attend to all their needs, act as their direct advocates, and never touch bribes, since for both neglect of their duties and oppression of their subordinates they will be subject to equal prosecution and punishment according to the laws.

§ 18. In the colonies, the Schulzen with their Assessors, should they be unable themselves to settle or reconcile minor quarrels and claims among the settlers, must report them without delay to the Head. And if reconciliation is not achieved even through his mediation, or if there remains dissatisfaction, they shall be granted leave to seek resolution at the Office; but if in this any of the disputants should prove obstinate and disobedient toward the Head's attempt at reconciliation, this must be reported to the Office with a full account of the circumstances of the case and the fault.

§ 19. When an administrative Head or Schulz decides some case unjustly, and this is exposed upon a complaint being brought to the Office, such a person must suffer a fine double the ordinary amount. And if any loss should result to the wronged party from this, he must, in addition to the fine, compensate him for it as well; conversely, for false accusations against their own Heads and Schulzen, everyone shall suffer merciless punishment from the authorities as a slanderer.

§ 20. Excluded from the jurisdiction of administrative and village Schulzen are any forcible seizures of another's property, theft, severe beatings, deliberately inflicted offenses against the appointed Heads and Schulzen, and especially beatings and any form of malicious injury: for this reason, offenders against these rules, and thieves caught with stolen goods — whatever has been stolen or seized by whom — are to be reported, with a detailed account of the offenses, in reports to the Office. From distant colonies, however, without presenting the offenders themselves, but having detained them under guard, a report is to be sent describing their offenses, and the decision of the Office awaited. But should someone commit a criminal offense, this must be reported to the Office as speedily as possible, the offenders themselves being delivered under guard; and in colonies distant from the Office, the village Schulzen, with a clear description of the occurrence, must deliver the offenders to the Lower Land Court, and likewise report to the Office without any delay.

§ 21. The Head must see to it that colonists do not, on their own, enter into written obligations with anyone without the knowledge and permission of the authorities, and moreover that any written obligations or contracts, powers of attorney, wills, accounts, monetary agreements — in short, any acts whatsoever — occurring either among the colonists themselves or with others, are without fail written not on plain paper, but on stamped paper; for without this no government office or authority will accept them or act upon them: hence all such transactions must without fail be duly declared and recorded at the Office. Moreover, promissory notes must also be written on stamped paper specially prepared for that purpose. The price set by the decree of December 18, 1797 for promissory-note sheets is: from 10 to 100 [1000] rubles, one ruble per sheet; above 1000 up to 5000 rubles, three rubles; above 5000 up to 10,000, five rubles; above 10,000 up to 25,000, twelve rubles; above 25,000 up to 50,000, twenty rubles; above 50,000 up to 75,000, thirty rubles; above 75,000 up to 100,000, forty-five rubles.

§ 22. The Heads throughout their entire Offices, and the Schulzen locally in the settlements, must most strictly observe that colonists do not sell drink in their homes, whether by the cupful, the glassful, or in any other manner, and that any abuse of this kind is suppressed and forever prevented: for the sale of drink in the colonies must be carried on in houses specially established for that purpose.

§ 23. Administrative Heads and village Schulzen are to watch diligently that colonists are not permitted to indulge in idleness, drunkenness, extravagance, and unruliness, but lead a sober and peaceful life, always engaged in labor appropriate to their condition — in agriculture, animal husbandry, and other matters pertaining to farming. And so that the settlers may see that diligence and good behavior secure their common welfare, the village Schulzen, under the special supervision of the Head, must compile registers both of those distinguished in their farming and of the negligent, which registers are to be submitted annually, signed by both, to the Office, to the end that the orderly and the disorderly may be distinguished, and that the diligent and honest may enjoy advantages of trust, while the negligent, on the contrary, are not only to be excluded from this but also punished with a fine, or kept on bread and water; moreover they are to be compelled, both to plow and sow their allotment and to perform other farm work, being assigned tasks; and for better success in this, tithingmen are to be attached to them. But if, despite repeated fines and inducements, someone proves obstinate and hardened in laziness and negligence, such a person, with an account of his acts of disobedience, is to be reported to the Office.

§ 24. No levies may be imposed on the colonists other than those established by this Instruction; in addition, fine money is to go into the common fund, which may be used for these burdens, such as the repair of bridges and roads, or the maintenance of almshouses; but apart from this, no colony and no administrative Head or Schulz may, without reporting to the Office and obtaining its permission, newly establish any monetary or grain levies on the colonists for any purpose, anywhere, or for anyone, nor use such funds on his own authority, whatever the sum of money involved. Otherwise, should even the slightest unauthorized levy or arbitrary use of money be discovered anywhere, not only the Schulz but also the Head, for failing to prevent it, shall be subject to prosecution and the strictest punishment according to the laws.

§ 25. Schulzen are not to impose any fines on their own without the Heads, unless the latter are absent, and even then only with the common consent of the Assessors and the leading men: the Heads, however, have the authority to impose fines themselves, whether in labor or money, with the common consent of the Schulzen; moreover, no Schulz has the right to impose a fine on his own account, but the Schulzen and Assessors petition the Head, while others seek satisfaction at the Office, or, during visits, from its Members.

§ 26. The Heads are instructed to send to the Office annually and without fail, by January 1st, lists and summary reports of births, marriages, and deaths; and, regarding livestock of every kind belonging to each householder, to submit summary reports to the Office twice a year, in May and November, so that the growth or decline of every household may be observed.

Article III. — On the internal administration of the colonies.

§ 27. The Heads and Schulzen are to keep special books for recording any verbal orders, decisions, and adjudications between settlements, as well as everything that may occur in the administration of any Head or Schulz, so that, in the event complaints of any kind reach the Office, justice may more readily be found; moreover, protocols are to be kept everywhere for recording orders received and reports dispatched, with numbers without fail marked on all of them.

§ 28. In every colony, upon notice given by the Head or Schulz through the tithingmen, the inhabitants — one from each household, or as many as ordered — must, on every occasion, promptly hasten to the assembly, where, in complete quiet, they are to heed the order and carry it out exactly; under penalty for disobedience or failure to appear at the summoned assembly of 50 kopecks, and for disorderly conduct and uproar, four times that amount.

§ 29. The Head is obliged to exercise guardianship over widows and orphans, reporting on them to the Office, appointing guardians for them with the consent of relatives and other householders, and overseeing these guardians so that they perform their duty with zeal and honesty for the genuine benefit of the widows and orphans entrusted to them, requiring an account from them twice a year, both of the growth or decline of their household and of their conduct and diligence, verifying their reports personally, or through the administrative Assessors, as often as possible. As for the households left behind after families have died out, guardians are to be appointed, and the remaining property, both in goods and livestock, is to be handed over to them by inventory for safekeeping without loss, over which they must exercise special oversight, and such households are to be reported to the Office without delay.

§ 30. The Head and Schulzen see to it that poor and destitute colonists do not wander about begging, nor beg alms in a mendicant manner. Such of them as are healthy are to be compelled, by means of diligent labor, to earn their own subsistence, while the aged and infirm are to be maintained by their relatives. If, however, they have neither relatives nor the strength to work, they are to be maintained at public expense, two houses being built near the church by common effort under the name of an almshouse, one for women and the other for men, where they are to be provided with food, warmth, and the clothing necessary to cover their nakedness. For such expenses, a box is to be kept at the almshouse under the seal and lock of the church elder, and a collection purse in the churches, by means of which money collected as alms on holy days and Sundays is to be added to the box, and, at the end of each month, taken out and used to maintain the almshouses, any shortfall being made up from the colony. For better order in these almshouses, the Priests of those churches must exercise chief oversight over them.

§ 31. Settlers must not, on their own, without the permission of the Office, divide their households; and, should there be any wish to do so, the Heads must diligently see to it that such divisions genuinely serve the settlers' common good and do not, on occasion, serve to disrupt the household; and to that end, in reporting to the Office those wishing to divide, it must be specifically explained whether there is good will to it on the part of parents or relatives, whether the one being separated will have sufficient land, farming implements, and livestock to establish a household, and, in short, care must without fail be taken in such cases that the first household is preserved intact and the second successfully established.

§ 32. No one is to surrender or sell his household under any pretext, except only in the case where someone, having no children or heirs, is, owing to old age, infirmity, and illness, wholly unable to manage it himself; but even in this case it may be surrendered only with the permission of the Office, and not on one's own by communal whim. Whoever takes over the household must then assume together with it all the state debts owed by such an elderly or ill person, and moreover must see to providing for his subsistence.

§ 33. Administrative Heads and village Schulzen are to watch closely that no colonist absents himself from his residence without cause or wanders idly about the colonies; but since absences for selling produce, for trade, and for occupations may be beneficial to them, these are not forbidden, provided, however, that farming does not suffer thereby and that the settlement remains answerable for the one who is absent. For such needs, the Heads may grant leave to those wishing to go to another settlement or to a Governorate or district town, issuing them a pass from the Office. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 123

Those, however, who need to travel to distant places and for long periods, or even to nearby settlements for some work but for a considerable time, must, having obtained leave from the Schulzen certified by the Head that there is no obstacle to their absence for the requested time, and that neither their farming nor their livestock will suffer any harm thereby, appear at the Office, where, upon receiving passports, they are obliged to return by the appointed date, on the further condition that the issued passports be returned to the Office.

§ 34. It is prescribed that all orders or instructions sent, and to be sent hereafter, by the Office be carried out most exactly in all colonies, without delay or omission, and that letters sent by the authorities be forwarded everywhere in turn, wherever required, from one settlement to another, without objection and with the utmost dispatch, under penalty of punishment. Should anyone prove disobedient in this, he is to be punished with three days of communal labor and assigned out of turn against his fellows twice over; to this end, for recording all envelopes received and dispatched, the Heads and all local village Schulzen are to keep a logbook, in which is to be noted in detail: when and from where envelopes were received, and likewise to where and with whom they were dispatched.

§ 35. The Schulzen are instructed that nowhere are horses and carts to be given to anyone whosoever without payment of the travel fee or placard fee and without a travel warrant or placard passport, nor any in excess of the number specified in the travel warrant or passport; hence the Heads, exercising unremitting oversight so that no burden may occur anywhere, are to establish special ledgers in the colonies, in which are without fail to be entered the names of travelers and by whom the travel warrant or passport was issued, for exactly how many horses, and whether that exact number was given; likewise who did the driving, and whether the traveler paid the prescribed travel or placard fees.

§ 36. The Schulzen are to inspect frequently to see that the boundary markers set up remain undamaged, and should any posts decay or any pyramids [mounds] crumble, this is to be reported immediately to their Head and repaired at once upon his order; for neglect of this, a fine is to be exacted into the common fund from the Schulzen of 1 ruble 50 kopecks, and from the Assessors of 50 kopecks; and should any be found deliberately damaged by inhabitants, this is to be reported to the Office for punishment according to the general laws.

§ 37. Colonists are not to be forbidden to hire workers, especially those with small families, the sick, and the well-off; the Schulzen must, however, exercise unremitting oversight that the householders themselves, who are able to work, are without fail engaged in agriculture and diligently occupied with their household; but should someone be unable to pay wages to workers, the hiring of such is to be forbidden to him.

§ 38. It is prescribed that no one, on his own, or with the agreement of only a few persons, shall presume to submit petitions of his own accord anywhere concerning common lawful needs of whatever nature, but that for any such needs a general assembly is to be held with the Head, Schulz, and Assessors, and communal resolutions made by the agreement of all settlers, with a detailed and clear description therein of their needs, also naming the proxy to whom it is specifically entrusted, that, pursuant to their written resolution, he may bring a complaint or submit a petition. Such resolutions of theirs, signed by all the settlers, the Schulz with the Assessors, and attested by the Head, are to be submitted to the Office; otherwise, should anyone dare to violate this order, he shall be dealt with according to the laws.

§ 39. The Heads must take special care that debt payments and the established land taxes be paid punctually and without arrears, at the appointed times, into the Office of Guardianship of Foreigners, from all the colonies within their jurisdiction. In the assignment of carts, both for postal relay service and under the Placard, as well as in all lawful village duties or obligations, matters are to proceed with genuine fairness, without the slightest burden to the settlers, with careful observance in every case of the actual rotation established by themselves, under penalty of strict and unremitting prosecution for failure to observe this.

§ 40. The Head and the other Schulzen in the villages must receive annually from the Office bound and sealed ledgers for recording in them both fines — noting specifically who is fined and for what — and other monetary levies, with a clear and accurate indication of why and from whom exactly how much was taken, and where or for what and when it was spent. At the end of each year, in order to audit these funds of the Head and the Schulzen, the colonists must elect from among themselves three trustworthy and knowledgeable householders and entrust them with the verification of the accounts, and then, having found any shortfall or deficiency in the ledgers, whatever is owed by the Head or by any Schulz, first report it to the Office, and, with its permission, recover it; the said ledgers, signed by the Schulzen and the leading men of the community, are to be submitted annually to the Office for examination and audit.

§ 41. Should it happen, contrary to expectation, that someone disturbs the peaceful possession [of land] in the colonies, the Schulzen must at once, without loss of time, report to the Head, with a description of the locations in which, by whom, and precisely what occurred; and the Head is to report to the Office, which, in the discharge of its duty, will be obliged to intervene and initiate proceedings in the order prescribed by the laws.

Article IV. — On village police and fire order.

§ 42. The Head, together with the Schulzen, must diligently observe and be answerable that the main roads, and the bridges and dams upon them, are kept in full repair and good order. Which settlements are to maintain them, and over what distance, depends on their own general arrangement.

§ 43. In the colonies, persons without written documents are on no account to be tolerated, and therefore, if someone comes to a settlement, whether for some business for a considerable time, or for work and hire, and does not have a pass or certificate, he is not to be admitted. And should unknown, suspicious, or fugitive persons be observed anywhere, they are to be sought out, apprehended, and sent to the Head, who, after conducting interrogations, must at once report in detail to the Office; he must also deliver the persons themselves together with everything found on them, as well as those who harbored them. Distant colonies, however, are to send such persons directly to the Lower Land Court, as stated in § 20 concerning criminal offenses.

§ 44. The Schulzen must strictly observe that no one gives shelter in his home to disreputable women or men; and should anyone be found doing so, the Head must immediately report both the householder and those engaging in such improprieties to the Office.

§ 45. Heads of the district office are to see to it that convicts of various categories being escorted through the colonies are strictly watched, so that no one may escape from DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 125

guard; for which purpose the Schulzes are to establish in every colony special notebooks in which are to be recorded precisely the names of the convicts being escorted, from whom and to which colony they were brought, with whom and when they were sent onward, and in which settlement to whom they were handed over; and in addition the receipts given upon acceptance are to be kept.

§ 46. It is strictly ordered to the Schulzes that they report to the Office immediately, with a detailed description through the district Head, concerning stray or newly arrived cattle that have come to their settlements or herds, for publication, while keeping the cattle themselves in the settlement where they turned up, but in a place separate from their own, under threat of penalty. When the owner of the cattle is found, they are to be handed over in the presence of the Schulz, upon payment for their upkeep. In the more remote colonies, the Schulz reports on newly arrived cattle of his district to the Lower Land Court.

§ 47. When colonists purchase horses, each purchase must be recorded in the Office, stating precisely when and from whom they were bought, at what price, the brand, and other identifying marks. Otherwise, in a suspicious case, one who fails to declare and record a horse bought or exchanged from someone will not only lose it but will also be brought to judgment; for this purpose the Heads are to establish special books for this in the Offices.

§ 48. Any enmity among the inhabitants, private quarrels, and slanderous reproaches are to be suppressed by the village Schulzes, first by admonitions, then by public works, and, in case of repeated offenses, by a fine into the common fund, collected only from the one who is the instigator of the quarrel, 25 kopecks each time.

§ 49. Luxury, and especially profligacy, the Schulzes must eradicate among the colonists with all their strength, bringing offenders to submission by assigning them the heaviest tasks in various communal works, so that they can never find time for such a harmful pursuit, until they come to acknowledge their fault. If they do not reform even by these means, such persons are to be sent to the Office with reports.

Note. By luxury is meant the following: if someone has immoderate expenses in his household, frequent gatherings of guests, and the like, giving occasion for the squandering of property; and profligacy is card-playing and other games for money or goods, the sale of one's own cattle or other property, without the knowledge of the Schulz and without any real need, for drunkenness or to satisfy other passions.

§ 50. The Schulzes are to watch diligently that every householder keeps his house, threshing floor, stables, cattle sheds, and fences in proper repair, tidiness, and cleanliness; otherwise, if anyone, despite all warnings, neglects and allows his rural buildings to fall into disorder, a monetary fine of 20 kopecks is to be taken from him, and in addition he is to be compelled to repair everything immediately, with a tithingman specially assigned to him to oversee this.

§ 51. The Schulzes are obliged to see that there is no filth in the streets of any colony; and for protection from storms, winds, and in case of fires, to order that various trees be planted along the streets near the yards and threshing floors, wherever convenient, according to the nature of the climate and soil, whatever kinds can grow there; and especially mulberry trees, which take root so readily everywhere and can bring the settlers significant benefit from sericulture.

§ 52. If anyone happens to find some lost item on the road or in a dwelling place, he must immediately declare it to his Schulz, keeping it safe in the meantime, and the Schulz reports it to the Head. When the owner is found, it is to be returned in the presence of witnesses; whereupon the finder is permitted to demand payment for his trouble, but by no means more than the legally established third part of what the found item is worth according to the Schulzes' appraisal; and whoever wishes to return it without payment, such disinterestedness will be all the more praiseworthy.

§ 53. The Head and the Schulzes are to watch diligently that all settlers treat their neighbors kindly and amicably, and visitors politely and hospitably, and that they avoid quarrels over land with the former on account of neighborliness, and the slightest rudeness toward the latter.

§ 54. If an extraordinary illness among people appears in any colony, the Schulzes must immediately give notice of it to the Head, and he is obliged to report it to the Office that very hour; as for what precautions are to be observed with regard to cattle plague, this can be seen from the instruction sent to the colonies on this subject, with which one must without fail comply; and when an outbreak occurs anywhere, it is to be reported to the Office at once, with a report following weekly both on the continuation or diminishing of it and on the progress made in carrying out the prescriptions of that instruction; the infected cattle are to be separated to a special place remote from the others, special shelters being made for this purpose at each settlement, in places distant from dwellings and from pasture, and contact of such infected cattle with other neighboring settlements is to be cut off. And when it happens that the settlements in which the infection appears are situated on streams and rivers, and there are other settlements below no farther than 10 versts away, then, so as not to cause the same harm to the neighbors through the watering place, the sick cattle are not to be watered at those sources, but water is to be carried by hand to the aforementioned shelters set up for that purpose; for which reason these are to be built closer to the water. Likewise the utmost caution is to be observed if such a misfortune should occur in settlements situated on the same streams, even if more than 10 versts away: for inexact fulfillment of this, the Head and the other Schulzes are to be fined.

§ 55. In every settlement, as a safeguard against fire and any theft, there are to be day and night watchmen specially assigned in certain places according to the size of the settlement, and in the middle of settlements where there are no churches, bells or iron plates are to be placed, so that if a fire or thieves are noticed in some house, the watchmen may sound the alarm, and the inhabitants of both sexes of full age immediately gather to help at that place; for which purpose all settlers are to be assigned by household as to what they should bring to a fire, with the provision that whoever fails to appear must pay a fine of 1 ruble into the common fund. In addition, every household must always keep ready water in special tubs; and for the whole settlement there must be kept in a designated place a number of special large iron hooks, pitchforks, barrels, and, for hauling water in turn, two horses, which should always stand ready.

§ 56. In case of a fire, which sometimes occurs not from carelessness but from unforeseen causes, whereby a settler is brought to complete ruin, it would be necessary to establish in the colonies, by agreement of all the settlers, a rule that everyone should render assistance to those who have suffered from fire according to his means, if not with money, then with labor or in some other way: toward which the Head and the Schulzes are obliged to encourage them. Such assistance is to be rendered through their mediation and under their direction.

§ 57. The Schulzes are to see that stoves in houses are made without fail with chimneys and are fired not from the entryway but from small kitchens specially built onto them, which are to be lined with brick and coated with clay for safety from DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 127

fire; moreover the chimneys must be cleaned every week, which the tithingmen must watch strictly. The Schulz or the Beisitzers oversee compliance with this, ordering the tithingmen monthly to inspect the chimneys.

§ 58. At night, no one is under any circumstances to walk in houses or along the streets with a splint-torch or with candles without lanterns, nor with lit pipes. Whoever is found guilty of this is to be punished with a monetary fine of 5 kopecks each time.

Article V. — Fines for damage caused

and compensation for it.

§ 59. Whoever sows someone else's land or plot, the grain sown is to be given to the one to whom the land belongs, a tenth part being taken from it into the common fund; but if that land lay fallow and the owner was unable to plow it for some reason, and consequently suffered no loss from this, then in such a case, only for the impudence, a fine of 12 kopecks per desyatina is to be collected into the common treasury, and the same amount is to be collected for the owner of that land; but if anyone under such circumstances plowed virgin land, nothing is to be given to the owner, because the plowing of virgin land will serve to the owner's benefit.

§ 60. If anyone, on someone else's land, whether at his own dwelling place or elsewhere, picks hops or other fruits, or spoils bait for game or fowl, then for what is spoiled and wasted, according to its appraised value, he must return the money to the plaintiff, and in addition a fine of 15 kopecks is to be collected into the common fund.

§ 61. If anyone seizes another's horse and keeps it for more than two days without declaring it to the Schulz of his village, then even if he performed no work on it at all, he must pay the owner 25 kopecks for each day; and if it is injured during that time and this can be clearly proven, then he must pay the owner the price as stated in the preceding paragraph.

§ 62. Whoever kills someone's cow or other livestock or fowl must, to the satisfaction of the injured party, pay for every animal or fowl according to its appraised value, and in addition, for such insolence, be punished with imprisonment on bread and water — for the killing of a horse or cow, four days, and for smaller livestock half of that, except for fowl and dogs.

§ 63. But if anyone kills or injures someone's livestock without intent, and this is clearly proven, then in such a case only two-thirds of the appraised value is to be collected for the killing and no fine at all is to be imposed, and he is to be ordered to have the unintentionally injured animal treated; and if he does not have it cured, he is to be compelled as stated for animals killed.

§ 64. If anyone forcibly takes away someone's livestock, fowl, or any other item, even under the pretext of a debt, the item taken is to be ordered returned to the owner, and the one who took it is to be reported to the Office as a robber.

§ 65. Whoever, notwithstanding the above-described fines and punishments, does not desist from insolent acts, such persons, with a description of their offenses, are to be brought under guard to the Office with a report, for proceeding against according to the laws.

§ 66. Since it is impossible here to enumerate all offenses and crimes, it is prescribed that if anyone commits some crime not mentioned in this instruction, it is to be reported through the Heads to the Office, and a new prescription is to be awaited from it.

Note. Although in various points of this instruction it is prescribed what fine is due for each offense, according to the crime; since crimes can never be of equal gravity, in adjudicating them one must proceed with the utmost prudence and caution — for example: if someone transgresses against the established rules deliberately or out of stubbornness, and some harm or loss to the settlement or to a neighbor results from it, such a person must be punished more severely or more perceptibly than one who transgresses unintentionally; or, even out of laziness but not out of stubbornness, and caused no harm to anyone, and moreover had never before been guilty of any vice — namely, the second should be punished a third or half less than the first, which is left to the discretion of the Schulzes.

Article VI. — On Economic and Other Useful

Establishments in the Colonies.

§ 67. To avert a shortage of grain that might arise from crop failure and other extraordinary circumstances, and for the general benefit of all settlers, grain storehouses are to be established, and accordingly it is prescribed: 1. To fill them, at the end of the harvest, half a chetverik of rye and, wherever it is grown, half a garnets of spring grain is to be collected annually from all settlers, from each revision soul; and however much grain is received into each storehouse, the Head, after its collection, must send to the Office detailed reports annually, without fail in the month of November. 2. In order that these stores may serve to the greater benefit of the settlers, and, in case of shortage and genuine need, be issued to them both for food and for sowing, it is absolutely necessary that the reserve grain be collected and kept in grain form. When anyone needs to take some part of it, it is to be issued to him by common communal decision and with the permission of the authority established over the colonies, with an entry made in a book; for which purpose such books are to be kept at every storehouse, both for receipts and for disbursements. 3. In order to keep the reserve grain fit for use and to protect it from spoilage, the grain contained therein is to be exchanged annually by the same settlers for fresh grain; this is to be carried out only by direction of the Office. The colonists themselves are forbidden to do this on their own without permission. 4. The keeping of the receipts and disbursements of this grain, as well as its safekeeping, is entrusted to one of the village Beisitzers, of whom two are established in each colony, with the provision that the Beisitzer keep the key to the storehouse, while the Schulz keeps the seal; therefore both are to be held responsible for its integrity.

§ 68. In general, both the district Heads and the Schulzes must make every effort toward the propagation in the colonies of all kinds of handicrafts and factories; toward which they must not only encourage everyone, but also compel anyone who, having both the ability and the knowledge for it, is unwilling to engage in it out of negligence. And since the principal economy of this region consists in livestock raising, and especially sheep raising, it is most fitting and natural for the householders to engage in the processing of wool, as the first abundant product of this region, and in general, from all livestock raising, in the tanning of hides, and in the establishment of soap- and candle-works.

§ 69. The Heads and Schulzes are obliged to make observations, according to the nature of the soil and climate on their lands, as to what may appear necessary for their common benefit, and to report this to the Office; and moreover to explain and impress upon the settlers the advantages contained therein.

§ 70. The Heads are to watch most strictly that efforts be made in all colonies toward the cultivation of forests on their lands and the sowing thereon of tree seeds suited to the nature of the soil, and especially to order the planting, by cuttings, of soft and fast-growing trees, such as: alder, willow, aspen, sallow, poplar, and asp-DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 129

en; and from the other trees, to gather the seeds when they ripen and sow them on well-plowed land; also to make certain efforts to plant mulberry trees as well, in accordance with the special instruction given to the Schulzes.

§ 71. In settlements that have forests on their lands, every excessive use is to be cut off and limited, so that the colonists, apart from what is necessary out of genuine need, do not profit by selling elsewhere, and by no means make an income for themselves from it; and further, in order that the forests may more conveniently be preserved, they are to be divided for cutting into different sections, and cutting of a second section is not to be permitted until the first has been finished; and the manner in which the divisions are made anywhere, the Head must report in detail for the Office's review. If anyone cuts timber beyond the section designated for that year, a fine is to be collected from him into the common fund double the value of what he cut according to price, and in case of inability to make such payment, he is to be assigned to public works until he has worked off that sum.

§ 72. The Head is to watch and endeavor that land throughout the colonies be divided everywhere into three fields, with trials being made of dividing it into 6 or 7 fields, and the Schulzes are to observe and urge the settlers that each of them, during the winter season, stock up on and have plows, wooden ploughs, harrows, carts, and other items necessary for fieldwork, and that oxen and horses be kept in good condition for work. And if any are found deficient in this not out of negligence but owing to other circumstances or unfortunate misfortunes, such persons are to be given all possible help by the combined effort of all the inhabitants.

§ 73. As soon as the prescribed time for plowing arrives, every Schulz must give notice that all the inhabitants go out to plow together in the very earliest morning hours and work with the utmost diligence; and tithingmen are to be assigned to oversee this. During the spring and autumn sowing, the Schulzes and Beisitzers of every settlement are obliged to inspect in turn the fields of each householder and to note whether they are worked as the nature of the soil requires, whether they were plowed deeply enough, and whether the soil is sufficiently loosened; and if they notice that some field has not been properly worked, they must without fail make the householders rework it in good time. Likewise they are to compel them to finish the sowing of both spring and winter grain without fail at the proper time; and in harvesting it they are to proceed according to the yield, ripeness, and the custom observed in such cases, which is already well known to all; threshing is to be done in good weather, and wattle-and-daub sheds are to be built for storage.

§ 74. So that the sown winter and spring grain not be choked out by weeds, every effort is to be made to harrow the plowed land as well as possible, so that no unbroken clods remain; then, after sprouting, if weeds appear anywhere, they are to be diligently weeded out, employing for this purpose young children from the age of 10, or whatever convenient and efficient tools may be available for this.

§ 75. During the haymaking season, care must be taken that everyone stocks up on a sufficient quantity of hay to feed his livestock through the winter, that the haymaking be carried out not in bits but all at once in proper order, and that hay by no means be carried home before it has been properly gathered into shocks and stacks; those who disobey in this are to be compelled, and are not to be released from the fields until they have done what is required.

§ 76. If, during the working season, some family, on account of illness, is unable to work its plot, harvest the ripened grain, and mow the hay, communal assistance is to be rendered to them, or else those sentenced for offenses to various works for the common good are to be employed for this purpose.

§ 77. The Schulzes must endeavor to keep the most accurate records of how many desyatinas of land each settler plowed at what time, how much of various grain he sowed on them, how much he harvested from it, and how much hay he mowed, which records are to be submitted through the Head annually in the month of November.

§ 78. In the winter season, care must be taken that none of the inhabitants remain idle, but that each labor at keeping proper watch over and orderly feeding and care of his livestock, attend to cleanliness, especially of the horses, to the repair of buildings, fencing around yards and gardens, endeavor to prepare all necessary supplies, stocking up for sowing with spring grain and other seeds and having everything ready; and those who know how to weave fine linens, tablecloths, and napkins, or other generally useful and profitable crafts, must engage in them. Women likewise should labor in spinning wool and flax, in raising various fowl, in gathering butter and the like — in a word, the strictest watch must be kept that no one remain idle in the winter season.

§ 79. Every colony must have a smithy and a blacksmith for various tasks and communal needs, who should keep in stock the material required for his craft and always be ready to give assistance through his work. If any craftsman is disobedient toward his Schulz, such persons are to be punished by assigned tasks and brought to compliance with what has been ordered; and if they fail to comply, a fine of 50 kopecks each time is to be collected into the communal fund. Above all, it must be observed that craftsmen do not demand excessive and immoderate prices from their fellows for their labor, but are always content with the prices established for their work by common consent.

§ 80. The Head and the Schulzes are obliged to attend to the whole of rural economy in general and to train the colonists:

1. That, in keeping with the custom of the places from which they came to Russia, they preserve in stone buildings the same style used there, and that due order be observed in the layout of houses in the colonies, so that they may be more quickly and conveniently protected in case of fire; and without the Office's permission, they are on no account to build new houses on their own.

2. As a safeguard against fire, to set up threshing barns as far as possible from the houses.

3. Not to leave their lands unused and their livestock without proper care, encouraging better cultivation of the land and the propagation of better breeds of livestock.

4. In accordance with the climate of each place, to sow seeds suited to the nature of the soil that provide the settler with the most convenient and profitable yield; and especially, pursuant to the report of the Senate confirmed by His Imperial Majesty on March 7, 1801, sesame for the production of oil from it.

5. To encourage the expansion of vegetable gardens and orchards with various needed fruits and produce; and especially to impress upon them the benefit of expanding potato cultivation where there is still little or none of it, and to endeavor that they sow their fields with it as well.

6. To watch most closely and to train each person, in attending to his own economy, to consider it necessary to keep the required supply of everything for his own use, and to have on hand double the seed of everything he is accustomed to sow in his fields and gardens, so that at the next sowing he will not feel any shortage. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 131

All the points set forth in this instruction are to be carried out by all Heads and the other Schulzes with the utmost exactness and without omission, under threat of the strictest and most unremitting penalty.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVI. Pp. 635-649.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 39.

Apart from a few points reflecting the specifics of Novorossiya, this document essentially coincides in content with the instruction for the Saratov colonies (doc. No. 38). The differences in form are far more significant: whereas the previous act was clearly prepared in haste, is poorly structured, is full of inaccuracies, and mechanically borrows the outdated vocabulary of the 1769 instruction, the present document is distinguished by a well-thought-out structure, clear style, and precise wording. It evidently bears the hand of an experienced official who was an expert on the matter. One may surmise that this was K.I. Gablitz, then a member of the Expedition of State Economy (see the Biographical Commentary).

---

## No. 40. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE RULES FOR THE RECEPTION AND SETTLEMENT OF FOREIGN IMMIGRANTS (1802)

20,259. — May 9. Nominal, given to the Novorossiysk Military Governor. — On the rules for the reception and settlement of immigrants from abroad.

Although the Manifesto of 1763 and the subsequent enactments, in permitting foreigners to enter and settle in all Russian governorates, laid down measures favorable to this policy and safeguarding the freedom of these immigrants and their means of subsistence; yet at the same time, on the one hand, in the manner of their reception at the border and of their assignment to particular state estates, under the guise of precautions, these same enactments subject them to many local formalities that hinder their settlement to such a degree that, having been received by the border guard, they are conveyed on foot and under escort over a great distance to its command, whence they are sent in the same manner to the Rural Police, and the Police forward them to the Provincial Board; and thus, wandering under guard for several hundred versts before they are able to choose an occupation, they are compelled to endure every extremity of want for a long time: on the other hand, the very regulation concerning the choice of their occupation, restricting it to merchantry, the burgher estate, or state service, excludes the most useful part of them, the farmers, from all means of subsistence; in order to remove these obstacles I find it necessary, in addition to previous arrangements in this matter, to establish the following: 1) As soon as people wishing to settle in Russia appear at the border, in all places where the reception of them is not prohibited by law, the border guard, receiving them and not detaining them in the least, shall issue them only cordon certificates indicating their names and where and when they appeared at the border, and with these certificates, without the slightest delay, shall release them further into the interior of the governorate without any special surveillance over them. 2) These certificates shall have the force of passports, with which their bearers may be received everywhere for a period of three months; but upon the expiry of this term, if the certificates are not presented for registration at a government office, as indicated below, they lose their validity, and the persons presenting them are considered without passports, of which they are to be informed at the time the certificates are issued. 3) The command of the border guard shall furnish the Provincial Board with monthly registers of the certificates it has issued, under penalty of unavoidable prosecution for any omission. 4) With these certificates, immigrants wishing to enter the burgher estate, the merchantry, or state service shall present themselves at the Municipal Magistracies or the Provincial Board, which shall proceed to assign them to an occupation in accordance with existing laws, with strict oversight on the part of the governorate's authorities to ensure that no delay or difficulty is permitted in this. 5) Those foreigners who do not wish to enter the above-mentioned estates may be received and settled by landowners on their lands according to the immigrants' wishes, but only on condition that they and their descendants are granted liberty and full freedom to move from one landowner to another. 6) Landowners, in receiving such persons wishing to settle on their lands, may make agreements with them concerning their obligations for a fixed term of years and present these agreements to the Lower Land Courts for registration and, if necessary, for the resolution of disputes in accordance with the laws on contracts. 7) Such settlers, established on landowners' lands, are exempt from all state taxes until the census; upon registration in the census, however, they shall pay these into the treasury on an equal footing with the landowners' peasants, without thereby losing any of their rights of freedom in relation to the landowner, so that no government office, either before or after their registration, may impose upon them any personal bondage, even should these immigrants themselves request it. 8) A landowner who has received such people onto his lands shall immediately present the cordon certificates issued to them for registration at the Land Court, and the latter shall report this monthly to the Provincial Board, which, by comparing these reports with the registers furnished by the border authorities, shall thereby be informed both of the number of these people and of the occupation they have chosen. Magistracies receiving these people into the merchantry and burgher estate shall likewise furnish information about them to the Provincial Board. 9) A landowner who fails to present a certificate for registration at the Land Court within three months shall be deemed to be harboring fugitives. 10) In implementing this arrangement for the reception of foreign immigrants, the authorities in the governorates must take all necessary precautions so that, under this guise, peasants belonging to Russian landowners, by colluding with other landowners willing to receive them, do not use this permission as a means of evasion and relocation from their own villages to other lands, thereby acquiring the right of freedom under the name of foreign immigrants. 11) In applying these general instructions to local circumstances, if the authorities in the governorates find anything that, in their judgment, would serve the better organization of this matter, they must submit their opinions thereon to Me for consideration and decision. 12) In addition to these measures easing the arrangements in this matter, I place under your special care, within the governorate entrusted to you, the provision to people of this kind of every possible assistance and convenience within your power, for the speedy and untroubled settlement of such foreign immigrants.

A decree of the same content was given to the Lithuanian Military Governor administering the civil department in both Lithuanian governorates, Baron Bennigsen.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVII. P. 136-137.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 40.

The document reflects the new methods of receiving colonists that became established during the reign of Alexander I. By this time a significant proportion of foreign settlers made their own way to Russia and settled on private (usually landowners') lands.

Bennigsen (Benigsen) Leontiy Leontyevich (Levin August Theophil) (1745–1826) — count (from 1813), general of cavalry, military governor of Vilna in 1801–1804.

Manifesto of [17]63 — doc. No. 11.
