## No. 44. SUPPLEMENT TO THE INSTRUCTION ON THE INTERNAL ORDER AND ADMINISTRATION OF THE NOVOROSSIYSK COLONIES (1803)

20,841. — July 7. Supplement to the Instruction on the internal order and administration of the Novorossiysk foreign colonies.

Section I. — On punishments.

§ 1. In the Instruction on the internal order and administration of the colonies it is prescribed in many cases that an offending colonist be punished by being put to public labor; but it may happen (as has already occurred) that at the very time when someone is to be punished in this manner, there is no public labor available; for this reason the district Office should, at the beginning of each year, after general deliberation with the most far-sighted householders, designate public works (*), the performance of which could serve at once as punishment for the guilty and for the common good.

(*) Note to § 1 of the Instruction.

§ 2. If anyone, by force of the Instruction, is sentenced by the district Office to a monetary fine and is unable to pay it, such a person is to be put to public labor for as long as it would take a hired laborer to earn that sum by performing it.

§ 3. If an offender has already been punished once or more by public labor but nevertheless does not mend his conduct, and is again found deserving of punishment, such a person is to be put, for a period fixed in proportion to the offense, into the stocks or the pillory while at public labor, and, after the day's work, is sometimes to be confined for the night in prison as well, which, like the stocks and the pillory with its post, is to be built from fine money, and, should that be insufficient, from public revenues.

§ 4. If any householder, owing to his offenses, becomes subject to frequent punishment by public labor and is thereby distracted from performing his own field work and managing his own household, or if likewise no useful public works happen to be available in the colony at that time, in such a case the district Office, with the general consent of several householders of good conduct, must impose upon him, in proportion to his guilt, corporal punishment, which is to be carried out only with the approval of the Office. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 137

Section II. — On preventing negligence toward grain farming and horticulture; on how these are to be carried out with greater diligence; also on engaging every year in various necessary and useful plantings, and on how these are to be handled.

§ 5. Notwithstanding that the region there abounds in manifold resources capable of assisting every industrious inhabitant in improving his condition, there are nevertheless few colonists who, in addition to farming, engage in any other useful trade or craft; even grain farming itself is in such a state of neglect in the colonies that, owing to the small area sown, even in the most fruitful years there is no abundant harvest, and consequently there can never be a reserve of grain there to guard against want in the event of a poor harvest; and if one considers that most colonists devote little attention to grain farming and engage in no other occupation besides; moreover, as is well known, farming in Novorossiysk Governorate is incomparably easier than elsewhere, since the fields there, owing to the nature of the soil and climate, need only be plowed once, while fertilizing them is not only unnecessary but is even considered harmful there in view of the customary droughts; it is thus clear that they spend more than half the year in idleness. — Should there occur (which God forbid) a cattle plague or a failure of the grain crop, these idlers must inevitably suffer famine; in such a case they rely on assistance from the Crown, which, although it does condescend to assist in time of need, does so only for those who have fallen into such straits through unavoidable misfortune and through no fault of their own; those, however, who have brought extremity and want upon themselves through their own unpardonable laziness, and who bear the burden of it themselves, ought not to expect such assistance at all.

To curb such harmful idleness and to avert the calamities arising from it, it is hereby prescribed that every householder shall sow grain every year, no less than 3 quarters of winter grain and 2 quarters of spring grain; and one who has in his family a greater number of grown sons or laborers must, beyond this quantity, sow as much more as he can manage to accomplish with due diligence. Likewise it is most strictly confirmed to all colonies that every householder shall provide himself with his own plow and other tillage implements, so that, for want of these, the working of the fields may not be delayed and the best sowing season missed. The district and village Offices must take the necessary measures and observe with all strictness that what is prescribed is exactly carried out. If anyone, without valid cause and from mere laziness, fails to attend diligently to farming, and it is found that he has not sown as much as prescribed, such a person shall be fined, the first time, one ruble for each unsown quarter, to be paid into the common fund; the second time, the Office shall send him in winter, for as long a period as it deems fit, to the house of correction; and if he still does not mend his ways and does not properly work his plot — in short, if he fails to fulfill exactly the duties of a settler — in such a case his land, homestead, tillage implements, and as much of his livestock and other property as, upon appraisal, would equal the sum of the state debt charged against him, are to be taken from him. All of this is to be given, according to inventory, to some exemplary person of known good conduct and industriousness who has no homestead of his own but wishes to have one, the entire state debt charged on that homestead being registered against him. If any colonist is found guilty of not using the loan received from the treasury for the improvement of his household and the acquisition of necessary tillage implements, but squandering it in an unpardonable manner, and moreover does not possess property equal to the amount of the state debt charged against him, such a squanderer of the state loan shall be dealt with according to law.

§ 6. The more varied the products that can be successfully cultivated in a region under a single climate, the more numerous are the means available to a poor settler for improving his condition. The excellent fruit and vineyard orchards existing in the vicinity of the Novorossiysk colonies are proof of that climate's suitability for horticulture and viticulture. For this reason the colonists are hereby charged with the duty of endeavoring to plant fruit and vineyard orchards; to this end every householder must first stock himself with wild saplings and, by grafting the best varieties of fruit-bearing trees onto them, improve their quality, and then apply himself to gradually expanding his orchard by sowing fruit seeds, whereby he will always be in a position to make good any loss of trees that may occur from time to time through drying out or freezing. The grapevines, of which each householder has already been given from 5 to 10 through the Office for planting, serve the purpose of gradually accustoming the colonists to and teaching them how to handle the grapevine, so that in time they may become properly proficient in viticulture. Since it has come to light, however, that many householders not only failed to preserve the vines given to them and did not follow the gardener's instructions in this regard, but even deliberately damaged, tore out, and discarded them, every householder found guilty of such negligence must, at his own expense, obtain, plant, and keep intact as many grapevines as were lost through his neglect. And should it happen in future that anyone, either deliberately or through negligence, allows livestock to gnaw, trample, or otherwise destroy grapevines, young fruit-bearing trees, or other useful trees on his property, such a person, depending on the circumstances of the case, is to be subjected to corporal punishment at a village assembly.

§ 7. That silk farming can be carried on with the desired success in that region admits of no doubt whatsoever, all the more so since experiments already conducted with success in the Novorossiysk colonies may serve as proof of this; for this reason it is prescribed, for strict compliance by each and every colony under the authority of the Novorossiysk Guardianship Office, that this most useful production of silk be introduced in them. Every householder must plant around his fences and gardens, each year, 20 mulberry trees, and continue doing so for as long as the surrounding space permits, taking care without fail to preserve them. The district and village authorities must in every way see to it that every householder sows, in the proper season, in autumn and spring, the mulberry seeds received from the Office, and does so properly, clears the young shoots of harmful weeds, and waters them as needed. As to the number of mulberry trees of one, two, three, or more years' growth possessed by each householder, the authorities of each colony must submit registers annually, by October, to the Office, reporting at the same time whether any householder, through laziness, neglects or disregards this useful undertaking; in such a case the guilty party is to be punished. And when the mulberry trees DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 139

in the colonies attain such growth that it becomes possible to proceed to the production of silk, they will then be given by the Office the necessary silkworm seed, together with instructions on how to handle it. Upon the perfection of this undertaking, when a certain quantity of the colonies' own silk production exists, but no convenient means is found to sell it, it will in that case be accepted by the treasury at reference prices, as is purchased from the inhabitants of the Caucasus, Astrakhan, Tauride, and other governorates.

§ 8. Since horticulture cannot be carried on successfully without proper attention to it, every householder must plant, in autumn and spring, willow, osier, and other fast-growing trees in such quantity as he needs to keep his fences in proper order.

§ 9. Although § 70 of the Instruction already most strictly prescribes to the district Heads and to all the Schulzen in general that they should make every effort to ensure that forest is sown in every colony, yet, owing to the importance and usefulness of this matter, this instruction is hereby further confirmed to all the authorities in the colonies, with the requirement that they compel the settlements under their jurisdiction to select in each, in proportion to the number of householders, a special site for forest planting, and that each autumn, or as circumstances permit, also in spring, they sow there properly, in addition to fast-growing trees, oak, elm, and other species capable of growing in Novorossiysk Governorate, taking care that the young shoots are properly preserved.

Section III. — On rural police.

§ 10. In every settlement there must be special herdsmen for the pasturing of calves, pigs, and domestic fowl, a separate one for each kind, whom the village Office must hire and maintain at the expense of the community. This is prescribed so that young fruit and mulberry trees, as well as grapevines and other produce, may not be damaged or entirely destroyed by livestock.

§ 11. Although § 50 of the Instruction most strictly requires the Vorsteher and Schulzen to keep unremitting watch that every householder maintains his house, threshing floor, stables, sheds, and fences in proper repair and cleanliness, and, failing this, to collect from them a fine of 20 kopecks into the common fund; yet since it turns out in practice that negligent, lazy, and stubborn householders would rather pay 20 kopecks than undertake such repairs, therefore any such householder who, without sound reason and solely out of stubbornness, laziness, or negligence, fails to repair his buildings and fences and allows them to fall into further disrepair, must pay a fine the first time of 20 kopecks. If the village authorities inform him of this a second time and he does not comply, in that case a fine of one ruble is to be collected from him; and the third time, for such disobedience arising from laziness and stubbornness, the guilty party must be subjected to corporal punishment, which the district Office is to determine for him and is to carry out only after submitting the matter to the Office for its consideration and decision.

§ 12. Since the colonists have hitherto had the custom of denoting the quantity of their produce by foreign measures and weights, which causes only confusion and misunderstanding, every district Office, and where there is none, the village Office, must accordingly provide itself with a stamped state measure — namely, the garnets, chetverik, and chetvert — as well as stamped pound and pud weights; by these every householder must then have similar ones made for himself and compare them with those kept as standards in the district Office, and when they are found to be entirely consistent, the district Office must then stamp them with its own seal.

Section IV. — On the use of the colonies' public revenues for useful economic establishments, for the development of profitable trades, and for the establishment of factories.

§ 13. The first point of the Instruction given to the Office of Guardianship of New Russian Foreign Settlers prescribes: to exercise, over the foreign colonies subordinate to it, "proper guardianship care and oversight, and to attend to economic arrangements pertaining to their present welfare and to rural economy"; and the eighth point: "to endeavor to encourage the foreign settlers toward the cultivation of artificial meadows, the planting of mulberry trees, grapevines, sesame seed and other useful plants, toward increasing the best breeds of sheep, and toward establishing linen, woolen, leather and other factories"; but since money is required to bring these two points into actual execution, it is for this purpose — as objects conducive to their own welfare — that the communal revenues in each district, obtained from the leasing out of drinking houses, meadows, fisheries, from distilling, monetary fines, and the like, are to be employed; and to that end every settlement is henceforth forbidden to divide communal monies among the householders as before, and likewise to use them at its own discretion; but all such revenues are to be paid into the district Prikaz [administrative office] into the common district treasury; the district Prikaz, in turn, must annually report to the Office on the state of such communal sums, presenting at the same time its opinion as to what these funds, in accordance with the above-mentioned prescription, might more fittingly be spent on for the common benefit of the colonists, and await the Office's authorization for this; and likewise it must give the Office a detailed annual account of their use.

§ 14. Experience shows that householders who, in addition to farming, also engage in some other craft are always able to secure sufficient sustenance for themselves, and even in times (may God preserve us) of crop failure, cattle plague, or other misfortunes, cannot be in want of it; whereas those who spend the whole winter and part of the other seasons in such ruinous idleness must inevitably suffer want in hard times. Since the weaving of linen and the like is the most advantageous craft for a settler — because in the time free from field work, men can earn by weaving, and women and even small children from 10 to 12 years of age by spinning — it is therefore most strictly confirmed to all colonies that they must by every means endeavor, as a sure means of improving the settlers' condition, to spread this craft in those places where it is already practiced, and in settlements where it is not yet practiced, to introduce it without fail. To achieve the desired goal in this, the district Prikazes, and where there are none, the village Prikazes, are obliged to impress upon householders who have grown boys that they should place their sons in apprenticeship with good weavers until they have thoroughly learned the craft. When the

DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 141

person who has learned the trade is not himself able to set up a weaving loom in order to practice this craft, in such a case the necessary assistance is to be given him from the common treasury, on the agreement that this debt shall be repaid by him in full at the appointed times. Moreover, the district Prikaz, and where there is none, the village Prikaz, must each year at the beginning of autumn take care and make such arrangements that in places well supplied with the best flax, a sufficient quantity of it be purchased, from which each householder might be supplied with such a portion as is needed to occupy his family with it. For such purchase of the best flax, the householders must make a monetary contribution as needed; in case of necessity, money may also be borrowed for this from the common treasury, but only on condition that it be repaid within a short time.

Section V. — On Internal Administration in the Colonies.

§ 15. Since not only from the village but even from the district Prikazes various reports, submissions, complaints and litigation cases arrive at the Office, for the most part written so poorly and unintelligibly that the Office is sometimes quite unable to grasp the true substance of the matter and to enter into its actual circumstances, it is therefore prescribed to every district and village Prikaz to maintain, at its own expense, one competent clerk who would be able, as required, to handle the written business of the Prikaz — that is, to know properly how to express clearly and intelligibly on paper all circumstances occurring both within it and throughout the colonies. To this end, the aforementioned boys and young men are to be employed in copying, making them also practice in the drafting of documents, so that in time they may acquire the proper knowledge in this.

§ 16. No decision of a district or village Prikaz shall be deemed valid unless the matter has been heard, deliberated and decided by all three members together — namely, in the district Prikaz by the Vorsteher and two Beisitzers, and in the villages by the Schultz with his Beisitzers. Since it may happen that one of them will be away on business, and another will fall ill by that time, so that the entire conduct of business in the Prikaz would depend on only two, or even one, person, whose sole judgment in deciding a matter pertaining to the Prikaz might be either insufficient or also based on bias, it is therefore necessary that, whenever village Elders are elected to the Prikazes by virtue of the Instruction, in addition to the three elected for each Prikaz, two more persons be appointed from among the most sensible and orderly householders, who, in case of the lawful inability of the first to be present at the Prikaz on the appointed days, must take their place and sign all resolutions, decisions and verdicts made therein in their presence.

§ 17. If anyone is summoned to the district or village Prikaz, he must appear there immediately. For failing to comply with this without good cause, he shall pay a monetary fine of 50 kopecks the first time, 1 ruble the second time, and 2 rubles the third time. In case of urgent necessity admitting no delay, he is to be brought to the Prikaz under guard, and such disobedience is to be reported to the Office. Upon the summoned colonist's arrival in the room where the Schultzes and Beisitzers perform their duties, he must, with due respect and without his hat, approach the village authority, ask permission to explain his matter, and then, in a decorous manner and without any commotion, state his need; and when, after being heard, he is told to leave the room, he must do so at once and wait until he is called again.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVII. P. 726-731.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 44.

The very titles of the sections of this document reveal which problems of colony administration seemed most important to the Russian authorities of the time. The provision on the corporal punishment of colonists (§ 4) is especially notable. Under the "despot" Paul I, this provision, which had been included in the temporary instruction for the colonies (1769), was not incorporated into the instruction for the Saratov colonies (doc. No. 38); this omission was rectified in the present document, issued under the "liberal" Alexander I. Although the document formally concerns only the Novorossiya colonies, its provisions were extended to all colonies in Russia by the Statute on Colonies of 1857 (doc. No. 115). In particular, Art. 481 of the Statute reproduces the aforementioned § 4, albeit supplied with a bashful qualification: "taking care that this [corporal punishment] should by no means become an execution, but should serve rather as a fear of shame and disgrace."

## No. 45. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE SETTLEMENT OF GERMAN COLONISTS IN THE CRIMEA (1803)

20,862. — July 24. Personal decree, given to the Kherson Military Governor Beklashov. — On the resettlement of colonists from various German provinces.

The Minister of Internal Affairs will deliver to you, together with this, information concerning the resettlement of colonists from various German Provinces under the direction of the Commissioners Ziegler and Schurter.

I charge you to assist, by all means at your disposal, in the sound and convenient settlement of these emigrants, in accordance with the arrangements made for them and prescribed in detail to the New Russian Guardianship Office.

Among these colonists there are many vine-growers. In order to turn their knowledge and skills to the benefit of viticulture, it will be necessary to provide them with the means to settle in the Crimean peninsula. If it proves impossible to provide them, in the highland part of the Crimea, with land suitable for the cultivation of vineyards, I charge you, without wasting time, to acquire the necessary quantity of such land by purchase from private persons, instructing at the same time the Tavrida Civil Governor to take special care of the colonists settling in the Crimea and to provide them with every means of restoring the neglected vineyards there.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVII. P. 786.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 45.

It is no accident that the document draws attention to the restoration of vineyards in Crimea — after Crimea's annexation to Russia (1783), many Tatars were forced to flee from there, and viticulture fell into decline. The first German colonies in Crimea arose in 1805 in Simferopol uyezd (the Neusatz district) and Feodosiya uyezd (the Zürichtal district) of Tavrida governorate.

Ziegler Franz — an agent who in 1803 was engaged in transporting colonists to Russia from southwestern Germany and Alsace; the settlers he transported founded all the first Crimean colonies except Zürichtal (see the note to doc. No. 47).

---

## No. 46. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE SETTLEMENT OF GERMAN COLONISTS IN NEW RUSSIA (1803)

20,988. — October 17. Personal decree, given to the Odessa City Governor, the Duc de Richelieu. — On the settlement, in the environs of Odessa and in other places of the Kherson, Yekaterinoslav and Tavrida Governorates, of colonists arrived from Germany.

The Minister of Internal Affairs has presented to me your report to him of September 26.

Approving and receiving with particular satisfaction all the arrangements you have made concerning the reception of the colonists arrived from Germany, and your care for them, I not only give My full consent that you should direct the settlement of those who may settle near Odessa, but I regard this as a personal favor to Me: so much do I wish that these poor people, having

DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________ 143

changed their fatherland, should find every possible assistance and not undergo the harsh trials which our first colonists experienced.

To further this aim, I find it necessary to prescribe to you the following:

1. Finding it useful that the colonists be settled, at least in part, near Odessa, I permit you to purchase the land of Count Wincenty Potocki, or other land at your best discretion, endeavoring to make this acquisition as advantageous as possible for the treasury. As for the land of Captain Vukovich, from the copy of the rescript to the former Kherson Military Governor Beklashov, herewith enclosed, you will see that, by the rights presented by the well-known Greek division, it was to be given to them; and although it is likely that the dispersal of these Greeks and their small number will be the reason that a significant part of this land remains with the treasury, nevertheless it is impossible to wait until this circumstance is brought to due clarity, and to leave the colonists without land until that time. The Kherson Civil Governor will, however, at the same time receive an order to proceed as quickly as possible with the execution of the aforementioned instruction given to Lieutenant General Beklashov.

2. Having thus obtained the land, you will not fail to communicate with the Office of Guardianship of Foreigners as to which of the colonists, by mutual agreement between you and the Collegiate Councilor Kontenius who administers it, according to the wishes and circumstances of each, may wish to settle in the environs of Odessa, and which may settle in other places of the Kherson, Yekaterinoslav, or Tavrida Governorates; and having thus divided the colonists, you shall take under your own special charge those who fall under your jurisdiction, while the rest will come under the ordinary supervision of the Office of Guardianship of Foreigners.

3. This Office shall be obliged to assist you in every way, and as it has all the necessary rules for the settlement of foreigners, and has already successfully settled many, you may obtain the necessary information on this through Collegiate Councilor Kontenius, with whom you should also come to agreement regarding the sums required for building houses for the colonists or their other needs: for some time ago thirty thousand rubles were allocated to the Guardianship Office, and appropriate sums will be allocated to it in future as well.

4. As to the expenses you have already incurred, the Guardianship Office must reimburse them to you immediately; and I, approving your resolve in this matter, wish that you proceed both with the repair of the barracks in which the colonists are to be housed for the winter, and with all other arrangements you deem necessary.

5. An order is being sent by the same courier to the Dubossary Quarantine Chief that he should not compel the colonists with unwarranted severity, nor burden himself unduly: for however necessary precautions may be in cases of genuine danger, in the present case they are unsuitable.

6. The Catholic and Lutheran priests you have requested will be found without delay and sent to you.

7. As for the overseer Gambinius, recommended by you for the two parties of colonists arrived in Odessa, I leave it to your discretion to grant him a monetary reward, and ask you to report to Me what other encouragement might be given to him, should you deem it necessary.

8. I greatly approve of the assurances you have given the colonists regarding their debts to the treasury, which may increase on account of their present idle stay in Odessa. In this respect it will indeed be possible to give them assistance, in proportion to whatever considerations they may deserve, whether their needs or their good conduct and diligence toward a swift and lasting settlement.

For the rest, I cannot sufficiently express here how much I wish that these colonists be as well cared for as possible, and lack nothing. Bound up with this is, first of all, the obligation that the people We have summoned should receive every possible assistance, and also Our own interest; for in proportion to the successes in the first foundations of these colonies, one may expect their expansion as well, should that be deemed advisable.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVII. P. 932-934.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 46.

The colonists who arrived in Odessa at that time were mostly settled in its environs. Between 1803 and 1806, 10 German colonies arose here, forming the Liebental district. The first Lutheran clergyman in these parts was Johann Christian Heinrich Pfersdorff (?–1819), a native of Thuringia, pastor in Odessa and the colony of Lustdorf (Olgino) in 1803–1806, and pastor in the colony of Gross-Liebental (Bolshoy Liebental, Bolshaya Akarzha) in 1806–1819.

## No. 47. REPORT OF THE MINISTER OF INTERNAL AFFAIRS ON THE RULES FOR THE RECEPTION AND SETTLEMENT OF COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1804)

21,163. — February 20. Report of the Minister of Internal Affairs, confirmed by His Majesty. — On the rules for the reception and settlement of foreign colonists.

Report. The foreigner Ziegler, who last year recruited a considerable number of colonists from Germany, having arrived here, offers his services for a similar recruitment this year as well. Having examined his proposals and considered all the circumstances of this matter, I make bold to submit most humbly to Your Imperial Majesty the following:

The recruitment of colonists began and continues to this day on the basis of the Manifesto issued in 1763. It was not specified exactly what kind of people were to be received, but this was extended generally to persons of every rank and condition, which is why, at first, there turned out to be many poor householders, for the most part the very poorest, who have so far brought little benefit to the State. The Saratov colonies and some of the New Russian colonies prove this truth.

As far as one can judge, the present recruitment, too, has been conducted by Ziegler and Escher without discrimination. From the descriptions of the colonists brought by the former, it is evident that there are among them many unnecessary craftsmen, decrepit, weak, solitary persons, and even some with chronic illnesses, to which must be added that most of them are extremely poor.

Empress Catherine II resolved upon the recruitment of foreigners, wishing to populate the empty steppes. But whereas the growth of population in the internal Governorates and the resulting overcrowding may now require the resettlement of Her own subjects, while land suitable for settlement in the southern region is no longer so abundant, one must now seek less to populate these lands with foreigners than to settle them with the former, unless it be a limited number of such newcomers who might serve as an example in agricultural pursuits or in handicrafts. Therefore, if it is desired to continue receiving people from foreign lands, this should be limited to the strictest necessity and solely to good and prosperous householders.

DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 145

At present their settlement is directed for the most part toward the New Russian region. But since it is known that there, too, few suitable state lands remain, and there is extreme difficulty in finding them, it is necessary, before permitting these people to depart, to determine where they are to settle, by selecting suitable state lands for the purpose or purchasing suitable plots from landowners; for owing to the untimely designation of land, and consequently the delay in settlement, they must live for about two years at the expense of the treasury and will cost considerable expense.

Once the lands have been designated and protected from any other use, it is necessary to restrict settlement upon them to only those foreigners who may be of most use to that region — namely, good farmers and people who have acquired sufficient skill in the cultivation of the vine, in the raising of mulberry trees and other useful plants, as well as those skilled in animal husbandry, and especially in the keeping and breeding of the best breeds of sheep, and possessing in general all the necessary knowledge of the best agricultural practices, should be given preference over others. Rural craftsmen, such as tailors, shoemakers, carpenters, blacksmiths, potters, coppersmiths, weavers and masons, may also be assured of acceptance; but all other artisans and craftsmen who are of no use for rural life shall not be enrolled among the colonists, except perhaps in the case where it may be deemed necessary, for the towns being established in the southern region, to recruit a small number of craftsmen.

Guided by this rule, it is likewise not considered advisable either to solicit or to induce, by whatever means, people to resettle, or to employ special commissions for the recruitment of colonists, or to appoint special agents for this purpose. Instead, it may be established that those who wish to emigrate to Russia for settlement should present themselves to our Ministers or other Agents, who, having examined the passports, certificates, or other documents presented by them, may issue them passports for travel to the Russian border; these certificates, issued by Magistrates or communities, must contain confirmation of the good conduct of the bearer.

It is also necessary here that, with regard to his present lord, he should have fulfilled everything he is obliged to under Imperial and Provincial law.

But since travel to the border may be attended with difficulties for one or two families alone, the Resident in Regensburg may be instructed that, having gathered from among those wishing to emigrate to Russia groups of 20 to 30 families, he should dispatch them at once in transports, whether by water or by land, whichever is deemed best, hiring vessels and carts at the expense of the Russian Government, and appointing one of their own number as Elder, whom all are to obey on the journey. To assist him in gathering the designated number of families from among those wishing to emigrate to Russia, in hiring boatmen and carters, in dispatching them, and in more precisely verifying the truth of the certificates presented by the colonists, as well as their actual condition, the foreigner Ziegler may be appointed, given his aptitude and efficiency for this task, being assigned, on the basis of instructions to be given him, a salary commensurate with his labors.

Several families, having agreed together to resettle, may choose one, two, or more persons and send them ahead to inspect the lands designated for them and to learn their quality.

Furthermore, the annual emigration of colonists from Germany in general must not exceed 200 families, for with other resettlements it is impossible to settle more than this number soundly. It is therefore necessary to establish that the Resident should receive and dispatch from 100 to 150 families per year, assuming that the rest may make their own way out from other places closer to the border.

In this connection, the Ministers at Foreign Courts to whom this may pertain must be instructed:

1. That they are to make no loan whatsoever to anyone, except payment for vessels and carts for those who will be dispatched in transports, as stated above.

2. That those who present themselves to them must produce certificates and reliable guarantees that they possess and will bring with them property, either in cash capital or in goods, of not less than 300 guilders; those who do not produce this are not to be accepted, for experience has taught that the establishment of those without sufficient means both proceeds slowly and succeeds poorly.

3. It goes without saying that those emigrating for settlement must be family people. Single persons are on no account to be accepted, unless someone should wish to take them into his family.

4. Families consisting only of husband and wife should, as far as possible, not be sent out; for experience shows how difficult it is for them to maintain a household and achieve a good condition, having no means to keep laborers.

For the rest, these emigrants may be granted all the rights and privileges accorded to colonists in general, as are now being settled in the New Russian region.

These rights consist of the following:

1. Freedom of religion.

2. Exemption from the payment of taxes and from all obligations for ten years.

3. After the expiration of these ten years they will pay the treasury a land tax, for the first 10 years from 15 to 20 kopecks per desiatina per year; and upon the expiration of this term, the tax shall be equalized with that which state peasants generally pay per soul in that locality. As to the other provincial obligations, the colonists are bound to bear these on an equal footing with those Russian subjects among whom they are settled, immediately upon the expiration of the exemption period, except for billeting, save however in those cases when military detachments are passing through.

4. Exemption from military and civil service. Anyone who wishes may enroll voluntarily, but this does not release him from the payment of his debt to the treasury.

5. Repayment of the money loaned by the treasury, after the expiration of the exemption years, is to be spread over the following ten years.

6. All colonists are given land free of charge, 60 desiatinas per family, except in the highland part of the Crimea, where special rules for distribution are to be established.

7. From the day of arrival at the border, the payment of subsistence money begins, at 10 kopecks per adult and 6 kopecks per minor per day, until the time they arrive at the place of settlement; and this money is charged to non-returnable expenses. However, should anyone wish to leave Russia, he must repay it.

8. From the time of arrival at the place of settlement until the first harvest of their own, 5 to 10 kopecks are paid per person, depending on the price of provisions; and this sum must be repaid by them together with the general loan.

9. The loan for building houses, purchasing livestock, and generally for setting up the whole household, extends up to 300 rubles; for people who arrive with good means, it may be increased if they require it for some useful enterprise.

10. They are permitted to import their property upon settlement, whatever it may consist of, duty-free, and in addition each family — meaning by this a husband and wife with minor children, or two adult laborers, or four women — is permitted, on one occasion, to bring in goods for sale to the value of up to 300 rubles, provided these goods are their own property and not entrusted to them by outside persons or taken on credit.

11. If anyone, at any time whatsoever, wishes to leave the State, he is granted freedom to do so, but on condition that, in addition to paying off all debt owed by him, he pay into the treasury, in a single payment, a tax equal to three years' worth.

12. It is permitted to establish factories and other necessary trades, to engage in commerce, to join guilds and corporations, and to sell their products anywhere in the Empire.

To this it is necessary to add that if any of those arrived for settlement should prove disobedient and insubordinate to the established Authority, or should fall into dissolute conduct, such a person shall without fail, after the debt owed by him to the treasury has been collected, be expelled beyond the border — a rule to be extended also to those already arrived, so that in this way a good morality in the colonies may be better established and the local Authorities may be shielded from those unpleasantnesses which they may encounter from the willfulness of colonists or other disorders.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVIII. P. 137-140.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 47.

This principal colonization act of Alexander I is often referred to in the literature as a "manifesto." The document reflects a new, more pragmatic approach to the reception of colonists — admitting only a limited number of well-to-do, married, and highly moral settlers, and moreover ones with experience in those branches of agriculture and craft that seemed promising for the colonies of southern Russia. As a result, the new colonies here avoided many of the problems characteristic of the colonies of Catherine's time.

This act for the first time provided for the recovery from colonists, in the event of their leaving Russia, of the subsistence money expended on their settlement (Art. 7).

Escher Hans Kaspar — major of the Moscow Dragoon Regiment, a Swiss, who organized the resettlement of colonists from Switzerland; the colonists he resettled founded the Crimean colony of Zürichtal in 1808.

Manifesto of 1763 — doc. No. 11.

---

## No. 48. REPORT OF THE MINISTER OF INTERNAL AFFAIRS ON LOCATIONS FOR THE SETTLEMENT OF FOREIGNERS IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA, APPROVED BY ALEXANDER I (1804)

21,177. — February 23. Report of the Minister of Internal Affairs, approved by His Majesty. — On locations for the settlement of foreigners.

Report. The inconveniences discovered in the measures taken at the founding of the first colonies in Saratov Governorate, and the necessity of establishing firm rules for the future settlement of foreigners in Russia, prompt me to present to Your Imperial Majesty the following proposals, most humbly requesting their approval, so that they might serve as guidance both to myself and to the various authorities that may take part in the arrangement of the colonists.

1. For the initial founding of colonies in the Governorates of Kherson, Yekaterinoslav, and Tavrida, locations nearest to the ports should be chosen, so that the settlers may find greater means of disposing of their produce; and thus, having laid these foundations, proceed, as the number of colonists increases, further into the interior of the lands.

2. Odessa and Feodosia (Kefa) are designated as such points.

3. In the vicinity of Feodosia and throughout the mountainous part of Tavrida, efforts should be made to settle vine-growers and people skilled in horticulture; for this purpose either crown lands should be considered, if any exist, or the necessary quantity thereof should be acquired by purchase.

4. Since the principal aim in settling immigrants in these places will be viticulture and horticulture, then, both for this reason and because of the generally smaller quantity of suitable land there than elsewhere, and the high price thereof, an allotment of 20 desyatinas for each family is deemed quite sufficient.

5. Furthermore, should there be found, besides the aforementioned type of foreigners, grain-farmers wishing to settle in Crimea, such persons should preferably be settled on the Molochnye Vody [Milk Waters], as a place bringing them closer to the Mennonites settled in Yekaterinoslav Governorate. But should the number of such settlers increase, they should then be settled on lands formerly occupied by the nomadic encampments of the Kalmyks, now transferred to the lands of the Don Cossack Host.

Likewise, the Mennonites, in accordance with their own wishes, should be settled on the Molochnye Vody as well, being given the two plots marked on the district plan under Nos. 60 and 61, currently occupied by the Nogais; the latter, upon being paid for their houses and winter quarters located there, and given certain assistance in relocating, should be transferred to other lands. In this resettlement of the Mennonites there is the advantage that they will be close to Taganrog, which will thereby add to their means of disposing of their produce in that city.

6. As for the other point, from which the settlement of foreigners is intended to extend as far as Odessa, grain-farmers chiefly are designated for settlement there.

7. For this purpose the colonists who have now arrived from Germany should be settled on the land being purchased from Count Potocki; as their numbers increase, they are to settle further into the interior of this region, in Tiraspol district, moving toward Olviopol.

<...>

9. Craftsmen of every kind should be settled in towns, wherever any of them may wish; and for the present, those who have now arrived from Germany should be established in Odessa, entrusting the implementation of this to the Duc de Richelieu and Collegiate Councilor Kontenius.

10. Having drawn up such a system or plan for the settlement of foreigners, it should be followed consistently, so as to put an end to the occasion for those changes and uncertainties which have hitherto caused substantial inconveniences.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVIII. Pp. 154-155.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 48.

This act specifies the places of settlement of colonists on the basis of the principles put forward in doc. No. 47. The provisions of the present document were subsequently implemented — alongside the colonies near Odessa, in Feodosiya uyezd, and in the Molochna Mennonite district, the following were established in subsequent years: the Molochna colonist district in Melitopol uyezd of Tavrida governorate (from 1804), and, in Kherson governorate, the Glückstal district in Tiraspol uyezd (from 1805), the Kuchurgan district in Odessa uyezd (from 1808), and the Berezan district in Odessa and Ananyev uyezds (from 1809).

## No. 49. REPORT OF THE MINISTER OF INTERNAL AFFAIRS ON PERMITTING FOREIGN COLONISTS TO PURCHASE LAND IN NOVOROSSIYA, APPROVED BY ALEXANDER I (1804)

21,192. — March 1. Report of the Minister of Internal Affairs, approved by His Majesty. — On permitting foreign colonists to purchase lands in the Novorossiya Governorates.

Report. By the decree of Your Imperial Majesty, issued on December 12, 1801, the right to acquire lands without peasants was granted to all Russian merchants, townspeople, state peasants, and freed persons.

DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 149

Taking into consideration that some of the emigrating colonists, being of sufficient means, might, without requiring lands for settlement from the treasury, wish to purchase such lands from private persons as their own property, or, having received from the treasury the quantity of land allotted to them, might wish to purchase additional plots at their own expense in order to expand and improve their establishments, I make so bold as to most humbly present to Your Imperial Majesty whether it might be pleasing to extend the aforementioned right, granted to Russian subjects, to purchase land, to foreign settlers wishing to emigrate to the Novorossiya region as well, subject to observance of the following rules:

1. Foreigners settled on land purchased by themselves must enjoy the same privileges as are generally granted to colonists.

2. They must be forever free from the special tax, but upon the expiration of the years of exemption they are obliged to pay the land dues generally imposed, or to be imposed in future, on landowners' lands in that region.

3. They must, from the time of their settlement, bear zemstvo obligations in every respect on an equal footing with the other native inhabitants of the region where they settle.

4. Should any of the settlers who own land as private property wish to leave the state entirely, he must, upon his departure, sell the land he has purchased to someone residing in Russia; otherwise it shall pass to the treasury without payment. This rule extends not only to the original acquirers of the land but also to their heirs, should the latter wish to leave Russia.

All of this I make so bold as to submit for the Most Gracious consideration of Your Imperial Majesty.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVIII. P. 177.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 49.

This is the first act permitting foreign colonists to purchase land. It acquired notable practical significance later on, once the colonists had accumulated the means necessary for this. It is worth noting that the acquisition of land by foreigners was excluded at the beginning of the 19th century in much the same way as in present-day Russia.

## No. 50. REPORT OF THE MINISTER OF INTERNAL AFFAIRS ON PERMITTING LANDOWNERS TO SETTLE COLONISTS ON THEIR LANDS, APPROVED BY ALEXANDER I (1804)

21,254. — April 12. Report of the Minister of Internal Affairs, approved by His Majesty. — On permitting landowners to settle colonists on their lands.

Report. In issuing various regulations concerning colonists, the Government has for the most part had in view only those resettlements which were established, with the treasury's assistance, on its own lands. No precise regulation has been made for the case in which landowners might wish to settle foreign colonists on lands belonging to them.

Meanwhile, many landowners have expressed such a wish, and will probably continue to do so in future; it is therefore necessary to determine in advance what rights and benefits may be granted to colonists moving from abroad onto landowners' lands.

Applying the general rules concerning colonies settled on crown lands, and the force of the decree of May 9, 1802, addressed to the border governors, the rights and benefits for colonists settled on landowners' lands may be summarized as follows:

1. Colonists settling on landowners' lands shall, on the basis of the manifesto of 1763, enjoy freedom of religion and be exempt from military and civil service for the entire period of their residence in Russia, unless someone voluntarily wishes otherwise.

2. In order to provide landowners with greater convenience and benefit in this manner of settlement, the general rule of a 10-year exemption for crown colonists shall be extended to colonists settled on landowners' lands as well, it being established that upon the expiration of this term the landowners shall pay into the treasury on their behalf the ordinary taxes paid by landowners' peasants.

3. Colonists must, from the time of their settlement, bear zemstvo obligations on an equal footing with the other inhabitants of the Governorate in which they are settled.

4. Colonists settled on landowners' lands must be free from any personal bondage, and although at the census they will be recorded on the lands where they settle, they do not thereby lose their rights, and no government office may effect any personal bondage upon them.

5. Landowners may make agreements with colonists regarding their obligations for fixed terms of years, and present such agreements to government offices for registration and, in necessary cases, for the resolution of disputes according to the laws on contracts.

6. Colonists, having fulfilled the obligations made with a landowner, may move from one landowner to another.

7. On these general grounds, all landowners are permitted not only to accept but also to bring in colonists from abroad and settle them on their lands by mutual and voluntary agreement as to the terms of obligations and labor.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVIII. Pp. 260-261.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 50.

Given the limited availability of free crown lands, the Russian authorities began to attach increasing importance to settling colonists on private (landowners') estates. This practice subsequently became widespread in New Russia, the South-Western governorates, and several other regions.

Decree of 9 May 1802 — doc. No. 40; manifesto of 1763 — doc. No. 11.

## No. 51. REPORT ON THE GERMAN THEATER IN ST. PETERSBURG, APPROVED BY ALEXANDER I (1805)

21,825. — July 5. Report of the Chief Director of Spectacles, the Military Governor of St. Petersburg, and the Minister of Finance, approved by His Majesty. — On the incorporation of the German troupe in St. Petersburg into the Theater Directorate and on the annual disbursement of 25,000 rubles from the treasury for its maintenance.

Report. It pleased Your Imperial Majesty to command that we examine the most humble petition of the manager of the German theater, Mire, in which he again requests Most Gracious assistance.

Mire, in this petition and in the submissions subsequently made by him to the Committee, shows a decrease in 1804 of 20,000 rubles in receipts from performances compared to before, and an increase of expenses for the troupe to 17,000 rubles (as is evident from his own account books), explaining: I. That, being unable to maintain the German theater on the 25,000 rubles he annually receives from the treasury, he requests that instead 47,000 rubles be provided,

DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 151

which now constitute the annual salary of the actors; that he be released from 41,986 rubles of debts incurred by necessity, and that the actors' salaries be satisfied, amounting from January 1 to June 15 of this year to 31,817 rubles; and 2. That if the Theater Directorate should take the German troupe under its own maintenance, then he be paid a lump sum of 30,000 rubles for the wardrobe, scenery, and other items, which cost him up to 174,000 rubles, that his debts of 73,803 rubles be paid, and that the 13,333 rubles issued to him as a loan for bringing actors here not be recovered from him, all of which, according to this latter proposal of his, amounts to a sum of 117,136 rubles.

The information we have gathered on the German theater shows that in 1801 Mire, under a contract concluded with the then Military Governor here, General of Infantry Golenishchev-Kutuzov, undertook to maintain the German troupe for 7 years, receiving assistance from the treasury only for the first three years at 5,000 rubles; but after only 2 years had passed, having incurred debts of up to 58,622 rubles, he petitioned Your Majesty for Most Gracious assistance. On November 11, 1803, Your Imperial Majesty, upon the report submitted by the Committee then in existence for the review of matters concerning the Theater Directorate in general, was Most Graciously pleased to command that Mire be released from debts of 58,622 rubles and that he be paid an annual assistance of 25,000 rubles from the State Treasury. Subsequently, on July 27, 1804, 15,000 rubles were issued to Mire as a loan for bringing German actors here, to be withheld over 3 years in equal portions from the 25,000 rubles disbursed to him, of which 1,667 rubles have already been deducted in the current May installment.

Having considered all of the foregoing, we find that, according to the original arrangement of the German theater and the contract concluded by its manager with the Military Governor, Mire has no right to any new assistance, all the more so since in 1803 he received such considerable assistance from Your Imperial Majesty's generosity. But since even that assistance did not render him solvent enough to continue maintaining the German theater, and he has instead fallen once again into unpayable debt, then new assistance to Mire offers no hope whatsoever that he will in future be capable of maintaining the German theater. For this reason it is our opinion: that Mire be refused the new Sovereign's assistance he requests, leaving him to seek by himself whatever means he may find best to settle with his creditors. But since Mire, being in dire straits and having lost his credit, cannot maintain the German theater, and it must therefore collapse, in that case, should it please Your Imperial Majesty that the German troupe continue to exist, it should be incorporated into the Theater Directorate, and for the maintenance of this troupe, in accordance with the proposal of the Chief Director of Spectacles, there should be disbursed from the treasury, in addition to the funds allocated for the maintenance of the theaters, the sum of 25,000 rubles annually — the same sum that Mire now receives.

Submitting all of this to the Most Gracious consideration of Your Imperial Majesty, we make so bold as to add whether it might not be pleasing, as a token of Sovereign mercy, to Most Graciously command that the 13,333 rubles issued to Mire in 1804 as a loan for bringing actors here not be recovered from him, in view of his disordered financial state.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVIII. Pp. 1116-1118.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 51.

Mire, Osip (Joseph) — a native of Strasbourg, staged performances in the theaters of Hamburg and Riga; in 1799 he founded a German theater in St. Petersburg, drawing German actors and singers into it. In 1800 he transferred the theater to the Theatrical Directorate, which paid off Mire's debts. In 1801 the directorship of the theater passed to the scholar-philologist Fyodor Pavlovich (Friedrich) Adelung (1768–1843), a corresponding member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (from 1809), and the theater was once again handed over to Mire. He was an expert in stage effects and staged very lavish productions — operas and operettas. A number of his performances at the Hermitage Theater attracted the attention of Alexander I and secured state support for Mire. Despite this, Mire again found himself in a critical financial situation, and in 1805 was forced to hand the theater over to the actor, poet, and playwright Christlieb Georg Heinrich Aresto (1764–1818) and left St. Petersburg. See: Stöckl E. Musikgeschichte der Rußlanddeutschen. Dülmen, 1993. S. 98–100, 102.

## No. 52. REPORT OF THE MINISTER OF INTERNAL AFFAIRS ON PAYMENTS BY THE ST. PETERSBURG COLONIES TO THE TREASURY, APPROVED BY ALEXANDER I (1805)

21,837. — July 18. Report of the Minister of Internal Affairs, approved by His Majesty. — On equalizing the St. Petersburg colonies in the payment of the loan and land dues they owe the treasury, in proportion to their means.

Report. At the original settlement of colonists in St. Petersburg Governorate, besides the general arrangements made by virtue of the manifesto of July 22, 1763, special conditions were made with them in 1765 and 1766, on the basis of which they were then settled in four colonies, of which Srednyaya Rogatka and Izhora were placed on lands belonging to the Tsarskoye Selo estate, while Novosaratovka and Yamburg received their plots from the general crown lands.

The essence of these conditions was to allot to the first two colonies 30 desyatinas of land per family, and to the latter 35, to build houses for each family and to carry out the entire economic establishment at the treasury's expense, to exempt them forever from all zemstvo obligations and taxes (1), and, upon the expiration of the years of exemption, to require them to pay only land dues of 1 ruble 22½ kopecks per desyatina, while also repaying, at a set time, the sum expended on their settlement.

(1) This latter circumstance is specifically included in the conditions for the Srednyaya Rogatka, Izhora, and Novosaratovka colonists. The Yamburg colonists, although they undertook, with respect to the maintenance of roads, billeting, and forest conservation, and in general with respect to police and civil administration, to be under the jurisdiction of the town of Yamburg, were nevertheless, upon coming under the jurisdiction and guardianship of the Expedition of State Economy, equalized with the others as regards obligations.

By the arrangement made at that time:

The Srednyaya Rogatka and Izhora colonies received an exemption of 5 years; repayment of the debt after the expiration of 15 years was set in 5 installments, that is, over two and a half years.

Novosaratovka likewise enjoyed a 5-year exemption, but repayment of the debt was to be made after the expiration of 10 years, in 6 installments, that is, over 3 years.

Yamburg was given an exemption of 13 years, and it was decided that the entire debt should be repaid in the last 3 exempt years.

These conditions were fulfilled with complete precision on the part of the Government; but when at the appointed time the same was demanded of the colonists, some, citing the unsuitability of the land, and others their own poverty, avoided all payment.

Under these circumstances, and chiefly out of special indulgence, the decree of 1779 ordered: that land dues be collected from them at half the established rate pending further decree, but that the debt to the treasury be paid in full without fail at the appointed time; yet even this arrangement had no effect whatsoever, and the colonists, after the expiration of the exemption, paid nothing more for over 20 years, until finally, upon better consideration of the circumstances, new undertakings were demanded of them for the exact payment of the established dues and the debt to the treasury. On this occasion similar indulgence was shown to them as before, and the decrees of 1792 and 1793 ordered the collection

DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 153

of land dues from the Srednyaya Rogatka and Novosaratovka colonists at 61¼ kopecks, and from the Izhora and Yamburg colonists at 30¾ kopecks, per desyatina of suitable land.

As regards the debt to the treasury, which for all of them amounted to more than 250,000 rubles, it was ordered to be repaid annually: by the Srednyaya Rogatka colonists at 10 rubles, and by the Novosaratovka and Izhora colonists at 5 rubles, per household, which they have indeed paid together with the land dues since 1792 without arrears. As for the Yamburg colonists, most of whom were resettled in 1793 to Yekaterinoslav Governorate, the debt and land arrears owed by them, amounting to more than 137,000 rubles, were forgiven them; the remaining 22 families were given, from that year, a new five-year exemption, upon the expiration of which they likewise pay the land dues of 30¾ kopecks per desyatina without arrears.

In 1797, the St. Petersburg colonists, having come, together with others, under the jurisdiction of the former Expedition of State Economy, it submitted a most humble report, which on June 20 of that same year was honored with Highest confirmation, so that, among other things, while confirming the payment of dues under the latest decrees, it be permitted, at the time most convenient for these colonists and once a noticeable improvement in their condition was evident, to endeavor to bring their land assessment, on the principles established for appanage estates, that is: first to a third, and then to a half of the annual income from each desyatina of arable land, and, in view of the proximity of these colonies to the Capital, to arrange matters so that no less than 30 desyatinas of land should be allotted per household; and since, under this arrangement, the Srednyaya Rogatka colony indeed lacked the full amount of land for the allotment of 30 desyatinas per family, in 1798, upon the submission of the Expedition, it was Most Graciously ordered that this be supplemented for them from the lands belonging to the Tsarskoye Selo estate, amounting to 226 desyatinas; for this purpose land was cut off from the village of Kamenka, whereby the needs of the colonists were fully satisfied, and, there remaining a certain surplus of this land, 4 families from among the most populous households separated off onto it with their own separate houses. These houses were, by Highest command, built of stone at the treasury's expense, and, for the convenient establishment and clearing of the land, overgrown with forest and marshy, they were given an exemption of 10 years.

Having thus provided the Srednyaya Rogatka colonists with the requisite quantity of land, and it having been observed that they are in a flourishing condition, it was recognized that they could, without any undue burden, pay the land dues designated in the original conditions; and, in consequence, a report on the collection thereof was submitted by the Governing Senate, which on October 10, 1799 was honored with Highest confirmation, and since then these colonists have paid annually 1 ruble 23 kopecks per desyatina.

After this, the Expedition of State Economy, wishing likewise to bring the obligations of the other three colonies into proper order, dispatched a surveyor in 1801 to make a new survey of the lands belonging to these colonies. This survey showed that in the Izhora colony there is 841 desyatinas and some sazhens of suitable land, that is, exactly the amount for which they pay land dues, and 1,728 desyatinas of unsuitable land; and that, on the contrary, in Novosaratovka and Yamburg there proved to be more suitable land than that for which they pay quitrent, namely 235 desyatinas in the former and 869 in the latter. In addition, closer inspections and investigations of all the lands belonging to the colonists revealed:

1. That as unsuitable lands in the Izhora and Yamburg colonies were marked off, even by the surveyors themselves, for the most part lands overgrown with timber and firewood forest, which, although in some places marshy in spring and autumn, may, with better management, through clearing and drying, be readily converted into hay meadows and arable land; and

2. That the numerous complaints made by the colonists to the previous authorities about the unsuitability of these lands arose especially from their avoidance of paying the dues owed. This was particularly noted in the Yamburg colony, which called unsuitable a tract of land covered with quite good timber and firewood forest, which it had laid waste, and in which there are no few hay-meadow clearings and places especially suited to grain-farming.

In view of these considerations, and taking into account that the condition of these colonies here, notwithstanding the advantages granted to them, superior to those elsewhere in Russia, and the various indulgences shown them, noticeably began to improve only from the time when the Government began to collect dues from them, and that those among them who must work harder in order to fulfill their obligations to the treasury are in a better condition, it is necessary to adopt measures whereby these colonies, without being burdened by dues, would be prompted to greater industriousness and would provide the Government with the greatest possible return of the expenses it has incurred on their behalf.

On this basis, I consider it expedient to make the following arrangements with regard to the payment of obligations by these colonies:

1. The Srednyaya Rogatka colony, which pays land quitrent and the debt sum more fully than the others and is distinguished from them by the expansion of its economy in every respect, should be left paying the land dues it currently pays, namely 1 ruble 23 kopecks per desyatina, while collecting, toward repayment of the debt, in accordance with the proposal made by the colony itself, 20 rubles per year per household instead of the 10 rubles now paid, beginning with the current year, this applying to those colonists originally settled there; while from those newly settled in the four houses, a similar levy should be collected, likewise in accordance with their voluntary agreement, upon the expiration of the years of exemption, that is, from 1808.

2. The Novosaratovka colony, which in point of advantages is not inferior to Srednyaya Rogatka, and in some respects even superior, should be assessed, instead of the land dues of 61¼ kopecks currently paid, at the same rate as Srednyaya Rogatka, namely 1 ruble 23 kopecks per desyatina, plus 10 rubles per household toward repayment of the debt, both levies beginning with the current year, and, moreover, the 235 desyatinas of suitable land which they hold in addition to the amount hitherto reckoned to them should be added to the land assessment, so that the entire portion of suitable land held by this colony will amount to 1,735 desyatinas.

3. The Izhora colony, which, not being equal to the other two in the quality of its land and its advantages, but nonetheless possessing a considerable tract, under the designation of unsuitable land, and paying no more than a quarter of the land dues and half the debt payment paid by Srednyaya Rogatka, should be placed under the obligation to pay 61½ kopecks per desyatina of land now considered suitable, it being left for future consideration to equalize it, as circumstances warrant, with the two above-mentioned colonies, and to make an addition to the debt payments it currently pays,

DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 155

as well as to establish a land due on those lands which shall in future be converted into suitable ones.

4. The Yamburg colony, which possesses all the necessary amenities but pays no more than 30¾ kopecks per desyatina, and that for only a very small quantity of land, should, while being left for the time being at its present quitrent, be required only to pay this levy, from the beginning of the current year, on the quantity of land recognized as suitable by the latest survey, namely for 1,378 desyatinas, it being left for gradual adjustment, in proportion to the advantages which this colony, possessing a quite considerable quantity of land, enjoys (for, in addition to the aforementioned suitable land, it also has 1,800 desyatinas of unsuitable land, with which the total amounts to more than 144 desyatinas per household), to equalize its obligations in proportion with the others. The unsuitable land, meanwhile, being for the present left in the colony's possession free of quitrent, it should be kept in view that, as the Government sees fit, people from other colonies might be settled upon it, should the need arise, or others, so that the land should not remain idle.

Submitting these proposals to the Highest consideration, and most humbly requesting their approval, I have at the same time the honor to present herewith a statement of the sum owed by the colonies situated in St. Petersburg Governorate.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVIII. Pp. 1128-1131.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 52.

With the normalization of the economic situation in the St. Petersburg colonies, the authorities began to raise both the colonists' payments toward the crown debt and the land tax levied on them.

Manifesto of 22 July 1763 — doc. No. 11; decree of 1793 — doc. No. 26; report of 20 June 1797 — doc. No. 28.
