## No. 76. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON HALTING THE RESETTLEMENT OF FOREIGNERS TO RUSSIA (1819)

27,912. — August 5. Regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On stopping the further resettlement of foreign émigrés to Russia.

The report of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs of August 3, No. 126, from the Department of State Economy and Public Buildings, entered in the Committee's journal under No. 1447, concerning foreign settlers, was heard.

The Committee resolved: 1) to confirm the opinion of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs, and, given the urgency of the matter requiring immediate resolution, to put it into effect forthwith. 2) At the same time, to authorize the Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs to make arrangements so that the further resettlement of foreign émigrés to Russia be completely stopped, placing responsibility for this on our Missions and Consulates; and 3) to bring all of this to the Highest attention; and, for due execution of this regulation, to communicate extracts from the journal to the Acting Ministers of Internal and Foreign Affairs.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXVI. P. 325.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 76.

Scholarship has advanced the view that the sudden cessation of the admission of foreign settlers was caused by a reassessment on the part of the authorities of the entire half-century-long policy of foreign colonization of Russia, since the colonies had not brought the country the universal agricultural upsurge originally expected of them (see: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. S. 174). If ruling circles indeed expected that the example of the German colonies would exert such a far-reaching beneficial influence on the Russian peasantry (and such hopes evidently did exist there), then the rulers were indulging in wholly groundless illusions. In reality, there were at that time no close contacts—nor could there have been—between the colonies and their neighbors, who farmed under entirely different conditions, if only because the German colonists had practically no knowledge of the local languages.

No known document from that period indicates that the authorities attempted to change this situation or even to introduce the colonists to the Russian language. The first tentative steps in this direction were taken only in the 1830s (see doc. No. 91), seventy years after the mass recruitment of colonists to Russia had begun. This, of course, can hardly be coincidental. Had the colonists mastered the local languages, they might well have tried, first and foremost, to impress upon their neighbors that serfdom, in whose grip those neighbors still had to live and farm, was hopelessly outdated and could in no way secure a "universal agricultural upsurge." The Russian authorities naturally sought to prevent the spread of such ideas at any cost, and it is entirely logical that the teaching of Russian to the colonists began to be seriously practiced only after the abolition of serfdom in 1861.

This act did not entail a complete halt to the influx of foreign colonists. In certain cases the authorities themselves introduced particular exceptions (an example being the settlement of Mennonites in the Volga region in the 1850s), and even more often those wishing to settle found ways to circumvent the restrictions imposed. In this connection, the mass influx of settlers into the South-Western governorates is especially notable, and it eventually gave rise to far-reaching consequences (see note to doc. No. 147).

---

## No. 77. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE PROHIBITION OF ISSUING PASSPORTS FOR RESETTLEMENT TO RUSSIA, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1819)

27,954. — October 25. Highest-confirmed regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On the prohibition of Russian Missions issuing passports to foreigners resettling to Russia and to the Kingdom of Poland.

It was announced to the Committee, in the memorandum of August 5 on the item entered in the journal under No. 1447 and put into execution, concerning foreign émigrés resettling to Russia, that the Sovereign Emperor consents that it now be decisively forbidden for our Missions to issue passports to foreigners resettling either to Russia or to the Kingdom of Poland.

The Committee resolved: to communicate this to the Acting Ministers of Foreign and Internal Affairs for execution, by extracts from the journal.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXVI. P. 362.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 77.

Along with a certain reassessment of values in matters concerning the colonists, it is difficult to find an exhaustive explanation for this document, as for the preceding one, unless one takes into account the general shift in policy during the final years of Alexander I's reign, when the emperor and his entourage moved ever further away from the markedly liberal "pro-European" course they had initially pursued.

Memorandum of August 5 — doc. No. 76.

---

## No. 78. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE ORAL OATH OF THE TRANSCAUCASIAN COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1819)

28,012. — December 2. Highest-confirmed regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On exempting the Württemberg colonists who arrived in Georgia in 1818 from the ordinary oath.

At the session of November 22, the report of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs of November 18, No. 213 (from the Department of State Economy and Public Buildings), entered in the Committee's journal under No. 2164, concerning the exemption of the Württemberg colonists who arrived in Georgia in 1818 from the ordinary oath, was heard.

The Committee resolved: to confirm this submission, having first sought the Highest consent thereto.

At the session of December 2, it was announced to the Committee that the Sovereign Emperor consents to this.

The Committee resolved: to communicate this to the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs for execution, by an extract from the journal.

Report. In the absence of the Chief Administrator in Georgia, General of Infantry Yermolov, who was on the Caucasus Line, the Commander of the Independent Georgian Corps, Lieutenant-General Velyaminov 1st, reported to the Ministry of Internal Affairs that the Georgian Office for the administration of the colonists settled there had made arrangements for preparing the Württemberg colonists, who had arrived in Georgia from Odessa in 1818 by special Highest command, to take the oath of allegiance as subjects.

Some of the village councils of these colonies replied that, according to the rules of their religion, it is forbidden for them to swear oaths; they therefore requested that they not be compelled to take such an oath. Lieutenant-General Velyaminov requests authorization as to whether these settlers should be compelled to take the oath, or exempted from it, DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 201

and, in the latter case, how to proceed in judicial matters, particularly criminal cases, where by law witness testimony must be confirmed by oath.

He also forwarded, in translation, two reports of the village councils of the Württemberg colonists, submitted to the Georgian Office.

From these it is evident that, according to their faith, the oath consists in their having to say: asking God to help them be loyal subjects of the Sovereign Emperor, and that anything beyond this is considered a sin.

Reference. 1. By the Highest manifesto of July 22, 1763, and by the rules Highest-confirmed in 1804 concerning the settlement of colonists in Russia, they are granted free exercise of their faith according to their statutes and rites, without hindrance.

2. In the charter Highest-granted on September 6, 1800 to the Mennonites, it is stated in point 1: "We confirm the freedom promised to them and their descendants in the unhindered exercise of their faith according to their church institutions and customs, with Most Gracious permission for judicial bodies, should the need arise, to accept from them an oath according to their custom, consisting solely of a verbal affirmation."

Taking the above-mentioned provisions into consideration, I propose not to require of the Württemberg colonists, of the sect called Separatists, the customary oath known to us, but to allow them to perform it in accordance with the rules of their faith, consisting solely of a verbal affirmation.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXVI. Pp. 405-406.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 78.

One of the principal reasons for the resettlement of the "Württemberg Separatists" to Russia was the conflict connected with their break from the Lutheran church. For them, unlike the Lutherans, the question of the form of the oath was just as fundamental as it was for the Herrnhuters or the Mennonites (see docs. No. 12 and 37). While living in Russia, the Transcaucasian religious separatists, though practically identical to the Lutherans in confession, never came under the jurisdiction of the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory (see doc. No. 114, art. 869).

Manifesto of July 22, 1763 — doc. No. 11; regulations of 1804 — doc. No. 47; charter of September 6, 1800 — doc. No. 37.

## No. 79. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE COLLECTION OF DEBT FROM THE ST. PETERSBURG COLONISTS (1820)

28,124. — February 2. Personal decree, announced to the State Council by its Chairman. — On the measure for collecting the repayable and non-repayable debt of the St. Petersburg colonists.

His Imperial Majesty, upon the opinion rendered in the General Assembly of the State Council concerning the debts of the new St. Petersburg colonists, was Highest pleased to command:

1) That the measure for collecting debts from the new St. Petersburg colonists, whereby no more than 50 and no less than 20 rubles is to be collected from each household, not be fixed, but rather be adjusted in proportion to the debtor's means; for it may easily happen that a payment of 50 rubles would be imperceptible to one, while another would be unable to pay even 20 rubles. In consideration of this, uniform payment from all households of a single colony is abolished, and this same rule is to be extended to the 48 families transferred from St. Petersburg to the New Russia territory.

2) That the measure of the land tax not be fixed, but that its assignment always be left to the Guardianship Committee, since it must be better acquainted with the quality of the land occupied by the colonists.

As for the remaining resolution of the State Council on this matter (confirming the proposal of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs in all respects), the Sovereign Emperor confirms it and has ordered it to be carried out.

Report of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs, Count Kochubey.

In 1809, by Highest command, German colonists were summoned from the former Duchy of Warsaw for settlement in St. Petersburg Governorate, numbering 91 families.

Part of them were settled near Oranienbaum, Peterhof, and in Strelna, and a larger number in Tsarskoye Selo district, in the so-called Izvarsky tract; but later, owing to significant inconveniences discovered at this latter location, pursuant to a Highest decree, in 1811, 31 families were transferred from there, some to Strelna and some to Kipen; and 48 families were sent for settlement to the New Russia territory.

All these colonists were settled on the basis of the rules on the settlement of colonists in Russia, confirmed pursuant to the Highest-confirmed report of the Minister of Internal Affairs of February 20, 1804.

For their settlement here — that is, for their departure from abroad, their subsistence en route, their settlement, the establishment of their households, resettlement anew, and other purposes related thereto — a total of 574,303 rubles 39¾ kopecks in assignat currency and 371 chervontsy have been expended from the treasury.

Upon review of all these expenditures, the Council of the Ministry of Internal Affairs found that, on the basis of the statutes issued regarding the collection of crown debts from colonists settled in Russia and the imposition of taxes upon them, and of prior precedents, of the said sum: a) 367,442 rubles 16¼ kopecks are to be converted into repayable debt to be collected from the colonists, which sum they are obliged, by statute, to repay, after the expiration of the years of exemption, in 10 equal annual installments thereafter. b) 33,359 rubles 86 kopecks are to be classed as non-repayable debt, which money is to be collected, insofar as it falls due from each, only if any of them should wish to leave Russia altogether. c) 173,501 rubles 37½ kopecks in assignat currency and 371 chervontsy are to be left entirely uncollected, as not properly pertaining to the settlement of the colonists, and d) the end of the 10-year exemption period for these colonists, on the basis of the general rules on this matter and the decree of the Governing Senate of September 27, 1806, is set at the expiration of this year, 1820.

Having examined all the circumstances of this matter, and taking into consideration that, although according to the rules on the settlement of colonists they are obliged to repay the repayable debt within 10 years, yet, as it appears from previous precedents, no colonists settled in Russia have ever been able to pay off their debts within the appointed time without utterly ruining themselves, I submitted all of this to the State Council in my opinion, which was as follows: 1). That the collection of the repayable and non-repayable debts from the colonists here be arranged so that the debts owed by each colony be apportioned equally among each household. 2). Having examined, through trusted officials, the condition of all the new colonists here, to impose upon them such an annual collection of debt that the colonists' obligation to repay remains firm while still allowing the colonists to improve their condition, collecting from each household from 50 to 20 rubles per year, provided that all households of one colony be assessed equally. 3). To proceed in the same manner in collecting the debt owed to the treasury from those transferred to the New Russia territory, leaving the examination of this matter to the Guardianship Committee for the colonists of the southern territory of Russia, on condition that it submit its conclusion thereon for confirmation by the MinisDOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 203

try of Internal Affairs. 4). As regards the collection of land tax from the colonists here, although, according to the rules on the settlement of colonists in Russia, they ought to pay from 15 to 20 kopecks per desyatina of land held per year; yet, since it is proposed to grant them an installment plan for the repayment of their debts to the treasury, they should be brought at least somewhat into line, in the payment of this tax, with the old colonists here, who pay from 1 ruble 50 kopecks to 2 rubles 50 kopecks per desyatina per year. 5). Wherefore, judging by the quality of the land they occupy and, in general, by the advantageous location of their settlements, to assess them a land tax of from 1 ruble 50 kopecks to 2 rubles per desyatina, paying it, on the basis of the Highest decree of September 12, 1811, into those departments to which the lands settled by the colonists belong. 6). That such an arrangement regarding payment of the land levy not be adopted as an invariable rule, but that the Government be authorized, as far as possible and as the condition of the colonists improves, to increase this tax in proportion to their advantages, and 7). that, as regards the imposition of such a tax upon the colonists transferred to the New Russia territory, it be collected from them equally, at no less a rate than that paid by the other colonists settled there, this too being entrusted to the Guardianship Committee, which, having made arrangements thereon, will not fail to submit a report here.

Such was the opinion that followed, upon my aforementioned submission, in the General Assembly of the State Council, Highest-confirmed on the 2nd day of this February, a copy of which I hereby submit to the Governing Senate, reporting at the same time that all necessary instructions and arrangements for its execution have been made by me to whomever it concerns.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXVII. Pp. 38-39.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 79.

The document attests to the authorities' desire to move away from uniform norms for colonists' payments to the treasury, since such norms did not take into account the particular circumstances of the various colonies and, as a rule, proved unrealistic.

Decree of 1811 — doc. No. 60; report of February 20, 1804 — doc. No. 47; decree of September 27, 1806 — PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 22293.

---

## No. 80. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON RAISING THE PAYMENT FROM THE ORIGINAL ST. PETERSBURG COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1823)

29,541. — July 13. Highest-confirmed opinion of the State Council. — On increasing the payment of debt monies to the treasury from the old St. Petersburg colonists.

The State Council, in the Department of State Economy and in the General Assembly, having examined the report of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs concerning an increase in the payment of debt monies owed to the treasury by the old St. Petersburg colonists, and finding the proposal of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on this subject to be correct, resolves to confirm it.

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was graciously pleased to confirm the opinion rendered in the General Assembly of the State Council concerning an increase in the payment of debt monies owed to the treasury by the old St. Petersburg colonists, and has ordered it to be carried out. For the Chairman of the State Council. Nikolai Mordvinov.

Report of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The St. Petersburg colonists, who came to Russia in 1765 and 1767 and were at that time settled in four colonies — Srednyaya Rogatka, Izhora, Novosaratovka, and Yamburg — had, apart from the general benefits granted by the Highest Manifesto of 22 July 1763, various terms for exemption and payment of taxes according to the agreements concluded with them, namely:

The Srednyaya Rogatka and Izhora colonists were given a five-year exemption, and were required to repay their debt to the treasury after the expiry of 15 years, in five installments, that is, over two and a half years.

The debt recorded against them was: for the Srednyaya Rogatka colonists, 28,870 rubles 14 kopecks, and for the Izhora colonists, 25,234 rubles 91¼ kopecks.

The Novosaratovka colonists were given a five-year exemption, with repayment of the debt after 10 years set in six installments, that is, over three years. Their total recorded debt was 90,125 rubles 89 kopecks; and the Yamburg colonists were given a 13-year exemption, with repayment of the debt set for the last three years; their recorded debt was 137,493 rubles 50 kopecks, but it was forgiven them by Highest decree of 17 August 1793.

After the expiry of their exemption, the said colonists, contrary to their obligations and under various pretexts, paid nothing for more than 20 years, until finally in 1792 it was ordered that a land tax of from 30 to 60 kopecks per desiatina be collected from them, together with 5 to 10 rubles per household toward repayment of the debt.

These colonists are not subject to local (zemstvo) obligations except those relating to government offices, the construction of major roads, and waterways, since a special exception was made for them on this account under the terms agreed with them in 1765.

Thereafter, pursuant to the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs confirmed by the Highest authority on 18 July 1805, the said colonists were assessed a land tax per desiatina ranging from 30 kopecks to 1 ruble 23 kopecks.

Toward repayment of the debt, the following was paid annually per household: from the Srednyaya Rogatka colonists, 20 rubles; from the Novosaratovka colonists, 10 rubles; and from the Izhora colonists, 5 rubles.

On the basis of the opinion of the State Council confirmed by the Highest authority on 12 March 1812, the aforementioned colonists of the earlier arrival now pay land tax annually per desiatina of usable land as follows: a) Srednyaya Rogatka colonists, 2 rubles 50 kopecks; b) Novosaratovka colonists, 2 rubles; c) Izhora colonists, 1 ruble 50 kopecks; d) Yamburg colonists, 1 ruble 23 kopecks.

Repayment of debts to the treasury has been left as before, as set forth in the aforementioned report confirmed by the Highest authority on 18 July 1805.

By this reckoning, each family in total pays annually from 51 to 95 rubles.

The present condition of these colonies is as follows: 1) In the Srednyaya Rogatka colony, according to the last census, there are 136 male souls and 26 households; the usable land in its possession is 750 desiatinas, and the treasury debt recorded against this colony as of 1823 is 16,890 rubles 14 kopecks. 2) In the Novosaratovka colony there are 411 male souls, 60 households, 1,735 desiatinas of usable land, and a treasury debt of 76,325 rubles 89 kopecks. 3) In the Izhora colony there are 191 male souls, 29 households, 841 desiatinas of usable land, and a treasury debt of 20,894 rubles 91¼ kopecks; and 4) in the Yamburg colony there are 136 male souls, 32 households, 1,378 desiatinas of usable land; no treasury debt is recorded against it, since it was, as stated above, forgiven them.

The new colonists settled in 1810 in this same governorate, in the colonies of Strelna, Kipen, Peterhof, Oranienbaum, and Kronstadt, have, on the basis of the opinion of the State Council confirmed by the Highest authority on 2 February 1820 and the resolution of the Committee of Ministers of 24 April of that same year 1820, been assessed since 1821 with land tax and payment of the debt to the treasury standing against them, namely: 1) The Strelna colonists, 40 rubles per household toward repayment of the debt, and 2 rubles per desiatina annually as land tax. 2) The Kipen colonists, 40 rubles toward repayment of the debt, and 1 ruble 80 kopecks per desiatina as land tax. 3) The Peterhof colonists, 45 rubles toward repayment of the debt, and 2 rubles per desiatina as land tax. 4) The Oranienbaum colonists, 30 rubles toward repayment of the debt, and 1 ruble 60 kopecks per desiatina as land tax; and 5) The Kronstadt colonists, 35 rubles toward repayment of the debt, and 1 ruble 80 kopecks as land tax.

In addition, these new colonists are obliged to discharge all local (zemstvo) obligations according to the assessment of the Provincial Administration, on an equal footing with the treasury peasants here.

Including these obligations as well, the total comes to from 70 to 120 rubles annually per family.

Taking into consideration: 1) that the aforementioned colonists of the earlier arrival of the Srednyaya Rogatka, Novosaratovka, Izhora, and Yamburg colonies not only received sufficient assistance from the treasury, but also enjoyed a far greater exemption than others, and, contrary to the terms agreed with them, made no payment whatsoever for more than 80 [20] years toward the expenses incurred by the treasury for their settlement, while the other colonists settled in this governorate began repaying their debt after 10 years of arrival in Russia and pay twice as much as they do; and 2) that according to the annual reports submitted on their welfare, these colonists, especially those of Srednyaya Rogatka and Novosaratovka, are in a decidedly prosperous condition and could, without the slightest hardship, be brought into equal standing with the other colonists settled here in the payment of debt.

I consider it just, for the speedier recovery of the treasury debt recorded against them, amounting to more than 114,000 rubles, to collect from them per household as follows: from the Srednyaya Rogatka colonists, instead of the 20 rubles now paid, 40 rubles; from the Novosaratovka colonists, instead of 10 rubles, 30 rubles; and from the Izhora colonists, instead of 5 rubles, 20 rubles.

In submitting this for the consideration of the State Council, I have the honor to add that, once my opinion is confirmed, collection of the debt according to the above calculation may begin from the first half of the year following its confirmation.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXVIII. Pp. 1103–1105.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 80.

The colonists settled near St. Petersburg in 1810 initially found themselves in a more favorable position than the first St. Petersburg colonists, since their settlement had been better planned and organized. By this point the condition of the first colonies had, at last, improved sufficiently for them to be placed on an equal footing with the later colonists in the repayment of the treasury debt.

Manifesto of July 22, 1763 — doc. No. 11; decree of August 17, 1793 — doc. No. 26; report of July 18, 1805 — doc. No. 52; opinion of March 12, 1812 — doc. No. 61; opinion of February 2, 1820 — doc. No. 79; statute of April 24, 1820 — PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 28252.

## No. 81. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON RAISING THE TAX FROM THE LIVONIAN COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1824)

29,833. — March 10. Highest-confirmed opinion of the State Council. — On raising the land tax paid by the Livonian colonists.

The State Council, in the Department of State Economy and in the General Assembly, having examined the report of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on raising the land tax paid by the Livonian colonists, in view of their having completed repayment of the treasury loan, and finding the opinion of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on this subject to be correct, resolves to confirm it.

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was graciously pleased to confirm the opinion rendered in the General Assembly of the State Council concerning the raising of the land tax paid by the Livonian colonists, and has ordered it to be carried out. Chairman of the State Council.

Report of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. In Wenden District of Livonia Governorate, on the treasury manors of Hirschenhof and Helfreichshof, German colonists were settled in 1766 and 1769 under a special contract concluded with them. That contract stipulated, among other things, that the land tax be collected from the colonists according to an assessment of their land.

These colonists, placed under the direct administration of the Livonian Civil Governor, have since 1797 paid to the treasury a land tax of 13 thalers, plus 2 thalers per household toward repayment of the loan made to them, on the basis of the decree of the Governing Senate to the Livonian Treasury Chamber of 5 September 1785, which also stated that, upon repayment of the debt, the land tax should be permanently increased to 15 thalers.

The treasury debt, which since 1815 has been collected in banknotes at rates set annually in the schedules of the Ministry of Finance, has been paid by the colonists in full and even with a surplus, amounting to 1,769 rubles 50 kopecks. The remainder of the debt was received from the colonists back in 1820.

On the occasion of this now fully completed repayment by the Livonian colonists of the treasury debt standing against them, the Livonian Treasury Chamber requested authorization last year: whether, on the basis of the decree of the Governing Senate of 5 September 1785, the quitrent monies from these colonists should be permanently raised to 15 thalers, and likewise whether, in future, the quitrent monies should continue to be collected at the rate previously set in the schedule, reckoning a 100 percent premium on the silver ruble; and in that case, whether the amounts overpaid by them to the treasury should be credited against the increased sums of 2 thalers per household still owed for 1821 and 1822.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs received a copy of this report of the Livonian Treasury Chamber from the Minister of Finance, and, taking into consideration, on the one hand, that the colonists, on the basis of the rules for their reception confirmed by the Highest authority on 20 February 1804, are, upon expiry of their exemption, placed on an equal footing in taxation with the treasury peasants of the same district or governorate, and, on the other hand, that under the contract concluded with the Livonian colonists it was stipulated that the land tax be collected from them according to an assessment of the land — that is, according to an assessment of the benefits which the colonists now derive from their land and holdings — sent to the place of settlement of those colonists one of the overseers of the St. Petersburg colonies, who, together with an official dispatched by the Livonian Civil Governor, inspected their condition and submitted detailed information on the whole matter, from which it emerged that the said settlers, without particular disruption to their circumstances, can pay from 15 to 17 thalers of land tax annually per household.

Having examined the information set forth, I found that although the Livonian colonists ought, on the basis of the rules for the reception of colonists confirmed by the Highest authority on 20 February 1804, and following the example of the Saratov colonists, to be placed on an equal footing in taxation with the local treasury peasants there, yet since the Livonian treasury peasants discharge their quitrent not in money but in labor, the colonists, who are not tenants, cannot be subjected to such a labor obligation, DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 207

and that a payment of 17 thalers annually per household will be, for the Livonian colonists, a land tax that is entirely not burdensome.

On this basis I proposed to collect from the Livonian colonists, who expect to improve their circumstances by that time, 15 thalers per household in annual land tax until 1826, reckoning from 1821, against which the 1,769 rubles 50 kopecks overpaid by them toward the debt are to be credited, and from 1826 to collect from them 17 thalers per household until a new regulation is issued.

I submitted this for the consideration of the State Council, adding that the authorization sought by the Livonian Treasury Chamber concerning the exchange rate at which it is to collect the land tax from the colonists would depend on the Ministry of Finance.

The State Council, having examined my aforementioned report on raising the land tax paid by the Livonian colonists, on the occasion of their having completed repayment of the treasury loan, in accordance with the minutes of the Department of State Economy of 30 November and of the General Assembly of 21 December 1823, confirmed it.

I have the honor to submit herewith to the Governing Senate a copy of this opinion of the State Council, confirmed by the Highest authority on 10 March of this year, requesting that it be pleased to instruct whomever is appropriate to carry it into due execution.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXIX. Pp. 211–212.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 81.

In effect, this act meant that the Livland colonists who had completed repayment of the treasury debt were placed on an equal footing, in terms of tax payments, with the state peasants of that area, as had earlier been prescribed with respect to the Saratov and the first Novorossiya colonists (see docs. No. 61, 65, and 71), although, given the local conditions of Livland mentioned in the document, this could not be carried out literally.

Regulations of February 20, 1804 — doc. No. 47.

## No. 82. SENATE DECREE ON THE TAXES AND OBLIGATIONS OF FOREIGN COLONISTS (1824)

30,172. — December 23. Senate decree, pursuant to the resolution of the Committee of Ministers confirmed by the Highest authority. — On the taxes and obligations of foreign immigrants belonging to the peasant estate.

The Governing Senate heard, firstly, the report of the Minister of Finance, to which he attached copies of a memorandum submitted by him to the Committee of Ministers and of an extract from its minutes, confirmed by the Highest authority on 11 March last, concerning treasury taxes and obligations owed by foreign immigrants; adding that particular cases giving rise to this new regulation would, strictly on the basis thereof, be resolved by instructions from the Ministry of Finance; but since these rules require universal notice and observance, would the Governing Senate be pleased to issue, to whomever it may concern, the necessary instructions for its execution? And secondly, the copies attached to this report of the memorandum of the Minister of Finance submitted to the Committee of Ministers on 31 August 1823, and of the extract from the minutes of that Committee, which state as follows. In the memorandum of the Minister of Finance: Last year the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, on the occasion of petitions received by him from foreign immigrants settled in Volhynia and Kiev Governorates on landlords' estates, corresponded with the former Minister of Finance regarding treasury taxes and obligations owed both by immigrants of this kind and by those who own land of their own in the Western Governorates. The laws on this subject state: <...> Regarding the taxes and obligations of immigrants settled on landlords' estates, Count Dmitry Alexandrovich [Guryev] held: 1) Mennonites and other foreigners who settled on landlords' estates in the Western Governorates, both before this territory's annexation to Russia and afterward, up until the issuance of the Highest decree of 9 May 1802, have no right to enjoy exemption from the payment of taxes, and must remain in the ranks and assessments in which they now stand; for prior to the issuance of the said decree, no legislation existed on this matter. Moreover, it would be extremely difficult, indeed impossible, to ascertain with due precision exactly when they arrived from abroad in the formerly Polish provinces, and whether they had not already availed themselves of some exemption. 2) Colonists who settled on landlords' estates after 9 May 1802, but before the promulgation of the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs confirmed by the Highest authority on 12 April 1804, ought, by the strict force of the Highest decree of 9 May 1802, to be granted exemption from the payment of taxes until the sixth census following that date. 3) Colonists who settled on landlords' estates after the promulgation of the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs confirmed by the Highest authority on 12 April 1804 should be reckoned a ten-year exemption from the payment of taxes from the time of their initial settlement on the landlords' estates. 4) After the expiry of the exemption period, treasury taxes are to be collected from all colonists settled on landlords' estates on an equal footing with the landlords' peasants; and they must discharge local (zemstvo) obligations from the time of their settlement. 5) Colonists who did not avail themselves of the legally established exemption in due time, or who were incorrectly assigned to a higher tax rate than the landlords' peasants, should be given due satisfaction by crediting all sums collected from them in excess against the taxes to be owed by them in future, at the rate applicable to landlords' peasants. 6) Colonists who have availed themselves of the ten-year exemption, or who, during the period of exemption, moved or shall move to other landlords' estates, or from one district to another, or from one governorate to another, are not to be granted a second exemption, and upon the expiry of 10 years from the time of their initial settlement, are to be assessed at the same rate as the landlords' peasants; to this end, the local authorities must ensure that colonists do not leave their settlements without their knowledge. 7) Landlords who have received foreigners onto their lands must, without delay, in accordance with the Highest decree of 9 May 1802, present the cordon certificates issued to them for registration with the District Court, which must at the same time report this to the Provincial Board; the latter, comparing the reports of the District Court with the notifications received from the border authorities, is obliged each time to inform the Treasury Chamber, as appropriate, of the number of such persons, the status they have chosen, and the time of their settlement, for its due action; without presentation of cordon certificates, no exemption may be granted to colonists, and landlords who fail to comply within three months, by force of the Highest decree of 9 May 1802, are deemed to be harboring fugitives. 8) The Treasury Chambers shall be obliged, having gathered the requisite information on all colonists under their jurisdiction on landlords' estates, to proceed, on the basis of the above rules, both in assessing their taxes and in satisfying their petitions. 9) Since existing legislation has granted colonists only exemption from military and civil service, and it is nowhere stated that they are entirely exempt from the recruit levy borne in Russia by all taxable estates DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 209

in kind or in money, and moreover, since complete exemption of colonists from the recruit levy for the future would result in an unwarranted burden on the rest of Russia's inhabitants, the obligation to pay the recruit commutation money of 500 rubles in lieu of a recruit should also be extended to colonists settled on landlords' estates, beginning with the forthcoming recruit levies. As for foreigners who own land of their own, the former Minister of Finance, taking into consideration that, by the report confirmed by the Highest authority on 1 March 1804, foreigners who have acquired land in ownership in the New Russia territory are ordered to pay such land dues as are levied on landlords' estates in that territory, and that peasants freed by their landlords to the status of free farmers pay taxes on the same footing as landlords' peasants, agreed with the conclusion of Count Viktor Pavlovich [Kochubei] that all foreigners who have hitherto come, and shall hereafter come, to Russia, who have purchased land in ownership and are not registered in any estate, should pay taxes on the same footing as landlords' peasants, and should discharge zemstvo obligations on the same basis as the treasury peasants living in the same governorate, subjecting them equally to payment of recruit money for the same reasons as those settled on landlords' estates. The Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, in the response now submitted to the Minister of Finance, finds that the question here raised regarding the recruit levy is not a matter for particular but for general consideration; for it must here be decided: are the colonists in general exempted forever solely from the provision of recruits in kind, or also from payment, after the expiry of the exemption period, of recruit commutation money? Although on this question the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs agrees with the opinion of the former Minister of Finance that the colonists are exempted forever only from the provision of recruits in kind, and not from the monetary levy that replaces this obligation, since the privileges granted to them speak only of military and civil service — exemption from which was probably prompted by the anticipated aversion of the colonists to military service among us, all the more so as it is contrary to the faith of some of them, namely the Mennonites, who, as is known, left their former dwellings and moved to us chiefly in order to avoid military service — yet, as he has made it a rule not to touch, during his temporary management of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, upon any general and important measures departing from the present order of things, he considers it best to leave the resolution of this question until the return of Count Kochubei; but in the present matter, which concerns only those colonists settled on landlords' lands, or on lands acquired by themselves, whose number is at present quite small, he considers it possible on this occasion, without touching upon the recruit tax, to resolve only the remaining questions relating to their other taxes and obligations, on which he, as well as the Department of State Economy and Public Buildings, agree with the opinion of the former Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance, finding for his part that if it should be deemed proper to postpone resolution of the question concerning the recruit levy on colonists until the return of Count Viktor Pavlovich [Kochubei], then in that case the local authorities of Volhynia and Kiev Governorates should nevertheless be instructed to cease all demands upon the colonists on this account, all the more so since subjecting them to the recruit levy cannot extend to past time, when no clear legislation existed on this matter — submitted this, together with the other proposals of his predecessor, for the further consideration of the Committee of Ministers. From the extract of the minutes of the Committee of Ministers of 3 November 1823 and 11 March 1824: at the session of 3 November, the memorandum of the Minister of Finance of 31 August, No. 3568 (of the Department of Various Taxes and Duties), submitted in the Committee's minutes under No. 18.95, concerning treasury taxes and obligations of foreign immigrants, was heard. The Committee, finding the opinion of the former Minister of Finance set forth in this report, with which the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs concurred, regarding taxes and zemstvo obligations, to be consistent with the existing enactments concerning foreign immigrants, resolved to confirm it; and as to the question of the recruit levy, the Committee, not considering it necessary to defer resolution of this question, and observing that the colonists settled in Russia, under the Manifesto of 22 July 1763 and the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs confirmed by the Highest authority on 12 April 1804, are in general exempt from military and civil service, recognizes for its part that, on the basis of these enactments, they are definitively exempt from the recruit levy, and that therefore to subject them to the obligation of paying to the treasury recruit commutation money of 500 rubles in lieu of a recruit would be a violation of the rights granted to them; this conclusion of the Committee is to be submitted to His Imperial Majesty, with a request for its confirmation by the Highest authority. At the session of 11 March it was announced to the Committee that the Committee's resolution had been confirmed by the Highest authority. The Committee resolved: to communicate this to the Minister of Finance for execution by extract from the minutes, and to give the same notice to the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Ordered: that, regarding this resolution of the Committee of Ministers confirmed by the Highest authority, for information and due execution by whomever it may concern, decrees be sent to the Civil Governors, to the Provincial and Regional Boards and Governments, to the Military Office of the Don Cossack Host, to the Treasury Chambers and government offices, and to the Ministers, Military Governors-General, Governors-General, Military Governors, managers of the civil department, and City Governors; and that notices be communicated to the Most Holy Governing Synod and to the Departments of the Governing Senate here and in Moscow.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXIX. Pp. 666–671.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 82.

As is evident from the present act, the occasion for its adoption was the increasingly frequent settlement of foreign immigrants on landowners' and privately owned lands in the South-Western governorates. The decisions taken in this connection, as reflected in the document, undoubtedly reinforced this already noticeable process. Besides this important circumstance, the document is notable in that it raises, for the first time, the question of the justification for exempting colonists from conscription duty.

Decree of May 9, 1802 — doc. No. 40; report of April 12, 1804 — doc. No. 50; report of March 1, 1804 — doc. No. 49; manifesto of July 22, 1763 — doc. No. 11.

## No. 83. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON THE COLLECTION OF DEBT FROM THE NEW RUSSIA COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1825)

30,281. — March 9. Opinion of the State Council, Highest Confirmed. — On the collection of the treasury debt from the New Russia colonists.

The State Council, in General Assembly, heard the journal of the Department of State Economy concerning the treasury debt due for collection from the New Russia colonists, and the information requested from the Administrator of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on the amount of land allotted to the Mennonites, together with a copy of the charter granted to them. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 211

The State Council, having weighed all the circumstances of this matter, resolves:

1. Mennonites not engaged in grain farming are not to be entered into any tax assessment when they belong to those families enjoying the privilege; for on the basis of that privilege the Mennonites pay a levy on the whole of the land, according to the number of families to which it has been allotted, rather than a poll tax; but should they engage in trade or crafts, then, according to the words of the charter, they shall be dealt with in accordance with the State statutes on that subject.

2. In consideration of the devastation suffered by the New Russia territory in 1824 from locusts, the collection of the treasury debt from those colonists whose exemption period has expired is to begin on 1 January 1826.

3. The apportionment made by the Trusteeship Committee for the colonists of the southern territory of Russia, as to how much debt each colony is to pay per year, is not to be regarded as fixed; rather, as the condition of the colonists improves — whether in general or in respect of any particular colony, and no later than upon the expiration of ten years from the start of payment — the Trusteeship Committee is to submit to the Ministry a proposal for raising the amount paid.

4. The remaining proposals of the Administrator of the Ministry of Internal Affairs are to be confirmed.

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was pleased to confirm, in the Highest degree, the opinion reached in the General Assembly of the State Council concerning the treasury debt due for collection from the New Russia colonists, and ordered it to be carried out. Chairman of the State Council.

Report of the Administrator of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The Ministry of Internal Affairs, bearing in mind the gradual expiration of the ten-year exemption established by statute for colonists settled and being settled in the New Russia territory, and the corresponding arrangements both for the return of the sums expended upon them and for the assessment of land tax upon them, instructed at various times the Chief Authority in the New Russia territory, under whose supervision these colonists were settled, to furnish full information on the sums expended and on the manner of their return to the treasury.

Subsequently, when a special statute on the chief administration of the colonists of the southern territory of Russia was issued, and by the decree of 22 March 1818 the Trusteeship Committee was established, the Ministry of Internal Affairs instructed that Committee: a) to present an opinion as to whether all colonists would be able to pay off the treasury debts owed by them within ten years in equal installments, or, failing that, to draw up a detailed statement of exactly how much money, judging by location and other advantages, each colony could contribute annually toward payment of the debt — such sum to be apportioned among the community of each colony in proportion to the means of each family therein; with the proviso that the sum imposed on the whole colony toward payment of the debt should on no account be less than that paid by colonists of earlier settlement; and b) to determine what tax might be imposed on landless colonists, for the sake of uniform equalization of taxes with the other settlers, all the more since they too enjoy the other general privileges granted to colonists.

In accordance with this instruction, the Trusteeship Committee in 1823 submitted detailed accounts of the expenditures on the New Russia colonists.

These accounts, after being put in order and verified in the Department of State Economy and Public Buildings, together with all the Committee's proposals, I submitted for consideration by the Council of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, which, having weighed everything together with the sums expended by the Ministry of Internal Affairs upon the departure of these colonists — both abroad and within our borders — and by the border Governors of Provinces in dispatching those colonists to their place of settlement, found that the Trusteeship Committee had expended, specifically on the New Russia colonists, 4,589,534 rubles 66 kopecks, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the border Governors 487,211 rubles 52½ kopecks in banknotes and 10,400 chervontsy, amounting in all to 5,076,746 rubles 18½ kopecks and 10,400 chervontsy; and that on the basis of the statutes issued regarding the collection of treasury debts from colonists settled in Russia and the assessment of taxes upon them, and likewise in accordance with the various amendments subsequently made thereto, and having taken into consideration that, although a period of ten years following the expiration of the exemption has been fixed for the collection of debts from the colonists, yet according to the installments of debt set by the Trusteeship Committee for collection, the term comes out considerably longer; nevertheless, since such an arrangement of installment payments was proportioned by the Committee to the condition and advantages of each colony so that payment of the debt should not disrupt their circumstances, and since it is moreover known that none of the previously settled colonists were able to repay their debt within the term fixed by the general statute thereon, the Council could not but agree to the installment plan proposed by the Trusteeship Committee, and therefore, in agreement with the opinion of the Department of State Economy and Public Buildings, proposed to collect annually from each family, such moneys to be paid into the District Treasuries, on the following basis:

I. Applying toward payment, as part of the debt to be repaid, the sums expended on the spot for provisioning, establishment, house construction, medicines, and the like — 3,915,933 rubles 66¼ kopecks — collection to proceed as follows:

For the Yekaterinoslav settlement: a) From the Mennonites, comprising 422 families, upon whom lies a debt of 174,356 rubles 83¾ kopecks, setting for each family an annual payment toward this debt of 35 rubles. b) From the colonists known under the names of Molochna, Crimean, Danzig, and Swedish, comprising 1,263 families, upon whom lies a debt of 715,928 rubles 77 kopecks, annually from each family 20 rubles until such time as they are equalized with the peasants in taxes, and after equalization 5 rubles, in the same manner as fixed for the old colonists. <...>

For the Odessa settlement. <...> b) From the German colonists, from the Bulgarian colony of Parkany, and from the new Montenegrins, comprising 2,228 families in all, upon whom lies a debt of 2,344,211 rubles 2 kopecks, annually toward payment of this debt, from those whose ten-year exemption has expired, 45 rubles, and from those approaching equalization in taxes with treasury peasants, 25 rubles. c) As for those placed in the old colonies — Khortitsa, Yamburg, Josephstal, and Rybalskoye — farming colonists and partly craftsmen, comprising 33 families, with a debt of 2,791 rubles 56¾ [kopecks], as well as the craftsmen in the towns of Yekaterinoslav, Novomoskovsk, Alexandrovsk, and Odessa, comprising 64 families, upon whom lies a debt of 63,585 rubles 21 kopecks: although the Trusteeship Committee made no mention of the apportionment of debts for the former, nevertheless, in order that this sum too be collected, the Trusteeship Committee is to be instructed to apportion this sum, amounting to 2,791 rubles 56¾ kopecks, for collection from those who received it, on the same basis as for the other colonists. DOCUMENTS____________________________________ __ _____________________________________213

The apportionment and collection of debt from the urban craftsmen are to be entrusted to the care of the Provincial or Municipal Authority under whose jurisdiction they fall and which is acquainted with their circumstances.

<...>

2. The 116,076 rubles 75¾ kopecks expended en route for the assistance of the settlers before their arrival at the place of settlement, which, on the basis of the rules confirmed in the Highest degree in 1804 for the settlement of foreign immigrants in the New Russia territory, are to be recovered from the colonists only in the event that any of them should wish to return to their own homeland or to enter another social estate.

To these expenditures must be added the moneys remitted abroad by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, as well as those expended within the border, and likewise those disbursed by the border Governors of the Grodno, Vilna, Białystok, and Volhynia Provinces — amounting in all to 10,400 chervontsy and 487,211 rubles 52½ kopecks in banknotes.

As to how much of these non-recoverable moneys is to be charged to each family, the Trusteeship Committee is to be entrusted with making the calculation, so that, in the event of a family's departure from colonist status, it may readily be possible to demand from it the return of the treasury moneys.

3. The 557,524 rubles 24½ kopecks expended on the construction of churches, the purchase of lands, salaries for officials, Pastors and Priests, and other expenses, <...> the purchase from the manufacturer Miller of Spanish sheep, and the rewarding of officials who took part in the settlement of the colonists, on the basis of the Highest orders and decrees issued — are to be left entirely without collection.

<...>

5. Those of the New Russia colonists for whom the fixed twenty-year exemption has by now already expired are to be equalized in taxes with the treasury peasants of that locality, just as the old colonists of that territory have already been equalized, following the example of the Saratov colonists, who were equalized with the peasants there in accordance with the report of the Ministry of Internal Affairs confirmed in the Highest degree on 18 December 1808.

6. Regarding the tax on Mennonites and colonists having no land, whom the Trusteeship Committee exempts from all taxation, the Ministry, having taken into consideration that these persons too personally enjoy all the rights and privileges of colonists, both within and outside the colonies, and that although they participate in making up the sum due from the whole colony according to the amount of land involved, they thereby benefit only their own community, while the community pays the State the same amount of land tax with them as it would without them, proposes: that all such landless and farmless settlers among the Mennonites, who enjoy considerably greater advantages than the other colonists, be taxed, upon expiration of the ten-year exemption, on an equal footing with settlers possessing land.

7. In the other colonies, in view of their lesser advantages, such landless colonists, upon expiration of the years of exemption — when all of them must be equalized with the treasury peasants in the payment of taxes and obligations — are to be assessed a tax equal to the poll tax among the treasury peasants, not excluding the zemstvo obligations either.

Having examined all the circumstances of this matter, I found the opinion of the Council of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to be thoroughly well-founded, all the more so since, although under the rules on the settlement of colonists they are obliged to repay the debt owed within ten years, yet, as previous examples show, none of the colonists previously settled in Russia were able to pay off their debts within the appointed time, and therefore all of them were granted, at various times, postponements and indulgences according to circumstances; wherefore I submitted the above-stated resolution on the payment of debts for the consideration of the State Council, together with the following opinion of my own: 1) That the collection toward payment of debts from all colonies whose exemption has already expired be begun on 1 January 1825, and that, as the exemption expires, other colonies be assessed accordingly on the same basis henceforth; and 2) that the amount fixed for debt collection not be regarded as fixed, but that, as the condition of all colonies in general, or of some in particular, improves, the Trusteeship Committee be obliged to submit to the Ministry of Internal Affairs a proposal for raising the sum paid and for requesting the State Council's authorization thereof.

The opinion reached upon this submission of mine in the General Assembly of the State Council, confirmed in the Highest degree on the 9th day of March of this year 1825, I hereby submit in copy to the Governing Senate, reporting at the same time that instructions for its execution have been given by me to the Trusteeship Committee for the colonists of the southern territory of Russia; but since the collection of debt from certain settlers must also be carried out by the Provincial Authorities of the New Russia territory, may it please the Governing Senate to issue a general instruction on this subject both to the Provincial Authorities of the New Russia territory and the Bessarabian Region, and to the Minister of Finance, for observance in the local Treasury Chambers and Expeditions.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XL. P. 131-136.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 83.

The act established the procedure for repayment of the treasury debt by the Novorossiya colonists, and also provided for placing the second group of these colonists on an equal footing with the state peasants in the payment of taxes.

A.S. Pushkin, during his period of exile in the South, was among those called upon to combat the locust infestation of 1824 mentioned in the document (art. 2).

Rybalskaya (Fischersdorf) — a Lutheran colony east of Yekaterinoslav, founded in 1789 by immigrants from Germany as well as from the nearby colony of Josephstal; it was not mentioned in previous documents because its inhabitants were counted among the Josephstal colonists. It formed part of the Josephstal volost of Novomoskovsk district; in 1897 it had 474 inhabitants, including 412 Germans.

Miller (Miller von Rehfenstein), Georg — a colonist who, together with the colonists Vassal and Rouvier, concluded an agreement with the government in the early nineteenth century for the development of sheep-breeding in the south of Russia, under which fine-wooled merino sheep were imported from Spain. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. S. 231.

## No. 85. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE REORGANIZATION OF THE COLONY OF KARRAS IN THE NORTHERN CAUCASUS, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1828)

2517. — December 15. Statute of the Committee of Ministers, Highest Confirmed. — On the new organization of the Scottish colony located in the Caucasus Region.

At the session of 4 December a memorandum was heard from the Minister of Internal Affairs, dated 30 November, No. 998 (from the Department of State Economy and Public Buildings), entered in the Committee's journal under No. 1929, concerning the new organization of the Scottish colony located in the Caucasus Region.

The Committee, having examined this submission, finds that the establishment of the Scottish colony must be considered from two aspects: first, from the standpoint of State economy, and second, from the ecclesiastical standpoint. On the first subject the Committee cannot but agree with the proposals of the Minister of Internal Affairs and of the Chief Administrator in Georgia, General Count Paskevich-Erivansky, for improving the organization of this colony. As regards the second subject, the Chief Director of the Postal Department, present at the Committee, stated that the late Sovereign Emperor, of blessed memory, in granting the Scottish Missionaries permission to settle in the Caucasus Region, had as his principal purpose that, through them, the mountain peoples might be converted to Christianity. There are accordingly no sufficient grounds for abandoning such a beneficent wish of His Majesty. The opinion expressed by the former Chief Administrator in Georgia, General Yermolov, that the admission of foreign Missionaries is, particularly in political respects, incompatible with Russia's interests, is too general a notion and cannot be applied to the present case. On the contrary, the twenty-five years of peaceful residence of the Scottish Missionaries in the Caucasus territory removes any apprehension on that score. And although their success in converting the mountain peoples to the Christian faith, judging by the number converted, is not very great, nonetheless a beginning has already been made. The establishment of a Russian society of clergy for the training of Missionaries among us, although likewise quite useful, has not yet been founded, whereas in the meantime opportunities may arise for the conversion of the mountain peoples; but were this forbidden to the Scottish Missionaries, such opportunities would be lost forever to Christianity. Weighing all this, the Committee proposes: 1) That the Scottish colony be left in possession of all the rights and privileges granted to it by the charter of 25 December 1806, without forbidding the Missionaries residing there from converting Mahometans and pagans among the mountain peoples to their own faith, whom they may afterward make members of their colony. 2) That the Basel Missionaries residing in the town of Shusha, in the Karabagh province, if the members of the Scottish colony agree to admit them, be permitted to settle in the Scottish colony, with the same rights and privileges which it enjoys. 3) That the Elder of this colony, Pastor Paterson, in recognition of his 25 years of labor and care for the benefit of the colony and of the local territory, be allotted, on the same site, 1,000 desyatinas of land, which is to be granted to him, on the basis of the charter, as hereditary possession. 4) That the nine families of baptized mountain peoples and the 10 families of Germans admitted as members of the colony be allotted, on the same basis, 60 desyatinas per family, amounting in all to 1,140 desyatinas. 5) That, in the event of the transfer of Basel Missionaries to the Scottish colony, or of an increase by other means in the membership of this colony, they too be allotted 60 desyatinas per family on the same basis. 6) That the former Saratov colonists now residing in the Scottish colony, in accordance with the proposal of General Count Paskevich-Erivansky, be left near the mineral waters, either on the land that remains after the allotment to the Scottish colonists, or, as convenient, be allotted other land from vacant treasury lands located near the mineral waters; permitting also other colonists who so wish to make settlements there, requesting in each case the prior consent of the Ministry of Internal DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 217

Affairs to their transfer. 7) That colonists newly resettling there be given a five-year exemption from payment and performance of all obligations, reckoned for each family from the day of arrival in the Caucasus Region, and that, upon expiration of the exemption, they be equalized, on the basis of the statute of the Committee of Ministers issued on the 29th day of September 1817, in taxes and obligations — except for the recruit levy — with the treasury peasants of the Caucasus Region. 8) That, in order to put an end to any disagreements between the Scottish and Saratov colonists, the lands and the internal administration itself be divided between them, entrusting to Paterson the management only of the Scottish colonists, while the Saratov colonists be allowed to elect communal elders on the general terms granted to colonists; and 9) That both groups of colonists be placed under the direct authority of the Commandant of Kislovodsk, who shall be obliged to watch over their welfare and to see that no discord of any kind arises between them; and should any arise, that, while taking measures to end it, he report the principal culprits to the Chief of the Caucasus Region.

At the session of 15 December it was announced to the Committee that the Sovereign Emperor was pleased to confirm, in the Highest degree, the Committee's resolution.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. III. P. 1142-1143.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 85.

The conflict between the Scottish missionaries and the German colonists had both objective roots (differences in social status and, correspondingly, in the value system) and subjective ones (the actions of the Scottish elder A. Paterson, referred to in the document as a pastor, although he had not officially been vested with that function in the colony). The measures prescribed in the present act did not lead to a normalization of the situation (see doc. No. 93).

Charter of December 25, 1806 — PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 22410; statute of September 29, 1817 — doc. No. 68.

## No. 86. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A SOCIETY FOR ORPHANS OF THE PROTESTANT CONFESSION, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1828)

2529a. — December 18. Imperially confirmed position of the Committee of Ministers. — On the establishment of a society for the care of orphans of the Protestant confession.

At the session of December 8, a memorandum of the Minister of Public Education of November 30 was heard, concerning the petition of the foreigner Schmidt for permission for several private persons to form themselves into a union of the German Orphan Institution and to purchase a house for it without payment of the statutory duties, as well as for the exemption of this house from all levies.

The Committee, recognizing that the institution for orphans of German origin established in St. Petersburg through private charitable contributions deserves the protection of the government, resolved: 1) To permit the persons named in the report of the Minister of Public Education, in order to sustain this institution, to form themselves, on rules proposed by them, into a society under the name of the Society for the Care of Orphans of the Protestant Confession. 2) In order that this institution may afford the government reliable assurance that it will not become a refuge for runaway children or children having no documentation whatsoever concerning their origin, the society shall be placed under the absolute obligation to admit into the orphan institution only children of free status possessing the proper documents concerning themselves obtained from the appropriate source; as for those not having such documents, the society shall apply to the police, or to those offices under whose jurisdiction they fall by virtue of their parents' status, and request precise certification of their origin; moreover, within the institution itself a register shall be kept for all orphans cared for there, faithfully noting their origin and the documents confirming it. 3) The house proposed for purchase for the orphan institution shall be exempted from payment of the one-percent tax into municipal revenues, following the example of state institutions in the capital, for as long as the orphan institution exists; but police levies, such as maintenance of the pavement, supervision of cleanliness near the house, and the like, must be performed by the orphan institution on the general basis. 4) For the further support of the said society and of the orphan institution maintained by it, they shall be placed under the protection of the Minister of Public Education and the St. Petersburg Military Governor-General; to this end a draft decree in the name of the latter shall be submitted for Imperial signature; and 5) Since the execution of the deed of sale for the house of the widow Müller, bargained for the orphan institution, without payment of the statutory duties would be contrary to proper order, it shall be submitted to His Imperial Majesty whether he might be pleased, out of regard for the charitable purpose of this institution and the insignificance of the duties payable to the treasury and for stamped paper upon execution of the deed of sale, to order that these duties be paid from His Majesty's Cabinet.

At the session of December 18 it was announced to the Committee that the Sovereign Emperor had been pleased to confirm the Committee's position, and the decree was signed in St. Petersburg on December 14, 1828.

Memorandum. By the Supreme command of His Imperial Majesty, Adjutant General Benckendorff forwarded to me a petition submitted to him by the foreigner Schmidt, in which he requests the solicitation of the Supreme consent of His Imperial Majesty for several persons to form a union of the German Orphan Institution (Verein der deutschen Waisenanstalt), and also for permission for them to purchase a house without payment of the statutory duties, and for the exemption of this house forever from all levies. In connection with this, Adjutant General Benckendorff communicated to me the Supreme will that Schmidt's petition be submitted to His Imperial Majesty through me.

I considered it my duty immediately to inspect the institution under Schmidt's charge, in which up to 40 orphans of both sexes are currently being raised, and found proper order in everything.

From the information furnished to me by Schmidt, the following emerged: in 1825 two Basel missionaries, Traub and Gebel, arrived in Russia intending to take part in bringing the light of the Gospel teaching to the Tatar tribes. Traub's illness compelled them to postpone their intention for a time. Meanwhile Gebel, being zealous for the common good, did not wish to remain idle. An encounter with an orphan begging for alms inspired in him the idea of establishing an orphanage for the care of poor and kinless children.

Having communicated his intentions to Gray, the teacher of the Lancasterian school for the poor, and to others, he soon, through their assistance, found the means to carry out his humane intention. A dwelling was promptly rented not far from the Lancasterian school, so that the pupils of both sexes might attend it and be taught there reading, writing, and the four rules of arithmetic (which is in fact carried out to this day). Thus the orphanage had its beginning.

For two and a half years the orphanage subsisted on the charitable contributions of various persons and lacked for nothing. Gebel subsequently handed over supervision of this institution to his colleague Traub, who administered it only briefly, suffering from a severe chest ailment (of which he soon died); at the beginning of this year, 1828, he was compelled to hand over the said institution to Schmidt, its present superintendent. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 219

Schmidt arrived in Russia in 1827; having completed his course of studies at the University of Berlin, he intended to take up a position as pastor in one of the German colonies of the southern region of Russia; but an illness that overtook him upon his arrival in St. Petersburg kept him from carrying out this intention, and meanwhile Traub persuaded him to take over the administration of the said institution. Soon after Schmidt entered upon his duties as superintendent of this institution, several benefactors donated 25,000 rubles for the purchase of a house to accommodate the orphans. But since the duty payable upon the purchase, as well as the annual levies on the house, would be burdensome for an institution having no reliable or steady income, he, Schmidt, resolved to petition for the solicitation of Supreme consent to purchase, without duties, the house belonging to the widow Müller, in the 1st Admiralty district, 3rd quarter, No. 170, which was found quite suitable for this orphan institution; and for its exemption from annual levies, and, for the further establishment of this institution, at the wish of the following persons: candidate Schmidt, the present superintendent, Court Councillor Hug, Gray the teacher of the Lancasterian school, Guval the tinsmith, the shoemakers Monstein and Kühn, Salman the manufacturer, Bötger the goldsmith, Geisig the weaver, and Stempel the cardboard-maker, that they form themselves, in the capacity of overseers, into the so-called union of the German Orphan Institution.

I had the honor of most humbly reporting on this to the Sovereign Emperor and on the 24th day of this November received His Imperial Majesty's own resolution in his own hand: "submit through the Committee of Ministers." In fulfillment of this Supreme will, I have the honor to submit Schmidt's petition for the consideration of the Committee of Ministers, and I consider it my duty to add that, since the house proposed for purchase, according to Schmidt's statement, costs only 28,000 rubles and the annual levies on it amount to no more than 200 rubles, then, taking into account, on the one hand, the real benefit of this humane institution for homeless orphans, and, on the other, the insignificance of the sacrifices requested from the treasury and the city, I consider that one may petition for the Most Gracious consent of His Imperial Majesty to the purchase of the house without duties, to its exemption from all levies for as long as this institution shall continue, and to the formation by the above-named persons of a union or society under the name of: guardians of the German Orphan Institution (Pfleger der deutschen Waisenanstalt), which name I find most fitting.

I have the honor herewith to append a draft of the rules of this institution.

Rules of the Union of the German Orphan Institution.

1. The purpose of the union is that its members shall jointly supervise the use of monies both already donated and to be donated in future, in accordance with the wishes of the donors, for the preservation for the future of the house which they intend to acquire by purchase for the benefit of the orphan institution, and in general for the maintenance of it in the best order.

Note. The house will be purchased in the name of the union of the German Orphan Institution, and not in the name of any single member, so that it may not subsequently pass by right of inheritance into the hands of strangers.

2. The duties of the members of the union are already evident from its purpose and further consist of: a) seeking out poor orphans and bringing them to the institution; b) finding for pupils discharged from the orphanage good places to enter into service or to learn some trade.

3. The number of members of the union is not fixed; at present there are ten of them, but it is proposed also to accept new members, provided they agree to fulfill all the obligations attached to this status.

4. Only legitimately born children of both sexes are admitted as pupils of the orphan institution.

5. Admission of pupils into the orphanage is carried out as follows: if it becomes known that somewhere there is a complete orphan compelled to beg for alms, two members of the union are immediately dispatched to investigate his situation. If it turns out that he is indeed in a helpless condition and there is a vacant place in the orphan institution, he is admitted into it. If there are many candidates, the poorest among them are chosen, and preferably those who have neither parents nor relatives.

6. Pupils remain in the institution only until confirmation; thereafter, once the members of the union have found good masters, they enter into apprenticeship with them. Female pupils, however, remain a further year in the institution and are taught household tasks; after this period they enter into service in households found for them by the members of the union.

7. Apart from these rules, the union of the German Orphan Institution has no others, for the persons composing it act solely at the prompting of the heart and in fulfillment of Christian duties.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Suppl. vol. III. Pp. 29-31.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 86.

Benckendorff, Alexander Khristoforovich (Konstantin Alexander Karl Wilhelm) von (1781–1844) — count, cavalry general; from 1826 to 1844, chief of the Corps of Gendarmes and head of the Third Section.
