## No. 87. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE ORGANIZATION OF THE LIVONIAN COLONIES, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1830)

3938. — September 23. Imperially confirmed position of the Committee of Ministers. — On measures proposed for the organization of the Livonian colonies.

At the session of September 2, a memorandum of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs of August 17 was heard, concerning measures proposed for the organization of the Livonian colonies.

The Committee, having examined this report, resolved: that all those proposals of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs which relate specifically to the organization of the Livonian colonists and which are contained in the first 7 points of his conclusion be put into effect forthwith; while the remaining matters, namely: concerning the plots of land belonging to these colonists, of which one is settled by state peasants of the Stockmannshof manor, and another is used by the Forest Master of the Wenden and Walk districts, and likewise concerning the levy collected from the colonists for timber and its allocation for the benefit of the Forest Master, are to be left to the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs to enter into correspondence with the Minister of Finance, and, once these matters have been brought to proper clarity regarding the transfer of the said peasants from their present place of residence, or their being left there with a corresponding allotment to the colonists elsewhere of the requisite amount of land, should a survey of the land they hold prove it insufficient, to submit the matter separately to the Committee.

At the session of September 23 it was announced to the Committee that the Sovereign Emperor had been pleased to confirm the Committee's position. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 221

Memorandum of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs. On the occasion of information received by the Ministry of Internal Affairs concerning disorders that have arisen among the German colonists settled in Livonia Governorate, it was decreed by the journal of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers, imperially confirmed on August 27, 1829: that a special official be sent by the Ministry to survey the present condition of the colonists and to devise measures for bringing them into proper order and ensuring their welfare in the future.

The execution of this was entrusted to Collegiate Councillor Baron Rosen, an official for special assignments attached to the Ministry, who was furnished for this purpose with instructions.

Upon this official's completion of the task entrusted to him, and upon examination in the Ministry of the report he submitted and of the information gathered on the spot, the following was found:

1. By force of the Supreme decree given in the name of Governor-General Browne on May 10, 1766, and of the contract concluded on the basis thereof with the Livonian colonists at the very time of their settlement, the lands of the state manors of Hirschenhof and Helfreichshof were given over to their exclusive use and ownership; and the peasants residing thereon were designated to be transferred to vacant lands lying near other manors; moreover, this contract set forth the general rights of the colonists, both as regards possession of these lands and as regards their internal administration.

But, contrary to these original provisions, the local authorities permitted, as early as 1768, the resettlement onto colonist lands of state peasants of the Stockmannshof manor; and in 1789 these peasants occupied a separate colonist plot of up to 70 desyatinas, and their village, numbering 114 souls, was named Silyan. As to how much land in total is occupied by them, and whether it is all from the land allotted to the colony or partly from adjoining state land, this cannot be determined from the information gathered by Baron Rosen; it is only apparent that the state peasants paid taxes to the treasury and sometimes helped the colonists in building houses and in working the land, while the colonists paid into the treasury the established fee for each day-laborer.

2. Also contrary to the said Supreme decree and contract, the elders of the colony, with the authorization of the local authorities, gave over from the lands belonging to it, into the possession of entirely outside persons, three plots: one, comprising more than 45 desyatinas, to the Latvian Jan in 1767, on the same terms as those granted to the colonists themselves; two of 90 desyatinas each, with houses and other structures, to the farmer Litz, from whom they subsequently passed by sale into the possession of various officials, and finally both these plots were sold in 1802 and 1810, for 1,100 thalers, to the physician Suk, by deeds confirmed in the local government offices, on condition that he pay annually into the colonists' fund 28 rubles in silver for them, which sum he does pay.

Although, following complaints lodged by the colonists in 1825 concerning various oppressions inflicted on them by the Superintendent Buddenbrock, the former Governor-General, Marquis Paulucci, ordered in 1828 that the local Provincial Board return the said three plots to the colonists, this was nevertheless conditioned on the colonists paying the person in possession of them, apart from state property, more than 1,250 rubles in silver for the buildings. And the Provincial Board, intending not to constrain the owners by compulsion to give up the plots to the colonists before the latter had compensated them for the improvements made, again submitted this matter for the consideration of Marquis Paulucci in 1829, and Baron Rosen was unable to ascertain what decision followed on this.

3. Owing to the growth of the population in the colony over the course of 63 years, many colonist families petitioned the local authorities for the surveying-out of new state lands for them; but this was not done because, according to the explanation of the Provincial Land Surveyor, most of the colonist plots contain more land than was assigned by the contract, and because, as Baron Rosen reports, scarcely half the land has been made fertile, since the colonists take no trouble either to drain the marshy and low-lying places or to clear the land of tree roots. Meanwhile he considers it necessary to re-survey the colonist lands.

4. In the colony there is a forest under state administration, with a special plot of land attached to it, which is used by the Forest Master of the Wenden and Walk districts. Although Baron Rosen applied to the Treasury Chamber for information on the time when this forest was separated from the colonies, and on the extent of this land, the Chamber informed him that this forest comprises 779 desyatinas, but that it could give no information as to from what year, and by virtue of what instruction, it was separated from the colony.

The colonists, for permission to remove and sell fallen timber from this forest, pay 12 kopecks per cubic sazhen and 6 kopecks in copper per log; these monies go to the Forest Master for his labors, on the basis of an instruction of the former Livonia Civil Governor Duhamel, given to the Superintendent of the colonists, Buddenbrock, on December 21, 1823.

5. By the arrangements of the Civil Governors, based on the opinion of the State Council, imperially confirmed on June 21, 1823, whereby, for all free persons not belonging to the peasant estate in Livonia Governorate, parish courts established for peasants were designated as the courts of first instance for the adjudication of their affairs, the colonists have been made subject to the Wenden parish court, to which are referred all those matters that cannot be concluded in the Rural Office. Such an arrangement does not correspond to the contract concluded with the colonists, point 17 of which states: "Should any of them be dissatisfied with the elder's adjudication, or consider himself wronged, he may present his case to the Imperial Economy, or to the Governor."

6. Although by force of the above-mentioned Supreme decree of May 10, 1766, and of the Supreme decree given in the name of the former Prosecutor General Prince Vyazemsky of November 14, 1784, whereby it was forbidden to have, attached to the Livonian colonies, any officials other than their own village elders; and likewise by the instructions issued by the former Expedition of State Economy and by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, no special Superintendent ought to be appointed for these colonies; instead, an arrangement should have been made whereby they, governing themselves, would remain, like state settlers, under the general oversight of the Rural Police, through which the Civil Governor would exercise administration over them; but, notwithstanding all this, it is evident from the information gathered by Baron Rosen that the Superintendent Buddenbrock (who is also the District Commissioner), appointed by the local authorities, not only has influence over the election of village elders, confirmation in which office is entrusted to him, but even administers all public levies and revenues and keeps their accounts; that, on the occasion of complaints brought against him by the colonists in 1825, a special commission was established, which uncovered irregularities in the bookkeeping, and the Governor-General, having reprimanded Superintendent Buddenbrock for this, although he ordered a register to be kept for recording income and expenditure of funds, nevertheless the order established for accountability is not observed in it; and that this Superintendent enjoys the following benefits: a) He possesses the Hirschenhof manor house, together with the garden and hay-meadow lands attached to it, in all 17 tonnenstellen or 8 desyatinas. b) In 1819 land was allotted to him, without specification of quantity, from what is called the forest remaining after the allotment to the colony. On it there is a homestead with a cattle yard, and winter and spring grain are sown. This land is worked for him by the above-mentioned state peasants transferred to the Hirschenhof manor, and he pays into the treasury, in place of these peasants' obligations, the sum due from them of 282 rubles 92¼ kopecks in assignat currency. c) He has in his possession the tavern located on the main road of the colony, belonging to the colonists, but given over in 1798, by order of the local authorities, to the Superintendent of the colony, in open violation of points 13 and 14 of the contract concluded with the colonists, whereby they are granted the use of the taverns and tavern sites, as well as the mills and mill sites, located on the manors of Hirschenhof and Helfreichshof. For this tavern he pays into the treasury 105 rubles in assignats in rent, while he himself receives an income of 250 rubles in silver a year. This tavern has been allowed by him to fall into such disrepair that it needs to be rebuilt anew. d) He enjoys the right to conduct tavern-keeping at the communal colonist mill, having persuaded the colonists, 11 years ago, to cede this right to him as a reward for his labors and troubles in administering the colonies.

7. Improper levies are collected from the colonists by Superintendent Buddenbrock, namely: a) to the parish Latvian teacher, who has no relation to them whatsoever, at the rate of 2½ loofs of grain per household; and b) 2 rubles 90 kopecks from each holder of a plot, toward the discharge of a debt imposed on them by Buddenbrock, which he made up out of various disbursements he made from the communal fund without receipts, but which, as they maintain, was already paid off by them before 1825, at the time of the payment of state taxes, and which Baron Rosen, owing to the confused state of the colony's accounts, was unable to clarify.

8. The Livonia Provincial Board, with the confirmation of the former Governor-General Marquis Paulucci in 1828, arranged to stop issuing to the colonists passports for residence outside the colony for various trades, in order to induce them either to occupy themselves with agriculture or to enter other occupations.

Opinion of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs. Having weighed all these circumstances against the laws relating to the colonists and the instructions of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, I propose to bring them to the attention of the Governor-General of the Baltic Governorates; and, in order to establish a sound organization for these colonists, to adopt the following measures:

1. The lands improperly held by outside persons, together with the state buildings on them, having been taken from them, are to be returned to the colonists. As for the compensation of the owners for improvements proposed by the former Governor-General, Marquis Paulucci, in accordance with the opinion of the Livonia Provincial Board, then, out of regard for the fact that these persons made various improvements on those lands specifically for their own benefit, of which they have already availed themselves, while the colonists, who have an indisputable right to possession of them, were deprived of them — the opinion of the Governor-General should be sought as to whether such compensation ought to be allowed, to what extent, and on what grounds; and, if it ought to be, whether it would not be proper to leave these temporary holders to seek such satisfaction from those offices and persons who permitted the execution of deeds upon state land granted to the possession of the colonists.

2. In order to establish with certainty the amount of land belonging to the colonists, and to allot them equitably the established proportion, a verification and survey of all the land belonging to the colony is to be carried out by means of local surveyors.

3. The referral of colonist affairs for resolution to the parish court, and the collection of money from them for its maintenance, is to be discontinued, leaving matters not concluded in the Rural colonist Office subject to adjudication by the Landgericht, in view of the fact that the colonists have been granted special rights and privileges, and, on the basis of point 17 of the contract, are permitted to bring complaints against their rural administration to the Imperial Economy, or to the Governor.

4. Superintendent Buddenbrock of the colony is to be immediately dismissed from this office, and no such officials are to be appointed in future; and the colonists are to be placed under the general oversight of the Rural Police, under the chief supervision of the Livonia Civil Governor.

5. Buddenbrock is to be ordered to hand over, according to inventories, to the Rural Office of the colony, in the presence of the official who will be sent by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, both the lands and establishments he holds in the colony and all the written records and accounts in his possession by virtue of his office as Superintendent, for the purpose of establishing order in the internal administration of this colony in accordance with the instruction given for such administration in the St. Petersburg colonies. Likewise, the said Buddenbrock is to be placed under the absolute obligation to bring, at his own expense, into proper repair everything among the state manor buildings, tavern, and public house in his possession that has been allowed to fall into disrepair, and to hand them over in such condition, likewise according to inventories, to the Rural colonist Office, in the presence of the same official. For the execution of this task, the Superintendent of the St. Petersburg colonies, Titular Councillor Strick, is to be sent, on condition that he use for the post-horses on both legs of the journey funds from the sum designated for travel in connection with these colonies, and that 500 rubles be issued to him from the State Treasury for travel expenses; an instruction to this effect is to be given to the Inspector of the colony, Bunin; and Superintendent Strick is to be furnished with instructions for the execution of this task.

6. The colonists are to be placed under the obligation to submit for confirmation, through the Rural Police, to the Livonia Civil Governor, the village elders whom they elect from among themselves.

7. In order, owing to the confused state of the accounts kept by the Superintendent of the colony, to have proper assurance as to the correctness or incorrectness of the use of the colonists' communal funds, an audit thereof is to be ordered; and, as regards all those levies on the colonists for which there exists no proper regulation, and which now appear to be the grain levy for the benefit of the Latvian teacher, whom the German colonists are under no obligation whatsoever to support, and the monetary levy of 2 rubles 90 kopecks from each householder, toward repayment of a debt which they disclaim and for which there is no proper evidence, the Livonia Governor is to be instructed to conduct an investigation in the lawful manner, excluding from any participation therein the Wenden Ordnungsrichter Hagemeister, a relative of Buddenbrock's, and to submit it to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, together with the conclusion of the said Governor.

8. The suspended issuance of passports to colonists leaving the colony, with the consent of the community, to go to towns for various trades, is to be permitted, by the right which not only the colonists but also the peasants enjoy.

9. As regards the plot belonging to the colony but settled by Latvian peasants, correspondence is to be entered into with the Minister of Finance, to ascertain the time and reasons for the settlement of state peasants on land belonging to the colony, their number, and the possibility or difficulty of transferring them elsewhere. Meanwhile, since it appears, among other things, from Baron Rosen's report that the colonists are negligent in bringing their lands into a condition suitable for tillage, and that upon re-surveying it may easily be found that they hold a quantity of land exceeding the proportion assigned to them by the contract, the said Latvian peasants might be left in their present locations, or, should the colonists lack land, the Minister of Finance might consider it convenient to allot them additional land from elsewhere, so as to leave the said peasants at their present settlement, should this be deemed necessary and beneficial.

10. The matter of the plot of land used by the Forest Master of the Wenden and Walk districts, as well as the payment made by the colonists, upon obtaining fallen timber from the forest belonging to them, of 12 kopecks per cubic sazhen and 6 kopecks in copper per log, and the allocation of this levy for the benefit of the said Forest Master, is to be submitted for the conclusion of the Minister of Finance.

I have the honor to submit this opinion of mine for the consideration and confirmation of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. V. Part 2. Pp. 52-57.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 87.

The picture presented in the document—the unlawful deprivation of colonists of their lands, the arbitrary conduct of the overseer (in this case, one who had, moreover, been appointed illegally)—was highly typical not only of the Livland colonies but of all the foreign colonies.

Duhamel, Osip (Joseph) (1768–1840) — a Courland nobleman, civil governor of Livland from 1811 to 1827, later a senator.

Hagemeister, Ferdinand August Nikolaus Christoph von (1785–1869) — Wenden Ordnungsrichter from 1812 to 1839.

Decree of May 10, 1766 — doc. No. 18.

## No. 88. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE RESETTLEMENT OF CHERNIGOV COLONISTS TO EKATERINOSLAV GOVERNORATE, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1831)

4616. — June 2. Most Highly confirmed decision of the Committee of Ministers. — On the resettlement of 124 families of Chernigov colonists to Ekaterinoslav Governorate.

The memorandum of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of May 15, on the resettlement of 124 families of Chernigov colonists, owing to a shortage of land in the colonies there, to Ekaterinoslav Governorate at their own expense, with the grant to them of a 5-year exemption from taxes and duties, was heard.

The Committee resolved: to permit the resettlement of the said colonists on the terms set forth in the present submission.

His Imperial Majesty was Most Highly pleased to confirm the decision of the Committee.

Memorandum. In 1820, the Chernigov Civil Governor represented to the Ministry of Internal Affairs a request to permit several families, from among the colonists settled in that Governorate, to resettle in the southern regions of Russia owing to a shortage of land.

In response to this, the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Active Privy Councillor Count Kochubei, instructed the Civil Governor to announce to the said colonists that they might choose land in the Novorossiisk region and Bessarabia, where 60 desiatinas would be allotted to farmers, and, depending on need, from 10 to 15 desiatinas to craftsmen, per family, but on the condition that they carry out the resettlement and establishment at their own expense, without requesting the slightest assistance from the treasury. In consideration, however, of the expenses that they would necessarily incur in resettling, they were promised that a petition would be made for a 5-year exemption from the payment of taxes and duties at their new place of settlement, on the understanding that, upon the expiration of that exemption, they would be assessed a land tax in the same amount as the local state peasants pay in poll tax and quitrent money, and would likewise perform all zemstvo duties on an equal footing with them.

As a consequence of this, in the month of August 1829 the Military Governor of Little Russia forwarded to the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Active Privy Councillor Engel, a petition submitted by the aforementioned colonists together with a list of 209 families who had expressed a wish to resettle, on the aforesaid terms, to vacant lands they had found in Ekaterinoslav Governorate, in Aleksandrovsk Uezd, in the neighborhood of the German colonists settled in Mariupol district.

The Military Governor considered it necessary, owing to the shortage of land, to permit the proposed resettlement, for the common benefit both of those moving and of those remaining in their former place of residence.

The Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Active Privy Councillor Engel, having compared this submission with the information available on the subject at the Ministry, and finding that the said colonists, given their present number of families, are short of up to 5,000 desiatinas of the land allotted to them in due proportion; that the plot they had chosen, comprising 13,000 desiatinas, belongs to the colonist department, is settled by no one, and is quite sufficient for the establishment of all 209 families that had expressed a wish to resettle; and that the Ministry had already consented to their resettlement — for his part also found it necessary to permit it; but, before proceeding to a final decision on the matter, proposed that the Guardianship Committee for Colonists of the Southern Region of Russia instruct the Ekaterinoslav Office for Foreign Settlers to ascertain personally, through one of its members, whether the 209 families wishing to resettle would in fact be able to move and fully set up their households in the new place of residence at their own expense, and to provide for their own subsistence for the first year without the slightest assistance from the treasury, and that, otherwise, those who proved insufficiently able to make the move on this basis, or who did not present written guarantees to that effect from their fellow colonists, should by no means be permitted to do so.

The Guardianship Committee, on the basis of a report from the Ekaterinoslav Office for Foreign Settlers, which had sent one of its members to the Chernigov colonies, reported the following.

Of the 209 families that had expressed a wish to resettle, 22 families withdrew entirely from resettlement, owing to poverty, ill health, and the death of their elders. In their place, 25 families joined those resettling, by reason of kinship,

and by mutual agreement they together formed only 124 separate families, comprising a total of 535 males and 512 females currently present, 1,047 souls in all.

These families undertaking resettlement have very little cash on hand, namely 2,840 rubles, but they will receive from the colonists remaining in place, in exchange for the households they are ceding to them, under an arrangement made among themselves, up to 75,000 rubles, and, moreover, some of those remaining in place have promised to render voluntary assistance for settlement to those among the resettlers who are without sufficient means.

Those resettling will take with them to the new place of settlement the necessary agricultural implements and the required number of draft animals: up to 750 horses and oxen. For the settlement of families possessing the necessary agricultural implements and draft animals, 400 rubles per family are required, according to the calculation of the Ekaterinoslav Board of Guardians.

The Guardianship Committee submitted a nominal roll of the resettling colonists, with a detailed account of their property and of the arrangements they had made regarding the transfer of their households. This roll shows that, upon receiving from their fellow colonists remaining in place the sums agreed by mutual consent for the households ceded to them, and in addition the promised assistance for settlement, each family will have from 400 to 1,400 rubles in cash, and that most of these families comprise from 4 to 12 males, and from 8 to 19 persons of both sexes.

In addition, the Committee submitted written undertakings by which the colonists taking over the households of those resettling obligated themselves, first, to have ready the sum designated for these households together with the promised assistance, with which they will unfailingly satisfy the resettlers as soon as permission for this follows, and, second, to answer for the payment of the treasury debt recorded against the households they are taking over.

The provisioning of the colonists in the first year of settlement in the new place, as the Guardianship Committee explains, will be fully assured by the grain they harvested in 1830 at their former location in Chernigov Governorate, of which at least more than 7,700 chetverts, of both winter and spring grain, will be available.

The Chief Trustee of Colonists of the Southern Region of Russia has notified the Ministry of Internal Affairs that, in view of the need for these colonists to take advantage of the time favorable for spring sowing, he has given permission for those among them with greater means to be allowed to begin their resettlement to the new place and to carry out sowing.

Reference. The Chernigov colonists were settled in 1767 and 1768, under terms specially concluded at the time of their establishment, by which 30 desiatinas of land per family were allotted to them.

In 1798, when they came under the jurisdiction of the then Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreign Settlers and Rural Husbandry attached to the Governing Senate, a review of their situation found a shortfall of land against the due proportion, which was subsequently made up, pursuant to a report of the Governing Senate Most Highly confirmed on August 21, 1800, and thus 30 desiatinas were allotted for each family, reckoning 4 male souls per family, amounting in all to 4,800 desiatinas for 160 families, plus a separate 180 desiatinas for three pastors.

According to the report on the condition of these colonies submitted by the Chernigov Civil Governor for the past year 1830, they comprise: 261 families, 1,280 male souls. At the established proportion of 30 desiatinas for every four male souls, 9,600 desiatinas of land are needed. But only 4,800 desiatinas have been allotted to them; hence there is a shortfall of 4,800 desiatinas.

In the event of the resettlement of 535 male souls to Ekaterinoslav Governorate, there will be a shortfall of about 800 desiatinas.

On the basis of the opinion of the State Council Most Highly confirmed on March 12, 1812, the said colonists pay 1 ruble for each desiatina of land they hold, and one half of this payment is credited toward the repayment of their debt to the treasury, of which, after the payment made by them up to the current year 1831, 1,822 rubles 45 kopecks remain outstanding. In addition, they perform zemstvo duties, except for the recruit levy, on an equal footing with the local state peasants.

They are under the charge of the Chernigov Civil Governor, and a special overseer is attached to them, maintained at their own expense.

Laws. I. By the decision of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers Most Highly confirmed on December 15, 1828, issued upon the submission of the Minister of Internal Affairs, colonists were permitted to resettle in the Caucasus Region and were granted a five-year exemption from the payment and performance of all duties from the day of their arrival in the Region.

II. By the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs Most Highly confirmed on February 20, 1804, it was decided, among other things, to allot colonists in the Novorossiisk region 60 desiatinas of land per family; and that, upon the expiration of 20 years, they would be assessed a tax equal to that generally paid by the state settlers of that place per soul.

<...>

Assessment of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Taking into consideration that the colonists settled in Chernigov Governorate have a very significant shortage of land against the 30-desiatina proportion established for each family; that as early as 1820 the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Active Privy Councillor Count Kochubei, granted them the right to choose land in the Novorossiisk region, proposing an allotment of 60 desiatinas for farmers, and from 10 to 15 for craftsmen, with a five-year exemption from taxes and duties; that, upon their choosing a vacant plot in Ekaterinoslav Governorate belonging to the colonist department, and upon inquiry made by the Colonist Administration into their circumstances, there appears to be no obstacle to permitting those families among them who are listed in the roll submitted by the Guardianship Committee as being of good standing to resettle on the land they have chosen; and finally, that although the proportion of land promised to them is twice that established for them, under the terms concluded with them as explained above, of 30 desiatinas for every four male souls, the families undertaking resettlement, in compensation, prove to be very numerous — for all these reasons, I am of the opinion:

Conclusion of the Manager of the Ministry. 1. To admit to resettlement, at their own expense, those of the Chernigov colonists who are listed in the roll submitted by the Guardianship Committee, to the plot of land they have chosen in Ekaterinoslav

Governorate, from which farmers are to be allotted 60 desiatinas, and craftsmen, depending on need, from 10 to 15 desiatinas per family.

2. In accordance with the promise made by the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in 1820, to grant them five years' exemption from the payment of taxes and duties, counting this from the time of their arrival in Ekaterinoslav Governorate; and, upon the expiration of this exemption, to assess them taxes and duties on an equal footing with the local state peasants.

3. To entrust the Military Governor of Little Russia with overseeing that the arrangements made by the resettling colonists with their fellow colonists who remain in their present place of residence, regarding the transfer of households, be carried out, and that the resettlers receive the moneys due to them, making it the absolute duty of the Ekaterinoslav Board of Guardians to keep watch, both over their solid establishment, and especially over the cultivation of the land allotted to them and the sowing of grain, so that they may not find themselves, after the harvest, without provisions of their own.

4. If, after the settlement of these resettlers, it should in time become necessary to further subdivide them on the same plot owing to the extreme populousness of families, their local Administration is to adopt as a rule that only such new families be separated out as have not fewer than four male souls, and that no more than 30 desiatinas of land be allotted to each such family, on the same basis they held in Chernigov Governorate, and

5. As regards the resettlers who remain thereafter in the Chernigov colonies, to inform the Military Governor of Little Russia that he should order it to be announced to them that, in the event of the growth of their families, they must by no means count on a similar resettlement, or on an increase of their land, but are obliged to endeavor to compensate for such shortage by improving their fields, advancing their agriculture, and training their children in various useful trades.

Which opinion of mine I have the honor to submit for the gracious consideration of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. VI. Part 1. P. 421-425.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 88.

Colonists from Chernigov who resettled in Yekaterinoslav governorate founded, in the Mariupol colonist district of Alexandrovsk county, five villages named after their mother colonies: Belye Vezhi, Gross-Werder (Great Werder, Marinovka), Kalchinovka, Klein-Werder (Yekaterinopol), and Rundewiese (Lugansk). These colonies were subsequently incorporated into the Alexandro-Nevskaya volost of Mariupol county. By the standards of the Novorossiya colonies they were of medium size: the population of Gross-Werder, the largest of them, was 502 in 1897, including 441 Germans.

Engel, Fyodor Ivanovich (1771–1837) — senator, member of the State Council.

## No. 89. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE RESETTLEMENT OF GERMAN COLONISTS FROM THE KINGDOM OF POLAND TO RUSSIA, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1831)

4617. — June 2. Most Highly confirmed decision of the Committee of Ministers. — On German colonists who have expressed a wish to resettle from the Kingdom of Poland to Russia.

The memorandum of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of May 15, on German colonists who have expressed a wish to resettle from the Kingdom of Poland to Russia, was heard.

The Committee resolved: to confirm this submission.

His Imperial Majesty was Most Highly pleased to confirm the decision of the Committee.

Memorandum. By the journal of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers of the past April, upon the memorandum submitted by the Manager of the Main Staff of His Imperial Majesty concerning permission for foreign craftsmen and colonists who had come from Prussia to the Kingdom of Poland to settle in Russia, it was resolved to refer this matter for the joint consideration of the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

In the aforementioned memorandum of the Manager of the Main Staff of His Imperial Majesty, it was explained that the Commander-in-Chief of the Active Army had informed him that several families of foreign craftsmen had expressed a wish to settle in Russia; he had permitted them to proceed to Białystok and to await there a decision on their establishment. After this, requests to the same effect were received by the Commander-in-Chief from many craftsmen and colonists, who had come for the most part from Prussia, of whom the former were almost all clothiers, and that, upon a report on this matter by Adjutant General Count Chernyshev to His Imperial Majesty, His Majesty was Most Highly pleased to order that it be submitted for the consideration of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers. In this connection, Count Chernyshev set forth his opinion that those of the said craftsmen who had already received permission from the Commander-in-Chief to proceed to Białystok should, in his view, be permitted to settle in Russia; while others, who, like the aforementioned émigrés, might come forward and ask to resettle in Russia, should be refused, since they might become a burden to the Government.

Reference. On March 3 of this year, Field Marshal Count Dibich-Zabalkansky informed the Minister of Internal Affairs that 20 families of German colonists, cloth manufacturers, who had resided in the Kingdom of Poland, Węgrów district, in the village of Wierzbka, had expressed a wish to resettle to Russia, and that he had permitted them to proceed to Białystok and to await there instructions for their further journey, having ordered that, owing to their poor circumstances, a one-time allowance of five chervontsy be issued to each family. Together with this, he forwarded a list of the said manufacturers, for the purpose of designating a place for their permanent settlement, and for reporting on the matter to His Imperial Majesty.

Since manufacturers in general fall under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Internal Affairs applied to him to learn whether he considered it possible to place them in the class of cloth manufacturers on an equal footing with the like colonist-manufacturers settled in Poltava Governorate; to which the Minister of Finance replied that the colonist manufacturers settled in the Kingdom of Poland, as was known to him, consist of weavers who prepare only raw cloth, who cannot support themselves on their own here, except by hire at cloth factories, or by settling near such factories and coming to an arrangement with the factory owners. As for the Poltava colonist manufacturers, to whom special houses had been given and to whom state-owned wool had been issued, with the raw cloth being taken into the treasury for the preparation of soldiers' cloth — they had not been able, by this means, to secure an adequate livelihood; their work was found unprofitable; as a consequence they were relieved of this obligation and permitted to occupy themselves with whatever they wished, working for themselves. — It is very disadvantageous to resettle such people from the Kingdom of Poland, and it is therefore highly undesirable that many of them should come to Russia: for Russian workers are no less skilled, while these resettlers would probably have to be fed by the treasury for a long time, and the matter, after many expenses, would come to nothing. He therefore found it necessary to notify the Commander-in-Chief of the Army of this.

The Minister of Internal Affairs, for the reasons set forth by the Minister of Finance, being in complete agreement with his opinion that the resettlement from the Kingdom

of Poland of poor colonist clothiers to Russia, which has its own good workers for the cloth trade, would cause the treasury only needless expense — in his report to His Imperial Majesty of March 27, proposed that Field Marshal Count Dibich-Zabalkansky be informed that he should not accept such persons for resettlement to us.

As for the aforementioned 20 families already sent to Białystok, who, owing to their poverty, received from the Field Marshal 5 chervontsy per family, taking into consideration that establishing them in colonist status would be very costly for the treasury, and useless to themselves, since they would have to turn to agricultural occupations in which they had never engaged, and moreover there are now no vacant lands in the colony districts; and basing himself on the Most Highly confirmed report of General of Infantry Count Vorontsov of June 1 of the past year 1830, by which Rumelian and Bulgarian resettlers were granted the right to choose their manner of life and to settle wherever they wished in accordance with their occupations, no one being forbidden to settle in towns, in state villages, on vacant plots, or on landowners' estates by mutual voluntary agreement, on the condition that those entering the townsman estate would be registered without the consent of the community, and granted a 10-year exemption from all taxes and from the recruit levy — he proposed to announce to these colonists that they should choose whatever manner of life they wished, on this basis, without any assistance from the treasury; and that, should they wish to register with towns or villages in the Great Russian Governorates, they be provided in such case with papers for travel to the places chosen, and issued for subsistence along the way 50 rubles in banknotes per family; but should they intend to register in the Governorates returned from Poland, only the assistance already given them by the Commander-in-Chief of the Army should be left to them.

To all of this His Imperial Majesty's Most High assent followed, and instructions for carrying it into effect were communicated at that time both to the Minister of Finance and to the Commander-in-Chief of the Army.

Conclusion of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Bearing in mind that, with regard to the foreign craftsmen and colonists already at Białystok, sent there from the Kingdom of Poland with the permission of the Field Marshal, a Most High order of the Sovereign Emperor has already followed, I do not consider it necessary to enter into any further consideration of this matter, and the Minister of Finance concurs with this conclusion of mine.

As for the future resettlement to Russia from the Kingdom of Poland of foreign craftsmen, whom the Committee of Messrs. Ministers recognizes as generally useful for our factories, and requires that rules be established regarding their resettlement and the granting of assistance to them: taking into consideration, first, the reasons set forth above in the memorandum most humbly submitted to the Sovereign Emperor by the Minister of Internal Affairs, on account of which it was found inconvenient to establish the aforementioned 20 families now at Białystok in colonist status, especially owing to the present absence of vacant lands in the colony districts; and, second, that by the Most High order announced to the Committee of Messrs. Ministers on October 25, 1819, further resettlement of foreign émigrés was entirely halted, of which the Ministry of Foreign Affairs was notified at that time, in order to instruct our Missions not to issue passports to foreigners resettling either to Russia or to the Kingdom of Poland — by virtue of this, I likewise find it impossible to permit foreigners to come now from the Kingdom of Poland to Russia to settle in the colonies; but I am of the opinion that, in consideration of their presently constrained situation, they may be allowed to choose their manner of life in Russia according to their wishes, without any assistance from the treasury, on the same basis as was applied to the aforementioned 20 families, in accordance with the Most Highly confirmed report of General of Infantry Count Vorontsov of June 1 (7), 1830, concerning the Rumelian and Bulgarian émigrés — that is, that, in accordance with their occupations, they may register with towns, state villages, vacant plots, and landowners' estates by mutual voluntary agreement, on the condition that those entering the townsman estate be registered without the consent of the communities, and granted a 10-year exemption from all taxes and from the recruit levy. For the support of those among them who lack the means to feed themselves during the journey, the Administrator of Białystok Region should be authorized, when providing them with papers for travel to the Great Russian or Novorossiisk Governorates, to issue, once only and without repayment, for subsistence along the way, 50 rubles in banknotes per family.

In agreement with this opinion of mine, the Minister of Finance, in his communication to me of the 8th of this May, also holds that, since all foreigners are permitted, under the established rules, to come to Russia, nothing prevents the aforementioned craftsmen from availing themselves of this permission as well, without requiring any assistance from the Government.

All of which I have the honor to submit for the gracious decision of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. VI. Part 1. P. 425-427.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 89.

The document attests to the desire of many colonists and artisans who had resettled from Prussia to the Kingdom of Poland, and who found themselves there in a difficult economic situation, to move on to the interior governorates of Russia. Whereas such colonists were often able to settle in the South-Western governorates, employment in Russia was frequently unavailable for the artisans (workers).

Dibich-Zabalkansky, I.I. — in 1830–1831, commander-in-chief of the army in Poland (see Biographical Notes).

Order of October 25, 1819 — doc. No. 76.

## No. 90. DECREE OF NICHOLAS I ON THE SETTLEMENT OF COLONISTS NEAR PETERHOF (1833)

6307 a. — July 9. Personal decree, announced to the Chief Administrator of Peterhof by the Minister of the Imperial Court. — On the settlement of colonists on crown land near Peterhof.

Upon my most humble report of the memorandum submitted by Your Excellency from the Inspector of the St. Petersburg colonies, Bunin, concerning the wish of 4 colonist families to settle on crown land near Peterhof, His Imperial Majesty has deigned to command the following: 1) That these colonists be allotted, for arable land, hayfields, and pasture, the requested quantity of land; but first the site they have chosen, along the Samsonievsky Canal toward the reserve pond where stakes have now been placed, is to be shown on a general plan, which is to be delivered to me for presentation to His Majesty. 2) Since there are no crown forest tracts near Peterhof from which forest lands could be allotted to the said 4 families, you are to communicate with the Inspector of the St. Petersburg colonies as to whether they might be permitted to use the same forest from which the colonists of the Sobstvennaya (Crown's Own) tract draw their needs. 3) Information is to be obtained as to how much will need to be issued in aid to these colonists for clearing the land for sowing, for establishment, and for subsistence. 4) Copies are to be made of the plan and elevations shown in the portfolio being returned herewith, under Nos. 1, 2, and 9; but on the elevation under No. 2, the crossed-out weathervane and the ornaments on the gates, wicket-gates, and DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________ 233

fence are to be removed, and in accordance with these designs an estimate is to be drawn up of the cost of building houses for the 4 colonist families, for each design separately,

In announcing this Supreme Will to Your Excellency for due execution, I propose that the said plans, elevations, and information be delivered to me for report to His Imperial Majesty. At the same time I inform you that His Imperial Majesty has been graciously pleased to confirm Bunin's submission concerning the granting to these colonists of a 10-year exemption, and of the same rights enjoyed by their brethren of the Novosaratovka and Srednyaya Rogatka colonies, as well as concerning the collection from them, after the 10 years have elapsed, of taxes and of payments toward their debt.

Memorandum of the Inspector of the St. Petersburg colonies.

In St. Petersburg Governorate nine colonies have been established for agriculture, of which four — Srednyaya Rogatka, Novosaratovka, Izhora, and Yamburg — were founded in 1765 and 1767, and the other five — Strelna, Peterhof, Oranienbaum, Kronstadt, and Kipen — in 1809.

The colonists of these colonies were settled as follows: the first four, on the basis of conditions specially concluded with them, with Supreme consent, at the time of their settlement, whereby they, in addition to the general rights granted to colonists, are exempt from payment of money toward zemstvo obligations; while the colonists of the other five colonies were settled on the basis of the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs, Highest confirmed on 20 February 1804 (21163), concerning the reception and settlement of colonists in Russia.

Under this decree the following was granted to those colonists: 1) Freedom from payment of taxes and from all obligations for 10 years. 2) Freedom of religion. 3) Freedom from military and civil service. 4) Freedom from military billeting, except for the passage of military detachments through their settlements. 5) Freedom to leave Russia should anyone so wish. 6) Permission to establish factories, engage in any trades, conduct trade, join guilds and crafts, and sell their products anywhere in the Empire.

The colonists of the four colonies of earlier settlement, on the basis of the opinion of the State Council, Highest confirmed on 4 June [13 July] 1823 (29541), pay land tax per year of from 1 ruble 23 kopecks to 2 rubles 50 kopecks for each desyatina of usable land they hold, while those of the five colonies of newer settlement, under the regulation of the Committee of Ministers Highest confirmed on 24 April 1820 (28252), pay from 1 ruble 60 kopecks to 2 rubles per desyatina.

Assistance was rendered to these colonists from the treasury, namely: 1) They were allotted crown lands of from 30 to 50 desyatinas per family, of which the necessary number of desyatinas was cleared for arable land for the first sowing. 2) Houses were built with yards and outbuildings. 3) They were supplied with horses and cattle. 4) Agricultural implements and other rural tools were purchased. 5) Subsistence money was paid until the first harvest.

All such expenses together then amounted to from 2,000 to 11,000 rubles per family. The colonists duly repay this treasury debt after the expiration of the exemption period, on the basis of Highest confirmed regulations, at from 20 to 45 rubles per year per family or household of the original settlement, and in addition pay state tax of 18 kopecks, and for land and water communications 30 kopecks, in total 48 kopecks per year per revision soul, and finally, the colonists of the new settlement also pay the sums assessed for zemstvo obligations.

The colonists who have declared their wish to resettle on the land situated near Peterhof most humbly request: 1) That they be allotted land in such quantity that its cultivation would cover their basic maintenance and crown taxes, considering that for arable land, hayfields, and pasture it will suffice to have the land they have chosen for 4 families along the Samsonovsky Canal, 700 sazhens in length and 300 sazhens in width toward the menagerie, forming a regular parallelogram, at those very points where they have placed stakes, and that, in addition, forest lands, even if at some distance, also be allotted to them. 2) That aid in money from the treasury be given them for clearing a certain amount of land for the initial sowing, for building houses, and for the necessary rural establishment and subsistence. 3) That an exemption of 10 years be granted to them, after the expiration of which they undertake to pay duly land tax of 3 rubles per desyatina, toward the crown debt 50 rubles per household, and the aforementioned taxes of 48 kopecks per revision soul per year, for which they have undertaken to give written pledges, and finally that they be granted the same rights enjoyed by their brethren of the Novosaratovka and Bessarabian [Srednyaya Rogatka] colonies.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Suppl. Vol. VIII. P. 18-20.*

## No. 93. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE REORGANIZATION OF THE CAUCASUS COLONY OF KARRAS, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1835)

8271. — June 26. Highest confirmed regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On measures for organizing the Scottish colony near the Caucasus Mountains.

The memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs of 27 April, on measures for organizing the Scottish colony near the Caucasus Mountains and concerning the right granted to the members of this colony and to the Basel missionaries residing in Shusha to convert Muhammadans and pagans to their faith, was heard.

The Committee, upon examining this matter, found that the principal circumstance contained in it is the right granted to the Scottish colonists to convert Muhammadans and pagans to their faith and thereby to increase the number of members of the colony.

On this subject the Committee could not fail to note that the actions of the colonists over more than 32 years, since the granting of this right to them, have been limited to the conversion of only nine mountaineers, and that since 1828, when the right was again confirmed to them, they have not converted a single person, whereas the preachers of the Ossetian mission, in the course of 17 years, have baptized 70,000 souls; such negligible success on the part of the colonists fully convinces one that they are not engaged in missionary work in the least, and consequently have not the slightest need of the right granted to them for increasing their colony.

As for the Basel missionaries settled in Shusha, it appears from the case that, since their establishment there, without having converted anyone to Christianity, DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 239

they have deviated from their true purpose, turning their attention instead to Armenian youth. Their conduct has provoked complaints on the part of the Armenian clergy which, according to the assurance of the local authorities, may have quite unpleasant consequences.

For this reason the Committee, fully sharing the opinion of the Chief Administrator in Georgia that the activities of all foreign-confession missionaries in general in the Transcaucasian territory should, for the reasons set out in detail in his explanation, be forever discontinued, and bearing in mind, moreover, the statement made in the presence of the Committee by the Synodal Chief Procurator, that the rules for the reorganization of the Caucasian ecclesiastical schools have already been honored with Highest confirmation, and that only the final considerations of Baron Rosen are awaited for the formation of a Greco-Russian missionary society beyond the Caucasus, which he, while here, promised to deliver immediately upon his arrival in Georgia — considered that there will then be no further need whatsoever to have foreign-confession missionaries in that territory.

Accordingly, the Committee proposed: 1) That the conclusion of the Minister of Internal Affairs regarding the measures he proposes for organizing the Scottish colony be confirmed. 2) That, having forbidden the members of this colony and the Basel missionaries settled in Shusha any missionary activity whatsoever, they be allowed henceforth to engage in agriculture, factories, and trades. 3) That the Basel missionaries, in order to remove any occasion for complaint on the part of the Armenian clergy, be further forbidden to accept Armenian youth into their schools. 4) That immediate oversight of this be entrusted to the Chief of the Caucasus Region, under the general supervision of the Chief Administrator of Georgia.

His Imperial Majesty was Highest pleased to confirm the Committee's regulation.

Conclusion of the Minister of Internal Affairs. — Having examined the details of this matter, I find in it two circumstances requiring resolution: 1) the organization of the Scottish colony; 2) the activities of the Basel missionaries, with respect to their influence on Armenian youth.

With regard to the Scottish colony, the investigation conducted on the spot and the report based on it by the Chief Administrator in Georgia, General of Infantry Baron Rosen, sufficiently establish that all the disorders that have occurred until now in the said colony arise from the colonist Paterson, who, retaining for himself without any right the title of elder, oppresses the colonists both in respect of land tenure and in the administration of communal affairs; wherefore the colony has for several years been subject to constant discord.

To put an end to such disorders and to bring order to the colony, I consider it necessary, in agreement with the opinion of General Rosen, to remove Paterson from the Scottish colony's community, and, on the basis of the Highest charter of 26 December 1806 (22410) and the Highest confirmed regulation of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers of 15 December 1828 (2517), to allot to the members of the colony a fixed proportion of land at 60 desyatinas per family, not excluding resettlers from the Saratov colonies, allowing them to establish an administration elected from among themselves consisting of an elder and two members, one from the Scottish and the other from the Saratov colonists, renewing this election every three years. The colonist Paterson is to be allotted the 1,000 desyatinas of land most graciously granted to him as a separate plot, set apart, as far as possible, from the colony's holdings, so as thereby to remove any occasion for new disputes.

As to the activities of the Basel missionaries, although the case contains certain remarks made in general against foreign missionaries by General Yermolov, later repeated by General of Infantry Baron Rosen, these remarks, having been considered by the Committee of Ministers in 1828, were left without action; and, on the other hand, taking into consideration that the conduct of Protestant missionaries in other states, and especially in Prussia, Sweden, and Denmark, has won the approval of their governments; that the Basel missionaries residing in the fortress of Shusha, during its siege by Abbas Mirza, likewise earned the approval both of the local military authorities and of the Commander-in-Chief of the Separate Caucasus Corps, Field Marshal Prince of Warsaw Count Paskevich-Erivansky; and finally, that in none of the documents concerning these missionaries is there anything definite to accuse them of any actions contrary to the interests of our Government — for these reasons I consider that the rights most graciously granted to them should remain inviolable. As for their influence specifically on the education of Armenian youth, in this case, basing myself on the assurance of the local civil and school authorities, who have recognized the missionaries' activities as very beneficial for the Armenian people, I would propose only, in accordance with the opinion of Prince of Warsaw Count Paskevich-Erivansky, to adopt certain measures to prevent, in future, disagreements arising between the missionaries and the Armenian clergy on account of the latter's apprehension regarding the drawing of Armenian youth into the Protestant faith. I would propose to limit these measures to those arrangements which the missionary society has already communicated for the preliminary consideration of General Rosen.

Accordingly, I propose: 1) That the colonist Alexander Paterson, for disorders and oppression of the colonists, be removed from the community of the Scottish colony of Karras. 2) That the members of this colony, on the basis of the Highest charter of 25 December 1806 and the Highest confirmed regulation of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers of 15 December 1828, be allotted from the tract situated at the Karras colony a fixed proportion of land at 60 desyatinas per family, not excluding resettlers from the Saratov colonies. 3) That the 1,000 desyatinas most graciously granted to the colonist Paterson be allotted to him as a separate plot, set apart as far as possible from the colony's holdings, so as thereby to remove any occasion for new disputes. 4) That, for the administration of the communal affairs of the Karras colony, the colonists be allowed to establish an Administration elected from among themselves, consisting of one elder and two members, with the election to be renewed every three years, and with the elder to be chosen in turn, once from among the Scottish and once from among the Saratov colonists. 5) That this colony be entrusted to the direct authority and protection of the District Chief of Pyatigorsk, who shall be obliged to watch over their welfare and to prevent any discord. 6) That, while leaving the Scottish and Basel missionaries in possession of the rights most graciously granted to them, the members of the Basel missionary society be permitted to accept into their schools not only Muhammadan but also Armenian youth, provided, however, that they, under pain of lawful prosecution, refrain from any DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 241

attempt to draw Armenians into their own faith, and that they select, with the confirmation of the local authorities, two honored trustees from among the Armenians for these schools, one from the laity and the other from the clergy.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. X. P. 767-769.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 93.

After an attempt at compromise in 1828 (see doc. No. 85), the authorities had to take radical measures to resolve the conflict between the Scottish missionaries and the German colonists who lived together in the North Caucasian colony of Karras.

Rosen, Roman Fyodorovich (Robert Fabian) von (1782–1848) — chief administrator in Georgia from 1832 to 1835.

Charter of December 25, 1806 — PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 22410; statute of December 15, 1828 — doc. No. 85.

---

## No. 96. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE APPOINTMENT OF AN OVERSEER FOR THE CHERNIGOV COLONY OF NOVYE MEZIRICHI, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1841)

14368. — March 18. Imperially confirmed statute of the Committee of Ministers, announced by the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. — On the appointment of a special Overseer for the colony of Novye Mezirichi.

The Brest first-guild merchant Isaev founded, on land he had purchased in Mglin district of Chernigov Governorate, an extensive manufacturing establishment for the production of woolen goods, called the colony of Novye Mezirichi, where he has, among other things, built housing for the workers, among whom are more than 70 families of German factory workers whom Isaev summoned from the Kingdom of Poland. In 1834, at Isaev's request, the local authorities appointed a special official to the said colony, with the title of police Overseer and with salary and other maintenance to be provided by the founder of that colony. Upon the introduction into force of the statute on rural police, Imperially confirmed on June 3, 1837, the colony of Novye Mezirichi was to pass, on the general basis, into the jurisdiction of one of the District Police Officers; but the Chernigov provincial authorities petitioned for the retention of the special Overseer already present there. In consequence, upon the submission of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the decision of the Committee of Ministers, a Highest command followed on March 18, whereby it was ordained: 1) That a special police official, with the title of Overseer, be appointed to the colony of Novye Mezirichi, Mglin district, Chernigov Governorate, leaving it to the discretion of the local authorities either to retain in this post the official already serving in it, with the permission of the former Little Russian Military Governor, or to appoint another. 2) That the Overseer of the Mezirichi colony be granted, in his administration of the police branch in the colony, the same rights and duties generally vested in District Police Officers, his position being reckoned in Class X of the civil service, in the 9th category for length-of-service pension, and in the 10th category under the uniform schedule of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. 3) That the maintenance of this official be charged to the owner of the colony, in accordance with the wish expressed by him to that effect, the salary being set at not less than 180 rubles in silver per year, plus a suitable apartment with heating. 4) That the owner of the factory also assign to the Overseer one constable for errands and other commissions. Concerning this Highest command, the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs submitted it for execution to the Governing Senate, adding that His Imperial Majesty had also been pleased to command that this be put into effect as a temporary measure, until the benefit and necessity thereof should be assessed by actual experience, this to be left to the further consideration, in due course, of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Minister of Finance.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XVI. Sec. 1. P. 191.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 96.

The colony of Novye Mezirichi (Neu-Meseritz), founded in 1833 and subsequently forming part of the Golubovka volost of Surazh county, Chernigov governorate, represents one of the few examples of the relatively successful creation in Russia of a purely artisanal (manufacturing) foreign colony. It is true, however, that the German colonists themselves made up only a small part of the colony's population: thus, in 1859 there were 348 inhabitants here, including 73 Germans.
