## No. 114. STATUTES ON THE SPIRITUAL AFFAIRS OF FOREIGN CONFESSIONS IN THE RUSSIAN EMPIRE (1857)

### BOOK ONE. ON THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE SPIRITUAL AFFAIRS OF CHRISTIANS OF THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CONFESSION.

#### SECTION ONE. ESTABLISHMENT OF THE SPIRITUAL AUTHORITIES AND ADMINISTRATIVE SEATS.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

On the composition of the dioceses.

11. In the Russian Empire there are seven dioceses of the Roman Catholic confession: the archdiocese of Mogilev, and the dioceses of Vilna, Telšiai (or Samogitia), Minsk, Lutsk-Zhitomir, Kamenets, and Tiraspol.

Note. The laws on the administration of the spiritual affairs of Christians of the Roman Catholic confession in the Kingdom of Poland are not included in this Digest.

1798 Apr. 28 (18504); 1840 Oct. 11 (13854); 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. I; 1848 Nov. 29 (22766); 1852 Nov. 6 (26748).

12. To the archdiocese of Mogilev belong the Roman Catholic churches: a) in the Mogilev governorate, b) all those which, according to the schedule set forth below (art. 13), are not included among the other diocesan districts of this same confession in the Empire, and c) in the Grand Duchy of Finland.

1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. I, para. 1; 1848 Nov. 29 (22766).

13. To the diocese of Vilna belong the Roman Catholic churches in the governorates of Vilna and Grodno (understanding the boundaries of these two, as well as of the following six, governorates as they stood in 1848); to Telšiai, in the governorates of Kovno and Courland; to Lutsk-Zhitomir, in the governorates of Kiev and Volhynia; to Minsk, in the governorate of the same name; to Kamenets, in Podolia governorate; to Tiraspol, in the governorates of Kherson, Yekaterinoslav, Taurida, Saratov, and Astrakhan, in the Bessarabian region, and in the Caucasus and Transcaucasian territory.

1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. I, paras. 2-7, and art. II; 1848 Nov. 29 (22766).

14. The number and names of the parishes of each diocese are determined by a specially approved schedule. Their number may be increased when required either by an increase in population or by the excessive size of existing parishes and the difficulty of communications.

1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, arts. II and XXXI.

15. For closer oversight of the parish churches and their clergy, the parishes of each diocese are combined into special districts called deaneries.

See the enactments cited under art. 36.

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On the ecclesiastical hierarchy.

16. In the archdiocese of Mogilev, the head is an Archbishop; in each of the other dioceses (art. 11), a Bishop.

1798 Apr. 28 (18504); 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. I.

17. By virtue of the privileges attached to the Mogilev Church of the Roman rite (de jure et dignitate Ecclesiae), the Archbishop of Mogilev is at the same time Metropolitan of all Roman Catholic churches in the Empire and the Grand Duchy of Finland. In these parts of the state he takes precedence over all clergy of his confession; the Bishops, presiding in the other dioceses, are at the same time Suffragans of the Metropolitan.

1798 Apr. 28 (18504); 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) para. 2; 1817 Oct. 24 (27106) § 141; 1848 Jul. 5 (new style), act of the Roman Pope; Nov. 29 (22766).

18. Under the Archbishop and each of the other Diocesan Heads (art. 16) there is a fixed number of Suffragan Bishops.

Note. The number of suffragan sees: in the archdiocese of Mogilev, three; in the dioceses of Vilna, three; Telšiai, three; Minsk, one; Lutsk-Zhitomir, two; Kamenets, one; Tiraspol, two.

1798 Apr. 28 (18504) para. 4; 1842 Jan. 1 (15188) staff regulations; 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, arts. III and IV; 1848 Nov. 29 (22766).

19. At each cathedral church there is a Chapter (Capitulum) composed of a fixed number of Prelates or senior members (Dignitates), Canons (Canonici), and Vicar Priests or Mansionaries (Mansionarii vel Beneficiarii).

1784 Apr. 17 (15982); 1798 Apr. 28 (18504); 1842 Jul. 17, detailed staff regulations; 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. VI; 1856 Jul. 16, information of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 271

20. Under the Archbishop and each of the other Diocesan Heads (art. 16) there are:

1) A Consistory, under the chairmanship of an Official, consisting of a Vice-Official, a Visitor of monasteries, and a fixed number of members from among the clergy. It has a Chancery consisting of a Secretary and other civil officials, on the basis of the staff regulations.

2) Personally attached to the Archbishop, a Chancery, and to the Bishop, a Secretary, on the basis of the staff regulations.

1839 Jul. 18 (12549); 1842 Jul. 17, detailed staff regulations; Dec. 16, Highest command; 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, arts. XVII-XIX.

21. For the examination and decision of matters common to all Roman Catholic dioceses (art. 11), specified below (art. 67), there exists in St. Petersburg a supreme spiritual body under the name of the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium, under the chairmanship of the Archbishop-Metropolitan (art. 17), consisting of two Members and seven Assessors from the dioceses. — Attached to the Collegium are: a) a Procurator, and b) a Chancery, on the basis of the staff regulations.

1801 Nov. 13 (20053) para. 1 and staff regulations; 1839 Mar. 15 (12122) staff regulations.

22. At each parish church there is a Rector, or a Priest holding the title of Rector (Administrator), and, under him, one or more Vicars. One of these Rectors performs the duties of Dean (Blagochinny) in the district to which his church belongs (art. 15).

1842 Jul. 17, detailed staff regulations.

23. Each male monastery has its own Superior, and each female monastery its own Mother Superior, according to the rules specified below (art. 78 et seq.). All these Superiors and Mothers Superior are subject, in the same way as the rest of the Roman Catholic clergy, to the jurisdiction and oversight of the Diocesan Heads.

1784 Apr. 17 (15982); 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) para. 5; 1832 Jul. 19 (5506) para. 12; 1842 Dec. 16, Highest command.

##### CHAPTER THREE.

On the procedure for appointing and dismissing clergy

and lay officials serving under the spiritual administration.

24. The Archbishop-Metropolitan, the Diocesan Bishops, and the Suffragan Bishops are appointed by His Imperial Majesty, upon prior agreement with His Holiness the Roman Pope, and canonical confirmation according to the accepted procedure. — His Majesty's Highest will regarding their appointment is expressed by his personal decrees to the Governing Senate.

1784 Apr. 17 (15982); 1817 Oct. 24 (27106) §§ 143, 144; 1824 May 15 (29914); 1826 Sept. 21 (593); 1832 Feb. 2 (5126); 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. XII.

25. After these clergy (art. 24) have taken the established oath of allegiance to His Majesty the Sovereign Emperor, Autocrat of All Russia, and to the lawful Heir to His Throne, they are permitted, upon the performance over them of the church rite, to take an oath also to the Supreme Pontiff of the Roman Church, according to the form Highest-approved for this purpose.

1784 Apr. 17 (15982) form of the oath; Fundamental State Laws, App. V.

26. In the event of the death of a Diocesan Head or his resignation from his office, the Vicar temporarily taking his place by election of the Chapter (art. 59) is likewise confirmed in this office by the Supreme Authority.

See the enactments cited under art. 24.

27. Only such clergy as have studied at the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Academy or the former Main Seminary and have received diplomas therefrom for ecclesiastical academic degrees are appointed as Cathedral Prelates and Canons (a). Those found worthy by the Diocesan Head are confirmed in these ranks by Highest decrees, announced by the Minister of Internal Affairs (b).

(a) 1784 Apr. 17 (15982); 1833 Jul. 1 (6296) § 83; 1842 Jan. 1 (15188) staff regulations; 1856 Jul. 16, information of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. — (b) 1817 Oct. 24 (27106) § 145; 1824 May 15 (29914); 1829 Mar. 14, Highest command; 1832 Feb. 2 (5126).

28. The appointment and dismissal of members of the Diocesan Consistory rests with the Archbishop or Bishop presiding in the diocese (art. 16). All of them are appointed, with the consent of the government, from among clergy. If the Diocesan Head deems it necessary to remove any one of them, he immediately appoints his successor, likewise with the consent of the government.

Note 1. Visitors of monasteries, who sit in the Consistories in addition to the other members, are confirmed, upon nomination and presentation by the Diocesan Heads, by the Minister of Internal Affairs.

Note 2. If, owing to illness or other valid reasons, the number of members required by law is not present in the Consistory, the Diocesan Head may invite members of the Chapter (art. 27) to sit temporarily therein, reporting this each time to the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium and to the Minister of Internal Affairs.

1798 Apr. 28 (18504) para. 5; 1804 Sept. 27 (21467); 1817 Oct. 24 (27106) § 148; 1832 Mar. 11 (5225); 1833 Jul. 1 (6296) § 83; 1842 Dec. 16, Highest command; 1843 Jan. 19 (16464); 1845 Nov. 29, order of the Ministry of Internal Affairs; 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. XVII.

29. The offices of members of the Consistory cease upon the death of the Bishop, or in the event of his resignation from the episcopal rank, and also upon the termination of the administration of a vacant diocese by the Vicar (art. 26). In the event of the death of the Bishop or his resignation from the episcopal rank, his successor, or the one temporarily taking his place (a Coadjutor with right of succession [cum futura successione], or the Vicar elected by the Chapter under article 59 for the temporary administration of the diocese), immediately forms a new Consistory, always, however, as stated above, with the consent of the government.

1804 Sept. 27 (21467); 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. XX.

30. Secretaries of the Consistories are appointed and dismissed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, from among persons of the Roman Catholic confession, upon the recommendation of the Diocesan Heads.

1804 Sept. 27 (21467) report; 1842 Jul. 17, Highest-approved staff regulations; 1856 Apr. 7, Highest-approved regulation of the Committee on Roman Catholic Church affairs. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 273

31. The other officials of the Consistorial Chancery are confirmed by the local Diocesan Head, upon the recommendation of its Secretary.

1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. XVIII.

32. Secretaries and other officials of the Consistorial Chanceries are considered to be in state service.

1804 Sept. 27 (21467); 1846 Sept. 23 (20458).

33. Secretaries attached to the Diocesan Heads for their official and private correspondence (art. 20, para. 2) are appointed directly and immediately by the Diocesan Heads themselves, who may, at their own discretion, choose them from among clergy as well.

1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. XIX.

34. Members of the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium are appointed, one from among the Bishops and the other from among the Prelates. They are appointed and dismissed by Highest decrees upon the recommendation of the Collegium, submitted by the Minister of Internal Affairs. Two candidates are presented for each vacancy.

1817 Oct. 24 (27106) § 142; 1832 Feb. 2 (5126); 1833 Jul. 1 (6296) § 83.

35. The Assessors of the Collegium are elected, each in his own diocese, by the Cathedral Chapter, every three years, from among the Prelates or Canons (art. 27) (a). — The Chapters ensure that persons elected to these offices combine knowledge of canon law with a thorough command of the Russian and Polish languages and of the state statutes (b).

(a) 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) para. 2; 1839 Mar. 15 (12122) staff regulations. — (b) 1815 Jul. 20 (25903).

36. Deans are appointed at the discretion of the Diocesan Head, preferably from among persons who have completed a course of studies at least at the diocesan Seminary.

1798 Apr. 28 (18504) para. 6; 1817 Oct. 24 (27106) §§ 144-146, 148; 1833 Jul. 1 (6296) § 83; 1842 Jul. 17, detailed staff regulations.

37. Parish priests, and Superiors and Mothers Superior of monasteries in the diocese, are appointed by its local Head (art. 16), wherever the right of patronage (jus patronatus) does not exist at all or has been temporarily suspended. Parish priests are appointed by the Diocesan Head, with the consent of the government, after preliminary examination and competition among candidates, in accordance with the canonical rules. — Superiors and Mothers Superior of monasteries are appointed according to special rules specified below in their place (art. 78 et seq.) (a).

Note. Attendant positions at churches are filled by hired persons (b).

(a) 1798 Apr. 28 (18504) para. 6; 1801 Nov. 13 (20053); 1817 Oct. 24 (27106) §§ 144-146, 148; 1832 Mar. 11 (5225); Jul. 19 (5506) para. 12; 1843 Jun. 11 (16939); 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, art. XXX; 1847 Oct. 6, order of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. — (b) 1838 Jun. 24 (11358); 1850 Jan. 11 (23817) § 5, note 3.

38. For positions of parish priests in all first- and second-class parishes, preference is given to those who have completed a course of studies at the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Academy.

1844 Dec. 14, Highest command.

39. The rank of Infulate (the right to wear the mitre during divine service in specified cases) is granted, upon the recommendation of the Diocesan Head, only with the Highest consent (a).

Note. All matters concerning appointment, dismissal, rewards, and penalties requiring Highest approval proceed to Highest consideration through the procedure defined above, in articles 8 and 10 (b).

(a) 1798 Nov. 3 (18734) para. 10; 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) para. 6; 1842 Jul. 17, detailed staff regulations; 1857 Jul. 10, Highest command. — (b) 1810 Aug. 17 (24326); 1856 Aug. 10 (30838).

40. Persons of the Roman Catholic clergy, upon their appointment as Rectors of a church or monastery, or as members of the Collegium, Consistory, or Academy, or to sit in civil government offices as deputies of this clergy (art. 55), take the oath of allegiance to the service before the civil authorities (Fundamental Laws, App. V).

1832 May 3 (5319); 1857 Dec. 31, information of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

##### CHAPTER FOUR.

Rights and duties of the authorities and offices of ecclesiastical administration.

Section One.

On the Archbishop-Metropolitan.

41. The Archbishop of Mogilev, possessing all the outward distinctions that, according to the rites of the Roman Church, belong to so preeminent a rank and office, enjoys also those rights that may be assigned to him not only in his own but also in the other dioceses of that Church, as its sole Metropolitan in the Russian Empire and the Grand Duchy of Finland (Art. 17).

1798 Apr. 28 (18504) pt. 8; cf. the enactments cited under Art. 17.

42. With respect to the other Diocesan Ordinaries, the Archbishop-Metropolitan acts within the limits of the spiritual authority assigned to him; in cases exceeding this authority, he applies to the Roman See and receives from that See authorizations, in the order established for that purpose (Art. 47, note).

1803 Dec. 13 (21078) pt. I, § 12, pt. 5; 1817 Oct. 24 (27106); 1824 May 15 (29914); 1832 Feb. 2 (5126); 1833 Jan. 24 (5931); cf. the enactments cited in the note to Art. 47.

43. In the administration of his own archdiocese the Archbishop-Metropolitan acts according to the general provisions concerning Diocesan Bishops set forth below, while in the consideration and decision of matters and cases common to all dioceses (Art. 11), as defined in article 67, he acts in accordance with the Statute of the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium, over which he presides.

Cf. the enactments cited under Arts. 44–56, 60–64, and 67–74.

Section Two.

On Diocesan Bishops.

44. Ecclesiastical justice and the administration of church affairs in each diocese belong exclusively to its Bishop, without however infringing the subordination established for him (a). He therefore has, within the bounds of his diocese, supreme oversight both of the secular and monastic clergy of his confession, and of the churches, monasteries, seminaries, and in general of all ecclesiastical institutions of the same confession and their properties (b).

(a) 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) pt. 1; 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman See, Art. XIII; cf. above in this Statute, Art. 3. — (b) 1772 Dec. 14 (13922) pt. 3; 1774 Feb. 6 (14122); 1780 Jan. 9 (14966); 1782 Jan. 17 (15326) pt. 11; 1783 Nov. 14 (15876); 1784 Apr. 17 (15982); 1798 Apr. 28 (18504) pts. 10 and 11; Nov. 3 (18734) pts. 3, 11, 16, 17, and 19; 1800 Dec. 11 (19684) pts. 8, 13, and 16; 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) pt. 5; 1832 Jul. 19 (5506) pt. 12; 1843 Jun. 11 (16939); 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman See, Arts. XXI–XXVIII.

45. The Diocesan Bishop administers the ecclesiastical affairs of his diocese with the assistance of his Suffragan Bishops (Art. 57), the Cathedral Chapter, the Consistory, the Deans, the parish rectors, and the local superiors of monasteries and schools (a); but, as the chief superior of all the ecclesiastical institutions of the Roman Catholic confession in his diocese, he is answerable to the higher government for the enforcement of the rules on oversight of the acts of these immediate superiors (b).

(a) See the enactments cited under Arts. 44, 57, 58, and others. — (b) See the enactments cited under Art. 44.

46. The Diocesan Ordinary is obliged, on the basis of the canonical rules, either personally or through others, to inspect the churches and other ecclesiastical institutions in his diocese, to eliminate abuses, and to correct morals.

Cf. the enactments cited under Arts. 85–87; 1844 May 5, order of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

47. When a Diocesan Bishop, in matters relating to the dogmas of the faith and to canonical rules, finds it necessary to obtain a higher ecclesiastical authorization exceeding his canonical power, he applies for it to the Roman See, and carries out its decisions, but only in accordance with the order established for relations with the Roman See.

Note. All Christians of the Roman Catholic confession, clerical and lay, among the subjects of the state, communicate with the Roman See on matters of their confession only through the Minister of Internal Affairs, who refers the matter to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. No bulls, briefs, or instructions of the Roman See may be put into effect in the Empire, the Kingdom of Poland, or the Grand Duchy of Finland without the authorization of His Imperial Majesty, requested by the Minister of Internal Affairs after prior verification that these acts contain nothing contrary to the state enactments and to the sacred rights and prerogatives of the Supreme Autocratic Power.

1798 Apr. 28 (18504) pts. 12 and 18; 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) pt. 3; 1803 Dec. 13 (21078); 1817 Oct. 24 (27106) § 12, pt. 5; 1824 May 15 (29914); 1829 Mar. 14, Imperial order; 1830 Mar. 10 (3522); 1832 Feb. 2 (5126); 1833 Jan. 24 (5931); 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman See, Art. XIII; 1857 Jun. 4, Imperial order.

48. Appointment to all ecclesiastical positions within a diocese, for the filling of which no special rules have been established in this Digest, is left to the discretion of the Diocesan Bishop, subject to the following rules (Art. 49 et seq.).

1817 Oct. 24 (27106) § 148.

49. Only Russian subjects may be appointed by Diocesan Ordinaries to ecclesiastical positions of their confession. The appointment of foreign clergy requires the higher authorization prescribed by the Laws on the Estates; once authorized, such clergy are obliged to take an oath of faithful service and due subject's obedience.

1780 Jan. 9 (14966); 1783 Nov. 14 (15876); 1784 Feb. 28 (15943); 1789 Nov. 26 (16820); 1795 Sept. 6 (17379) pt. 6 and (17380) pt. 5; 1798 Apr. 28 (18504) pt. 7; 1820 Mar. 13 (28198); 1844 Mar. 16, Imperial order.

50. To the office of Preacher at Cathedrals only such clergy are appointed as hold an academic theological degree; the same is observed, as far as possible, in appointing Instructors of Religion in all educational institutions and in all ecclesiastical positions in the capitals.

1833 Jul. 1 (6296) § 83; 1844 Dec. 14, Imperial order.

51. In distributing parishes according to church rules, the Diocesan Bishop retains none of them for himself in his own diocese and may not hold any in other dioceses. Nor may he, under any pretext, give more than one parish to a single person.

1801 Nov. 13 (20053) pt. 6.

52. He may not transfer or accept into his diocese any clergyman of another diocese without the prior consent of the local Diocesan Ordinary and without the knowledge of the government.

1842 Dec. 16, Imperial order.

53. The Diocesan Bishop may not, on his own authority, order a general solemn prayer service throughout the diocese in memory of any deceased private person, apart from the customary sermon at burial, the requiem, and commemoration according to the church rite (a).

Note. Laypersons may not be permitted to deliver speeches at these religious rites, either inside the church or outside it (b).

(a) 1826 Dec. 4 (726). — (b) 1836 Nov. 15 (9706).

54. It is among the duties of the Diocesan Ordinary, on the basis of the Censorship Statute, to conduct the prior review of all kinds of Roman Catholic religious books, and to appoint censors for manuscript sermons (a).

Note. In general, persons of the Roman Catholic clergy are strictly forbidden, in the sermons they deliver in churches, to touch upon political matters, even in general terms, or to publish writings on political affairs, especially those relating to the internal governance of the state (b).

(a) 1828 Apr. 22 (1979) § 23; 1832 Mar. 11 (5225); 1853 Feb. 18 (27017). — (b) 1798 Nov. 3 (18734) Art. 22; 1800 Dec. 11 (19684) pt. 19; 1832 Mar. 11 (5225) pt. 5.

55. The Diocesan Ordinary appoints permanent deputies from among the clergy under his authority to sit in the secular courts of law in civil matters relating to church and monastery properties, and in criminal matters, whenever clergy of the Roman Catholic confession are implicated.

Note. Permanent deputies are appointed, from one to four in each district (uezd), in proportion to the number of churches, the extent, and the local circumstances of the district. They are appointed preferably from among the secular clergy, but where such clergy are few, deputies may also be appointed from the monastic clergy, upon the instructions of the Diocesan Ordinary to the Superiors of the monasteries. — The office of deputy may also be entrusted to a clergyman who has studied only at a seminary and not at an academy. It may not be combined with other duties that would hinder its performance, except the office of Dean. — Deputies, upon their appointment, must, pursuant to Art. 40, take an oath of faithful service. — For investigations and court proceedings, deputies are always required from the nearest places. — The dismissal, and, in case of misconduct, the removal from office, of a deputy rests with the Diocesan Ordinary.

1810 Oct. 18 (24380); 1832 May 3 (5319); 1833 Jul. 1 (6296) § 83; 1846 Nov. 4 (20581); 1847 Dec. 16 (21804).

56. The remaining rights and duties of the Diocesan Ordinary, owing to their close connection with the rules concerning the ecclesiastical institutions subordinate to him, are set forth below, each in its proper place.

Section Three.

On Suffragan Bishops and Cathedral Chapters.

57. Suffragan Bishops assist the Diocesan Ordinary, upon his instructions, in discharging the duties entrusted to him with respect to the diocese.

See the enactments cited under Art. 18.

58. The Cathedral Chapter constitutes, in accordance with the canonical statutes of the Roman Church, the Council of the Diocesan Ordinary, assists him in affairs, and celebrates solemn divine service together with him.

See the enactments cited under Art. 19.

59. In the event of the death of a Diocesan Ordinary, or of his resignation from his office, if there is no Coadjutor Bishop with right of succession, the local Chapter, on the basis of the canonical rules, within the period fixed by them, elects a Vicar to administer the vacant diocese until the appointment of a successor to the deceased or otherwise departed Ordinary.

1798 Apr. 28 (18504) pt. 5; 1832 Mar. 11 (5225); 1842 Jan. 1 (15188) establishment; 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman See, Art. XX.

Section Four.

On Consistories.

I. On the subjects of the Consistories.

60. In diocesan administration, the following judicial and administrative matters are subject to the prior review of the local Consistory:

§ 1. Matters relating to the diocesan clergy: a) Disciplinary matters in general. However, of these matters, the less important ones, which do not entail removal from office or confinement for a longer or shorter period, are decided by the Diocesan Ordinary without the prior opinion of the Consistory, unless he himself deems it necessary to refer these matters as well, like the others, to the prior review of the Consistory. b) Disputed matters between clergymen concerning movable or immovable church property. c) Complaints and suits against clergymen, brought by clerical or lay persons alike, for injuries or damages, or for non-fulfillment of undisputed obligations, in cases where the plaintiff, to protect his rights, applies to the ecclesiastical rather than the secular authority. d) Cases concerning the invalidity of monastic vows, examined and decided according to special church rules.

§ 2. Matters relating to lay persons: matrimonial cases, certifications of the legitimacy or illegitimacy of a marriage, records of birth, records of baptism, death, and so forth.

Note 1. The first instance of ecclesiastical judgment in matrimonial and other spiritual matters is constituted by the local Diocesan Bishop, or Archbishop, together with his Consistory, on the basis of Article 61; the second instance, for matters decided in the first instance by Bishops, is constituted by the Archbishop, while for those matters that were decided by the Archbishop himself together with his Consistory acting as the first instance, it is constituted by the Bishop of one of the dioceses nearest to the archdiocese, previously designated for that purpose by His Holiness the Roman Pope. If the decisions of the two first instances of this ecclesiastical court differ, as likewise in the event of appeal, complaint, or protest, the examination of matrimonial cases is referred to the Roman See (a).

Note 2. Matrimonial cases are carried from the first instance to the second without any appeal. If the second instance renders a decision consistent with that of the first instance, and both parties are satisfied with it, the case is considered finally decided (b).

§ 3. Mixed matters: cases in which church penance is to be imposed for some crime or offense, after the case concerning it has been decided in the secular courts.

§ 4. Matters of an economic nature: the schedule or estimate of sums allotted for the maintenance of the clergy, the verification of expenditures and accounts relating to these sums, matters concerning the repair or construction of new churches, chapels, and so forth.

Note. In addition, the Consistory is obliged to draw up lists of the clergy and parishioners of its diocese, and to circulate circulars and other announcements that do not relate to the administrative affairs of the diocese (v).

(a) 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman See, Art. XIV; 1848 Nov. 29, special agreement with the same See. — (b) 1798 Jun. 22 (18560). — (v) 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman See, Art. XIV.

61. The above-named matters (Art. 60) are decided by the Bishop after their examination in the Consistory. The voice of the Consistory is, however, merely advisory. The Bishop is not obliged to explain the grounds of his decisions even where his opinion should not accord with the conclusion of the Consistory.

1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman See, Art. XV.

62. The remaining matters of the diocese, which are called administrative and which include matters of conscience (casus conscientiae, fori interni), as well as, as stated above (Art. 60, § I, pt. a), those disciplinary matters that entail only minor corrective penalties or pastoral admonitions, depend exclusively on the authority of the Diocesan Ordinary and are decided at his own discretion.

*Ibid., Art. XVI.*

63. In disciplinary matters, appeals to the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium are permitted against decisions ordering removal from office and, in general, any significant penalty (Art. 60, § 1, pt. a); but those sentenced to such punishment in the diocese may not leave their place of residence without the permission of the authorities.

1798 Jun. 22 (18560); 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) pt. 4.

64. Criminal cases and civil cases, other than those indicated above, are not subject to diocesan jurisdiction: their investigation and trial are conducted according to the general rules of the secular courts, with the participation only of deputies of the clergy (a).

Note. If a clergyman is accused of violating the prohibitions specified in Articles 4 or 5, he is likewise subject to the general criminal court (b).

(a) 1798 Nov. 3 (18734) pt. 4; 1800 Dec. 11 (19684) Art. 4; 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) Arts. 1, 8; 1806 Dec. 13 (22395); 1807 May 15 (22528); 1810 Oct. 18 (24380). — (b) 1840 Jan. 27 (13116).

II. On the conduct of cases in the Consistories.

65. The order of conducting, deciding, and executing cases in the Consistories, the accounting of matters and sums, and the duties and responsibilities of those serving therein are determined by the general rules established for the civil service and by a special instruction of the Minister of Internal Affairs.

1804 Sept. 27 (21467); 1856 Apr. 7, Imperially confirmed resolution of the Committee on the Affairs of the Roman Catholic Church.

66. In cases of particular importance, such as: the delivery to the proper parties of ecclesiastical orders accompanying Imperial manifestos or decrees for publication and reading in the churches, likewise the forms for the commemoration of the Imperial family at the litanies, tables and additions to these forms, transmission is made through the rural post, by means of the District Courts (Zemsky Sud), the Stanovoi Pristavs (district police officers), and the sotskys (village constables).

1826 Nov. 24 (694); 1837 Jun. 3 (10306) §§ 4–6; Jun. 3 (10307) § 8.

Section Five.

On the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium.

I. On the subjects of the Collegium.

67. In the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium are concentrated, for the entire administration of the Roman Catholic clergy, the following matters:

1) Complete records of all Roman Catholic churches, monasteries, clergy, educational and other ecclesiastical institutions, and movable and immovable properties (a).

2) Supervision of the proper and successful conduct of business in the Diocesan Consistories, review of their decisions, and measures of correction upon appeals, complaints, and private grievances or protests, except in matrimonial and other spiritual matters (b).

3) Examination and submission to the higher government of all kinds of proposals of the diocesan authorities relating to the general good of the state together with that of the church (v).

4) Matters concerning the admission of those wishing to enter the monastic state (g) <...>.

5) Management of the auxiliary fund of the Roman Catholic clergy in the Empire, according to special rules on this subject (e); likewise management of a special repair fund allocated for the construction and repair of churches, and the use of only its interest for these purposes, at the Collegium's own discretion, as loans or as non-returnable grants (zh).

6) Audit of the accounts of the auxiliary and repair funds (pt. 5), and audit of the accounts of the use of all sums disbursed for the maintenance of the Roman Catholic clergy from the state treasury. Both audits are conducted in accordance with the rules established in the General Accounting Statute and in the Accounting Statute of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, under the special supervision of that Ministry (z).

II. On the order of conducting, deciding, and executing the affairs of the Collegium.

68. The Collegium meets in session three times a week, on the days appointed for that purpose, and in summer, from June 15 to August 15, only once a week.

1844 Apr. 29, Imperial order; 1852 Feb. 25 (26023).

69. All matters of the Collegium are conducted according to the general provisions concerning collegial institutions, and are decided in its session by a majority of votes, according to church rules. In the event of a tie, the side is preferred with which the presiding Archbishop-Metropolitan agrees (Art. 21).

1801 Nov. 13 (20053) intro. and pt. 8.

70. Matters coming before the Collegium under Article 67, pt. 2, from the Mogilev archdiocese (Art. 12), if they were decided personally by the Archbishop-Metropolitan, as Diocesan Ordinary (Art. 43), before being submitted to the Collegium, are decided in the Collegium without his presence.

1801 Nov. 13 (20053); 1803 Oct. 26 (21010).

71. Matters requiring higher authorization, or the consideration and resolution of other state authorities and offices, are submitted by the Collegium to the Minister of Internal Affairs, who gives these matters their proper course, appending to each his own conclusion. Excepted from this are judicial matters: in these the Collegium applies directly to the Governing Senate and to the Minister of Justice.

1817 Oct. 24 (27106) §§ 131, 132; 1832 Feb. 2 (5126).

72. In the event of disagreement with a decision of the Collegium, the Minister of Internal Affairs presents to it his opinion. If the Collegium finds any inconveniences in carrying out this opinion, it reports them to the Minister, and thereafter proceeds according to his resolution.

1817 Oct. 24 (27106) § 133; 1832 Feb. 2 (5126).

73. The Procurator attached to the Collegium is obliged to submit to the Minister of Internal Affairs memoranda and reports on matters decided in the administrative sphere, and is answerable to the Minister for their prompt and proper delivery and for oversight in this regard. If the Procurator observes anything to the contrary and the Collegium does not accept his proposal, he submits his protest to the Minister (a).

Note. During the period from June 15 to August 15, when the Collegium sits only once a week (Art. 68), the Procurator has the right to open packets addressed to it that arrive on non-session days and to forward them to the Chancery for preparation for report to the session of the Collegium (b).

(a) 1817 Oct. 24 (27106) § 131; 1832 Feb. 2 (5126). — (b) 1844 Apr. 29, Imperial order.

74. The Collegium communicates with the Governing Senate by reports and receives decrees from it, and with the Ministers of Internal Affairs and Justice by representations and receives proposals from them (a); it sends decrees to the Diocesan Ordinaries and Consistories and in general to the offices and persons subordinate to it, and receives from them representations and reports (b); with the provincial establishments it communicates by official communications (v).

(a) 1803 Oct. 26 (21010); 1817 Oct. 24 (27106) § 133; 1832 Feb. 2 (5126); cf. 1845 Jan. 2 (18580) Arts. 176–180. — (b) 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) pt. 1. — (v) Cf. 1845 Jan. 2 (18580) Art. 180.

On the parish clergy.

75. The immediate administration of each church and the performance of the religious rites in its parish belong to the Parish Priest (a).

Among the duties of the Parish Priest is, among other things, the reading in church, after the conclusion of divine service, of Imperial manifestos and decrees issued with the words "to be proclaimed to the people," as well as of those enactments and instructions of the secular authorities that it may be deemed necessary to make most widely known among the people, and concerning the reading of which in the churches the ecclesiastical authority, in relation to the provincial authority, shall make arrangements for all parish churches.

Note. The special duties of priests regarding the administration of parish churches in the settlements of foreign colonists in the Empire are set forth in the Statute on Colonies.

Section Eight.

On certain general duties

and rights of the Roman Catholic clergy.

89. In the dioceses, the Roman Catholic clergy, secular and monastic, strictly observe the rules of subordination to their immediate and general diocesan authority; it is obliged to carry out with complete exactness all lawful orders and instructions of these authorities (a).

Note. In sermons on the duties of a subject toward the Sovereign, the clergy follow special instructions issued for this purpose (b).

(a) 1798 Nov. 3 (18734) pt. 2; 1800 Dec. 11 (19684) pt. 2; see also the enactments cited under Arts. 45 and 46. — (b) 1832 Jul. 26 (5521).

90. No one belonging to the Roman Catholic clergy may leave his place of residence or service without a permit from his proper authority; passports for distant absences are issued by the Provincial Governors, upon the request of the Diocesan Ordinaries, for all provinces.

Note 1. The Minister of Internal Affairs has the right, on his own authority, to authorize Diocesan Ordinaries to make temporary absences to other dioceses on church business and to grant them, as well as members of the Ecclesiastical Collegium and members of the Consistories, leaves of up to four months without retention of salary.

Note 2. Permits are issued to members of the monastic clergy only with the consent of the Archbishop or Bishop to whose diocese they belong. In case of overstaying their permits, they are sent back to their Diocesan Ordinary under escort.

1800 May, undated (19437); 1830 Oct. 15 (3794); 1831 May 6 (4544) pt. 12; 1832 Feb. 2 (5126); 1856 Dec. 4 (31214).

91. All Roman Catholic diocesan administrations, and the cathedral, parish, and monastery clergy, as well as those serving in various branches of the civil, military, and naval administration, receive maintenance from the state treasury and from the interest of a special fund under the Minister of Internal Affairs, according to the establishments and other regulations, in a manner proportionate to the needs of the offices and persons and befitting the rank and standing of each (a). No deductions are made herein for hospital purposes (b). Monasteries, moreover, are given, by the department of state properties, servants from among peasants of non-Orthodox confession, exempted from taxes (see Statute on Taxes), or special sums for their hire (v).

Note. On the basis of the note to Article 47, the Roman Catholic clergy may not remit its income abroad without Imperial authorization (g).

92. In the event that the government assigns positions or temporary commissions entailing travel from one place to another, clergy of the Roman Catholic confession are paid, in addition to their permanent salaries, travel money (progony) from the state treasury: 1) to the Archbishop-Metropolitan, for twelve horses; 2) to a Diocesan Bishop and a Member of the Ecclesiastical Collegium, for ten horses; 3) to a Suffragan or Vicar Bishop, for eight horses; 4) to an Assessor of the Ecclesiastical Collegium and to an Official or Chairman of a Consistory, for six horses; 5) to a Vice-Official, an Assessor of a Consistory, a Prelate, a Canon, the Rector of the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Academy, and a Visitor, for four horses; 6) to Visitors of churches and Superiors of monasteries, priests of the secular and monastic clergy, for three horses, and to clerks (prichetniki) for two horses.

Note. Travel money is also paid for the journeys of seminary students from their own to another diocese for their ordination as priests, when there is no local Bishop, and for the dispatch of clergy, in case of misconduct, to monasteries for correction.

93. To persons detailed as deputies to attend investigations or courts (Art. 55, note), travel money is likewise disbursed from the state treasury, upon the requisitions of the secular courts and officials and with the authorization of the local Treasury Chamber.

94. To those detailed by order of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to places distant from their permanent residence, per diem money is paid from the treasury, in addition to travel money, at sixty kopecks silver per day each (a). — In the Tiraspol diocese, whenever the religious needs of the Roman Catholics there <...> require that the Bishop send priests on circuit to attend to them, the necessary sums for travel expenses and the maintenance of those sent are allocated by the government (b).

96. Those serving in the land or naval military department have the same right to pensions and one-time benefits as clergy of other Christian confessions serving in the same department (a). Likewise, the regulations existing in the educational branch of the Ministry of Public Education concerning the granting of pensions and one-time benefits to teachers are extended to Instructors of Religion of clerical rank of the Roman Catholic confession, in the same way as to those of other Christian confessions in educational institutions of the same department. These pensions or benefits are granted to them with the consent of their ecclesiastical authority, independently of whatever provision they may receive through the ecclesiastical department, but only to those Instructors of Religion who were in actual teaching service under Imperially confirmed establishments, or under arrangements Imperially approved (b).

Note. To clergymen of the Roman Catholic confession, as likewise to clergymen of other foreign Christian confessions, and, if the latter have families, to their families as well, for long and blameless service at state-owned mining works and similar institutions, pensions and one-time benefits may be granted in proportion to the salaries paid to them, when it is impossible to provide for them by other means, upon separate representations for each case by the Ministers and Chief Administrators. In this they are not subject to the rules and categories of the General Pension Statute, except for the division of the pensions of clergymen not of the Roman Catholic confession between their widows and children, and the discontinuance of the payment of their shares (v).

97. Prelates, Canons, and other clergy have the right, by virtue of their academic ranks, to wear special (distinctive) crosses, bearing upon them the image of the Russian state emblem.

1832 Nov. 26 (5773); 1833 Jul. 1 (6296) § 84.

98. The most zealous and well-intentioned priests of the Roman Catholic confession have the right, like the clergy of other foreign Christian confessions, to be awarded pectoral crosses, specially established for this purpose.

Note. On the front of this cross is depicted the Crucifixion, and on the reverse the inscription: "To the pastor who gives his flock an example by word and by life. Established in the Pious Reign of the Great Sovereign Emperor Nicholas I, May 26, 1843."

1843 May 26, Imperial order.

99. Beyond these distinctions (Art. 97 and 98), clergy of the Roman Catholic confession may be admitted to the Russian Imperial and Tsarist orders.

100. The aged and those afflicted with incurable diseases are cared for in staffed monasteries. They receive heating and lighting from the monasteries, and from the auxiliary fund of the Roman Catholic clergy (Art. 129) each of them is paid, according to merit, from fifty to one hundred rubles in silver annually.

1832 Jul. 19 (5506) para. 11; 1843 Oct. 30, Imperial Command.

101. The remaining personal and property rights of the Roman Catholic clergy, secular and monastic, are set forth in the Laws on Estates (Status).

#### SECTION TWO. ON THE ADMINISTRATION OF ECCLESIASTICAL EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS.

102. For the education of Roman Catholic youth wishing to devote themselves to the clerical estate, Seminaries have been established in the Roman Catholic dioceses, and in St. Petersburg a Theological Academy of this confession.

1842 Jun. 9 (15729); 1843 Jan. 19 (16464); Nov. 19 (17341); 1848 Nov. 29 (22766); 1852 Nov. 6 (26748); 1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, Art. VII, XXI–XXIX.

103. The Roman Catholic Theological Academy is established for the higher education of clergy destined for the principal offices of the Roman Catholic Hierarchy in the Empire.

1833 Jul. 1 (6296).

104. To the Bishops belongs the supreme administration over matters of upbringing, learning, and internal discipline in the Seminaries of their dioceses, on the basis of canonical rules.

<...>

1847 Jul. 22, treaty with the Roman Court, Art. IX and XXI.

105. The choice of Rectors, Inspectors, Professors, or Teachers of diocesan Seminaries is left to the Bishop. Before their appointment he must satisfy himself that, as regards the civil conduct of these persons, their selection for these positions will be approved by the government. If the Bishop deems it necessary to remove the Rector or Inspector or any of the Professors or Teachers, he shall immediately, and on the aforesaid basis, appoint a successor for him. He is entitled to suspend temporarily the teaching of one or several courses of study in his Seminary. In the event that he finds it necessary to suspend all courses of study at once and to send the students back to their parents, he shall report this without delay to the government.

*Ibid., Art. XXII.*

106. The Archbishop-Metropolitan of Mogilev enjoys the same authority in respect of the St. Petersburg Roman Catholic Theological Academy as each Bishop enjoys in respect of his diocesan Seminary. He alone presides over it and has supreme administration of it. The Council or administration of the Academy has only an advisory character.

*Ibid., Art. XXIII.*

107. The choice of the Rector, Inspector, and Professors of the Academy is made by the Archbishop, upon the recommendation of the Academy Council. The provisions contained in Article 105 apply equally to these choices.

*Ibid., Art. XXIV.*

108. Professors and Adjuncts of Theological sciences are always chosen from among ecclesiastical persons. Other teachers may be chosen from among lay persons professing the Roman Catholic faith, preferably from among those who have completed a course of study at one of the higher educational institutions of the Empire and have been awarded academic degrees.

*Ibid., Art. XXV; 1851 Mar. 23, Imperial Command; 1857 Dec. 31, information of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.*

109. Confessors of the students, both of the Seminaries and of the Academy, take no part whatsoever in overseeing the maintenance of internal discipline in the institution; they are chosen by the Bishop or Archbishop, as the case may be.

1847 Jul. 27, treaty with the Roman Court, Art. XXVI.

110. The Archbishop, in consultation with the Diocesan Bishops, determines once and for all how many students are to be sent from each diocese to the academy.

*Ibid., Art. XXVII.*

111. The program of studies for the Seminaries is drawn up by the Bishops, and for the Academy by the Archbishop, after prior consultation with the members of his Academic Council.

*Ibid., Art. XXVIII.*

#### SECTION THREE. ON THE ADMINISTRATION OF PROPERTY BELONGING TO ECCLESIASTICAL INSTITUTIONS.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

General provisions.

112. All monasteries, churches, and other ecclesiastical institutions of the Roman Catholic confession own property, both movable and immovable (except property populated by serfs), lawfully come to them and coming to them by grant, donation, and other means of acquisition (see the Civil Laws), as well as the increments thereof, on the basis of the general provisions on this subject.

Note. Collections made in churches on Sundays and feast days, and offerings in favor of the churches, as distinct from the Priests, made in the performance of religious rites (jura stolae), are likewise reckoned as part of the property of the churches or, as the case may be, of the monasteries.

1769 Feb. 12 (13252) paras. 25, 26, 27; 1772 Dec. 14 (13922) para. 3; 1774 Feb. 6 (14122); 1786 Feb. 26 (16333); 1793 Jul. 11 (17141) Art. VIII; 1798 Nov. 3 (18734) Art. 5, 6, 11, 14; 1800 Dec. 11 (19684) paras. 5, 6; 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) para. 7; 1832 Jul. 19 (5506); 1841 Dec. 25 (15153); 1843 May 10 (16829); 1844 Feb. 28 (17673).

113. Direct management of the property of each monastery and church belongs to their Superiors, under the oversight of the local diocesan authority, but at the same time this property, like that of other ecclesiastical institutions, remains under the protection and oversight of the government.

1782 Jan. 17 (15326) paras. 9, 12; 1798 Nov. 3 (18734) Art. 5, 6; 1800 Dec. 11 (19684) paras. 5, 6, 9, 12; 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) paras. 6, 7, 8.

114. Monasteries may not newly acquire any immovable property without Imperial authorization. Acquisition of immovable property for churches in the amount of up to five thousand rubles is authorized by the Minister of Internal Affairs, while for acquisitions above five thousand rubles Imperial authorization is likewise sought.

1786 Feb. 26 (16333); 1810 May 29 (24246); 1819 Jan. 4 (27622); 1852 Jan. 28 (25944) Art. 44; 1853 Feb. 18 and 1856 Jun. 22, Imperial Commands; 1857 Dec. 31, information of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

115. Monasteries and churches are not forbidden to accept sums of money bequeathed to them by testament. In this connection, no inheritance duties are levied on capital designated for the construction or restoration of the monasteries or churches themselves, or for charitable institutions established at them, as distinct from capital for the private benefit of monastics or the parish clergy.

Note. Acceptance of bequeathed and donated capital and objects for the benefit of ecclesiastical institutions is authorized by the Minister of Internal Affairs for any sum. He reports each donation exceeding ten thousand rubles separately to the Emperor, and reports the rest every half year.

1832 Dec. 20 (5840); 1857 Jun. 4, Imperial Command.

116. Churches receive by law one-fourth part of the movable property remaining after the death, intestate, of clergy who had been attached to them.

Note. The inheritance by monasteries of the property of monks and nuns is set forth in the Laws on Estates.

1772 Aug. 16 (13850); 1793 Mar. 27 (17108); 1796 Dec. 12 (17634); 1801 Sep. 9 (20004); cf. Laws on Estates, Art. 356, 357.

117. All buildings of churches, monasteries, ecclesiastical-educational, and charitable institutions, except those let out for rent, are exempt from military billeting and from all police and municipal obligations, except for the repair and upkeep of pavement cleanliness and the lighting of street lamps.

1801 Nov. 13 (20053) para. 7; 1846 Mar. 6 (19805) § 3, para. 2; 1855 Jun. 13 (29408). DOCUMENTS 287

118. The property of ecclesiastical institutions may not be alienated or mortgaged without special Imperial consent; only property not needed by the churches and their dilapidated buildings may be sold with the authorization of the Governing Senate and other authorities.

Note. The sale of unneeded immovable property and dilapidated buildings belonging to Roman Catholic churches is authorized as follows: by the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium up to three hundred rubles; by the Department of Ecclesiastical Affairs of Foreign Confessions up to one thousand rubles; by the Minister of Internal Affairs up to five thousand rubles; and above this amount, for any sum, by the Governing Senate. The sale of unneeded movable property is authorized by the same institutions as follows: by the Collegium up to six hundred rubles; by the Department up to two thousand rubles; by the Minister up to ten thousand rubles; and above this, for any sum, by the Governing Senate. Confirmation of the sale itself, of both immovable and movable property, is left to the said offices and authorities within the limits set for the confirmation of public auctions; in this connection the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium enjoys the rights of provincial offices (see the Civil Laws).

1798 Nov. 3 (18734) Art. 6; 1800 Dec. 11 (19684) Art. 6; 1801 Nov. 13 (20053) para. 7; 1822 May 31 (29060); 1831 May 6 (4544); 1852 Jan. 28 (25944) Art. 42.

119. Lands of ecclesiastical institutions may be let for rent or lease with the authorization of the Diocesan Superior, for a term of years fixed under the Civil Laws, on the condition, among others, that any building erected on them by the lessee shall, upon expiration of the term, belong to the owner of the land, albeit with some compensation to the lessee fixed in advance by agreement (a).

Note. The exchange of church or endowment (fundusz) lands for municipal or private lands is authorized by the Minister of Internal Affairs (b).

(a) 1832 Nov. 1 (5711). — (b) 1831 May 6 (4544); 1857 Jun. 4, Imperial Command.

120. Monetary capital belonging privately to an ecclesiastical institution must, for its increase and use for its benefit, be deposited in state credit institutions. But if the authorities of that institution find it possible to place this capital more advantageously in private hands, under reliable security, then, with the authorization of the Minister of Internal Affairs, it may be lent out in this manner as well.

Note. Regarding the general capital, known as the auxiliary fund, held in common by the ecclesiastical institutions of the Roman Catholic confession, provision is made below (Art. 129 et seq.). — Interest on church capital is paid by the credit institutions three months after the deposit.

1829 Mar. 30 (2787); May 28 (2892); 1832 Aug. 2 (5539).

121. The use of capital privately belonging to ecclesiastical institutions, and of all sums designated for the maintenance of the Roman Catholic clergy, is exempt from audit by the State Comptroller, but is subject to accounting before the Ecclesiastical Collegium (Art. 67, para. 6), under the oversight of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

1842 Jan. 28 (15251a); 1844 Oct. 23, Imperial Command.

122. Suits and litigation concerning the property of ecclesiastical institutions with various other institutions and private persons, except for the matters specified in Article 60, § 1, are conducted and decided in the general courts, according to the rules concerning treasury property, with deputies from the ecclesiastical side present.

See the General Provincial Institution and the Statute of Civil Judicial Procedure; 1840 Jul. 12 (13658); Oct. 15 (13866).

##### CHAPTER TWO.

Special provisions.

I. On the administration of church property.

123. Church Superiors are obliged to keep intact the property belonging to the churches, not to combine it with their own property, and to render the established account thereof, in its administration and use, to the appropriate authority.

1803 Dec. 23 (21100).

124. In the details of economic administration of church property, where no special rules have been laid down, Church Superiors are guided by the regulation appended to this article on the administration of the property of the St. Petersburg Roman Catholic Church of St. Catherine.

1772 Dec. 14 (13922) para. 3; 1774 Feb. 6 (14122); 1823 Aug. 13 (29586).

125. Regarding the construction and repair of Roman Catholic churches, the following rules are observed:

1) Roman Catholic churches may be newly built only where this is required either by growth of the population, or by the excessively large extent of existing parishes (Art. 14) and difficulty of communications (a).

Note. Within a small area, a church parish having one Priest must consist of no fewer than one hundred parishioner households (b).

2) Persons or societies wishing to build a new church (para. 1) are obliged to apply with a petition to the local provincial authority, which, after communicating with the appropriate diocesan authorities of the Orthodox and Roman Catholic confessions, must satisfy itself that there are no obstacles to authorizing the construction, and communicate this information together with its opinion to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, for final consideration and disposition on the basis of the Building Statute (v).

<...>

4) The repair of churches and the construction of new ones in place of those that have become dilapidated, or that have been destroyed by some unfortunate occurrence, are carried out with the authorization of the ecclesiastical authority. This rule extends also to the so-called filial churches of the Roman Catholic confession and to chapels (kaplitsy) existing with the authorization of the government (d).

5) The repair of churches, once duly authorized, is carried out without hindrance at the expense of the communities or of private persons wishing to bear the costs themselves. If their means are insufficient, they may apply to the government with a petition for assistance (e).

<...>

6) The establishment of domestic chapels and portable altars is permitted for persons who have earned a right to special respect, and who, while devoted to the House of God, cannot attend church owing to illness or advanced age. Authorization for this is sought in the same manner as prescribed above, in paragraph 2, for the construction of new churches (z). DOCUMENTS 289

Note. The remaining rules on the construction of churches are set forth in the Building Statute. Penalties imposed for violation of the rules established regarding the construction of churches are set forth in the Statute on Punishments (i).

XXXI. — (b) 1832 Jul. 19 (5506) para. 5. — (v) 1782 Apr. 8 (15379) Art. 58; 1828 Oct. 19 (2358); 1832 Feb. 2 (5126); 1837 Jun. 3 (10303) § 88; 1845 Jan. 2 (18580) Art. 3. <...> (d) 1856 Dec. 10 (31240). — (e) Ibid.; 1847 Jul. 2, treaty with the Roman Court, Art. XXXI. <...> (z) 1846 Aug. 27 (20365). — (i) 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) Art. 1350–1352.

III. On the administration of the auxiliary fund

of the Roman Catholic clergy.

129. In addition to the repair fund and the capital privately belonging to Roman Catholic ecclesiastical institutions, a special fund known as the auxiliary fund is maintained, out of interest, in state credit institutions or in private hands, intended for meeting the essential needs of poor Roman Catholic churches, monasteries, schools, and other institutions of public benefit, as well as other expenses established by law in connection with the Roman Catholic ecclesiastical administration.

See the enactments cited in the following articles.

130. The sources from which this auxiliary fund is formed are determined by special rules (a).

Note. The tithe collection, where it is levied for parish churches under the former rules, is likewise included in this fund (b).

(a) 1822 Nov. 26 (29227); 1829 May 28 (2892); 1832 Jul. 19 (5506) para. 9; 1843 Oct. 30, Imperial Command. — (b) 1808 Mar. 14, Imperial Command; 1825 Feb. 16 (30231); 1828 Jul. 30 (2190); 1843 Dec. 15 (17403).

131. Subsidies charged to the auxiliary fund (Art. 129) must be paid only out of the interest received on it, without ever touching the capital itself. These subsidies are authorized, upon representations of the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium, by the Minister of Internal Affairs up to nine hundred rubles in silver, and above that sum, with Imperial consent (a). But if a subsidy is sought for the repair or construction of church buildings and other buildings of the ecclesiastical department, the Minister of Internal Affairs may authorize disbursement on his own authority up to ten thousand rubles (b).

132. The auxiliary fund is under the authority of the Roman Catholic Ecclesiastical Collegium. All certificates of credit institutions for the deposits of this fund are kept there. New deposits are consolidated into a single sum every three years.

### BOOK TWO. ON THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL AFFAIRS OF CHRISTIANS OF THE PROTESTANT CONFESSION.

#### SECTION ONE. STATUTE OF THE EVANGELICAL LUTHERAN CHURCH.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

On doctrine.

134. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in the Russian Empire professes a doctrine founded on the Prophetic and Apostolic writings of the Old and New Testament, and, as Symbolic books expounding them, recognizes the Apostles', Nicene, and Athanasian Creeds, the Unaltered Augsburg Confession, and the other works included in the collection known as the Liber Concordiae.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 1.

135. No member of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in the Empire may permit himself to disseminate, orally or in writing, opinions contrary to the doctrine of this Church.

*Ibid., § 2.*

136. Evangelical Lutheran Preachers, upon entering office, are bound by oath to preach and teach in accordance with the rules of their Church.

*Ibid., § 3.*

137. Professors and Teachers of the Law of God, Church Law, Church History, and all branches of Theology in educational institutions established for the education of Lutheran youth must belong to the Evangelical Lutheran Church, and likewise, upon entering office, are bound by oath to instruct and teach in accordance with the rules of their Church.

*Ibid., § 4.*

138. Members of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in the Empire must carefully refrain from any violation of the proper respect due to other faiths freely professed in the Empire, on the basis of the general state enactments, and especially from proselytism, which is strictly forbidden by these laws.

*Ibid., § 5.*

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On divine worship.

Section One.

On public worship.

139. In all Evangelical Lutheran parishes in the Empire, public worship, with singing, preaching, and prayer, is to be performed on Sundays, feast days, and certain other days specially designated for the purpose.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 6. DOCUMENTS 291

140. The order of public worship, as well as the other church rites and customs which are to be observed in the Evangelical Lutheran churches in the Empire, are set forth in detail in the special service book of these churches, called the Agenda. Changes in liturgical provisions are permitted only with the authorization of the higher authority, in the manner established.

Note. The service book published in 1832, together with the Statute of the Evangelical Lutheran Church and the Instruction to its clergy, under the title Agenda, does not form part of this Digest.

*Ibid., § 7.*

141. The pericopes (selected passages of Holy Scripture) fixed, prior to the promulgation of this Statute in 1832, as texts for sermons must in general continue to serve as the basis for sermons, as before. Local Consistories may, however, sometimes, with the authorization of the General Consistory, designate other texts for sermons.

*Ibid., § 8.*

142. In the Evangelical Lutheran churches in the Empire, besides Sundays, the following days are celebrated: two days for the Nativity of Christ (December 25 and 26), New Year's Day (January 1), the Epiphany of the Lord (January 6), the Annunciation (March 25), Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, the first and second days of Easter Week, the Ascension of the Lord, two days for the feast of the Descent of the Holy Spirit, the Nativity of the Forerunner (June 24), the day of general repentance and prayer (the Wednesday after the Sunday of Invocavit), the harvest festival (on the first Sunday after the day of St. Michael the Archangel), Reformation Day (October 19/31, or the first Sunday thereafter), the day of commemoration of those who died during that year (Todtenfeier), on the last Sunday of the Church Year (Kirchenjahr), and finally the day of the consecration of the church (Kirchweihfest), where the custom of celebrating it already exists, or where the parishioners wish to introduce it.

Note. When the Annunciation falls during Holy Week, or on one of the first two days of Easter Week, in the former case it is celebrated on Palm Sunday, and in the latter, on the Tuesday of Easter Week.

*Ibid., § 9.*

143. In addition to the church feasts, in all Evangelical Lutheran churches in Russia the birthdays and name days of the Sovereign Emperor, the Sovereign Empress, the Heir to the Throne the Sovereign Tsesarevich Grand Duke, and other days, are celebrated as indicated in a special schedule drawn up annually by the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

*Ibid., § 10.*

144. Where, on certain other days during the week as well, sermons and hours of prayer have been established, this arrangement is to continue to be strictly observed as before (1832 Dec. 28). Moreover, special hours of prayer and sermons during the week must be appointed in all Evangelical Lutheran churches, at least for the period of Lent, for contemplation of the sufferings of our Lord Jesus Christ.

*Ibid., § 11.*

145. As to the number of sermons to be delivered on the days appointed for that purpose, and the appointment of hours for the beginning of the service, each church must conform to the rules that existed in it prior to December 28, 1832. Changes to these are made only by order of, or with the authorization of, the local Consistories, which, for any proposed change of this kind, seek the consent of the General Consistory, which in turn reports the decision it has made to the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

*Ibid., § 12.*

146. During public worship, only such sacred hymns are sung as have, with the approval of the higher authority, been included either in the collection of church hymns (Gesangbuch) common to all Evangelical Lutheran parishes in the Empire, or in the special collection for each Consistorial district. Exceptions to this rule are permitted in special cases with the authorization of the local Consistories.

*Ibid., § 13.*

147. Catechization (Katechisationen) and examination of young people and other parishioners in knowledge of the Law of God, where these have been established, must be carried out as before (1832 Dec. 28). This custom is to be introduced gradually into the other parishes as well.

*Ibid., § 14.*

148. During public worship in the churches, proper order, silence, and reverence must be observed in all respects. Violators of this rule are subject to punishment under the laws.

*Ibid., § 15.*

Section Two.

On prayer in the home.

149. Every head of household has the right to appoint, for himself and his family, a time for common domestic prayer, but without in any way hindering anyone from attending public worship.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 16.

150. Private prayer gatherings going beyond the bounds of family or common domestic prayer are permitted only with the authorization of the Consistory and with the knowledge of the local civil authority. In this connection the following rules must be observed: 1) that at these gatherings no one shall have the right to preach (freie Vorträge zu halten) or to administer the Holy Sacraments, and that all their proceedings shall be limited to the reading of Holy Scripture without any commentary, or to the reading of discourses of religious content approved by the Consistories, likewise without any additions or commentary, and to the singing of sacred hymns, or the recitation of prayers, also reviewed and approved by the Consistories; 2) that these gatherings shall not be appointed during the time of public worship and shall in no case become an occasion for schisms objectionable within Christian society, or for any violation of church or civil order.

*Ibid., § 17.*

##### CHAPTER THREE.

On the Performance of the Sacraments and Other Sacred Rites.

Section One.

On the performance of the sacraments and other sacred rites in general.

151. The sacraments and other sacred rites designated in this chapter of the Evangelical Lutheran Church may be performed only by Preachers properly appointed to this office. Excepted from this are only baptism in case of necessity and burial in certain instances.

1832, Dec. 28 (5870) § 18.

152. In performing the sacraments and other sacred rites of the Evangelical Lutheran Church, every Preacher is obliged to follow the prescriptions of the Agenda (Art. 140).

*Ibid., § 19.*

Section Two.

On Holy Baptism.

153. All infants born alive and in a fully formed state (hinlaenglich ausgebildete) of parents of the Evangelical Lutheran confession must be baptized according to the order established for this confession, within the first eight days, or at the very latest not later than six weeks after their birth.

Note. Exceptions to this rule are permitted only for special reasons worthy of respect, which must in every instance be explained to the parish Preacher.

1832, Dec. 28 (5870) § 20.

154. If the parents, or, in their absence, the nearest relatives, without sufficient cause and despite the Preacher's admonition, allow the six-week period fixed by Article 153 for the baptism of an infant to pass, then for this purpose, and only in this case, the Consistory appoints a special guardian, who is obliged immediately to bring the infant to the holy font.

*Ibid., § 21.*

155. Baptism must preferably be performed in church and, if possible, on a day when public worship is held. It may, however, also be performed in a private house.

*Ibid., § 22.*

156. The sacrament of holy baptism must be performed by the Preacher of the parish to which the infant's parents belong, or of that in which they reside.

*Ibid., § 23.*

157. Godparents at holy baptism, whose names are announced to the Preacher beforehand, must belong to one of the Christian confessions, have received Holy Communion, and be at least fifteen years of age.

*Ibid., § 24.*

158. In the Baltic governorates, Evangelical Lutheran Preachers perform, observing the same order, holy baptism also over the illegitimate children of mothers of the Evangelical Protestant confession, with the latter's consent, as well as over abandoned or foundling infants whose parents are unknown (see the Statute on the Prevention of Crimes, Section I).

*Ibid., § 25.*

<...>

160. If an infant is so weak that it appears likely to die before the Preacher's arrival, and likewise if there is no Evangelical Protestant Preacher near the place of its birth who could perform the rite of baptism over it within the legal period (Art. 153), or in other extraordinary cases, the performance of so-called baptism in case of necessity is permitted.

*Ibid., § 27.*

161. To perform baptism of this kind (Art. 160) it is sufficient that a devout Christian, whether male or female, pouring pure water mixed with nothing else over the newborn infant, pronounce over it the following words: "In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, you are baptized, infant NN," and thereupon, commending the newborn to the protection of the Almighty, bless it and read over it the Lord's Prayer: Our Father.

*Ibid., § 28.*

162. The infant's parents and the person by whom baptism in case of necessity was performed must immediately inform the parish Preacher, or, if his place of residence is very distant, another nearby Preacher, or a Probst.

*Ibid., § 29.*

163. Baptism performed in case of necessity must, as soon as circumstances allow, be confirmed by the parish Preacher; and if in performing it the rules set forth in Article 161 were not observed, the infant is to be baptized by him according to the established order.

*Ibid., § 30.*

Section Three.

On Confirmation.

164. Young men and young women belonging to the Evangelical Lutheran Church must, before receiving Holy Communion, be instructed in the Law of God and duly confirmed.

1832, Dec. 28 (5870) § 31.

165. The basis of the instruction of Evangelical Lutheran youth preceding confirmation must be Luther's Small Catechism.

*Ibid., § 32.*

166. The rite of confirmation is performed on young persons of both sexes not earlier than fifteen and not later than eighteen years of age. Exceptions to this rule are permitted only for special reasons, with the authorization of the Consistory.

*Ibid., § 33. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 295*

167. Those being confirmed must at least be able to read and must firmly know the principal dogmas and precepts of their Church.

*Ibid., § 34.*

168. The rite of confirmation is performed by the Preacher of the parish in which the person being confirmed resides.

*Ibid., § 35.*

Section Four.

On Repentance and Holy Communion.

169. Repentance, as a necessary preparation for Holy Communion, must precede it.

1832, Dec. 28 (5870) § 36.

170. In general confession, all persons participating in it inwardly confess their sins according to the formula read by the Preacher, and receive absolution from him.

*Ibid., § 37.*

171. Confession of sins in private is permitted by the Evangelical Lutheran Church.

*Ibid., § 38.*

172. All who wish to proceed to repentance and receive Holy Communion must notify the Preacher of this beforehand, declaring to him at the same time their name, status, rank, or trade.

*Ibid., § 39.*

173. Members of the Evangelical Lutheran Church who belong to a particular parish must apply for admission to repentance and Holy Communion to their own parish Preacher; from this they may be released only by his written consent, or by special authorization of the Consistory.

*Ibid., § 40.*

174. Anyone who owns property in different parishes may receive Holy Communion in one or the other, at his own choice.

*Ibid., § 41.*

175. In towns where Lutherans are not divided into parishes, everyone is permitted to choose for himself, as his spiritual father, one of the Preachers of his confession, according to his own discretion. Anyone who subsequently wishes to choose another may not be admitted by him to repentance and Holy Communion until he presents a proper parish certificate (Parochialschein) issued by the first.

*Ibid., § 42.*

176. In the case of sudden and dangerous illness, of an unexpected and speedy departure, and in other extraordinary cases, any Evangelical Lutheran Preacher may administer Holy Communion to one who so desires, even without presentation of a parish certificate.

*Ibid., § 43.*

177. Foreigners, and all persons at a great distance from their former place of residence, may, if they so wish, be admitted to repentance and Holy Communion in the Evangelical Lutheran parish in which they reside. If it is not known with certainty whether they belong to the Evangelical Protestant Church, a written declaration signed by them is required, in which it must be stated that they do not belong to the Church of the Orthodox confession (see the Statute on the Prevention of Crimes, Section I).

*Ibid., § 44.*

178. In churches with many parishioners, the sacrament of Holy Communion must be administered, for those wishing and prepared for it by repentance, every Sunday; in other churches, twice, or at least not less than once a month.

*Ibid., § 45.*

179. Admission to Holy Communion is generally granted only in church. Only those who, by reason of illness, old age, or other special causes, are unable to be present in church may receive communion outside it: in this case their families and household members, if they so wish, are also permitted to receive communion together with them.

*Ibid., § 46.*

180. If anyone appears to receive Holy Communion in an indecent and scandalous state, the Preacher is obliged immediately to order him removed, and, in case of disobedience, to hand him over to the police authorities as a disturber of public order and of due reverence for the sacred.

*Ibid., § 47.*

181. Every member of the Evangelical Lutheran Church is obliged to receive Holy Communion annually, unless prevented by some special reason worthy of respect.

*Ibid., § 48.*

Section Five.

On Marriage (Trauung).

182. The performance of the marriage rite for persons belonging to the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Russia is a necessary condition for the validity of lawful marriage.

1832, Dec. 28 (5870) § 49.

183. The following are necessary for the validity of a marriage: 1) the question put by the Priest to both parties entering into marriage, whether their consent to enter into this marriage is voluntary and genuine; 2) the expression of this consent by them; 3) the established blessing of the marital union.

*Ibid., § 50.*

184. The marriage rite must be performed in the presence of at least two witnesses, by a duly appointed Preacher, and if possible by one of the parish to which the bride belongs.

*Ibid., § 51. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________   297*

185. The marriage rite must preferably be performed in church; it may, however, also be performed in a private house.

*Ibid., § 52.*

186. The marriage rite in the Evangelical Lutheran Church may not be performed during Holy Week, nor likewise on the eve of, or on the very days of, the feasts of the Nativity of Christ, Easter, and the Descent of the Holy Spirit.

*Ibid., § 53.*

187. Private persons entering into marriage may not authorize others to take their place in the performance of the marriage rite.

*Ibid., § 54.*

Section Six.

On Burial.

188. The death of every member of the Evangelical Lutheran Church must be announced to the Preacher of the parish in which it occurred. This duty falls upon the deceased's nearest relatives, and, in their absence, upon the owner or manager of the house in which he died.

1832, Dec. 28 (5870) § 55.

189. The custom of notifying the parish of the death of one of its members by several strokes of the bell, or by an announcement from the pulpit, is to be preserved wherever it existed before December 28, 1832.

*Ibid., § 56.*

190. The rite of burial must be performed by the Preacher of the parish in which the deceased died, or by the Preacher of the parish to which the deceased belonged, if the former consents to this. When this parish is at a great distance, permission from the government is sought for the transport of the body to it.

*Ibid., § 57.*

191. In towns where Lutherans are not divided into parishes, the deceased's spiritual father, or, in his absence or in case of other obstacles, any other Preacher, may, upon invitation, perform the rite of burial over him.

*Ibid., § 58.*

192. If the Preacher to whom the right to perform this rite belongs is unable to proceed with it for some reason worthy of respect, and there is no other Preacher in that place, then, with his consent and under his instruction, the body is buried by one of the church servitors.

*Ibid., § 59.*

193. Funeral orations in church may be delivered only by Preachers.

*Ibid., § 60.*

194. Persons sentenced to death, or to punishments replacing it, who die before the execution of the sentence, or from the effects of the punishment, are buried without any solemn church rites, orations, or gatherings (in der Stille).

*Ibid., § 61.*

195. The bodies of suicides are buried on the basis of the rulings issued in each such case by the civil authorities.

*Ibid., § 62.*

196. The bodies of members of the Evangelical Lutheran Church are buried only in places consecrated according to the established order and designated for this purpose, whether for entire parishes or for individual families.

*Ibid., § 63.*
