The summons must state: 1) which Consistory is summoning the person to appear; 2) the name, surname, and rank or status of the person summoned; 3) the case, or the circumstance of the case, for which he is summoned; 4) the day and hour on which the person summoned must appear before the Consistory, with a statement of the consequences of non-appearance.

*Ibid., § 340.*

485. Pursuant to the summons, every person is obliged to appear personally before the Consistory, or to send an attorney, by the appointed deadline. No one may refuse to fulfill this obligation, except for some special lawful reason.

*Ibid., § 341.*

486. When the person summoned is abroad, or his place of residence is unknown, the summons is announced three times in the public gazettes. The deadline set for the person summoned is counted from the day of the last publication.

*Ibid., § 342.*

487. The order of judicial proceedings in the Consistories, depending on the type of case, is either investigative (Untersuchungs-Prozess) or private (Verfahrungs-Civil Prozess).

*Ibid., § 343.*

488. All cases concerning clergy accused of crimes or omissions in the performance of their duties, as well as all cases arising from complaints brought against any of their actions contrary to the clerical calling, are conducted by the investigative procedure.

*Ibid., § 344.*

489. All disputed and other cases between private persons subject to the Consistory's review are conducted by the private procedure.

Note. The private procedure may be ordinary or summary. In conducting a case by the summary procedure, all the essential forms of the ordinary private procedure relating to the hearing of both parties are observed, but it is given the swiftest possible course, through the shortening of deadlines and postponements, and by providing that the disputing parties present, with their initial petitions, all the explanations and evidence that can be presented at that time.

*Ibid., § 345.*

Section Two.

On the investigative procedure.

490. Denunciations concerning any crime or omission by a clergyman in the performance of his duties may be accepted only on the basis of the general laws on this subject, when they are accompanied by proper evidence of the truthfulness of the accusations. Otherwise, the denunciation is disregarded, and the Consistory has no right to undertake any investigation on its account.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 346.

491. The Consistory, upon learning, from a private denunciation worthy of credence, or from an official report, of some crime or omission by a clergyman in the performance of his duties, entrusts one of its members, or the district Probst, or one of the Church Wardens or Elders, with the task of discovering the true state of the matter by questioning the accused beforehand while avoiding any premature publicity; but if particular circumstances and the gravity of the case so require, it appoints an extraordinary church visitation for this purpose.

*Ibid., § 347.*

492. When this preliminary investigation reveals that there are insufficient grounds to accuse the Preacher and the case itself is not of particular importance, the Consistory releases him from trial and further investigation until such time as clearer evidence is presented that could give cause for a new review of the case. If, however, the case appears for some reason exceptionally important, or if, upon preliminary investigation, the suspicions against the Preacher have not diminished but rather increased, the Consistory summons him before it for a personal response, or appoints a special commission to examine the case on the spot, consisting of two lay members and one clerical member, or of one lay member and two clerical members.

*Ibid., § 348.*

493. In the case of a formal complaint against a Preacher for violation of his official duties, the Consistory, in order to discover the truth, is guided by the same rules established in the preceding Articles 490, 491, and 492.

Note. If, in a complaint filed against a Preacher, he is accused of not very serious omissions, and sufficient evidence of its truthfulness is attached to it, the Consistory instructs the accused to satisfy the petitioner within a deadline set for this purpose, under threat of a fine, or to present, within the same deadline, lawful reasons for dismissing the complaint. In this latter case, the Consistory, having reviewed the Preacher's response, either proceeds to a final decision or to further conduct of the case by the investigative procedure.

*Ibid., § 349 and note. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 353*

494. Special commissions of inquiry established by the Consistories observe, in the conduct of their proceedings, the rules established by this Church Statute and by the general state laws or the local laws of the governorate.

*Ibid., § 350.*

495. Upon the appointment of a commission, the Consistory notifies the authorities of the governorate in which it is established, so that they do not refuse the commission assistance should the commission make such a request. In addition, the commission has the right to request directly from the police and other offices of first instance in the governorate in which it is located the necessary information and assistance, upon presenting only the order it has received from the Consistory establishing it.

*Ibid., § 351.*

496. Upon completion of the investigation, the commission submits all its case records together with its opinion to the Consistory.

*Ibid., § 352.*

497. Upon completion of the preliminary or formal investigation by the commission, the Preacher may, if he wishes, appear personally before the Consistory to present evidentiary explanations regarding circumstances that were not known during the investigation.

*Ibid., § 353.*

498. In cases where a clergyman is accused of, or has already been convicted of, a crime unrelated to his calling, the Consistories are guided by the rules established in Articles 241, 242, 375, 376, and 444 of this Statute.

*Ibid., § 354.*

Section Three.

On the private procedure.

I. On the order of judicial proceedings in private matters in general.

499. Cases conducted by the private procedure begin with the filing of a petition with the Consistory.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 355.

500. The petition must state: 1) the substance of the matter; 2) the claimant's demand.

*Ibid., § 356.*

501. It is not permitted to combine claims arising from different suits in a single petition.

*Ibid., § 357.*

502. When the petition has all the required legal attributes and there is no reason to return it to the person who submitted it, then, within the first seven days thereafter, or, in cases admitting of no delay, immediately upon receipt of the petition, a proper summons (citatio) to appear before the Consistory is sent to the respondent.

*Ibid., § 358.*

503. Upon receipt of notice that the summons has been delivered to the Consistory, the proceedings in the case are considered to have begun, and neither of the disputing parties may thereafter evade the jurisdiction of this Consistory, even if the respondent should in the meantime change his place of residence.

*Ibid., § 359.*

504. To the respondent who appears, or to his attorney, is handed—or, if he is absent and has no attorney, is forwarded to him at his request—a certified copy of the petition filed against him, and he is informed that he must, within a set two-week deadline, submit his explanations in response.

Note. The claimant and the respondent are required to submit exact copies of all those petitions, explanations, and evidence of theirs which must be communicated to the opposing party.

*Ibid., § 360.*

505. The respondent is obliged to give clear and precise explanations on all points of the petition, both with respect to those statements and demands of the claimant which he acknowledges as true and those which he disputes, so that it may be conveniently possible, by separating everything in which he agrees with the claimant from that in which he contradicts him, to determine accurately and fully what constitutes the subject of the dispute (status controversiae).

*Ibid., § 361.*

506. Excepted from the general rule are only those cases in which the respondent, in his explanations, instead of the ordinary refutation of the claimant's statements, must draw the Consistory's attention to circumstances which, although not relating to the substance of the case, must suspend its progress (exceptiones dilatoriae), or to such circumstances as would render the very grounds of the suit void (exceptiones peremtoriae). In these cases the respondent is obliged to present to the Consistory, at one and the same time, at the very outset of the proceedings, all circumstances which in his opinion must suspend or alter the course of the case (exceptiones dilatoriae). As for circumstances of greater importance that nullify the grounds of the suit (exceptiones peremtoriae), he may present them later, that is, after consideration of the former, but likewise before the formal commencement of the case, and likewise stating all these circumstances in one and the same petition, except only those which become known to him after the filing of this petition. All explanations of this kind are examined by the Consistories under the summary procedure.

*Ibid., § 362.*

507. Having received the respondent's explanations, the Consistory, within the first seven days, delivers a certified copy of them to the claimant and sets him a two-week deadline for presenting his evidence, or, should he not consider it necessary to present it, for filing, within the same deadline, his second petition (replica). At the same time as the claimant, the respondent is likewise given a two-week deadline for presenting his evidence, if he considers this necessary.

*Ibid., § 363. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 355*

508. If neither party presents evidence and the claimant files a second petition (replica), it is communicated, in a certified copy, to the respondent within the first seven days thereafter, with a ten-day deadline likewise set for him to present his second explanations (duplica), of which the claimant may, if he wishes, obtain a copy for his information.

*Ibid., § 364.*

509. Upon receipt of these second explanations of the respondent, the Consistory no longer accepts any new petitions or statements from either him or the claimant, and proceeds to render its judgment.

*Ibid., § 365.*

510. If, on the contrary, one or both parties present evidence, the filing of second petitions and explanations by both the claimant and the respondent is postponed until the completion of the proceedings concerning the evidence; thereafter a ten-day deadline is set, first for the claimant and then for the respondent, for filing second petitions and explanations (replica et duplica), at which point they are given the memorandum compiled by the Consistory from the witness testimony (scrutinium), and the respondent is furthermore given a certified copy of the claimant's second petition.

*Ibid., § 366.*

511. When the disputing parties present any papers (documents) as evidence, the Consistory, within the first seven days thereafter, communicates to the opposing party certified copies of these papers and of the statements filed with them, for the presentation, not later than within two weeks, of final explanations concerning this evidence.

*Ibid., § 367.*

512. When referring to witnesses, the claimant and the respondent must state in writing the name, surname, rank or status, and place of residence of each of them, indicating also, in brief points and with due precision (articuli probatoriales et reprobatoriales), exactly who is to be questioned and on what circumstance.

*Ibid., § 368.*

513. This statement is likewise communicated to the opposing party within the first seven days thereafter: first, so that it may present, not later than ten days thereafter, particular questions which, at its request, must be put to the witnesses (interrogatoria specialia); second, so that it may object to witnesses on grounds of suspicion within the same deadline.

*Ibid., § 369.*

514. General questions concerning the names, surnames, confession, rank or status of the witnesses, their age, their relationship to the litigants, whether they expect to gain or lose from the outcome of the case, whether they are at enmity with the party against whom they are called as witnesses, and similar matters that may serve to determine the degree of credibility of their testimony (interrogatoria generalia), are put to the witnesses by the Consistory without the assistance or request of the litigants.

*Ibid., § 370.*

515. Before giving their testimony, witnesses must take the prescribed oath according to the rite of the faith they profess, in the presence of the Consistory, and, should the disputing parties express a wish to that effect, also in the presence of the parties themselves or their attorneys. However, by mutual agreement of the litigants, witnesses may be admitted to give testimony without an oath.

*Ibid., § 371.*

516. Testimony is taken from witnesses and recorded in the presence of the Consistory in the manner prescribed by law, on the basis of the points submitted by the party referring to them (articuli probatoriales et reprobatoriales) (see Article 512) and the questions (interrogatoria specialia) (see Articles 513 and 514), beginning with the general questions from the Consistory (interrogatoria generalia).

*Ibid., § 372.*

517. When witnesses, owing to the remoteness of their place of residence or for other lawful reasons, cannot appear before the Consistory, it applies to another appropriate office to have them questioned, forwarding to it the questions and informing it whether the litigants wish to be present at the witnesses' oath. In this case the Consistory requires of the witnesses a written undertaking to appear for this purpose at the appropriate office by the deadline it has set.

*Ibid., § 373.*

518. A special memorandum (scrutinium) is compiled in the Consistory from the witnesses' testimony, which, duly certified, is communicated to the disputing parties, as indicated in Article 510.

*Ibid., § 374.*

519. With regard to the taking of so-called testimony for perpetual memory (in perpetuam rei memoriam), the existing rules on this subject are strictly observed, which permit a witness to be questioned, if the claimant or respondent so requests, even before the case has begun, or during the course of litigation before the proceedings concerning evidence have begun, namely, if the witness is departing on a journey and will not soon return, or if advanced old age or dangerous illness give cause to doubt that his life will continue.

*Ibid., § 375.*

520. Once the case has thus been reviewed, the proceedings on it are deemed concluded, and a report (relatio) is compiled from it.

*Ibid., § 376.*

521. The report must contain: 1) a brief and clear statement of the substance of the case; 2) the principal circumstances on the determination of which the decision of the case itself depends; 3) the laws relating to the case.

*Ibid., § 377.*

522. Upon the compilation of the report, the hearing of the case begins with its reading; at this point all the original papers pertaining to the case are presented.

*Ibid., § 378. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 357*

523. Thereupon the Consistory, having put the case up for deliberation, proceeds to render its decision in strict compliance with the laws existing on the matter.

*Ibid., § 379.*

II. On the oral hearing of private cases.

524. Oral hearing is permitted only for special reasons, namely, when written proceedings prove burdensome for the disputing parties owing to their poor circumstances.

*Ibid., § 380.*

525. In the case of an oral hearing of cases, the papers submitted by the disputing parties, in accordance with the rules set forth above, are composed from their own words in the Consistory itself, in the form of minutes, and, after being read and confirmed, are signed by the petitioners, or, if they are illiterate or physically unable to do so, in their place and at their wish, by one of the members of the Consistory.

*Ibid., § 381.*

526. The Consistory, in entering these minutes in the record, must remain within the bounds of its judicial office, giving the disputing parties no advice whatsoever regarding their case.

*Ibid., § 382.*

III. Special rules of procedure for marriage cases.

527. In judicial proceedings concerning marriage cases, the Consistories, guided by the provisions of Chapter Four of this Statute on marriages and by the provisions of the preceding articles of this chapter on disputed and judicial matters in general, observe in addition the following special rules (Articles 528 et seq.).

*Ibid., § 383.*

528. In all marriage cases, the claimant and the respondent may defend their own rights before the Consistory in person, even if, under existing laws, they would not otherwise be entitled to bring suits and answer to them on their own behalf in other matters.

*Ibid., § 384.*

529. In divorce cases, persons who, without lawful cause, fail to appear before the Consistory by the deadlines set for them under threat of fines (Articles 479, 480, and 481), are summoned for a third deadline not under threat of forfeiture of the right of defense (praeclusio), if the consequence of such forfeiture would be the dissolution of the marriage, but only under threat of compulsion through the appropriate offices or other authorities.

*Ibid., § 385.*

530. From the general rule that the claimant must bring his suit in the judicial venue under whose jurisdiction the respondent falls, an exception is permitted in marriage cases, but only for abandoned spouses and brides deprived of their honor, or for maidens seduced under promise of marriage, who, under Articles 223, 226, and 256, are granted the right—the former to petition for divorce, and the latter for the solemnization of marriage: they may bring these petitions to the Consistory of their own place of residence.

Note. The rules governing proceedings for the dissolution of marriages contracted between persons of different confessions are set forth in the Laws on Civil Judicial Procedure.

*Ibid., § 386.*

531. If a suit for the dissolution of an unlawful marriage—though not deemed invalid—is brought not by the spouses but by a third party claiming to have the right to do so, and is brought by him within the prescribed period (Article 249), the Consistory shall first endeavor to end the matter through reconciliation, and only when these efforts prove fruitless shall it proceed to the ordinary judicial proceedings.

*Ibid., § 387.*

532. The same rule is observed in all petitions for divorce based on the grounds specified in Articles 252, 253, 255, 260, 261, 263, 264, and 265, even when the divorce is sought on grounds of malicious desertion (Article 256), but only when, pursuant to an ordinary summons or one made through the gazettes, the accused party appears before the court.

*Ibid., § 388.*

533. For the reconciliation hearing (Sühneversuch), which must precede the ordinary trial, both parties appear personally before the Consistory, within the deadline it sets. If, however, owing to great distance or other lawful reasons, personal appearance of the disputing parties is deemed impossible, the Consistory applies to the secular office, requesting it, together with a deputy of the Consistory—that is, one of its members, the district Probst, or some other clergyman appointed by it—to endeavor to reconcile the disputing parties.

*Ibid., § 389.*

534. When, owing to great distance or other reasons deserving of consideration, the disputing parties cannot appear together, either before the Consistory or before another office, then various Probsts or Preachers are respectively instructed to exhort and induce each of them, so far as it concerns them, to reconciliation; for this purpose all the circumstances of the case stated in the complaint are communicated to them.

*Ibid., § 390.*

535. In the event of the claimant's failure to appear at the reconciliation hearing without presenting lawful reasons for it, a second summons of the respondent to the proposed reconciliation must not be issued until the claimant has compensated him for all losses incurred as a result of his non-appearance.

*Ibid., § 391.*

536. When the claimant, without lawful cause, fails to appear by the deadline even upon a second summons to the reconciliation hearing, the respondent is released from all consequences of the complaint filed against him, and the claimant has no right to file a second petition for divorce on account of circumstances and events already known to him prior to the setting of the reconciliation hearing on his first petition.

*Ibid., § 392. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 359*

537. In the event of the respondent's failure to appear by the deadline for the proposed reconciliation, he must pay, for the first and second occasions, the fines established in Article 481, and compensate the losses incurred by the opposing party as a result of his non-appearance. On the third occasion, the Consistory, in summoning the respondent, declares to him that if he fails to appear even upon this summons, he will be compelled to appear by the secular office (citatio realis).

*Ibid., § 393.*

538. If the prescribed measures for reconciliation have been employed but have not achieved the desired success, a certified copy of the petition filed against him is communicated to the accused, and he is given the deadline set by Article 504 for presenting his explanations on the matter.

Note. Statements made by the parties in the course of the reconciliation hearing are deemed as if they had never been made, if the spouses do not reconcile, and references to such statements or admissions are not subsequently permitted by the Consistory.

*Ibid., § 394.*

539. On petitions for the solemnization of marriage following betrothal or a given promise, the Consistory likewise endeavors to reconcile the disputing parties and acts in this case according to the rules set forth in Articles 533–537, with only this difference: that if the accused, having missed the first two deadlines set under threat of a fine, fails to appear even at the third and final one, the petition of the opposing party is deemed justified strictly on the basis of Articles 224 and 226.

*Ibid., § 395.*

540. If the Consistory receives reliable notice of the solemnization of a marriage that must be deemed invalid, it is obliged to conduct the appropriate investigation into the matter without delay. Upon confirming the accuracy of the information it has received, the Consistory dissolves the marriage and sentences the Preacher who performed the marriage to the appropriate punishment; as for the other persons at fault in the matter, it leaves it to the secular offices to render judgment according to the laws.

*Ibid., § 396.*

541. The Consistory may not, on its own authority (ex officio), conduct investigations into marriages which, although unlawful, are not deemed invalid. It proceeds to investigate and resolve matters relating to such marriages only when a formal petition has been filed to that effect.

*Ibid., § 397.*

542. When the Consistory finds the statements set forth in a petition on this matter to be well founded, it imposes on the guilty parties the obligation to fulfill, so far as possible, the necessary conditions for a lawful marriage that they failed to observe, or to remove all obstacles thereto.

*Ibid., § 398.*

543. The Consistory returns, with an endorsement, petitions for the dissolution of marriage: 1) if they are not based on any of the lawful grounds for divorce specified in Articles 251–253, 255, 256, 258–265; 2) if it is not also proved that the matter falls within its jurisdiction, for which purpose a certificate must be attached showing that the marriage of the disputing parties was solemnized according to the rites of the Evangelical Lutheran Church.

*Ibid., § 399.*

544. In marriage cases, household members (Hausgenossen), and even relatives of the disputing parties, are admitted as witnesses in the absence of others, with the exception only of those descending in a direct line from either party.

*Ibid., § 400.*

545. If, in a marriage case, one party's own admission, whether oral or written (Article 252), could result in the dissolution of the marriage sought by one or the other party, further evidence is required in addition to it.

*Ibid., § 401.*

546. The disputing parties are not permitted to require one another to take an oath as to the truth or falsity of statements which, were such an oath to be taken, would result in the dissolution of the marriage.

*Ibid., § 402.*

547. In the ruling dissolving the marriage the following must be indicated: 1) the reason for the divorce; 2) whether one of the parties is found guilty, which one specifically, and of what; 3) which of the spouses, in the event of adultery or malicious desertion, is forbidden, as punishment therefor, to enter into a new marriage (Arts. 256 and 257); 4) which of them is to raise some or all of the children born of this marriage, and to what age; and 5) which of the parents must bear the expenses of the maintenance and upbringing of these children (Art. 266).

*Ibid., § 403.*

548. Upon the entry into legal force of the Consistory's ruling on the dissolution of the marriage, this dissolution is solemnly performed in the Consistory itself, in the presence of the disputing parties, if there are no lawful obstacles to their appearance, according to the following special rite: the General Superintendent, Superintendent, or another clerical member of the Consistory, in a session thereof, having first delivered a brief exhortation to the spouses being divorced, declares their marriage dissolved, takes their wedding rings, and separates them by lowering the hand joined between them.

*Ibid., § 404.*

549. When a marriage is dissolved on account of the proven fault of one of the spouses (and not for other lawful reasons), then upon declaring the marriage annulled, the General Superintendent, Superintendent, or another clerical member of the Consistory, uses the following formula:

"Inasmuch as it has already been sufficiently shown, by the evidence presented and by his (her) own admission (or only: by the evidence presented), that this your husband or this your wife NN, forgetting the fear of God and contrary to His holy word, has become guilty (or has become guilty) of adultery or of maliciously deserting you, or of cruel treatment of you, or the like, and et cetera, and has thereby forfeited all of his (her) marital rights over you; I therefore declare you, NN, in the name of God and by the power of His holy word, free from the marriage DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 361

in which you were bound, and grant you, NN, the right to enter into a new marriage, where and when you see fit; whereas to you, NN, on the contrary, it is hereby most strictly forbidden, until further ruling, to enter into a new marriage."

*Ibid., § 405.*

550. If, for lawful reasons, both spouses being divorced cannot appear at the Consistory at the same time for the dissolution of the marriage, this rite (Art. 549) is performed, with the necessary changes to the formula and other rules, over each of them separately. In the case of great distance or other circumstances preventing the spouses being divorced from appearing at the Consistory, it may instruct the local Preacher to perform the rite of dissolving their marriage, in the presence of two Church Elders.

*Ibid., § 406.*

551. Each of the parties is issued a certificate stating that their marriage has been solemnly dissolved.

*Ibid., § 407.*

Section Four.

On the announcement of rulings.

552. The Consistory notifies the disputing parties who are present in the place where the Consistory resides, or who have attorneys there, of the day appointed for the announcement of its final decision in the case, and summons them to hear it by special notices, for the receipt of which they are obliged to give signed acknowledgments, and summons those absent by publication in the gazettes. For those present, or having attorneys, in the place where the Consistory resides, a seven-day period is set for appearing to hear the decision, counting from the day the notice was delivered, and for those absent a six-month period, counting from the day of the last publication in the newspapers. At the wish of the litigants, the Consistory's decisions may also be announced to them through their superior authorities, or through the local presence offices.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 408.

553. The same procedure is observed also in announcing the Consistory's interlocutory rulings, with the sole difference that absent parties are summoned to the hearing not by publication in the gazettes, but by posting a notice on the doors of its Presence chamber, and that a two-month period is set for their appearance.

*Ibid., § 409.*

554. If any of the disputing parties present in the place where the Consistory resides, having given a signed undertaking to appear at the Consistory to hear its final decision in the case, fails to appear on the day appointed in the notice and does not present an attorney on his behalf, the decision is nevertheless deemed announced to him as of that same day which was appointed in the notice, and consequently the periods set for lodging an appeal and interlocutory complaints (querelae) are counted from that same day.

*Ibid., § 410.*

555. Owing to the failure of one of the disputing parties to appear on the day appointed for the announcement of the final or interlocutory decision, the announcement of that decision to the other party, who appeared in time, is not postponed.

*Ibid., § 411.*

556. If the disputing party, or his attorney, fails to appear on the day appointed by the Consistory in the notice for hearing the final or interlocutory decision, and no signed acknowledgment of receipt of that notice has been presented to the Consistory, then he is deemed absent, and, on the basis of Articles 552 and 553, a six-month or two-month period for appearance is set for him by publication in the public gazettes, or by posting a special notice on the doors of the Presence chamber.

*Ibid., § 412.*

557. If the disputing party deemed absent, or his attorney, appears at the Consistory either of his own accord or by its direction, before the summons has yet been made through the newspapers or through the posting of a notice on the doors of the Presence chamber, or after that but before the expiry of the period appointed in the summons, then the Consistory announces the decision to him, and the periods for lodging an appeal or interlocutory complaint (querelae) are counted from the day the decision was announced.

*Ibid., § 413.*

558. If, however, the disputing party fails to appear even within the period appointed for him in the summons for hearing the decision, then the verdict, with respect to him, is deemed to have entered into legal force.

*Ibid., § 414.*

Section Five.

On the transfer of cases upon appeals and complaints.

559. Cases are transferred from the local Consistories to the General Consistory upon appeals and interlocutory complaints (querelae).

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 415; 1847 Jul. 29 (21450).

560. Appeals and interlocutory complaints are not permitted: a) against orders for the execution of verdicts that have entered into legal force; b) against decisions based on an oath taken by mutual consent; c) against decisions in investigative cases concerning offenses of the clergy against their office and their non-observance of the rules of subordination, when the penalty imposed therefor is a simple reprimand, or a fine not exceeding forty-five silver rubles.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 416; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

561. Against the decisions of Consistories in matters pertaining to the performance of the Preacher's office, to teaching, to the conduct of divine service, and to religion in general, appeals and complaints are permitted even in cases where the matter did not arise from a petition submitted by a plaintiff.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 417.

562. Complaints against the final decisions of Consistories may be filed only by way of appeal.

*Ibid., § 418.*

563. A party wishing to lodge an appeal with the General Consistory is obliged, within seven days counting from the day the decision was announced, either personally or through an attorney, to notify the Consistory thereof, indicating all those points of the decision by which he considers himself aggrieved (gravamina), and stating, in a signed declaration in lieu of an oath, that to the best of his understanding and in good conscience he considers DOCUMENTS________________________________ ___________________________________________ 363

his case to be just and the grounds for lodging the appeal to be lawful; together with this he shall submit seven rubles fifty kopecks in silver for the transfer of the case. Anyone who fails to fulfill any of these requirements when appealing shall be refused permission to lodge the appeal.

*Ibid., § 419; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).*

564. Those points of the decision against which no dissatisfaction was noted at the time the appeal was announced enter into legal force upon the expiry of the aforementioned seven days (Art. 563).

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 420.

565. Those who, owing to poverty, cannot pay the sum set for the transfer of the case (Art. 563), shall submit proper certification thereof and, being thereby exempted from payment of this sum, shall obtain the right to lodge an appeal without it.

*Ibid., § 421.*

566. Upon the announcement of the appeal in the aforementioned manner within the lawful period, it is admitted by the Consistory, provided there is no lawful obstacle thereto by reason of the nature of the case (Art. 460). Thereupon the Consistory issues to the appellant a certificate of the permission granted him (attestatum concessae appellationis); this certificate states not only the six-month period set for lodging the appeal, counting from the day the decision was announced, but also the entire procedure to be observed in filing the appeal.

*Ibid., § 422.*

567. The appellate petition is submitted by the appellant personally, or through an attorney, to the General Consistory, or is forwarded to it by post, together with a copy of the verdict on stamped paper and the proper amount of the statutory duty.

*Ibid., § 423.*

568. Upon receipt of the appellate petition, the General Consistory, within the first seven days, issues a copy thereof to the opposing party, who appears in person or through an attorney for that purpose; and in the event of that party's failure to appear, it forwards this copy to him through the proper local authorities, and sets for him a period of four weeks, or longer depending on the remoteness of his residence, for submitting his explanations thereon (refutatio appellationis); and if the residence of the opposing party is unknown, the General Consistory summons him by publication in the gazettes, setting a four-month period for appearance.

*Ibid. § 424.*

569. The Consistory reports in advance to the General Consistory on the proposed transfer of the case (Art. 566), and then, having received from it notification of the appeal's admission, submits the case itself to it.

*Ibid., § 425.*

570. Having received the opposing party's explanation on the appellate petition, the General Consistory no longer accepts any further papers. The appellate proceedings are deemed concluded, and, after a report memorandum has been drawn up from them, the General Consistory shall decide the case in the order established for the hearing thereof.

*Ibid., § 426.*

571. If the appellate petition, with the proper attachments (Arts. 566 and 567), is not submitted in time, the right of appeal is deemed forfeited and the Consistory's decision deemed to have entered into legal force. The General Consistory notifies the local Consistory of this lapse of the period set for lodging the appeal. Likewise, the opposing party (appellatus), by allowing the period set for him to lapse, also forfeits the right to submit explanations against the appellate complaint.

*Ibid., § 427.*

572. Interlocutory complaints may be brought only against rulings that are likewise interlocutory (interlocuta), which do not contain decisions on the very subject matter of the dispute that gave rise to the litigation, and which relate only to circumstances incidental to the case (puncta incidentia), such as the manner of conducting the litigation, the procedure for presenting evidence, and the like.

*Ibid., § 428.*

573. Whoever wishes to bring a complaint to the General Consistory against an interlocutory ruling of the Consistory must, within seven days counting from the day such ruling was announced, notify the Consistory thereof in writing, precisely indicating all the points of the ruling against which he declares dissatisfaction. Otherwise the interlocutory ruling enters into legal force.

*Ibid., § 429.*

574. Upon such notice of dissatisfaction being given, the Consistory shall, within the first seven days thereafter, issue to the petitioner a certificate admitting the interlocutory complaint (attestatum concessae querelae), if it is in general recognized by law as permissible (Arts. 460 and 461); this certificate shall state the two-month period set for lodging the complaint, counting from the day the interlocutory ruling was announced, and shall affirm that, should the period lapse, the right of complaint will be deemed forfeited and the ruling deemed to have entered into legal force.

*Ibid., § 430.*

575. Thereupon the petitioner lodges the interlocutory complaint with the General Consistory, but is not obliged to pay any duties.

*Ibid., § 431.*

576. Upon receipt of the interlocutory complaint, the General Consistory delivers copies thereof to the local Consistory and to the opposing party (querulatus), requesting explanations. These explanations must be submitted within a two-week period, or longer depending on the distance involved, as set by the General Consistory; and if the residence of the opposing party is unknown, the General Consistory summons him by publication in the gazettes, indicating a two-month period for appearance.

*Ibid., § 432.*

577. The General Consistory also requires the local Consistory, if the petitioner so desires, to provide, at his expense, copies of all the papers contained in the case, or only certain ones as designated by him.

*Ibid., § 433. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 365*

578. An interlocutory complaint halts the proceedings in the case only with respect to those circumstances against which it was filed. If those circumstances are such that the decision of the case itself, or of its principal part, depends on them, then the entire proceedings in the case are halted, and this is reported to the General Consistory.

*Ibid., § 434.*

579. The General Consistory affirms or overturns the ruling of the local Consistory, and, if the disputing parties or their attorneys do not appear to hear the decision, sends it to the local Consistory for proper execution.

*Ibid., § 435.*

580. In announcing final and interlocutory decisions, both the General Consistory and the local Consistories are guided by the rules set forth in Articles 552–558.

*Ibid., § 436; 1847 Jul. 29 (21450).*

581. Upon the dissatisfaction of one or both parties, appeals or complaints against the interlocutory rulings and final decisions of the General Consistory are admitted to the Governing Senate on the general basis, in all those cases which are not excepted therefrom by the rules established in Art. 461.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 437.

##### CHAPTER NINE.

On the Evangelical Lutheran Synods.

Section One.

On the Synods in the Consistorial Districts.

582. The Evangelical Lutheran General Superintendents and Superintendents, with the exception of the Moscow one, shall annually convene, at a convenient time and place appointed by them for that purpose, the Provosts and Preachers of their Consistorial district for an Evangelical Lutheran Synod, or general clerical council. The purpose of these councils among the clergy of the district is the improvement of each, through the mutual exchange of thoughts, local observations, and information on spiritual matters, on the discharge of Pastoral duties, on the difficulties encountered along this path, and on the means for overcoming them.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 438.

583. Clergy who reside far from the place of assembly, and generally outside the boundaries of the governorate in which the Evangelical Lutheran Synod is convened, may be excused from the obligation of attending the Evangelical Lutheran Synod.

*Ibid., § 439.*

584. In extensive Consistorial districts, even though composed of a single governorate, instead of all the Preachers, only half of their number is obliged to appear annually at the assembly of the Evangelical Lutheran Synod, according to a distribution made in advance for that purpose by the General Superintendent. He likewise designates a separate place, depending on convenience, for each of these assemblies, first asking the opinion of the Provosts on the matter.

*Ibid., § 440.*

585. The Evangelical Lutheran Synods are presided over by the General Superintendents, or Superintendents; they open these assemblies with a solemn divine service in church and conclude them with prayer and a blessing. The assemblies of the Evangelical Lutheran Synod shall not last longer than eight days.

*Ibid., § 441.*

586. The subjects of business of the Evangelical Lutheran Synods consist of:

1) Mutual explanations and communications on purely spiritual matters, on the spiritual state of the parishes, on the progress of catechization, on unusual and generally important occurrences in the discharge of Pastoral duties, etc.

2) Discussions of learned theological subjects: members read compositions prepared by them on questions of theoretical and practical theology, offer one another their observations, and report news of the latest theological books, etc.

3) Deliberations on the economic affairs of the church, widows' funds, etc.

4) Deliberation on the means for improving the condition of the churches in their district.

*Ibid., § 442.*

587. All members of the Consistory have the right to attend these Evangelical Lutheran Synods. Candidates for the clergy may also be present at these assemblies, but they take part in the deliberations only with the special permission of the General Superintendent or Superintendent. The minutes of these assemblies are submitted through the General Superintendents or Superintendents to the Consistories, and from them forwarded in copies to the General Consistory; the originals are kept in the archives of the Consistories.

*Ibid., § 443; 1847 Jul. 29 (21450).*

Section Two.

On the Synods in the Provostial Districts.

588. The Provostial Evangelical Lutheran Synods that existed prior to December 28, 1832, in certain places may continue to be convened on the former basis, but this does not exempt anyone from the obligation to attend the general Evangelical Lutheran Synod of the Consistorial district. The minutes of these Provostial Evangelical Lutheran Synodal Assemblies are submitted each time to the General Superintendents, and from them to the Consistories.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 444; 1847 Jul. 29 (21450).

589. In the Saratov, New Russia, and Bessarabia colonies, whose Preachers, owing to the remoteness of their parishes, cannot often attend the Evangelical Lutheran Synods, the Provosts shall annually convene the Preachers subordinate to them for a district Evangelical Lutheran Synod; at it everything established in Articles 585 and 586 concerning the opening, continuation, business, and closing of the Evangelical Lutheran Synods in the Consistorial districts shall be observed. The minutes of these assemblies are submitted to the General Superintendent for entry into the local Consistory, and from it forwarded in copies to the General Consistory.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 445; 1847 Jul. 29 (21450).

Section Three.

On the General Synod.

590. In order to present to the government more precise and detailed information on the needs of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in the Empire and on the means for further perfecting its institutions, a General Evangelical Lutheran Synod is convened from time to time.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 446.

591. To attend the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod, all Consistorial districts appoint deputies, each one, alternately clerical or lay. When the St. Petersburg, Livonia, Courland, and Reval districts appoint clerical deputies, then from Moscow, Estonia, Ösel, and Riga lay deputies are chosen; at the following assembly of the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod these latter districts appoint clerical deputies, and St. Petersburg, Livonia, Courland, and Reval lay ones. In addition to these eight members, the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod is attended by the clerical Vice-President of the General Consistory, the Professor of the Theological Faculty of Dorpat University, as appointed by that University, and, alternately, the lay Presidents or clerical Vice-Presidents of the Consistories of St. Petersburg, Livonia, Estonia, Courland, and Moscow, or, when they cannot attend the assembly owing to significant obstacles, then in their stead the senior lay or clerical Assessors of these Consistories. In this it is observed that when a lay deputy has been elected by a Consistorial district, then a clerical one is appointed by the Consistory itself, and vice versa.

*Ibid., § 447.*

592. The election of lay and clerical members to the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod, apart from those appointed from the Evangelical Lutheran Consistories, is conducted in the same manner as established above in Article 437 for the election of lay and clerical members of the Consistories. The Ministry of Internal Affairs, having received from the chief administration of the Baltic governorates, from the General and other Consistories, and from the Ministry of Public Education, notice of the members intended for the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod, submits a list of them for the Highest consideration.

*Ibid., § 448.*

593. The Evangelical Lutheran General Synod is presided over by one of its lay members, or by another person of the Evangelical Lutheran confession, as appointed by His Imperial Majesty.

*Ibid., § 449.*

594. The Evangelical Lutheran General Synod convenes in St. Petersburg, at the discretion and by the calling of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, with the Highest permission.

*Ibid., § 450.*

595. It is granted to the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod, in its assemblies: 1) To resolve questions put to it by the General Consistory, upon instruction or with the authorization of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. 2) To propose measures for the more precise execution of the provisions of the Statute of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in the Empire. 3) To bring, through the Ministry of Internal Affairs, to the Highest attention its thoughts and conclusions on the condition, needs, and administration of the Evangelical Lutheran churches in the Empire.

*Ibid., § 451.*

596. The conduct of business in the sessions of the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod is managed by the Chairman. The minutes of sessions are drawn up by one of the members, as chosen by the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod.

*Ibid., § 452.*

597. At all assemblies of the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod there is present the Procurator of the General Consistory, or, in the event of his illness or absence from St. Petersburg, another official appointed by the Minister of Internal Affairs; he acts on the basis of the rules prescribed for Procurators in collegial institutions.

*Ibid., § 453.*

598. The chancellery of the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod, depending on the number of cases submitted for its consideration, is composed of officials detailed from the General Consistory, or specially appointed for that purpose. Arrangements in this regard depend on the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

*Ibid. § 454.*

599. The sessions of the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod last from four to six weeks; when it is necessary to extend them, the Highest permission is requested through the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The Evangelical Lutheran General Synod is opened and closed with a solemn divine service.

*Ibid., § 455.*

600. The Minister of Internal Affairs submits the deliberations and conclusions of the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod for the consideration of His Imperial Majesty.

*Ibid., § 456.*

601. Members of the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod, during its sessions, may be excused only by the Highest commands of His Imperial Majesty, upon the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs.

*Ibid., § 457. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 369*

602. Upon the conclusion of the sessions of the Evangelical Lutheran General Synod, the Chairman submits its minutes to the Ministry of Internal Affairs; and certified copies thereof are forwarded to the General Consistory.

*Ibid., § 458.*

##### CHAPTER TEN.

On the administration of the properties of Evangelical-Lutheran churches.

Section One.

On the composition and use of church properties.

603. Any movable or immovable property intended for the maintenance of any Evangelical-Lutheran church, or of charitable institutions attached thereto, whether assigned to it at the very founding of the church, by testament, deed of gift, or otherwise (bona dotalia), or subsequently acquired by it through lawful means (bona acquisita), is called church property and is protected by the special rights granted to properties of this kind (a).

Note. Pastorate glebes (Widmen) constitute the incomplete ownership (dominium utile) of the clergy, while so-called gracious hakens and other lands constitute the property of the church; but the clergy possess the right of use both of the glebes and of these hakens and lands, the receipt of all income from them, and their internal administration (b). Therefore the Kurland Forstamt does not participate in the administration and disposition of the glebe forests in Kurland governorate (v).

(a) 1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 459. — (b) Code of Local Statutes of the Baltic (Ostsee) Governorates, Part I, Art. 927. — (v) 1840 Dec. 26 (14090); 1854 Jan. 27 (27886) Art. 6, note 3.

604. Capital and income granted from the Monarch's bounty, and likewise received by the church under testaments or deeds of gift, must be used only for the purpose specified in the act of grant, or in the testament or deed of gift. This purpose may be changed only with the Highest permission, which is sought only in the following two cases: 1) when the testator or donor himself consents to the intended change, and 2) when, after the death of the testator or donor, it is proved that the use of the capital or income received from him by the church for its original purpose has for some reason become impossible.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 460.

605. The acquisition of immovable properties for Evangelical-Lutheran churches is authorized: by the General Consistory for a sum up to three hundred rubles, by the Department of Spiritual Affairs of Foreign Confessions up to one thousand rubles, by the Minister of Internal Affairs, upon resolution of his Council, up to five thousand rubles; for acquisitions above five thousand rubles the Highest permission is sought.

*Ibid., § 461; 1852 Jan. 28 (25944) Art. 44.*

606. Evangelical-Lutheran churches may not, without the Highest permission, alienate any of their immovable properties, except for the sale of unneeded land or the necessary exchange of their land for other land. The sale of unneeded church immovable properties is authorized: for a sum up to three hundred rubles by the General Consistory, up to one thousand rubles by the Department of Spiritual Affairs of Foreign Confessions, up to five thousand rubles by the Minister of Internal Affairs, and above this, for any sum, by the Governing Senate; the confirmation of such a sale is entrusted to the same authorities, at the amount set for the confirmation of public auctions, whereby the General Consistory enjoys the rights of provincial institutions (see Civil Laws). — The exchange of church lands for municipal lands is authorized by the Minister of Internal Affairs.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 461; 1852 Jan. 28 (25944) Art. 42, cl. 1 and 3; 1857 Jun. 4, Highest Directive.

607. The granting of church immovable property on perpetual, emphyteutic, or other long-term lease intended to last more than twelve years is likewise permitted only with the Highest permission.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 462.

608. Collections and offerings of any kind for the benefit of the church, permitted prior to December 28, 1832, on the basis of lawful regulations or ancient customs, may not, without the Highest assent, be either increased, diminished, or abolished (a).

Note. Persons who, by their confession, do not belong to the Protestant Church, are obliged to pay to the benefit of this Church or its clergy only those dues which may follow on the basis of agreements concluded on their part under proprietary right, that is, for the use of church land; from all other dues in favor of this Church and its clergy they are free (b).

(a) Ibid., § 463. — (b) 1853 Dec. 29 (27815).

609. Capital bequeathed or donated to churches up to three hundred rubles in silver, as well as items whose value does not exceed this sum, may be accepted by the Church Wardens (Kirchen-Vorsteher) without special permission of higher authorities; the Chief Church Wardenships (Ober-Kirchen-Vorsteher-Aemter), Municipal Church Councils, Collegiums or Convents, and all bodies of equal standing with them in the administration of church economic affairs, have the right to accept offerings up to one thousand five hundred rubles; for the acceptance of offerings above this sum, confirmation of the General Consistory is required; and when it exceeds three thousand rubles, the General Consistory submits the matter to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, which grants permission under Article 115 (note). But regarding capital and items bequeathed or donated to churches with the stipulation of any special conditions attached, the matter is always submitted through the General Consistory to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. If the conditions intended by the testator or donor are not accepted, the offering is returned to him or to his lawful heirs.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 464; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867); 1857 Jun. 4, Highest Directive.

610. Items and other movable properties of Evangelical-Lutheran churches, other than monetary sums, may be alienated by the Church Wardenships (Kirchenvorstand) only for reason of noted deterioration, or complete unfitness for their intended use, and upon verification that their sale will be advantageous to the church. Where

Chief Wardenships have been established, their prior consent is sought for this, and when the value of the movable property exceeds ninety rubles in silver, also the permission of the General Consistory, which for its part, regarding the sale of items worth more than six hundred rubles in silver, submits the matter to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Every submission concerning the sale of any church movable property must be accompanied by a valuation of it made on a lawful basis.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 465; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867); 1852 Jan. 28 (25944) Art. 42, cl. 2.

611. The sale of unneeded movable church property is conducted only by public auction, according to the rules established in the Civil Laws. If it is deemed more advantageous to sell church property in a district or provincial town, the consent of the parish is required for this.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 466.

612. Church Wardenships may, under the same responsibility with which they are generally entrusted with the administration of church property, transfer free of charge to another church movable items no longer needed by their own churches but useful to another, particularly items serving to adorn the church, or suitable for use in divine services and in the performance of spiritual rites, or for the internal arrangement of the church. This transfer is carried out: first, when the value of the movable property being transferred, according to a valuation made on a lawful basis, does not exceed thirty rubles, without prior consent of the parish, though with the obligation to mention every such transfer in their annual reports to the General Consistory or the Chief Church Wardenships; second, when the value of the movable property exceeds thirty rubles, with the consent of the parish; and finally, third, concerning the transfer of items worth more than ninety rubles, the permission of the General Consistory is sought through the lawful channel, either directly or through the Chief Church Wardenships and equivalent bodies for the administration of church property, and the General Consistory, for its part, regarding the transfer of items worth more than six hundred rubles, submits the matter to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. — The Ministry, if the value of the items being transferred exceeds ten thousand rubles, seeks the permission of the Governing Senate.

1837 Oct. 23 (11600); 1839 Nov. 9 (12867); 1852 Jan. 28 (25944) Art. 42, cl. 2.

613. Disbursements of monetary sums for the needs of the church up to one hundred fifty rubles in silver may be made by the Church Wardens; but they thereby assume responsibility for the necessity or benefit of these expenditures; for the disbursement of sums from one hundred fifty to six hundred rubles, the consent of the parish or its authorized representatives and the permission of the Chief Church Wardenships, or bodies of equal standing in the administration of church economic affairs, are required. — Municipal Church Councils, Collegiums, and Convents likewise have the right to make disbursements up to one hundred fifty rubles directly on their own authority, and from one hundred fifty to six hundred rubles with the consent of the parish or its authorized representatives. — For the disbursement of sums from six hundred to two thousand rubles, the permission of the General Consistory is required. The Minister of Internal Affairs authorizes the disbursement of sums for the needs of Evangelical-Lutheran churches up to ten thousand rubles, and for disbursement above this sum the Highest permission is sought.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 467; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867); 1852 Jan. 28 (25944) Art. 58; 1857 Jun. 4, Highest Directive.

614. At each church there must be a true and detailed inventory, certified by the Preacher and members of the Church Wardenship, of all church immovable properties, items, and monies, as well as of all income due to that church by any right or special privilege, and a bound and sealed book, under the seal of the Preacher and Wardens, for entering into it all monetary receipts and expenditures of the church.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 468.

615. At every church there must be, in a secure place, a special church chest for the safekeeping of all documents relating to church property, monetary sums, and such church vessels as are not necessary for daily or at least frequent use. This chest must, depending on the number of Church Wardens, have three or at least two different locks and be sealed with the church seal. The keys to the locks are kept by the Preacher and one or two of the members of the Church Wardenship (Kirchenvorstand), one each; they must all invariably be present each time the chest is opened. If the member holding one of the keys to the chest cannot, for lawful reasons, come to the place where the chest is located, and the chest must nevertheless be opened, he sends his key sealed to the Preacher, and in his place another witness from among the parishioners is invited, as designated by the Preacher and the Church Wardenship.

*Ibid., § 469.*

616. All church vessels in private use are kept by the Preacher.

*Ibid., § 470.*

617. Offerings collected in the church and other contributions made for its benefit, received by the Preacher, are submitted by him to the Church Wardenships at the end of each month.

*Ibid., § 471.*

618. Church capital is placed to accrue interest in state or public credit institutions. The placement of this capital in private hands may be permitted only when, owing to special local circumstances, such a transaction is deemed convenient and advantageous for the church, and the sum thus entrusted is secured by a reliable pledge. — Church Wardenships shall see to it that large sums of money do not remain in the church chest without need.

*Ibid., § 472.*

619. All instruments concerning monetary sums belonging to the church, placed to accrue interest, or held in private hands for any other reason, must be drawn up in the name of the church, or of the charitable institutions belonging to it.

*Ibid., § 473.*

620. Incurring debts in the name of the church is not permitted under any circumstances; in all church expenditures authorized by law or by higher authority, payment is made in cash, and for anything taken without payment, the Church Wardens are liable as for their own personal debt; and on this basis, no suit against the church or its property and income may be brought or entertained by any government office.

*Ibid., § 474.*

621. The properties of churches are preserved intact, without any detriment, under the same right as state properties, by which right they must also be protected, under the liability, for any unlawful expenditure or loss thereof, of all persons responsible therefor to whom the administration or safekeeping of these properties has been entrusted (a).

Note. Civil government offices, when handling church affairs of the Protestant confession, are obliged to invite deputies from the clergy to be present during the deliberation and decision of such matters, applying for this purpose to the appropriate ecclesiastical institutions (b). — Special rules are attached herewith concerning the procedure in cases of boundary disputes in the demarcation of pastorate lands in Livland and Kurland governorates with state and private estates (v). — Penalties for sacrilege are set forth in the Penal Code, Articles 253–267, in which the aforementioned division of items belonging to churches into sacred, or merely consecrated through use in divine service, is adopted as a rule also for the Evangelical-Lutheran confession (g).

(a) Ibid., § 475. — (b) See Civil Laws. — (v) 1837 Jun. 8 (10311). — (g) 1847 Jan. 7 (20779).

622. Evangelical-Lutheran churches, the buildings attached to them and not let out for rent, as well as the buildings of the charitable institutions belonging to them, and the houses of clergy of this confession occupied by themselves, are free from billeting and from all police and municipal duties, except, however, for the repair of pavement, the oversight of its cleanliness, and the maintenance of street lamps.

Note 1. Those churches which, prior to December 28, 1832, were granted special rights in this respect, retain them on the former basis (a).

Note 2. In St. Petersburg, buildings and other immovable properties belonging to churches of foreign Christian confessions are exempt from payment of the municipal assessment levy (b).

(a) 1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 478. — (b) 1842 Mar. 30 (15441); 1846 Mar. 6 (19805) § 3, cl. 2; 1855 Jun. 13 (29408).

Section Two.

On the administration of church properties.

623. The administration of the properties of Evangelical-Lutheran churches in St. Petersburg, Moscow, and generally in all towns of the Empire, with the exception only of the three Baltic governorates and the town of Narva, as well as the administration of the properties of the Church of St. James in Riga and the Toompea (Domberg) Church in Reval, depends directly on the so-called Church Councils, Collegiums, or Convents existing at each of them. The property of all other Evangelical-Lutheran churches is managed directly by the Church Wardens (Kirchen-Vorsteher) attached to them, who in Mitau, Bauske, Goldingen, and Windau are under the supervision of the local Church Inspections there, in Libau, Dorpat, Pernau, Arensburg, Narva, Riga (except for the Church of St. James), and in Reval (except for the Toompea Church), under the supervision of the Magistrates of these towns, in the Evangelical-Lutheran colonies of Saratov governorate, under the supervision of the Saratov Office of Foreign Settlers, and in the colonies of Novorossiysk Krai and Bessarabia Province, under the supervision of the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers of the Southern Krai; in all other urban and rural parishes these Wardens are subordinate to the Chief Church Wardenships (Ober-Kirchen-Vorsteher-Aemter).

Note. There are four Chief Wardenships in Livland governorate, four in Estland, five in Kurland, one in St. Petersburg governorate (Ingermanland), one in Vilna and Grodno governorates, and one on the island of Ösel. Their division in Livland governorate remains on the former basis, in Estland it corresponds to the districts of the counties, and in Kurland to the districts of the Ober-Hauptmann Courts (a). The Shavli (Šiauliai) Evangelical-Lutheran Church Convent is independent of the local Chief Church Wardenship; the filial parishes also participate in the election of the four members of this Convent, or else, apart from them, each filial church has one deputy in it, with the right to vote in all important matters and resolutions (b).

(a) 1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 477. — (b) 1838 Aug. 4 (11454).

624. The supreme oversight of the administration of the properties of Evangelical-Lutheran churches is entrusted to the Evangelical-Lutheran General Consistory.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 478.

I. On Church Councils, Collegiums, or Convents.

625. Municipal Church Councils, Collegiums, or Convents must consist of no fewer than four and no more than twelve members, who are called Church Elders or Wardens and are elected by the parish for three years. In addition, the parish Preachers are also present in the Church Councils, Collegiums, or Convents with all the rights of members. They are presided over, at the appointment of the parish, either by the honorary patrons attached to the churches, elected to this office for life, or by one of the Church Elders or Wardens, or by one of the Preachers (a).

Note. The composition of the Convent of the Reval Toompea Church and the procedure for electing its members are determined by special rules (b).

(a) Ibid., § 479. — (b) 1839 Apr. 25 (12261).

626. The election of Chairmen and members takes place at a general meeting of the parishioners, by a majority of votes of those present. To these meetings are invited all military and civil officials, landowners, scholars, artists, capitalists, merchants, manufacturers, and craft masters belonging to the parish. During the election, for the observance of order, an official assigned by the local civil authority is present. The parish is notified of the time and place of the election by a threefold announcement from the pulpit on Sundays, and where possible by a threefold publication in the public gazettes (a). In Narva, the Church Wardens, upon election by the parish, are confirmed by the local Magistrate; among these Wardens are included, with all the rights of members, also the Pastors there, each at the church of the parish in which he serves as Preacher (b).

(a) 1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 480. — (b) 1838 May 7 (11219).

627. New members of the Church Council, Collegium, or Convent, upon entering office, are obliged, having verified the integrity of the church property, to accept it from their predecessors according to the inventory drawn up on the basis of Article 614.

1832 Dec. 28 (5870) § 481.

628. The oversight of the integrity of church property, the administration of church income, the maintenance of the Preacher and church servants, where this is provided by the parish, the handling of church affairs in the appropriate government offices, the construction of church buildings, all repairs thereto, the letting of them for rent, the appointment and dismissal of the Secretary or Notary of the Church Council, Collegium, or Convent, and of all church servants, and all such matters, as well as likewise the care of the poor belonging to the parish, and the concern for the burial of those who leave neither property nor relatives, fall within the scope of duties of the Church Councils, Collegiums, or Convents. These bodies generally act as authorized representatives of the parish; however, in important matters they have the right to require from the community a special power of attorney at as full a gathering of parishioners as possible. Having received this power of attorney, they are, for those actions specifically prescribed to them at this meeting, thereafter released from all liability before the community. The parishioners are notified of the time and place of these meetings, as stipulated in Article 626, by announcements from the pulpit and in the public gazettes.

Note. Church Councils, Collegiums, or Convents have no right to make changes in the allowances for the maintenance of the Preacher or church servants without first obtaining, firstly, the consent of the parish, and secondly, the permission of the General Consistory.

*Ibid., § 482.*

629. Church Councils, Collegiums, or Convents set the days and hours of their meetings at their own discretion and in accordance with the number and nature of the matters at hand. Minutes are kept of all meetings by one of the members, or by a specially appointed Secretary or Notary, in which the opinions of the members on each item are recorded. Resolutions are adopted by majority vote, and in case of liability for any matter, only those members who agreed with the majority are subject to it.

*Ibid., § 483.*

630. At the end of the year, the Church Councils, Collegiums, or Convents must render before the general meeting of parishioners a full account of all their actions in the administration of the economic affairs of the church, and in particular of the state of its treasury. For the verification of accounts, inventories, and for the inspection of church buildings, the parish may elect special representatives, to whom the members of the Church Council, Collegium, or Convent are obliged to provide all explanations required of them. At the beginning of each year, the Church Councils, Collegiums, or Convents submit to the General Consistory an extract from this report and a statement of all monetary sums at their disposal.

*Ibid., § 484.*

631. At the end of the three-year term, members of the Church Councils, Collegiums, or Convents may be elected again to this office.

*Ibid., § 485.*

II. On Church Wardens and Elders.

632. The number, procedure of election, appointment, and dismissal of Church Wardens (Kirchen-Vorsteher), where they already existed prior to December 28, 1832, remains on the former basis. In Church Wardenships newly established thereafter in rural parishes, Wardens must be elected by the Church Convent, which is composed of all parishioners possessing any immovable property, and confirmed by the Chief Church Wardenship. In small parishes one Warden is appointed, and in larger ones, two. They are elected for three years and, upon expiry of this term, may be elected again. In those rural parishes of St. Petersburg (Ingermanland), Vilna, and Grodno governorates in which there are no landowners of the Evangelical-Lutheran confession, as well as in the colonies of foreign settlers of Saratov and of the Southern Krai, the office of parish Preacher is combined with that of Church Warden, and he is obliged, upon assuming office, immediately to report to the body to which he is subordinate as Church Warden on the state of the property and economic affairs of the church.

*Ibid., § 486.*

633. The duties and relations of Church Wardens to the parish, to the parish Convent, and to their higher authorities, insofar as not changed by the provisions of this Statute, remain on the former basis. They are entrusted with the direct oversight of the integrity of church property, care of the economic affairs of the church, the convening of parish Convents for deliberation on the most important matters of the parish in church respects, the execution of the resolutions of these Convents, upon obtaining, when necessary, the permission of higher authority, proposals for the distribution, with the consent of the Convent, among the parishioners of expenses intended for church construction and repairs, oversight of the conduct of such construction and repairs, care of the beggars and poor belonging to the parish, oversight of parish cemeteries and roads leading to the church, and finally the preservation of order and decorum during divine services, and generally all the so-called church police (Kirchen-Polizei). Church Wardens submit to their immediate superiors, at the beginning of each year, a statement of the receipts and expenditures of the monetary sums at their disposal.

*Ibid., § 487.*

634. To assist the Church Wardens in the economic affairs of the church and in matters of church police, Church Elders drawn from the peasantry are subordinated to them (Bauer-Kirchen-Vorsteher, Sechsmänner oder Unter-Kirchen-Vorsteher); reliable peasants are appointed to this office in all rural and colonist parishes. In those parishes where the Preachers are also Church Wardens, these Church Elders co-sign with them the reports to higher authority on the state of the property and economic affairs of the church. Church Elders in St. Petersburg governorate (Ingermanland) and in the colonies are elected by the parish for three years and confirmed by the Preachers acting as Church Wardens; in the Baltic governorates they are appointed by those possessing immovable property in that parish and are likewise confirmed by the Church Wardens after obtaining the opinion of the Preacher. The whole parish is informed of those elected. The number of these Church Elders drawn from the peasantry is determined by the extent of the parish and the greater or lesser number of estates, villages, or colonies belonging to it.

*Ibid., §§ 488 and 489.*

635. At the end of the three-year term, Church Elders drawn from the peasantry may be elected again to this office. For incompetence, they may be dismissed at any time by the Wardens.

*Ibid., § 490.*

636. Special privileges granted in certain places to Church Elders drawn from the peasantry for the duration of their tenure in this office are retained by them also for the future after December 28, 1832.

*Ibid., § 491.*

III. On Chief Church Wardenships and Inspections.

637. Chief Church Wardenships (Ober-Kirchen-Vorsteher-Aemter) are composed of a Chairman, bearing the title of Chief Church Warden, one lay member, and one clerical member.

*Ibid., § 492, cl. 1.*

638. Chief Church Wardens are elected by the nobility in Livland and Estland governorates and on the island of Ösel from among the Landrats, and in Kurland, Vilna, and Grodno from among the local nobles of the Evangelical-Lutheran confession possessing immovable property. The lay Assessors, who must likewise be of the Evangelical-Lutheran confession, are elected by the nobility from among its own members for three years; at the end of the three-year term they may be elected again.

*Ibid., § 492, cl. 2.*

639. The Chief Church Wardens and lay Assessors elected by the nobility in the Baltic governorates are confirmed by the provincial authority, which immediately communicates their confirmation to the General Consistory; in Vilna and Grodno governorates, the Provincial Boards notify the General Consistory of those elected, and the General Consistory confirms them.

*Ibid., § 492, cl. 3.*

640. For the rural parishes in St. Petersburg governorate (Ingermanland), the President of the St. Petersburg Evangelical-Lutheran Consistory is the Chief Church Warden; in place of the lay Assessor, the General Consistory appoints one of the nobles of the Evangelical-Lutheran confession possessing immovable property in this governorate, or one of the honorable residents of St. Petersburg of this faith, with their consent, or else one of the lay members of the St. Petersburg Evangelical-Lutheran Consistory.

Ibid., § 492, cl. 4.

641. The place of the clerical member in the Chief Church Wardenships in Livland, Estland, Kurland, and St. Petersburg governorates is always occupied by the senior of the Provosts of the district subordinate to the Wardenship, in Vilna by the Vilna Provost, and on the island of Ösel by the local Superintendent.

*Ibid., § 492, cl. 5.*

642. When the clerical member sitting in the Chief Wardenship cannot, for lawful reasons, be present therein, another senior member from among the Provosts or Preachers of the district subordinate to the Chief Wardenship is called in his place.

*Ibid., § 492, cl. 6.*

643. Clerical affairs in the Chief Church Wardenships in Kurland and Estland governorates and in Vilna are handled by Notaries appointed by the Chief Church Wardens; they are assigned small salaries for their maintenance from the churches and parishes within the district of the Wardenship. — In the St. Petersburg Chief Church Wardenship, the office of Notary is performed by the Notary of the St. Petersburg Consistory, and on the island of Ösel by the Consistory Secretary, both without any special salary for this office. — In Livland governorate, the appointment and maintenance of Notaries in the Chief Church Wardenships remains on the former basis existing prior to 1832 (a).

Note. In the Chief Church Wardenships of Kurland governorate, Notaries receive an annual salary of thirty rubles and seventy rubles for office expenses, from a special levy raised until the churches are able to maintain them by their own means. This levy is raised on the following basis: 1) The sum required for the maintenance of the Notaries is divided into four parts. One part is imposed on the churches of the district of the Chief Wardenships, in proportion to the amount of their church capital, excluding churches having capital of no more than one thousand rubles, and those parishes in which church properties are administered not by Wardenships but by special Inspections; these churches and parishes are entirely exempt from the levy. The levy falling on the remaining churches is paid into the Chief Church Wardenship by the Church Wardens semi-annually. 2) The second part of the sum is collected from the estates of private and crown manors; but from those lessees of crown manors whose contracts have not expired since 1837, this levy is raised only with their own consent. 3) The last two parts are apportioned, by number of souls, among the peasants of the Evangelical-Lutheran confession belonging to private and crown manors.
