798. The St. Petersburg Evangelical Reformed society consists of two societies: French and German, which nevertheless constitute one Whole.

1778 May 11 (14748); 1834 Apr. 17 (6999); 1837 Mar. 31 (10086).

799. The St. Petersburg Evangelical Reformed church is to be regarded as common to both united societies.

Note. This church was founded by the French society, and it has therefore been granted the right to be named in all acts before the German society.

1778 May 11 (14748) pt. 1.

800. Each society (art. 798) has its own Pastor. Both receive their maintenance from the revenues of the church.

*Ibid., pts. 2, 3.*

801. Divine services in the church are performed for each society at different times, determined by their mutual agreement, with the knowledge of the ecclesiastical authorities.

*Ibid., pt. 4; 1797 Mar. 30 (17896).*

802. Both societies are permitted, should they unanimously wish it in order to conserve the church's revenues, to maintain only one Pastor, capable of conducting the service in both languages. In this case, for the election of the Pastor each society appoints an equal number of parishioners, and they, in the presence of a lay deputy delegated by the Reformed Session of the St. Petersburg Evangelical Lutheran Consistory (art. 790), elect the Pastor by a majority of votes; in case of a tie the choice is decided by lot.

1778 May 11 (14748) pt. 5.

803. Church property and, in general, the economic affairs of the church, are managed by a special Church Council.

*Ibid., pt. 6.*

804. The Church Council consists of three Elders or Trustees of the French society and an equal number of Elders of the German society. On church matters the Pastors are also invited to the Council: on such matters they have the first voice.

*Ibid., pt. 7.*

805. The Elders of each society are elected by it for three years.

*Ibid., pts. 7, 8.*

806. Entrusted to the care of the Church Council are: the management of church revenues of every kind; the maintenance of the servants attached to the church; all necessary repairs to buildings belonging to it, and other similar matters of economic administration.

*Ibid., pt. 9.*

807. Should the church's revenues prove insufficient to cover expenses, in particular the maintenance of both Pastors, the additional sum required to cover these expenses shall be apportioned for collection between both societies.

*Ibid., pt. 10.*

808. Among the objects of economic administration of the Church Council is also the letting of the church house; in this the Church Council arranges matters so that the Pastors of both societies, on equal terms of advantage to one another, and likewise the church servants, are lodged in this house. Revenues received from the letting of apartments are added to the general church funds (a).

Note. The rules set forth above (art. 622) concerning the exemption of buildings belonging to Evangelical Lutheran churches and to the clergy of this confession from equal obligations are extended with equal force to the houses of churches and clergy of the Evangelical Reformed confession (b).

(a) Ibid., pt. 11. — (b) Statute on Zemstvo Obligations, art. 270, pt. 4.

809. Upon the expiration of the three-year term, the Elders are obliged to render before the assembly of the whole society a full account of all their actions in the administration of the church's affairs and in particular its revenues, and to obtain thereupon an approving certificate from the society. Having rendered their account, the Elders are discharged from their office, but may also remain in it if the society consents thereto and the Elders themselves do not decline to continue serving.

1778 May 11 (14748) pt. 12.

810. For the auditing of the accounts (art. 809) both societies are permitted to elect one or two trustees knowledgeable in bookkeeping; the Elders are obliged to furnish them with all explanations required for this audit.

*Ibid., pt. 13.*

811. The society (art. 798) has the right to submit, through the Church Council, to its higher ecclesiastical authority (arts. 790, 795), any rules it considers necessary to supplement the provisions set forth above.

*Ibid., pt. 15.*

II. On the Administration of the Spiritual Affairs

of the Moscow Evangelical Reformed Society.

812. The Evangelical Reformed church in Moscow is regarded as common to the followers of the Evangelical Reformed confession there, excepting only those who are attached to some other parish in Moscow.

1830 Oct. 14 (3998) § 1.

813. The parish maintains at this church one or two Pastors, at the discretion of the society, having regard to the circumstances and needs of the parishioners.

*Ibid., § 2.*

814. The election of Pastors is carried out in a general assembly of the parish, by a majority of the votes of those present. The parish society is notified of the time and place of the election by a threefold announcement from the pulpit on Sundays and by a threefold publication in the newspapers.

*Ibid., § 3.*

815. To observe order at the election of the Pastor, a deputy from the local provincial authorities must be present.

*Ibid., § 4.*

816. Upon the election of the Pastor, the Church Council (art. 817) submits him for confirmation to its ecclesiastical authority (arts. 790, 795).

*Ibid., § 5.*

817. The church and economic affairs of the parish are managed by the Church Council.

*Ibid., § 6.*

818. The Church Council consists of eight Church Elders, elected for three years; during this time they act as representatives on behalf of all parishioners.

*Ibid., § 7.*

819. The Church Council is chaired by the Pastor, except only in cases where the Council deliberates on complaints against him and other matters to which he may be party; in matters of this kind the Pastor has no vote and does not attend the Council.

*Ibid., § 8.*

820. The election of Elders is carried out by the same procedure as the election of Pastors. At the election an official from the local provincial authorities is likewise present to observe order.

*Ibid., § 9.*

821. Upon entering office the Elders are obliged carefully to examine the state of all matters relating to the administration of the church, and to draw up a detailed inventory of all church plate, valuables, and moneys.

Note. The church treasury is kept in a special church chest, under the church seal and three different locks; the keys to them are held by the Pastor and two of the Church Elders, each holding one, and all three must be present each time the chest is opened.

*Ibid. § 10.*

822. The management of church revenues of every kind, the maintenance of the Pastor and of the servants necessary for the church, the conduct of church business in the proper judicial places, the construction of church buildings, all repairs thereto, and everything of like nature, is entrusted to the care of the Elders. In important matters the Church Elders have the right to require special authorization from the society, in as full an assembly of parishioners as possible. Having received this authorization, they are, for those actions specifically prescribed to them at such an assembly of parishioners, freed thenceforth from all responsibility before the society. The parishioners are notified of the time and place of these assemblies, as stated above in article 814, by announcements from the pulpit and in public newspapers.

*Ibid., §11.*

823. In case of insufficiency of the church's revenues for its necessary needs, and especially for the maintenance of the Pastor, the additional sum required shall be apportioned among all the parishioners, with regard to the means of each of them.

*Ibid., § 12.*

824. All sums collected and to be collected for the church, from whatever sources they may be received, are regarded as the common property of the whole parish, and are placed to accrue interest in state credit institutions. For current expenses the Council has the right to keep in its treasury up to one hundred fifty silver rubles.

*Ibid., § 13; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).*

825. Sums granted from the Monarch's bounty, and likewise those received by the church under wills or deeds of gift, must be applied to no other purpose than that specified in the grant, the will, or the deed of gift.

1830 Oct. 14 (3998) § 14.

826. All church capital is preserved intact and without loss, on the same footing as state property; it is protected under this right, with liability, for any unlawful expenditure or loss thereof, first on the part of the Elders who caused it, and then, in case of their insolvency, on the part of all who consented to their election.

*Ibid., § 15.*

827. Upon the expiration of the three years, the Elders must render before the general assembly of parishioners a full account of all their actions in the administration of the church's affairs and in particular its revenues. The society may, if it deems fit, give them written certification that the church's affairs and funds have been received from them in due and complete order.

*Ibid., § 16.*

828. Upon the expiration of the three years, the Elders may be re-elected to this office.

*Ibid., § 17.*

829. The society may, for the auditing of the accounts, elect one or two trustees knowledgeable in bookkeeping; the Elders are obliged to furnish all explanations required of them by these trustees.

*Ibid., § 18.*

830. The society has the right to submit, through the Church Council, to its higher ecclesiastical authority (arts. 790, 795), any rules it considers necessary in addition to the provisions set forth above (arts. 812—829).

*Ibid., § 19.*

III. On the Administration of the Spiritual Affairs of the Riga, Mitau,

and Reval Evangelical Reformed Societies.

831. The rules set forth above concerning the procedure for the appointment of Pastors (art. 796) and the conduct in the Evangelical Lutheran Consistories of matters concerning Evangelical Reformed societies (art. 795) are extended likewise to the Evangelical Reformed societies existing in Riga and Mitau.

1830 Jul. 15 (3796).

832. In general, in the Baltic governorates, the administration of the property of the Evangelical Reformed churches and of the schools and charitable institutions attached to these churches is left entirely to the societies themselves.

*Ibid.*

833. The Evangelical Reformed society in Reval is under the charge of the Reformed Session of the St. Petersburg Evangelical Lutheran Consistory (arts. 790, 795).

1837 Mar. 31 (10086).

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On the Administration of the Spiritual Affairs

of the Arkhangelsk Evangelical Parish.

834. The Evangelical Lutheran and Evangelical Reformed parishes in Arkhangelsk, united, with the Highest consent, in 1817 into one parish, constitute a separate society under the name of the Arkhangelsk Evangelical Parish.

1838 Jun. 30 (11374) § 1.

835. For the divine services of the Arkhangelsk Evangelical parish, the Church of St. Catherine located in Arkhangelsk is designated.

*Ibid., § 2.*

836. Public divine services, the sacraments, and other sacred rites are performed in this church according to the order determined in the special act of union of the Arkhangelsk Lutheran and Reformed parishes drawn up on 30 November 1817, and in the protocol of 25 April 1836 based thereon.

*Ibid., § 3.*

837. The parish maintains at its church one or several Pastors, at the discretion of the society, having regard to the circumstances, means, and needs of the parishioners.

*Ibid., § 4.*

838. The election of Pastors is carried out in a general assembly of the parish, by a majority of the votes of those present. The society is notified of the time and place of the election by a threefold announcement from the pulpit on Sundays or by means of a circular, through the sexton.

*Ibid., § 5.*

839. To observe order at the election of the Pastor, a deputy from the local provincial authorities must be present.

*Ibid., § 6.*

840. Only persons who, under the regulations issued for Protestants in the Empire, have the right to enter the office of Preacher are admitted to election.

*Ibid., § 7.*

841. The person elected is submitted each time, through the chief provincial authorities, for confirmation by the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

*Ibid., § 8.*

842. When a Preacher, owing to old age or illness, requests his discharge from office, the parish, according to its means, provides for the maintenance of the one being discharged.

*Ibid., § 9.*

843. A Pastor who wishes to lay down the office of Preacher not for the reasons indicated in the preceding article but of his own will, gives notice thereof to the parish six months in advance.

*Ibid., § 10.*

844. The church affairs of the Arkhangelsk Evangelical parish are managed by its Church Council.

*Ibid., §11.*

845. The Church Council is composed of an Honorary Patron, as chairman, of the Pastor, two Church Elders, and three Church Trustees. The latter divide among themselves the management of the church and its property in such a way that each of them manages for one year, and at the expiration of that year hands over the church protocol, the account books, and the report for the past year, together with the church treasury, to his successor, in the presence of the Church Council and the society.

*Ibid., § 12.*

846. The Honorary Patron and the Church Elders are elected for life, and the Trustees for three years, so that each year one of them is discharged and a new Trustee is elected in his place; the one discharged, however, is not forbidden, at the unanimous wish of the society, to remain in the former office of Trustee for the following three-year term as well. The Honorary Patron, in case of need or at his own wish, has the right to transfer the office of Chairman to the Trustee then in charge.

*Ibid., § 13.*

847. The election of the Patron, Elders, and Trustees is carried out by the same procedure as the election of Pastors. In this, an official from the local provincial authorities is likewise present to observe order.

*Ibid., § 14.*

848. The Patron is submitted, through the local chief authorities, for confirmation by the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The election of the Elders and Trustees is likewise brought to the notice of this Ministry in the same manner.

*Ibid., § 15.*

849. Oversight of the order of divine services, on the basis of the act of union and the protocol indicated in article 836, the disposal of the annual church revenues, the maintenance of the Pastor, the appointment and maintenance of the servants necessary for the church, the construction of the church and church buildings, all repairs thereto, the conduct of church business in the proper judicial places, and in general everything concerning the welfare of the Arkhangelsk Evangelical parish, is entrusted to the care of the Church Council; but as concerns family and marital matters, such as: the conciliatory examination of spouses seeking divorce, the issuing of certificates on the proper securing of children's property in the event of a parent's remarriage, and the like, all this belongs exclusively to the duties of the Pastor.

*Ibid., § 16.*

850. In important matters the Church Council has the right to require special authorization from the society, in as full an assembly of parishioners as possible. Having received this authorization, the Church Council is, for those actions specifically prescribed to it at such an assembly of parishioners, freed thenceforth from all responsibility before the society. The parishioners are notified of the time and place of these assemblies by threefold announcements from the pulpit, or, in case of special need, owing to the small size of the society, through the sexton.

*Ibid., § 17.*

851. In marital matters, examined according to the rules set forth above in the Evangelical Lutheran Church Statute, the Arkhangelsk Evangelical Church Council is subordinate to the St. Petersburg Evangelical Lutheran Consistory and the General Consistory of this confession, but in all other matters directly to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, to which it makes its submissions through the chief local authorities.

Note. Concerning the number of parishioners of both sexes, born, married, and deceased, the Pastor furnishes the appropriate information to the Ministry of Internal Affairs annually, in the month of January, addressing his reports to the Department of Spiritual Affairs of Foreign Confessions. To this Department the Pastor generally reports directly on all matters in which the Department finds it necessary to communicate with him.

*Ibid., § 18.*

852. In case of insufficiency of the church's revenues for its necessary needs, and especially for the maintenance of the Pastor, the additional sum required shall be apportioned among all the parishioners, with regard to the means of each of them.

*Ibid., § 19.*

853. All the property of the church, as well as sums coming into it from whatever sources, are regarded as the common property of the whole parish, and are placed to accrue interest in state credit institutions. For current expenses the revenues collected in the preceding year are used; as for the remainder of revenues arising from the general collection and from interest, the society, at its discretion, in a full annual assembly in the month of January, deliberates and determines whether to send the surplus to be added to the capital, or to apply it to expenses for the following year, reducing the collection accordingly.

Note. The collection of revenues designated for the church, as well as their disbursement for the benefit of the church, in accordance with the general resolution of the Church Council thereon, is the duty of the Church Trustee then in charge; the church treasury is likewise kept under his single lock.

*Ibid., § 20.*

854. Sums received by the church under wills or deeds of gift are to be applied to no other purpose than that specified in the will or deed of gift.

*Ibid., § 21.*

855. All church capital is preserved intact and without loss, on the same footing as state property; it is protected under this right. For unlawful expenditures and losses thereof the Church Council is answerable.

Note. The Pastor is exempt from all responsibility in the economic and monetary affairs of the church.

*Ibid., § 22.*

856. Every year, in the first half of January, a full assembly of the society is convened. It must: a) verify the account books through a Committee elected for this purpose; b) hear the report of the Church Council on the management of all the church's affairs and revenues; c) determine and authorize the expenses for the current year; d) deliberate on necessary construction, plans for improvement, and changes in the collection, as need requires; and finally e) certify the discharge of the outgoing Trustee and elect another in his place.

*Ibid., § 23.*

857. The society has the right to submit, through the Church Council and the chief local authorities, to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, any additions it considers necessary to the preceding rules (arts. 834—856).

*Ibid., § 24.*

##### CHAPTER THREE.

On the administration of the spiritual affairs

of the German colonists in the Transcaucasian territory.

858. The German colonist societies in the Transcaucasian territory (Georgia) profess the doctrine of the Evangelical Lutheran Church according to the writings of the Old and New Testaments and as set forth in the Augsburg Confession and other Symbolic Books of this Church.

1841 Nov. 25, rules for the German settlers in Georgia, art. 1.

859. These societies form part of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in the Russian Empire and generally are governed by the Statute of this Church and its clergy, set forth in the first section of this book (arts. 134—789), in everything not superseded by the following articles (860—884) (a).

Note. The Evangelical Lutheran parishes in the Transcaucasian territory, populated by colonists belonging to the Separatist sect, were formerly governed, in spiritual matters, by a special Church Statute of 1829. In 1835 it was decreed that, in matters of divorce and in certain other cases, at the discretion of the general colonist Synod, these parishes should be governed by the provisions of the general Statute of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of 1832 (arts. 134—789); from November 25, 1841, the effect of the Church Statute of 1829 was entirely abolished, and this general Statute of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of 1832 was extended to the Georgian German colonies, and the provisions indicated below were issued at the same time as a supplement to it, as rules embodying the special rights and privileges of these colonies in spiritual matters, granted to them at the very time of their settlement in Georgia (b).

(a) 1841 Nov. 25, art. 2. — (b) 1829 Feb. 7 (2659); 1835 Feb. 12 (7853); 1841 Nov. 25 (15059).

860. The order of public worship and other church rites is determined by the Old Württemberg Church Agenda, which the colonists have long followed. Hymns are also sung from the Old Württemberg Collection of spiritual songs.

1841 Nov. 25, arts. 3 and 8.

861. The basis for public sermons is, as has always been the case in the Evangelical Lutheran Church, the texts (Pericopen) of the Holy Gospel and the Epistles of the Holy Apostles, selected and introduced for Sundays and feast days.

*Ibid., art. 4.*

862. In addition to Sundays and generally the church holidays of the Evangelical Lutheran confession and the state ceremonial days, the colonist societies also observe days dedicated to the memory of the Holy Apostles (a).

Note. Those wishing to do so are permitted to sell their produce or goods on all days, without exception for Sundays and holidays (b).

(a) Ibid., art. 5. — (b) See the Statute on Colonies.

863. In addition to the above (art. 862), on the first Friday of every month gatherings are held for repentance and prayer, and in those societies where weekly Wednesday prayer meetings exist, these meetings remain in force.

1841 Nov. 25, art. 6.

864. On Sundays and church holidays, a sermon is delivered in the morning, and in the afternoon catechization of the youth is carried out, which all unmarried persons of both sexes up to the age of eighteen attend.

*Ibid., art. 7.*

865. For the instruction of youth in the catechism, the basis is the compilation made in Württemberg, based on the Lutheran Catechism of Brenz, known as the Extract from the book: Instruction for the Salvation of the Soul (Auszug aus der Katechetischen Unterweisung zur Seeligkeit). This work, together with the accompanying Collection of Biblical texts, also serves as a guide in the public preaching of the Law of God.

*Ibid., art. 9.*

866. The sacrament of holy baptism is performed within the first eight days after the birth of an infant; the number of witnesses invited for this purpose must not exceed six persons.

*Ibid., art. 10.*

867. Confirmation is performed annually on the Sunday of Thomas Week (am Sonntage quasi modo geniti); children who have reached the age of fourteen, who have acquired all the necessary knowledge, and who, from the first Sunday after the Epiphany of the Lord (Epiphanias) until confirmation, have diligently attended the Pastor's lessons in the Law of God for six hours each week, are admitted to confirmation.

*Ibid., art. 11.*

868. For the preparation of youth for confirmation, the basis is the Instruction on the Confirmation of Christian Youth (Das Würtembergische Evangelische Unterrichtsbüchlein), published in Württemberg.

*Ibid., art. 12.*

869. The Transcaucasian Evangelical Lutheran colonist societies are not subordinate to the Consistories of this confession (arts. 790 and 795), but are under the spiritual jurisdiction of the Colonist Synod and the Ober-Pastor, and these in turn are directly subordinate to the Viceroy of the Caucasus.

*Ibid., art. 13; 1856 Aug. 10 (30838).*

870. Pastors are appointed and confirmed in their positions by the Viceroy of the Caucasus, either directly or in consultation with the Ministry of Internal Affairs, in accordance with the recommendation of the Ober-Pastor of the colonies; in doing so, the wishes expressed on this matter by the societies themselves are always taken into consideration.

1841 Nov. 25, art. 14; 1856 Aug. 10 (30838).

871. The order of ordination and appointment of Pastors, the performance and resignation of their office and their departure from the clerical estate generally, follows the same procedure as prescribed above in the Statute of the Evangelical Lutheran Church (section 1), and thereafter the clergy of the German colonies in the Transcaucasian territory enjoy equal rights with the other Pastors of this Church in the Empire.

1841 Nov. 25, art. 15.

872. The Pastors, as Church Trustees, together with two Church Elders and with the assistance of the Church Convention, administer church property and render an annual account thereof, in the month of January, to the colonist Synod (a). The decision as to which of the colonists may be admitted to fill the positions of Church DOCUMENTS______________________________________________________________________ 415

Elders or members of the Church Convention and Synod is left to the local authorities, according to rules established for this purpose with the confirmation of the Viceroy of the Caucasus, with the requirement that persons of bad conduct, or otherwise unreliable for any reason, must not acquire influence over the colonist societies (b).

(a) Ibid., art. 16. — (b) See the Statute on Colonies; 1856 Aug. 10 (30838).

873. In the event that a colony has no Pastor, the society may, pending the appointment of a new Preacher, elect from among its own members a capable spiritual teacher, who must be examined and installed in office by the Ober-Pastor.

1841 Nov. 25, art. 17.

874. The immediate superior of all the colonial Preachers is the Ober-Pastor. He is appointed by the Viceroy of the Caucasus, either directly or in consultation with the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

*Ibid., arts. 14 and 18; 1856 Aug. 10 (30838).*

875. The Ober-Pastor, as superior and overseer of the other Preachers, supervises their teaching, morality, and precision in the performance of their office, and generally attends to the welfare of the Church and schools in the colonies. He communicates to the Pastors all instructions of the Viceroy of the Caucasus and other local authorities, gives the Pastors necessary authorizations in special cases, and receives reports from them for submission, when necessary, to the proper authority. The Ober-Pastor visits the colonist societies located in the Transcaucasian territory annually, to inspect their church and school affairs, and draws up a protocol of each such visitation, which is signed by the Ober-Pastor himself, the local Preacher of the colony, and the Church Elders. He is empowered to petition the civil authorities on Church matters, to convene the colonist Synod at set times, to direct its deliberations, and to report to the Viceroy of the Caucasus on matters to be resolved in the Synod and on all cases in the spiritual sphere in the colonies that deserve the government's attention. He reports to the Viceroy on the death of Pastors, presents candidates for vacant Pastoral positions, on the basis of article 870, and, upon confirmation of those elected, installs them in office. Finally, the Ober-Pastor annually, in the month of February, submits to the Viceroy information on the number of births, marriages, and deaths in the colonies for the past year, as well as on the number of churches, clergy, and parishioners in the colonies.

1841 Nov. 25, art. 19; see the Statute on Colonies; 1856 Aug. 10 (30838).

876. In the event of the death of the Ober-Pastor, or of an illness preventing him from performing the duties of his office, this office, until his recovery or the appointment of another, is performed by the senior, by length of service, of the Pastors of the five colonies located near Tiflis.

1841 Nov. 25, art. 20.

877. For deliberation and judgment on important matters concerning the Church, the Ober-Pastor convenes a Synod, composed of the Ober-Pastor himself, as Chairman, two senior Pastors by length of service from the colonies nearest to Tiflis, as spiritual members, and four secular members, deputies elected by all the societies for three years and, to avoid unnecessary expenses, only from the five colonies located near Tiflis. From these colonies the Synod also elects one Pastor to conduct written business, and it meets in Tiflis twice a year, namely in the early days of March and October.

*Ibid., art. 21.*

878. The secular deputies of the Synod, upon presentation by the Superintendent of the colonies, are confirmed by the Governor of Tiflis, who notifies the Ober-Pastor of those elected. Each of these deputies receives from all the societies collectively, in addition to travel expenses, eighty kopecks in silver per day for his maintenance, for the entire period of his attendance at the Synod.

*Ibid., art. 22; 1846 Dec. 14 (20701).*

879. In the most important matters concerning an entire individual society or colony, that society or colony is permitted to send its Pastor and a special deputy to the Synod; in such a case the Synod itself has the right to require their presence.

1841 Nov. 25, art. 23.

880. The colonist Synod is especially obliged to ensure that the Pastors, in all their actions, precisely follow the general Evangelical Lutheran Church Statute (arts. 134—789), in accordance with the special rules for the Transcaucasian German settlers (arts. 858—884), and that in their teaching and manner of life they act according to the words of the Holy Gospel. It is obliged to strive to remove all obstacles that may arise to this end, to put a stop to any deviations therefrom, and, employing all measures for the preservation of the Church's welfare, to submit reports thereon, in important cases, for the consideration of the authorities.

*Ibid., art. 24.*

881. The colonist Synod examines and decides all disputes and complaints regarding marriages and divorce cases, in strict accordance with the Evangelical Lutheran Church Statute (arts. 134—789) (a).

Note. Every German colonist of the Transcaucasian territory is given the freedom, upon reaching the age of seventeen or eighteen for males and fifteen or sixteen for females, to enter into marriage with persons of any age of majority (b).

(a) Ibid., art. 5. — (b) See the Statute on Colonies.

882. The period for entering into a new marriage, in the event that the whereabouts of one of the spouses are unknown, is set at five years from the time of his absence for Transcaucasian German colonists (a). Such permission to enter into marriage is also allowed in cases where the remaining spouse, husband or wife, though aware of the other party's whereabouts, has no prospect whatsoever of that party's return (b). The investigation of the reliability of the statements of those colonists who, owing to the long absence of a husband or wife, request permission to enter into another marriage, as well as the determination of the cases in which permission may be granted to dissolve a marriage on account of the long absence of one of the spouses, is entrusted to the Tiflis Chamber of State Domains, with a deputy on the spiritual side (v).

(a) See the Statute on Colonies. — (b) Ibid. — (v) Ibid.; 1846 Dec. 14 (20701). DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 4Т_7

883. The Synod confirms village teachers in their positions; it ensures that they, under the supervision and guidance of the Pastors, perform their duties precisely, and generally attends to everything relating to the schools. In the event of important changes in this regard, the Synod seeks the authorization of the authorities.

1841 Nov. 25, art. 26.

884. The Synod oversees the administration of church property of all the societies, and therefore strictly examines and verifies all reports and annual accounts thereon submitted to it by the Pastors and Church Conventions of all the colonies, and submits a statement on this matter, through the Ober-Pastor, to the Viceroy of the Caucasus.

*Ibid., art. 27; 1856 Aug. 10 (30838).*

##### CHAPTER FOUR.

On the administration of the spiritual affairs of the Evangelical Brethren societies

of the Augsburg Confession in Sarepta and the Baltic governorates.

885. The Sarepta Evangelical Brethren Society is granted freedom in the practice of its faith according to the statute, doctrine, and rites existing among the Evangelical Brethren.

1764 Feb. 25 (12057); 1767 Mar. 27 (12852); 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 1; 1801 Sept. 15 (20013); 1826 Oct. 10 (611).

886. The Sarepta Evangelical Brethren Society is permitted to build churches with bell towers and to have bells on the latter, while observing all the requirements of the Construction Statute concerning the building of churches of foreign Christian confessions.

1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 2; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 3; 1801 Sept. 15 (20013); 1826 Oct. 10 (611).

887. With the permission of the government, the Sarepta Evangelical Brethren Society may establish public schools and special houses for keeping not only children but also adults of both sexes until their marriage. In these houses, arranged according to the spiritual rite of the Evangelical Brethren Society, each sex is kept separately.

1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 1; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 3; 1801 Sept. 15 (20013); 1826 Oct. 10 (611).

888. The House belonging to the Sarepta Brethren Society in St. Petersburg, designated for worship and for housing members of this society, is exempt from billeting and other police duties, on an equal footing with the houses of other churches and clergy of the Protestant confession.

1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 11; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 10; 1801 Sept. 15 (20013); 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 10; 1826 Oct. 10 (611); see the Statute on Colonies.

889. The freedom granted to the Sarepta Evangelical Brethren Society in the practice of its faith according to the statute, doctrine, and rites existing among the Evangelical Brethren extends also to members of the Evangelical Brethren societies in the Baltic governorates.

Note. In the Highest decree of May 3, 1834, it was explained, among other things, that the proposal of the Evangelical Lutheran Consistory to admit those wishing to become members of the Brethren society, with a solemn declaration to that effect, could not be permitted, firstly because the Herrnhuters living in the Baltic governorates do not constitute either a separate colony or a distinct religious community, professing generally the Evangelical Lutheran faith, and secondly because all the rights and privileges specified in the Highest charters of October 27, 1817 and October 10, 1826 were, and could only have been, granted to actual members of the Brethren society, that is, to those who arrived in Russia already holding this status, and not to those who might arbitrarily choose to assume this designation.

1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 1; 1826 Oct. 10 (611); 1834 May 3 (7049) art. 6; see also the Statute on Colonies.

890. Members of the Evangelical Brethren Society in the Baltic governorates are permitted to maintain under their supervision, for spiritual benefit, prayer houses or meetings for Latvians, Estonians, and other willing persons in towns, settlements, and villages, with the consent of the landowner and with the knowledge of the town authorities, without any hindrance otherwise. All who wish may freely gather in these prayer houses or meetings, during time free from work, except during the hours designated for ordinary church worship.

1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 2; 1834 May 3 (7049) art. 1.

891. The above-mentioned (art. 890) prayer houses and meetings are under the direction and management of the Elders and members of the Evangelical Brethren Society.

1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 2.

892. Those in charge of the prayer houses and meetings (art. 891) must be Russian subjects, unless they entered upon these positions before May 3, 1834.

1834 May 3 (7049) art. 1.

893. New prayer houses and meetings of the Evangelical Brethren Society in the Baltic governorates may be established only in compliance with the conditions established above, in articles 150, 690, and 691, regarding the establishment of such private prayer meetings as go beyond the bounds of family or household communal prayer, namely:

1) New prayer houses and meetings may be established only with the authorization of the local Evangelical Lutheran Consistories.

2) The Consistories are obliged, upon any intention to establish a prayer house or meeting under their jurisdiction, to bring this to the attention, beforehand and with their opinion, through the chief local authority and the General Consistory, of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, for report to His Imperial Majesty.

3) The Consistories, in authorizing the establishment of new prayer houses and meetings, notify both the local civil authority and the Preacher in whose parish the prayer house or meeting to be established is to be located.

4) The Consistories permit the establishment of prayer houses or meetings only to persons who enjoy general respect in their parishes, who have not been noted for any unlawful acts or acts bringing shame and dishonor, who are Russian subjects, and who are permanent residents of the place where they intend to hold meetings.

1832 Dec. 28 (5871) § 23; 1834 May 3 (7049) art. 1. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 419

894. Priests ordained by Bishops of the Evangelical Brethren Society in the Baltic governorates are permitted, among their brethren of German origin who are actual members of that society, to perform in accordance with their office all spiritual rites which, under the statutes of the society, they are to perform.

1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 5; see the Statute on Colonies.

895. In all prayer houses and meetings without exception (arts. 890—893), only Pastors have the right to preach (freie Vortraege zu halten), and those candidates in Theology who, after due examination by the Evangelical Lutheran Consistory, in accordance with article 274 of this Code, have received a certificate of permission to preach (pro venia concionandi), or Priests properly ordained by Bishops of the Brethren society.

1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 5; 1826 Oct. 10 (611); 1834 May 3 (7049) art. 2.

896. Preceptors (Vorbeter) elected by members of the Evangelical Brethren Society in the Baltic governorates for prayer meetings, if they do not have from the Evangelical Lutheran Consistory the certificate of permission to preach (pro venia concionandi) specified in article 274 of this Code, must, on the basis of article 150, confine themselves to reading Holy Scripture without any interpretation, or to prayers, hymns, and spiritual discourses from books approved by the Evangelical Lutheran Consistories, likewise without any interpretation.

1834 May 3 (7049) art. 3.

897. In accordance with article 691 of this Code, parish Pastors and district Probsts in the Baltic governorates not only have the right, but are obliged, under strict personal responsibility, to visit the prayer meetings of the Evangelical Brethren Society as often as possible, and to observe the precise fulfillment of everything established in article 691.

*Ibid., art. 4.*

898. All gatherings not held in properly established prayer houses, but in private homes, must be forbidden, but with strict observance that this pretext not be used for harassment and oppression.

*Ibid., art. 5.*

##### CHAPTER FIVE.

On the administration of the spiritual affairs of the Scottish colonists at Karras,

the Basel colonists at Shusha, and the Mennonites.

899. Members of the Scottish colony of Karras near the mineral waters in Stavropol governorate are granted the practice of their faith according to the statute, doctrine, and rites existing in their society.

1806 Dec. 25 (22410) art. 2; 1828 Dec. 15 (2517) art. 1; 1835 Jun. 26 (8271).

900. The public affairs of this colony (art. 899), including those relating to matters of faith, are handled by a special Administration composed of persons elected by the society of colonists.

1806 Dec. 25 (22410) art. 5; 1828 Dec. 15 (2517) art. 1; 1835 Jun. 26 (8271).

901. Members of the Scottish colony of Karras and the Basel missionaries settled in Shusha are forbidden all missionary activity (they are permitted to engage in agriculture, manufacturing, and crafts, but not in the conversion of persons of other faiths to Christianity).

1806 Dec. 25 (22410) arts. 12, 13; 1828 Dec. 15 (2517) art. 1; 1835 Jun. 26 (8271).

<...>

903. The Mennonites conduct their affairs of faith without hindrance, according to their church institutions and customs.

1800 Apr. 6 (19372); Sept. 6 (19546); 1801 May 23 (19887).

904. Spiritual teachers of the Mennonites, in performing the duties of their office according to the rules of their confession, must not under any circumstances interfere in secular or other matters unbecoming to the priestly rank.

1801 May 16 (19873) §3.

Digest of Laws of the Russian Empire (SZRI). 1857. Vol. XI. Part I. Pp. 7—171.

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 114.

This document contains complete information on the statutes of the Russian Empire issued up to its appearance (1857) concerning practically all the confessions that spread among the Russian Germans. The one notable exception is the Baptists, officially legalized in Russia in 1879, that is, after this act was issued, and who numbered 19,900 adherents among the country's German population in 1897 (1.1% of that population).

The present edition omits fragments of the document that have no bearing on the Germans, as well as the articles devoted to the Catholic monastic clergy (Arts. 78—88) and the administration of monastic properties (Arts. 126—128), since colonists in Russia were forbidden to establish monasteries.

It is worth noting that the portion of the document devoted to Catholicism is considerably smaller in volume than the Evangelical Lutheran portion. This is due above all to the fact that many aspects of the Catholic Church's activity were regulated not by Russian legislation but directly by the Holy See (by agreement between it and the Russian government). It evidently also played a role that the Evangelical Lutheran Church was noticeably more influential in the Russian Empire than the Catholic Church: the Lutheran confession was not uncommon in the very highest strata of society and even among members of the imperial family.

In 1897 there were 242,200 Catholics (13.5%) among the German population of Russia. Russian Germans of the Catholic faith belonged for the most part to parishes attached either to the Archdiocese of Mogilev (mostly townspeople) or to the Diocese of Tiraspol (colonists, some townspeople). In the Diocese of Tiraspol they constituted the great majority of the parishioners. The Archdiocese of Mogilev was founded in 1782; the Diocese of Tiraspol (known until 1852 as the Diocese of Kherson) was created in 1847, and from 1856 its seat was located in Saratov (Arts. 12, 13).

The German colonists' parishes of the Diocese of Tiraspol belonged to the following deaneries: Saratov (Saratov and Samara governorates), Kamenka (Saratov governorate), Yekaterinenstadt, Marienthal, Zelman (all in Samara governorate), Berdyansk (Taurida and Yekaterinoslav governorates, Don Cossack Host Region), Yekaterinoslav (Yekaterinoslav, Taurida, and Kherson governorates), Simferopol (Taurida governorate), Nikolayev (Kherson and Yekaterinoslav governorates), Odessa (Kherson governorate), and Pyatigorsk (Kuban Region) (Art. 15).

The Archdiocese of Mogilev was headed until 1917 exclusively by Poles or Lithuanians. By contrast, among the heads of the Diocese of Tiraspol there was only one Pole — Wincenty Lipski (1795—1875), who administered the diocese in 1864—1872. All its other heads were German bishops: Ferdinand Helanus Kahn (1787—1864) — 1850—1864, Franz Xaver von Zottmann (1826—1901) — 1872—1889, Anton Johannes Zerr von Padua (1849—1934) — 1889—1901, Eduard Yulyevich (Eduard Michael Johann) von der Ropp (1851—1939) — 1902—1903, Joseph Aloysius Kessler (1862—1933) — 1904—1929. Kahn was born in Galicia, Zottmann in Germany, von der Ropp in Courland, while Zerr and Kessler came from Russian German colonist families (Art. 16).

The theological seminary of the Diocese of Tiraspol, founded in 1856, was located in Saratov. From 1865 all subjects, except the Russian language, Russian literature, and Russian history, were taught here in German. By 1882, 68 priests, including 49 Germans, had graduated from the seminary. The seminary was opened on the initiative and with the participation of Bishop Kahn. Among those who studied there and subsequently served as its professors and inspectors were the future bishops Zottmann (the first professor of German origin), Zerr, and Kessler; Zottmann was also rector of the seminary (Art. 102).

In 1897 there were 1,360,800 Lutherans (76.0%) among the German population of Russia. The basis of the Lutheran portion of the present document was the Statute of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Russia of December 28, 1832, together with the accompanying Instruction to the Lutheran Clergy (PSZRI. Coll. 2. Nos. 5870 and 5871).

The term "preachers" (проповедники) used in this document (as in many other Russian-language documents) with reference to Evangelical Lutheran pastors (Art. 136 and following) is incorrect. In German the word "preacher" (Prediger) was customarily used for Lutheran clergy who had not been ordained or who served military units, or for clergy of certain Protestant confessions (Mennonites, Baptists, etc.) that reject church hierarchy. In Russian (if one wishes to avoid using the foreign word "pastor") Lutheran pastors should be called parish priests, as is done in the Catholic portion of the present document, or simply priests.

The colonies had the following provostal districts: the Volga region (Moscow Evangelical Lutheran Consistory) — Right Bank (the upland side of the Volga; Saratov governorate) and Left Bank (the meadow side of the Volga; Samara governorate); the south of Russia (St. Petersburg Evangelical Lutheran Consistory) — 1st South Russian (Bessarabia Region, Kherson governorate) and 2nd South Russian (Yekaterinoslav, Taurida, and Kherson governorates, Don Cossack Host and Kuban Regions) (Art. 401).

The lay presidents of the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory were: Pavel Ivanovich (Paul) von Tiesenhausen (1774—1864) — 1833—1845, Yegor Fyodorovich (Georg Otto Wilhelm) von Meyendorff (1794—1879) — 1845—1879, Theodor Bruhn — 1880—1888, Fyodor Karlovich (Theodor) Giers (1824—1891) — 1888—1891, Alexander Alexandrovich (Alexander Karl Abraham) von Uexküll-Gyllenband (1840—1912) — 1891—1896, Emil von Scholtz (1841—1913) — 1897—1913, Yuly Alexandrovich (Julius Karl) von Uexküll-Gyllenband (1852—1918), brother of A.A. von Uexküll-Gyllenband — 1914—1917. The spiritual vice-presidents and general superintendents of the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory were: Johann Friedrich August Vollborth (1768—1840) — 1832—1840, Friedrich Nikolaus von Paucker (1778—1856) — 1840—1856, Karl Christian Ulmann (1793—1871) — 1856—1868, Yuly Ivanovich (Julius Wilhelm Theophil) von Richter (1808—1892) — 1868—1892, Konrad Reimund Freifeld (1847—1923) — 1892—1918. Vollborth was born in Germany, Paucker and Richter in Courland, Ulmann and Freifeld in Livonia. Vollborth became a Doctor of Theology at Dorpat; Ulmann, Richter, and Freifeld studied at the University of Dorpat, where Ulmann also served as professor of theology and rector (Art. 452).

In 1897 there were 64,000 persons (3.6%) of the Reformed faith among the German population of Russia. In addition to the Evangelical Reformed parishes mentioned in this document, such parishes also existed in Russia in Vologda and Yaroslavl (1670—1704), in Odessa (from 1844), in the Volga colonies — North Yekaterinenstadt (1768—1905), Kukkus (from 1767), and others, and in the colonies of southern Russia — Rohrbach-Worms (from 1861), Neudorf (from 1862), and Shabo (from 1846).

Reformed sessions [committees] existed in the St. Petersburg, Moscow, Courland, and Livonia Evangelical Lutheran Consistories (Art. 790).

The French and German Evangelical Reformed communities in St. Petersburg formed a single body from 1775 to 1858 (Art. 798); the French community was founded in 1724, the German community in 1775 (Art. 799).

The Evangelical Reformed parish in Moscow existed from 1635 (Art. 812); the Reformed parish in Arkhangelsk existed from 1660 (the Lutheran one from 1686) (Art. 834).

The first Evangelical Lutheran parishes in the German colonies of Transcaucasia arose in 1825—1832 (Art. 859).

Until 1884 the chief pastors (Oberpastoren) of the Transcaucasian colonies were, as a rule, the pastors of the colonist community of Tiflis (the colony of Neu-Tiflis): Johannes Bernhard Saltet (1792—1830) — 1825—1830, August Heinrich Dittrich (1797—1855) — 1833—1838, Christoph Heinrich Bonwetsch (1804—1876) — 1838—1845, Johannes Huppenbauer (1816—1887) — 1845—1851, Christian Gottlieb Roth (1802—1872) — 1852—1853, 1858—1864, Alexander Martin Geyer (1820—?) — 1853—1858, Karl Rudolph Roos (1825—1910) — 1865—1884; in 1884—1905 — the pastor of the colony of Yelenendorf, Markus Miller (1847—1905), who was killed during the revolutionary disturbances; in 1905—1909 — the pastor from Yelenendorf, Oskar Georg Rudolph von Wiren (1866—1950); in 1910—1915 — Heinrich Heinzelmann (1865—?), a former pastor of the colonies of Alexandershilf (Alexandrovo), Elisabethtal, and Yekaterinenfeld, who was exiled to Siberia in 1915. Owing to the peculiarities of religious life in the Transcaucasian colonies, the origins of the chief pastors here differed considerably from what was usual at that time for the Evangelical Lutheran churches of Russia. Saltet, Dittrich, Bonwetsch, Huppenbauer, Roth, and Miller were graduates of the Basel Mission Society; all of them, except Miller, a native of Switzerland, were born in Germany. Only from the second half of the nineteenth century did natives of the Russian Empire, graduates of the University of Dorpat — Geyer, Roos, von Wiren (Heinzelmann's origin has not been established) — begin to occupy the post of chief pastor in Transcaucasia (Art. 874).

The five colonies near Tiflis are the colonies of Tiflis governorate: Neu-Tiflis, Elisabethtal, Yekaterinenfeld, Marienfeld, and Alexandersdorf (Art. 877).

The Evangelical Brethren community (Herrnhuter community) in Sarepta arose in 1765 and existed until 1894, when it merged into the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Russia (Art. 885).

The Evangelical community in the colony of Karras (Stavropol governorate, later Terek Region) arose in 1805; until 1825 it was served by Scottish clergy, and thereafter by German clergy; from 1866 it was served by the Pyatigorsk parish (Art. 899).

In 1897 there were 65,900 Mennonites (3.7%) among the German population of Russia (Art. 903).

## No. 115. STATUTE ON COLONIES OF FOREIGNERS IN THE RUSSIAN EMPIRE (1857)

**STATUTE**

**ON COLONIES OF FOREIGNERS IN THE EMPIRE.**

**COMPENDIUM**

**OF INSTITUTIONS AND STATUTES**

**ON COLONIES OF FOREIGNERS IN THE EMPIRE.**

#### PART ONE. THE DIVISION OF COLONIES AND THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THEIR ADMINISTRATION.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

Division of colonies.

Art. 1. The colonies of foreigners settled in the Russian Empire are: 1) colonies established on state lands (a); 2) colonies settled on lands acquired in ownership by foreign immigrants (b); and 3) colonies settled on private lands, under contracts with their owners (v).

Note. Provisions concerning colonies of foreigners settled on lands allotted to them from the treasury constitute properly the subject of the first eight parts of this Compendium; while the rules concerning other settlers, as exceptions from the general provisions, are set forth separately in Part IX.

(a) Cf. the enactments cited in Chapter III [II] of this part. — (b) 1804 Mar. 1 (21192). - (v) 1765 Nov. 1 (12503): 1804 Apr. 12 (21254); 1817 Aug. 25 (27022); Oct. 1 (27072); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

2. The colonies settled on state lands are the following:

I. The colonies of the southern region of Russia, by which are meant all existing colonies of foreigners in the three New Russia governorates and in the Bessarabian region (a).

II. The Saratov colonies (b). DOCUMENTS_______________________________ ____________________________________________ 421

III. The Northern colonies, namely those established in St. Petersburg Governorate (v).

IV. The Livonia colony, settled in Wenden district of Livonia Governorate, on the estates of Hirschenhof and Helfreichshof (g).

V. The colonies of Members of the Evangelical Brethren Society, established in Sarepta and in the three Baltic governorates (d).

VI. The Belovezh colony, in Chernigov Governorate (e).

VII. The Rybensdorf colony, in Voronezh Governorate (zh).

VIII. The colonies of Württemberg settlers, in the Transcaucasus region (z).

IX. The German colony, in Stavropol Governorate near the mineral waters (k).

X. The German colony, settled near the town of St. Krest (l).

XI. The Karras colony, near the mineral waters in Stavropol Governorate, founded by Scottish missionaries (m).

XII. The colony of the Basel missionaries, settled near the town of Shusha (n).

XIII. The German colony near the town of Yeysk (o).

Note I. The woolen manufacturers settled near the towns of Poltava and Konstantinograd (p), although they had been received into the charge of the Poltava Chamber of State Domains, nevertheless, since these manufacturers occupy land within the town boundary, are under the jurisdiction of the town police for police matters, and since a special Committee of six members, elected by the society of these manufacturers from among themselves, under the chairmanship of a Guardian of the colonies appointed to that office by the local authorities (r), has been established to direct their affairs, these manufacturers have been removed from the department of the Chamber of State Domains (s).

Note 2. In 1851 it was Most Highly permitted for Prussian Mennonites, numbering one hundred families, to settle in Samara Governorate, under specially established rules on the matter (t).

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On the department and administration of the colonies.

4. Foreign settlers (art. 2) are under the guardianship of the Ministry of State Domains (a), through the First or Second Department of this Ministry, depending on the governorate in which the colonies of foreign settlers have been established (b). In the governorate administration, foreign settlers, in each governorate where they are located, are either under the guardianship of the Chamber of State Domains, through its Economic Division (v); or are subordinate to the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers of the southern region, or to the Saratov Office of Foreign Settlers, and beyond the Caucasus to the Expedition of State Domains under the Main Administration of the Transcaucasus Region (g).

Note. In the district administration, foreign settlements are subject to District Chiefs only in those governorates in which the Chambers of State Domains are subordinate to the Second Department of State Domains (d).

Division One.

On the local administration of the colonies of the southern region.

I. Composition of the local administration.

7. For the administration of the New Russia and Bessarabian foreign and Jewish settlements there exist: 1) the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers of the southern region; 2) the Administration of the Trans-Danubian immigrants.

1845 Nov. 1 (19434).

8. The Guardianship Committee consists of a Chairman and two Members.

1845 Nov. 1 (19434) staff [establishment] I; 1850 Jan. 25 (23873) para. 1.

11. Under the department of the Guardianship Committee are the Overseers of the settlements (colonies).

1818 Mar. 22 (27312) art. III, para. 3; 1819 Dec. 29 (22054[280541).

17. In the District and Village Board there must be a clerk, under whose supervision young people of the colony are employed for correspondence work (a).

Note. For the training of capable teachers from among colonist boys for village schools and clerks for the Boards, as well as Surveyors and Architects, with the aim moreover of spreading through them knowledge of the Russian language in the colonies, a school has been established in the Bessarabian colony of Sarata, under a special regulation concerning it (b).

18. The colonists of each settlement constitute its communal society.

1801 May 16 (19873).

19. In each communal society a village communal assembly is established.

*Ibid.*

20. Colonists, at least one from each household, are summoned to the assembly by the Head or Schulz, sent for this purpose through Tithingmen with notices.

*Ibid.*

21. Colonists, having assembled for the meeting, must maintain quiet and attentively occupy themselves with what is proposed to them.

II. Procedure for the appointment of officials.

22. The appointment and dismissal of members of the Guardianship Committee and of the Administrator of the Trans-Danubian immigrants is at the discretion of the Minister of State Domains.

*Ibid. and 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).*

23. All other officials and clerical staff are appointed and dismissed by the Guardianship Committee itself.

*Ibid.*

24. Heads, Schulzes, and Beisitzers are appointed by election by the society of colonists.

1801 May 16 (19873) § 9.

25. The Head is elected for three years, and District Beisitzers for two years, from all the villages of the colony assigned to the Board. After a year has passed following the initial election, one of the Beisitzers is dismissed, and whoever is to take his place then remains in office for a full two years without fail. For Village Schulzes and Beisitzers, the election is held for two years, under the special supervision of the Heads, with the consent of each settlement, but with the same annual rotation of Beisitzers as in the District Board.

*Ibid., § 10.*

26. Those settlements which, because of their distance from others, cannot conveniently be assigned to any of the District Boards, elect a Schulz for three years, and two Beisitzers for two; those thus elected perform all the duties assigned to a District Board, independently of it.

*Ibid., §11.*

27. In electing district and village officials, in addition to the three persons appointed for each Board, two more should be elected to fill the posts in case of absence or illness.

1803 Jul. 7 (20841) § 16.

28. Elections are conducted by majority vote, from among adult colonists who have their own household, who are prudent, just, of good behavior, diligent and exemplary in their household management, and above all skilled in agriculture, horticulture, and animal husbandry.

1801 May 16 (19873) §9.

29. In the election, each casts his vote in turn, for whomever he chooses for whatever office, without any servility and following neither friendship nor enmity.

*Ibid.*

30. At the conclusion of the elections, those who have received the most votes are confirmed by the signed agreement of all, and are submitted for final confirmation by the Guardianship Committee.

*Ibid., §§ 9 and 10; 1833 Jul. 1 (6298).*

31. Tithingmen are rotated monthly.

1801 May 10 (19873) § 10.

32. Clerks are appointed for a special wage by voluntary hire.

1803 Jul. 7 (20841) § 15.

33. The Chairman, the members of the Committee, the Administrator, and all other officials of the administration of the New Russia and Bessarabian foreign settlements receive maintenance in the amount fixed by the establishment. The establishment sum is made up by a levy on the New Russia and Bessarabian foreign settlers under the Committee's jurisdiction, and from revenues of the leasehold items in the foreign settlements (a).

Note. The levy on the New Russia and Bessarabian foreign settlers has been increased by three kopecks for every male revision soul released from the exemption period, to cover the expenses under the establishment of a special Control Division of the Committee, set up in 1850. This additional levy is paid into the District Treasuries within the time limits established for the payment of taxes, while the sum fixed by the establishment is disbursed from the state treasury on the general basis (b).

35. The Head receives a salary of five rubles seventy-two kopecks, and the District Beisitzers four rubles twenty-nine kopecks, from all the settlements belonging to the Board; the Schulz is allotted two rubles eighty-eight kopecks from the settlement in which he was elected.

IV. Subjects and duties.

37. The subjects of the Guardianship Committee are:

1) The reception of foreign settlers establishing themselves in the status of colonists.

2) Their settlement on the basis of the rules established for this purpose.

3) The department of lands allotted or hereafter to be allotted for the settlement of colonists.

4) The protection of all benefits, rights, and privileges granted and hereafter to be granted to colonists.

5) Supervision of the fulfillment of the obligations they have undertaken.

6) The inspection of the colonies and the examination of complaints and petitions submitted by colonists (a).

Note. The authorities of the foreign settlers of the southern region also participate in the arrangements for the provisioning of local horses, for the travel of Their Highest Highnesses, on an equal footing with the other persons designated for this purpose (b).

38. In addition to this, the following are assigned to the department of the Guardianship Committee:

1) All matters of rural police in relation to the colonies entrusted to them; the timely and proper collection of taxes due to the treasury; the conduct of investigations in the colonies; fines, penalties, etc.

2) Care of the economy and household management in the colonies.

3) Encouragement of the improvement of agriculture, horticulture, and animal husbandry, and of the establishment of factories suited to the climate and local possibilities.

4) The apportionment of state debt sums among families, the safekeeping of payments made, their verification, and their forwarding as appropriate.

5) The issuance of passports to colonists, their release into other statuses, and their departure abroad.

6) The confirmation of district and village officials in the manner established for this.

7) Judicial matters among colonists under the rules set forth in Part VIII of this Compendium.

41. Heads, Schulzes, and Beisitzers, being distinguished and respected above all other villagers, are obliged to promote their welfare and warn them against any harm; in the performance of their office, they must exact compliance strictly but with order, treat the villagers kindly, receive all their petitions patiently and attend to all their needs, be direct advocates for them, and by no means engage in bribe-taking, since they will be subject to prosecution and punishment under the laws both for neglect of their duties and for oppression of their subordinates.

V. Procedure for the conduct of business.

43. In the conduct of business the Committee follows the procedure established in the Chambers of State Domains; matters are brought before the General Presence at the direction of the Chairman.

1845 Nov. 1 (19434) para. 5.

1803 Jul. 7 (20841) § 16. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 427

At the request of a District or Village Board, every colonist must appear before it immediately; upon the summoned colonist's arrival in the room in which the Schulzes and Beisitzers perform their office, he must, with due respect and without his hat, approach the village authorities, ask permission to explain his matter, and then decorously and without any commotion present his need; and when, after being heard, he is told to leave the room, he must do so at once and wait until he is called back in.

*Ibid., § 17.*

48. Whoever, upon being summoned by a District or Village Board, fails to appear before it at once without good cause, shall be liable under article 307 of the Code of Punishments; and in cases requiring urgency admitting of no delay, he may be brought to the Board under guard, and such disobedience is to be reported to the Guardianship Committee.

1803 Jul. 7 (20841) § 17; 1833 Jul. 1 (6298); 1840 Aug. 31 (13750); 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 295.

VI. Nature and limits of authority.

49. The jurisdiction of the Guardianship Committee extends to all colonies already existing or hereafter to be settled on state lands in the three New Russia governorates and in the Bessarabian region, of whatever nation they may be, and to settlers from among Russian subjects, settled under the rules issued for colonists, only until such time as they are transferred to the general governorate department.

VII. Subordination and procedure of communications.

51. The Guardianship Committee is directly subordinate to the Minister of State Domains.

52. The Committee receives instructions and proposals from the Minister of State Domains, and carries them out precisely.

54. In matters admitting of no delay, the Committee is guided by the interest of the treasury or the necessity of the settlers, reporting nevertheless immediately on everything to the Minister.

The Committee has no direct communication with other higher authorities, except for reports to the Senate on the receipt of decrees, which are sent to the Committee on an equal footing with other higher government offices. In all cases requiring communication with other offices, the Committee submits to the Minister of State Domains.

57. Necessary communications with the Governor-General of New Russia and Bessarabia, as the chief local authority in civil matters, are conducted either directly by the Committee according to the forms used in the Ministries, or, by its resolutions, in the name of the Committee's Chairman. The Governor-General is obliged to satisfy all lawful requirements of the Committee in matters concerning colonists, while notifying it at the same time of his own dispositions.

The lower officials of the governorate in which the subordinate colonies are located, such as Town Governors, District Police Officers, and others, are obliged to comply immediately with the requirements of the Committee or of its Chairman in all cases in which such requirements pertain to their duties.

77. The Administrator of the Office, its Members, and all other officials receive maintenance fixed by the establishment. The establishment sum is made up by an eighteen-kopeck levy on the colonists subordinate to the Office. Surpluses from the establishment allocation are used, with the permission of the Minister of State Domains, for those purposes to which a similar sum is applied, made up of surpluses from the establishment allocations for the Chambers and District Administrations of State Domains.

1845 Nov. 1 (19434) staff [establishment], note; 1854 Jan. 6 (27841) staff [establishment], note.

78. District and Village Boards are organized entirely in conformity with those established in the colonies of the southern region, and likewise, in various particulars of administration, are obliged to conform to the rules prescribed for the local administration of the southern colonies.

This is evident from a comparison of the Instructions for the Saratov and New Russia colonists.

Division Three.

On the local administration of the St. Petersburg colonies.

79. For the administration of the St. Petersburg colonies an Overseer with an Assistant is appointed; one clerical servant is allotted to them.

1833 Jul. 1 (6298) staff [establishment]; 1840 (14108) staff [establishment].

80. The appointment and dismissal of the Overseer of the St. Petersburg Settlements and his Assistant is at the discretion of the Minister of State Domains.

1833 Jul. 1 (6298); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

81. The Overseer, his Assistant, and the Boards administer the colonists in application of the rules prescribed for the local administrations of colonists of the southern region and of Saratov.

1797 Jun. 20 (18006) para. 7-9; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798); 1809 Aug. 7 (23773).

82. Under the department of the Overseer are District and Village Boards, which are established on the same basis as those existing in the colonies of the southern region of Russia.

1803 Jun. 16 (20798) art. II, §§ 8-11.

83. The Overseer, his Assistant, and the clerical servant receive their salary at the expense of the settlers themselves, per establishment.

1833 Jul. 1 (6298) para. 8; 1840 (14108) staff [establishment]. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 432

84. The colonist-manufacturers of Tsarskoye Selo are not under the general administration of the St. Petersburg colonists, but are administered by the town authorities of Tsarskoye Selo (a), while the colonists of the Alexandria colony, settled on land of the palace department near Peterhof, are entirely under the jurisdiction of the Peterhof town authorities (b).

(a) 1819 May 28 (27818); 1825 Aug. 20 (30459). - (b) 1852 Jun. 9, Most Highest] command].

Division Four.

On the local administration of the Livonia colony,

settled in Wenden district.

85. The Livonia colonists are administered by Elders chosen from among themselves, whose confirmation they must submit, through the District Chief under whose department they are, to the Livonia Chamber of State Domains; they are subject to the general oversight of the rural police.

Conditions concluded with these settlers upon their establishment, 1766 Nov. 21, para. 17; 1783 Nov. 14 (15873); 1798 Jun. 14, rescript addressed to the Livonia] Civil] Governor] Richter; 1830 Sept. 23 (3938) art. 56 [6], para. 4 and 6; 1841 Jun. 12 (14643).

Division Five.

On the local administration of the colonies

of Members of the Evangelical Brethren Society, established in Sarepta

and in the three Baltic governorates.

I. Local administration of the Sarepta colony.

86. The Sarepta colony is administered solely by the Administrator of the Office of Saratov Foreign Settlers; it has, moreover, its own special Board, whose composition, under the name of the Board of the Evangelical Brethren Society, is defined in Part VIII of this Compendium.

1797 Jun. 20 (18011) para. 4; 1833 Jul. 1 (6298) staff [establishment]; 1834 Aug. 8 (7337).

II. Local administration of Members of the Evangelical Brethren Society

living in the Baltic governorates.

87. Members of the Brethren Society in the Baltic governorates are permitted to have their own authority among themselves, consisting of Elders.

1817 Oct. 27 (27113) para. 8.

88. These Elders are granted the right to have a special seal.

*Ibid.*

Division Six.

Local administration of the Belovezh colony

in Chernigov Governorate.

89. The Belovezh colony is under the authority of the Chernigov Chamber of State Domains, which is obliged to administer it according to the laws generally issued concerning colonists.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1809 Jul. 2 (23737) pt. 1; 1838 Apr. 30 (11189) pt. I, § 57; 1844 Aug. 8 (18132).*

Section Seven.

Local administration of the Ryebensdorf colony

in Voronezh Governorate.

90. The Ryebensdorf colony is subordinate to the Voronezh Chamber of State Domains.

*1833 Jul. 1 (6298) pt. 3; 1838 Apr. 30 (11189) pt. I, § 57.*

91. The colonists elect from among themselves a Vorsteher, who in everything relating to rural administration acts according to the rules prescribed for Volost Heads in state-owned villages.

*1833 Jul. 1 (6298).*

Section Eight.

Local administration of the colony of Württemberg settlers

in the Transcaucasian Territory.

92. Supervision of the Transcaucasian settlers is entrusted to the Expedition of State Domains under the Main Administration of the Transcaucasian Territory (a).

Note. The German colony located near Tiflis, beyond the Kuki suburb, has been assigned to the city of Tiflis, and moreover in 1852 it was decreed: having secured the colonists' present rights, to grant to each householder as private property the land and houses individually held by them, provided, however, that these may not be transferred to outside persons not belonging to the membership of the colony; 2) to permit colonists to resettle in other places and to pass into other estates; those who are discharged into another estate may remain in the estate of colonists only if they undertake to fulfill the obligations of both statuses, in accordance with articles 139 and 140 of this Statute; 3) to grant them, for internal administration, the right to have their own Board [Prikaz], on the model of the Rural [Board], on the former basis and with the former rights, on condition that the Board collect from them all state and municipal taxes and dues and remit them where required; 4) with the assignment of the German colony to the city of Tiflis, to place it under the jurisdiction of the Tiflis municipal police, on condition that the police adjudicate complaints against the actions of the Board according to the rules set forth in this Statute, within the limits of authority granted to the Colony Warden, and refer matters requiring the decision of higher authority to the Tiflis Provincial Board. The Viceroy of the Caucasus has been authorized, on this basis, to define in special rules the relations of the Tiflis police to the colonists and their Board (b).

(a) 1833 Jul. 1 (6298) pt. 2; 1841 Jan. 5 (14157) § 17; 1846 Dec. 14 (20701) pt. 7; 1849 Dec. 21 (23753) §§ 1, 2, 31, 32. - (b) 1852 Sept. 11 (26578).

93. The Colony Warden, the Bookkeeper — who is at the same time the officer in charge of colony affairs — and the clerical staff are appointed and dismissed by the Expedition of State Domains and receive salaries according to the staff schedule at the expense of the settlers themselves.

*1833 Jul. 1 (6298); 1838 Apr. 30 (11189); 1841 Jan. 5 (14157) § 17.*

94. The Colony Warden, being directly subordinate to the Expedition, acts under its direction on the basis of instructions given to him with the approval of the Viceroy of the Caucasus.

*1849 Dec. 21 (23753) §§ 1, 2, 31, 32.*

Section Nine.

Local administration of the German colony

settled in Stavropol Governorate near the mineral waters.

95. The German colony near the mineral waters, formed of settlers from Saratov, is under the authority of the Chamber of State Domains and is administered according to the general rules established for the administration of the Saratov foreign settlers and the colonists of the southern territory.

*1835 Jun. 26 (8271); 1838 Apr. 30 (11189).*

Section Ten.

Local administration of the German colony

near the town of St. Cross [Svyatoi Krest].

96. These colonists have a special Warden, maintained at their own expense, for their administration; in other respects they remain under the direct authority of the Chamber of State Domains.

*1817 Sept. 29 (27070) pt. 3; 1838 Apr. 30 (11189) pt. I, § 57.*

Section Eleven.

Local administration of the colony

founded by Scottish missionaries at Karras.

97. For the administration of the public affairs of the Karras colony, the colonists are granted the right to establish a Board [Uprava] by electing from among themselves one Elder and two members.

*1835 Jun. 26 (8271) pt. 4.*

98. The election is renewed every three years, and the Elder is chosen in turn: once from the Scottish and once from the Saratov colonists.

*Ibid.*

99. This colony is under the direct authority and protection of the Chamber of State Domains, which is obliged to watch over the welfare of the colonists and to prevent all discord among them.

*Ibid., pt. 5; 1838 Apr. 30 (11189) pt. I, § 57.*

Section Twelve.

Local administration of the colony of Basel missionaries

settled near the town of Shusha.

100. The local administration of the colony of Basel missionaries is in every respect based on the same rules as the administration of the Scottish colony (a). This colony is under the Administration of the Expedition of State Domains under the Main Administration of the Transcaucasian Territory (b).

(a) 1821 Dec. 17, Highest Order; 1828 Dec. 15 (2517). - (b) 1841 Jan. 5 (14157) § 17; 1846 Dec. 14 (20701) pt. 8.

Section Thirteen.

On the administration of the German colony near the town of Yeysk.

101. The German colony near the town of Yeysk is under the immediate subordination of the Investigative Authority of the Yeysk district, where it has been settled under the general authority and protection of the Host Administration of the Black Sea Host.

*1852 Mar. 20 (26077), pt. 5.*

102. For the settlement of cases, the observance of order, and the exact fulfillment of everything relating to the economy, police, and moral condition of the colonists, they appoint from among themselves Elders and Deputies.

*Ibid.*

103. The Elders and Deputies act on the basis of the duties defined above (arts. 16, 45, etc.) for Schulzes and Beisitzers.

*Ibid.*

104. The Investigative Authority acts with the powers of the Colony Warden (art. 75), and the Host Administration with the powers of the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers of the southern territory.

*Ibid.*

105. Criminal cases of the colonists are referred for decision to the Host judicial bodies.

*Ibid.*

Section Fourteen.

On the administration of the Jewish colonies

located in the New Russia governorates.

106. The administration of the Jews in the New Russia governorates is subordinate to the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers.

*1846 Nov. 5 (20582); 1847 Mar. 5 (20977) pt. 16.*

107. For local oversight, the Guardianship Committee appoints in each of the New Russia governorates a special Trustee with an Assistant, and in the settlements Boards [Prikazy] are established on the same basis on which they exist in the German colonies, under the direction of one of the best German colonists, or, in the absence of such, of trustworthy persons of another estate. Jewish settlements situated among the colonies of foreign settlers may be placed under the nearest Colony Warden (a).

(a) 1847 Mar. 5 (20977) pt. 17. <...>

108. In order to attract to the Jewish settlements German colonists who, by the example of their husbandry, might be of benefit to the Jews and, moreover, might be appointed to the offices of rural officials, the Guardianship Committee is authorized to invite the best householders among the German colonists to move to the Jewish settlements, as leaseholders, for an extended term, granting them plots of land from twenty to forty desyatinas for the first ten years, on an equal footing with the Jews, free of charge, and thereafter, over the course of the next DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 435

ten years, upon payment of half the quitrent. If, however, the colonists wish to remain on these plots beyond the twenty-year term, they shall be required to pay the full quitrent (a).

#### SECTION TWO. ON THE CIVIL STATUS OF COLONISTS.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

On entry into the estate of colonists.

110. Only those foreigners are recognized as colonists who are settled either on state-owned, or private, or purchased lands, in the capacity of farmers or of craftsmen needed in the agricultural condition; foreigners arriving singly or with families for trade and crafts, or for registration in some estate within towns, are in no way to be counted among them (a).
