Note. From 1819, the recruitment of foreigners was firmly discontinued (b), but subsequently, at various times, the resettlement of foreigners to Russia was again permitted (v).

(a) 1763 Jul. 22 (11880); 1804 Feb. 20 (21163); Mar. 1 (21192); Apr. 12 (21254); 1817 Aug. 25 (27022); 1818 Mar. 22 (27312) art. 1, pt. 8; 1827 Oct. 5 (1443). - (b) 1819 Oct. 25 (27954); 1831 Jun. 2 (4617). - (v) 1842 Jan. 27 (15248); 1851 Nov. 19 (25752, a); 1852 Mar. 20 (26077).

111. The Ministry of State Domains is granted the right to admit into the number of colonists, singly and without any assistance from the treasury for settlement, but with the grant of the statutory allotment of land, such foreign émigrés as, having arrived from abroad to visit relatives long settled in Russia in the estate of colonists, or having been summoned by the latter, should for whatever reason wish to remain permanently in Russia in this same estate (a), and to authorize, at its discretion, the admission into the estate of colonists of foreign craftsmen useful to the colonies who, according to the certification of the local authorities, will be able to settle without assistance from the treasury, provided the colony community consents to their admission (b).

Note. In 1832 and 1837 the Chief Trustee of the colonies of the southern territory was authorized to admit into the said colonies, in order to replace families lost to plague and cholera, German emigrants departing from the Kingdom of Poland, without requesting special permission of the Ministry of State Domains for this, provided, however, that such emigrants be admitted to the class of colonists only with the consent of the communities and if they prove able to settle without any assistance from the treasury, taking care that, in order to avoid overcrowding in the settlement, their number should not exceed the number of colonists lost (v).

(a) 1831 May 6 (4539) pt. 4; 1837 Dec. 26 (10834). - (b) 1832 May 31 (5404); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834). - (v) 1832 Oct. 18 (5684); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

112. The rural craftsmen who are permitted to be enrolled among the colonists (art. 111) are: tailors, shoemakers, carpenters, blacksmiths, potters, coppersmiths, weavers, and masons; all other artisans and craftsmen who are of no use for village life may not be recognized as colonists.

*1804 Feb. 20 (21163).*

113. Upon entry into the estate of colonist, the foreigner must give a signed undertaking to observe the internal laws of the colony.

*1763 Jul. 22 (11880) pt. 5; 1764 Mar. 19 (12095) art. 4.*

114. Each colonist takes the oath of allegiance according to his own faith and rites.

*1763 Jul. 22 (11880) pt. 5.*

<...>

116. Mennonites, as well as Württemberg colonists of the Separatist sect, are not required to take the oath of allegiance, but are permitted to perform it in accordance with the rules of their faith, by a single verbal affirmation consisting in the pronouncement of the word "yes."

*1800 Sept. 6 (19546) pt. 1; 1819 Dec. 2 (28012).*

117. Should any colonist refuse to take the oath of allegiance, such persons, after everything that may have been given to them for their settlement has been taken back, shall be sent abroad immediately.

*1814 Jul. 17 (25622).*

118. The formal admission of persons wishing to join as members of the Evangelical Brotherhood Society in the Baltic governorates, and their solemn declaration thereof, is prohibited.

*1834 May 3 (7089) pt. 6.*

<...>

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On the civil rights of colonists.

120. All colonists settled in Russia enjoy freedom in the practice of their faith according to its statutes, teachings, and rites.

*1763 Jul. 22 (11880) art. 6; 1764 Feb. 25 (12057); 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) pt. 1; 1804 Feb. 20 (21163); 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) pt. 2; 1814 Jan., Privilege to the Warsaw colonists settled in Bessarabia, pt. 6; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) pt. 1; <...>*

121. Colonists are permitted to establish churches on the lands allotted to them and to maintain at these the requisite number of Priests, Pastors, and other clergy; the construction of monasteries, however, is prohibited.

*1763 Jul. 22 (11880) art. 6; 1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 2; 1814 Jan. b. pt. Privilege to the Warsaw colonists settled in Bessarabia, pt. 6.*

122. Under pain of the full rigor of the law, colonists are forbidden to entice and draw into agreement with their own faith or society any persons living in Russia who profess the Orthodox faith or, in general, any other Christian faith.

*1763 Jul. 22 (11880) art. 6. — Cf. Statutes on Foreign Confessions.*

**<...> DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 437**

124. Colonists and their descendants are granted civil rights not only in their colonies, but throughout the Empire.

*1763 Jul. 22 (11880) art. 6; 1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 4; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) pt. 5; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546).*

125. Colonists and their descendants enjoy full freedom and power to dispose of their own property within the state as they see fit.

*1797 Jun. 20 (18011) pt. 9; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) pt. 8.*

126. In the event that a colonist exports acquired property abroad, he is obligated to pay a three-year tax on the capital accumulated in Russia, in whatever amount is declared according to his conscience and that of the authorities of the settlement in which he resides (a).

Note 1. The particular civil rights of colonists, both personal and in respect of property and obligations, are set forth in detail in Section III; the rights of colonists to engage in trade and to establish factories and works are set forth in Section V of this Code.

Note 2. Concerning the rights granted to foreign armorers of the Zlatoust factory, see the Mining Statute (b).

(a) 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) pt. 9; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) pt. 8. - (b) 1832 Mar. 11 (5224); 1833 Feb. 28 (6018).

##### CHAPTER THREE.

On the acts of civil status of colonists.

127. The acts of civil status of colonists are: 1) revision tales [census lists], and 2) parish registers.

Cf. the laws cited in the following articles.

Section One.

Revision tales.

128. The census of colonists is conducted at the same intervals and on the same rules as the general census; and therefore the compilation and form of the revision tales, as well as their submission, is carried out in the same manner as prescribed by the Statute on the Census generally for all taxable estates subject to enumeration.

*1802 May 9 (20259); 1815 Dec. 8 (26013).*

Section Two.

Parish registers.

129. The duty of keeping accurate parish registers in the colonies, both of those married and of those born and deceased, is placed upon the Priests and Pastors, who must submit copies of them to the authorities at the end of each half-year.

*1800 Sept. 17 (18562[19562]) art. 3; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 8 [6]; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 6.*

130. Heads and Schulzes are obliged to send lists and summary registers of births, marriages, and deaths annually by the first day of January.

*1801 May 16 (19873) § 26; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 24.*

##### CHAPTER FOUR.

On the termination of the civil status of colonists.

131. The rights of civil status of colonists are terminated by: 1) transfer into other estates (a); 2) departure abroad (b); 3) a crime entailing the deprivation of all rights of status (v).

(a) Cf. the laws cited in the following articles. — (b) Cf. the laws cited in Sect. II, Ch. IV, Section VI. — (v) 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 24.

132. It is forbidden to discharge colonists into other estates by entire settlements, or in such numbers from a single settlement that it might thereby fall into disorder.

*1812 Nov. 27 (25276) pt. 1.*

133. A colonist wishing to transfer into another estate must have: 1) a discharge from the local authorities, and 2) the written consent of the entire community.

*Ibid., pts. 2, 4 and 8; 1826 Jan. 31 (116).*

134. A discharge may be granted to a colonist by his authorities only when he has definitely chosen another way of life and presents a receipt from the Colony Warden for payment of the portion of the state debt owed by him.

*1812 Nov. 27 (25276) pts. 3 and 4.*

135. Should it be found that the reckoning of the debt of a discharged colonist was made incorrectly, responsibility shall be borne by the Warden who issued the receipt; once all accounts have been put in order, however, responsibility passes, in the colonies of the southern territory, to the Guardianship Committee, and in the Saratov colonies, to the local Office.

*Ibid., pt. 4; 1833 Jul. 1 (6298).*

136. The community has no right to detain a colonist if he presents someone else in his place to continue his husbandry.

*1812 Nov. 27 (25276) pt. 3 [2].*

137. One who has received a discharge, upon entry into another estate, enjoys, equally with others, all the rights and privileges granted to that estate.

*Ibid., pt. 5.*

138. On the basis of these rules, the local authorities discharge colonists into other estates on their own authority, without prior communication on the matter with the Minister of State Domains.

*Ibid., pt. 8; 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).*

139. Those discharged into another estate may at the same time remain in the estate of colonist, fulfilling the obligations of both statuses.

*1812 Nov. 27 (25276) pt. 6.*

140. On this basis, that is, with the fulfillment of the obligations of both statuses, colonists are permitted to be registered into other statuses both by entire settlements and in unlimited numbers.

*Ibid.*

< >

#### SECTION THREE. ON THE CIVIL RIGHTS OF COLONISTS.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

On the family customs of colonists.

Section One.

On marriage and divorce.

142. The necessary conditions for the marriage of colonists of the Protestant faith and the lawful impediments thereto, likewise the contracting of marriage, its dissolution, and matters of divorce generally, are defined in the Statute on Spiritual Affairs of Foreign Confessions, Book II.

*1832 Dec. 28 (5870) §§ 66-135.*

143. Divorce cases of colonists of the Protestant faith are conducted in the local Consistories.

*1808 Nov. 3 (23339); 1825 Mar. 13 (30292); 1828 Aug. 7 (2217 a).*

144. Colonists are exempted from payment of fees for stamped paper in dispensation cases.

*1828 Aug. 7 (2217 a) pt. 1.*

145. For the Württemberg settlers in the Transcaucasian Territory belonging to the Separatist sect, it has been decreed with regard to marriage that every one of them is free, upon reaching the age of majority — that is, seventeen or eighteen years for males, and fifteen or sixteen years for females — to enter into marriage with bridegrooms or brides of any age, provided they too have reached the age of majority.

*1829 Feb. 7 (2659) pt. 7; 1835 Feb. 12 (7853); 1841 Nov. 25 (15509[15059]).*

146. The term for entering into a new marriage, in the event that the whereabouts of one of the spouses is unknown, is set for these same colonists at five years from the time of their absence.

*1829 Dec. 3, Resolution of the Committee of Ministers.*

147. Such permission to enter into marriage is also allowed in cases where the remaining husband or wife, although the whereabouts of the other party may be known, has no prospect whatsoever of that party's return.

*Ibid.*

148. The investigation of the veracity of the statements of those settlers who, owing to the prolonged absence of a husband or wife, request permission to enter into another marriage, as well as the determination of the cases in which permission may be granted for the dissolution of a marriage on account of the prolonged absence of one of the spouses, is entrusted to the Transcaucasian Expedition together with a deputy from the ecclesiastical side.

*Ibid., and 1841 Jan. 5 (14157) § 17; 1849 Dec. 21 (23753).*

Section Two.

On guardianship and majority.

149. District Heads and Schulzes are obliged to appoint guardians over widows and orphans, and likewise over the idle and negligent, with the consent of their relatives and other householders; they themselves exercise chief guardianship over such persons.

*1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 16, pt. 2; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 29; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 27.*

150. Heads and Schulzes must see to it that guardians perform their duty with diligence and honesty, and must require of them, twice a year, an accounting both of the increase and decrease of their household and of their conduct and diligence, personally, or through Beisitzers and Deputies, verifying their statements as often as possible and reporting everything to the authorities.

*Ibid.*

151. Heads and Schulzes must likewise appoint guardians over the estates remaining after extinct families, and, having handed over to them, by inventory, all the remaining property, report thereon to the authorities without delay.

*1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 16, pt. 2; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 27 [29]; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 27.*

152. Guardianship over a minor ceases upon his reaching the age of twenty.

*1764 Mar. 19 (12095) art. 4.*

153. At that time the minor enters into all the rights of an adult, and the guardian is obliged to render a full accounting, receiving as a reward one-quarter of the movable property acquired under his administration.

*Ibid.*

154. Mennonites are granted the freedom to choose guardians according to their own rules.

*1800 Sept. 6 (19546) art. 8.*

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On the right to property.

Section One.

On the allotment of land to colonists from the treasury.

155. Colonists are allotted plots of land from the treasury in a quantity commensurate with the conditions concluded at the time of their settlement.

Note. The quantity of plots with which colonists have been allotted is as follows: 1) the Saratov colonists were allotted, for each soul according to the fifth revision, twenty desyatinas of land (a); 2) of the St. Petersburg colonists, the Sredniaya Rogatka and Izhora colonists were allotted thirty desyatinas each, while the Novo-Saratov, Strelna, Peterhof, Oranienbaum, Kronstadt, Kipen, and Yamburg colonists were allotted thirty-five desyatinas per family (б); 3) the Livonian colonists were allotted thirty desyatinas per family, or, by Livonian measure, sixty so-called "tonnenstellen" (в); 4) of the colonists of the Southern Territory: the Danzig, Swedish, and Yamburg colonists received land at fifteen desyatinas per soul (г); the Josephstal colonists were provided thirty-two and a half desyatinas per family (д); <...> while all the rest, both the New Russia and Bessarabia colonists, were allotted sixty desyatinas of land (ж); and the Mennonites sixty-five desyatinas per family (з); 5) the Scottish missionaries settled in Stavropol Governorate, the Basel missionaries located in the town of Shusha, and the colonists settled near the mineral waters in Stavropol Governorate, as well as near the town of St. Krest, were allotted sixty desyatinas per family (i); 6) the Chernigov colonists were assigned thirty desyatinas per family at the time of their settlement (и); 7) the Lutheran and Reformed pastors in the colonies were assigned one hundred twenty desyatinas of arable and hay-mowing land, and the [Catholic] priests sixty desyatinas, plus three desyatinas for a house and garden. Should DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 441

any of the priests wish to farm on a larger scale, they may be given a number of desyatinas equal to that assigned to the pastors; otherwise the excess is to be taken back from them (к).

(a) 1797 Jun. 30 (18[0]22) art. 8; 1797 Dec. 4 (18263); 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) para. 13; 1802 Sept. 4 (20403) para. 1, and Dec. 19 (20556) para. 1; 1808 Dec. 18 (23408). — (б) 1797 Jun. 20 (18006); 1805 Jul. 18 (21837); 1811 Sept. 12 (24776[24766]). — (в) Conditions concluded with the Livonian colonists, 1766 Nov. 21, art. 2. — (г) 1800 Apr. 6 (19372) arts. III, IV, V. — (д) Ibid., art. II. <...> — (ж) 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) para. 6; 1814 Jan., Privilege granted to the German colonists who relocated to Bessarabia from the former Duchy of Warsaw, para. 3. — (з) 1800 Apr. 6 (19372) art. 1, and Sept. 6 (19546) para. 2; 1801 May 23 (19887). — (i) 1817 Sept. 29 (27070); 1828 Dec. 16[15] (2517). — (и) This is evident from the special conditions concluded with these colonists at the time of their settlement. — (к) 1809 Aug. 25 (23807); 1810 Mar. 23 (24166); 1814 Jul. 17 (25622); 1817 Sept. 18 (27056).

156. In the plots of land allotted to colonists, only usable land is counted (a); all other lands, such as: rivers, lakes, marshes, bogs, chalk deposits, salt flats, clayey, sandy, and other places unsuitable for plowing and haymaking, are not counted at all, but are given over to the common possession of the whole village or hamlet (б).

(a) Cf. all the enactments cited above in this section. — (б) 1764 Mar. 19 (12095) art. 4, para. 6; 1802 Dec. 19 (20556) paras. 4 and 5.

157. Should precious metals be found anywhere, such places are excluded from the allotted holdings.

1764 Mar. 19 (12095) art. 4, para. 6.

158. For the Saratov colonists in particular it is prescribed that unusable lands be considered not only those recognized as such by the Land-Surveying Instruction, but also all those which, through trials conducted by the colonists over the course of several years, proved unsuitable either for plowing or for haymaking (a).

Note. In general, it has been decreed that the Saratov colonists be allotted, in addition to making up the existing shortfall against the twenty-desyatina proportion per soul of the fifth revision, such a quantity of land that a total of fifteen desyatinas would fall to each soul of the eighth revision (б).

(a) 1802 Dec. 19 (25556[20556]) paras. 4 and 5. — (б) 1840 Mar. 12 (13255).

Section Two.

On the colonists' right of possession of lands

allotted to them by the treasury.

159. All lands allotted for the settlement of colonists are assigned to them in indisputable and perpetually hereditary possession, but not as the personal property of any individual, but as the communal property of each colony.

1764 Mar. 19 (12095) art. 4, para. 4; 1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 1; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) para. 2; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) para. 2; 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) para. 3; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) para. 3; <...>

160. Therefore the colonists may not, under any pretext whatsoever, sell or cede even the smallest portion of their land, nor execute any deeds thereof, without the will of the authority established over them, so that such lands may never fall into outside hands.

The same enactments.

161. All water mills situated on lands allotted to the colonies, regardless of whose funds were used to build them, constitute the property of the colonist communities of the very settlements to which the land belongs.

1801 Aug. 7 (19967); 1803 Mar. 28 (20692); 1808 Nov. 26 (23371).

162. Every colonist is permitted, without hindrance, to build a windmill on his own plot.

1808 Nov. 26 (23371).

163. Whoever wishes to build a windmill on communal land must without fail have permission from the entire settlement for this, and must pay it an annual quitrent for the site, not exceeding, however, sixty kopecks.

*Ibid.; 1829[1839] Nov. 19[9] (12867).*

164. Persons not belonging to the estate of colonists may under no circumstances have this right.

1808 Nov. 26 (23371).

165. Should, contrary to expectation, the peaceful possession within the colonies be disturbed by anyone, the Schulzes must immediately report to the Head or Overseer, describing the localities in which, by whom, and precisely what occurred, and these officials must report to their local administration, which is obliged to intervene and initiate proceedings in the order prescribed by law.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562); 1801 May 16 (19873) § 41; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 39.

Section Three.

On the right to acquire land as property.

166. Colonists are permitted, for the expansion and improvement of their farming, to purchase and in general acquire land as property from private individuals.

1804 Mar. 1 (21192); <...>

167. With respect to such lands, colonists enjoy all the rights assigned to other rural inhabitants over their private property.

*Ibid.*

<...>

Section Four.

On inheritance and division of property.

169. The right of inheritance in lands allotted to colonists from the treasury is established on the following rules.

170. In plots of land allotted from the treasury, the youngest son generally inherits, and only in the case of his incapacity may the father designate another heir from among his elder sons, or from among relatives.

1764 Mar. 19 (12095) art. 4, paras. 1, 2.

171. When the father fails to do this during his lifetime, then, owing to the complete incapacity of the lawful heir, the local authority gives the plot to those of the near relatives who do not have plots of their own, or, in the case of equal rights among several persons, disposes of it by lot.

*Ibid., art. 4, para. 2. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 443*

172. Brothers and relatives are permitted, by mutual consent, to live in one household, on the condition, however, that one person alone, not all of them, be the master of that household.

*Ibid.*

173. Should colonists wish to divide their household, this may be permitted only with the authorities' permission; the Heads and Schulzes must ensure that such divisions serve the direct benefit of the settlers and do not disrupt their farming, and to this end, in presenting the names of those wishing to divide, they must specifically explain the good will of the parents or relatives toward this; also whether the party being separated off will have sufficient land, implements, and livestock to set up a household, and, in short, on this occasion it must without fail be observed that the first household is preserved intact and the latter is successfully established.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 38; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 31; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 29.

174. If, after a colonist's death, only a widow with daughters remains, they hold the land plot jointly until the marriage of the mother herself, or of one of the daughters. The first man to enter such a household through marriage receives the hereditary land into permanent possession; however, before the marriage is concluded, he must give a written undertaking, witnessed by the Pastor and the elders of the settlement, that he will keep and support his mother-in-law in his household until her death, and his wife's stepdaughters and sisters until their marriage, unless they themselves wish to leave earlier than that time.

1764 Mar. 19 (12095) art. 4, para. 4.

175. Lands allotted to church servants of a colonist settlement do not pass by inheritance to their children, but fall to their successors in office.

*Ibid., para. 5.*

176. Each colonist may bequeath his own personal property according to his own will, without any restriction.

*Ibid., para. 3; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) para. 9; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) para. 8; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) para. 9.*

177. If, by a will, movable property lawfully acquired in Russia by a colonist is bequeathed to his relatives residing abroad, the authorities of the settlement where the testator resided, having appraised such property in good conscience, are obliged first to pay out of it all debts, both to the treasury and private, and to deduct a three-year tax on the whole of the acquired capital.

1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 10; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) para. 9; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) para. 8; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) para. 9.

178. In the event of a colonist's death without a will, the movable property remaining after him is divided on the following basis: the widow of the deceased is given one-fourth of it, all the daughters together receive an equal fourth, and the remainder is divided in equal shares among the sons.

1764 Mar. 19 (12095) art. 4, para. 3.

179. If a colonist of the Sarepta or Baltic Evangelical community dies without leaving heirs and without making a will, his estate is given over into the possession of the community of the whole colony without any levy to the treasury, subject only to the obligation to pay the debts of the deceased.

1797 Jun. 20 (18011) para. 9; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) para. 9.

##### CHAPTER THREE.

On obligations.

180. Colonists may not, of their own accord, without the knowledge and permission of their authorities, enter into written obligations; the Heads and Schulzes must exercise oversight in this regard.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 31; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 21; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 19; 1827 Dec. 31 (1673).

181. Colonists, especially those with small families, the sick, and those of insufficient means, are permitted to hire workers; but anyone unable to pay wages to workers is forbidden to hire them.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 23; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 37; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 35.

182. Colonists enter into obligations with the treasury only in matters pertaining to their trade, according to the rules laid down in the Civil Laws.

1830 Oct. 17 (4007) §7.

183. Written obligations of colonists must be executed at public offices and with the permission of their authorities.

1827 Dec. 31 (1673).

184. Should it be discovered that any written obligation of a colonist was executed without the permission of his authorities, the entire responsibility for it must fall upon the person or office that approved it, and the act itself is deemed invalid.

*Ibid.*

185. A contract for leasing out water mills on a farming-out basis may be executed only with the general consent of the colonists of the settlement to which the mill belongs, and for a term of not less than one year and not more than twelve years.

1803 Mar. 28 (20692); 1808 Nov. 26 (23371).

186. All written obligations or contracts, agreements, promissory notes, powers of attorney, wills, accounts, and other instruments, whether executed among colonists themselves or with outside persons, must be written on the prescribed stamped paper, without which no public office or authority of theirs shall accept them or take any action upon them.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 81[31]; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 21; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 19.

#### PART FOUR. ON THE DUTIES AND TAXES OF THE COLONISTS.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

On exemption.

187. Colonist communities, at the time of their initial settlement, are granted years of exemption from the performance of duties and the payment of all kinds of taxes.

1763 Jul. 22 (11880) art. 6, para. 2; 1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 8; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) para. 11; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) para. 9; 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) para. 2; 1806 Dec. 25 (22401[22410]) para. 4. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 445

188. The term of exemption established for the colonies is determined by the conditions concluded at the time of the colonists' settlement and in the charters granted to them.

Note. Although the manifesto of 1763 Jul. 22 (11880) granted settlers coming to Russia a thirty-year exemption, and subsequently, by the decree of 1806, Sept. 27 (22293), a ten-year exemption from the payment of taxes was established for all foreigners in general wishing to settle in the Empire; nevertheless, from the particular conditions concluded with the colonists at their settlement and from the charters granted to them, it appears that the term of exemption established for each colony differs, namely: the Saratov and Sarepta colonists enjoyed a thirty-year exemption (**) (a). Of the St. Petersburg colonists, the Sredniaya Rogatka, Izhora, and Novo-Saratov colonists received five years of exemption, while the Yamburg colonists received thirteen years (б); all the rest, namely: the Strelna, Kipen, Peterhof, Oranienbaum, and Kronstadt colonists, as well as the manufacturer-colonists of Tsarskoye Selo, were given ten years of exemption (в). Of the Livonian colonists, those who received into their possession fully cultivated lands were assigned four years of exemption, while those who received lands partly cultivated and partly uncultivated were assigned six years; the rest, who received one-third or one-quarter cultivated land and two-thirds or three-quarters uncultivated land, were given eight years of exemption; while those who settled on vacant and wholly uncultivated land enjoyed an exemption of from nine to ten years (г). The Scottish missionaries settled at Karras in Stavropol Governorate, and the Basel missionaries settled near the town of Shusha, were granted thirty years of exemption (д). The Mennonites and all the other New Russia and Bessarabia colonists received ten years of exemption (*[**]) (е); with the exception of: 1) the Württemberg and Bavarian émigrés who settled in Bessarabia in 1817 and received seven years of exemption, (ж) <...>

Note 2. To the Marienfeld colonists settled beyond the Caucasus, a ten-year exemption from the payment of taxes and duties was Most Graciously granted, counting it from 1849; and to the six-year term for which they were given in 1845 a loan of one thousand five hundred rubles interest-free for setting up their households, a further four years of exemption were added, after which it was prescribed that the collection of the loan monies should begin in 1856, over the course of ten years, in equal annual installments [(и)].

(a) 1763 Jul. 22 (11880); 1767 Mar. 27 (12852); 1808 Dec. 18 (23408). — (б) 1797 Jun. 20 (18006); 1805 Jul. 18 (21387[21837]); 1807 Dec. 4 (22706). — (в) 1820 Feb. 2 (28124) and Apr. 24 (28252); 1823 Jul. 13 (29541); 1825 Aug. 20 (30459). — (г) Conditions concluded with these colonists, 1766 Nov. 21, art. 3. — (д) 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) para. 4; 1828 Dec. 15 (2517); 1840 Apr. 10 (13386[13368]) § 5. — (е) 1809[1800] Apr. 6 (19372); Sept. 6 (19546) para. 9; 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) para. 2: Privilege to the Warsaw colonists settled in Bessarabia in 1841[1814], para. 1; <...> 1825 Mar. 9 (30281); 1830 Oct. 14 (3993). — (ж) 1817 Aug. 2[28] (27029). <...> — (и) 1852 May 2, resolution of the Committee of Ministers.

(**) Subsequently, the exemption for the Sarepta colony was extended to 1806; 1797 Jun. 20 (18111[18011]) para. 11.

(*[**]) As, according to the inspection of the Mennonite settlements conducted in 1800, they were found to be in a state of poverty, and, owing to the cramped conditions in the Khortitsa area, some families were at that time relocated to other lands, the ten-year exemption granted to the Mennonites was extended for those who remained on the sites of their earlier settlement by a further five years, and for those relocated, by ten years (1800 Sept. 6, Charter granted to the Mennonites [19546] art. 9).

189. Colonists relocating to Stavropol Governorate to the mineral waters are given a five-year exemption from the payment of taxes and the performance of all duties, counted for each family from the day of arrival in Stavropol Governorate.

1828 Dec. 15 (2517).

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On the duties in kind of the colonists.

Section One.

On the recruitment duty.

190. All colonists settled in Russia, together with their descendants, are forever exempted from the recruitment duty, both in kind and in money (a).

Note. In 1851 it was decreed: that the Mennonites, who in future may be permitted by the government to settle in Russia in new colonies under the rules set forth in this Statute, be granted exemption from military service for a period of twenty years from the time of settlement, and that, upon the expiry of this term, they be assessed, by calculation, a permanent monetary levy, under the name of recruitment money [(б)].

(a) 1763 Jul. 22 (11880), art. 6, para. 7; Conditions concluded with the Livonian colonists, 1766 Nov. 21, art. 10; 1767 Mar. 27 (12852) para. 7; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) para. 8; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) para. 6; 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) para. 4; 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) para. 4; 1814 Jan., n.d., Privilege granted to the Warsaw colonists settled in Bessarabia, art. 5; 1817 Sept. 29 (27070) para. 2; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 7; <...> 1824 Dec. 23 (30172); 1825 Aug. 20 (30459); 1828 Dec. 15 (2517) para. 7; 1831 Jun. 28 (4676) § 10, para. 5. — (б) 1851 Nov. 19 (25752 a).

191. Should a colonist, however, voluntarily wish to enter military service, this is permitted him, and, moreover, upon assignment to a regiment he is given, in addition to the ordinary pay, a one-time award of nine rubles. They may also hire themselves out as recruits (Statute on Recruits, art. 356, para. 4).

1763 Jul. 22 (11808[11880]) art. 6, para. 7; 1840 Aug. 31 (13750).

192. The military authorities must under no circumstances accept colonists into military service on their own initiative; but if petitions are received from colonists, they are first obliged to communicate with the authority of the colonies to whose department they belong, regarding whether the colonists petitioning to enter military service have paid off the treasury debt owed by them, or whether their relatives have taken over payment of it, and whether there are any other obstacles to their release from colonist status; and upon receipt of such replies, the military authorities must submit the matter, together with all the papers received concerning them, to the Inspector Department of the Ministry of War for consideration, and await a decision before making the appointment.

1821 Jul. 15 (28692).

<...>

Section Two.

On the general natural zemstvo duties of the colonists.

200. By the term general natural zemstvo duties of the colonists are meant those which they perform on an equal footing with the other inhabitants among whom they are settled.

1763 Jul. 22 (11880) art. 8; 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) para. 3. See also the enactments cited in the following articles.

201. Such duties include: 1) the construction and repair of roads, bridges, and dams, and the maintenance of ferry crossings; 2) the billeting duty; 3) the provision DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________ 447

of relay horses; 4) the escorting of prisoners; 5) the maintenance of fire-fighting equipment in the settlements; 6) the preservation of internal order, cleanliness, and tidiness in the settlements.

Note. The last three types of these duties are set out in detail in Chapter III of Part VI; the remainder are set forth in the following articles.

See the enactments in the following articles.

I. On the construction and repair of roads, bridges,

and dams and the maintenance of ferry crossings.

202. From the roads, bridges, and ferry crossings lying along the main highways and maintained by the zemstvo, sections must be allocated to colonist settlements.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 27; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 42; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 40.

203. Oversight and responsibility for the colonists' maintenance, in good order, of the sections allotted to them rests with the Heads and Schulzes. Which settlement is to maintain such sections, and over what distance, depends on general arrangement.

*Ibid.*

204. The Heads are obliged to act in this matter with strict fairness, without the slightest burden to the colonists, and with careful observance in every case of the actual rotation established by the colonists themselves, under penalty, for failure to observe this, of strict and unremitting exaction.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 12; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 39; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 37.

205. Of the country roads and the bridges and crossings situated on them, colonists are obliged to maintain in good order only those which lie within their own holdings.

Conditions concluded with the Livonian colonists, 1766 Nov. 21, art. 10; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) art. 7; 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) art. 4; 1820 Feb. 2 (28124); 1823 Jul. 13 (29541).

206. Heads, Assessors of the District Office, Schulzes, and clerks are personally exempted from all levies and labor duties; Rural Assessors and tithingmen, however, are not excluded from the performance of such duties.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 17; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 13; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 12.

II. On the billeting duty.

207. Some colonies are entirely exempted from any kind of billeting or quartering; these are:

1) The Brethren of the Evangelical community, settled in Sarepta and in the Baltic governorates (a);

2) The Livonian colonists settled in Wenden District (б);

3) The Scottish and Basel colonists (в), and

4) Of the St. Petersburg colonists: the Sredniaya Rogatka, Izhora, Novo-Saratov, and Yamburg colonists, and the manufacturer-colonists settled in Tsarskoye Selo (г).

(a) 1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 7; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 8; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 7. — (б) Conditions concluded with the Livonian colonists, 1766 Nov. 21, art. 10. — (в) 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) para. 4; 1821 Dec. 17, Most Gracious order communicated in a report of the Ministry of Spiritual Affairs to the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs. — (г) 1805 Jul. 18 (21837); 1823 Jul. 13 (29541); 1825 Aug. 20 (30459).

208. All other colonists perform this duty only when military units are passing through some locality; in such a case, quarters must be assigned to them in the colonies free of charge, and only for the shortest possible time, such as for an overnight stay or a rest.

1763 Jul. 22 (11880) art. 6, para. 2; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) para. 7; 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) para. 3. — Privilege granted to the Warsaw colonists settled in Bessarabia in 1814, art. 5; <...>

209. The house in St. Petersburg belonging to the Sarepta Evangelical Brethren, granted to them for divine worship and for lodging their agent and brethren arriving temporarily from the colonies, is exempted from billeting.

1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 11; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 10; 1826 Oct. 10 (611).

III. On the provision of relay horses by colonists.

210. Colonists are obliged to provide relay horses: 1) as assigned, in aid of the postal service; 2) for the escorting of prisoners; 3) for officials traveling on official business, and 4) for private persons traveling with lawfully required papers.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 33; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 30[35]; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 33.

211. The assignment of relay horses from colonist settlements in aid of the postal service may take place only pursuant to a Most Gracious order.

212. Relay horses are given by colonist settlements free of charge for sick prisoners only in the case that their transport route lies through the zemstvo, and not through way-stations.

Both of these articles are based on the general enactments concerning such duties.

213. Schulzes must see to it that colonists give no one traveling through, except officials of the rural police, who by the Statute on Zemstvo Duties are entitled, while traveling on official business, to take relay horses free of charge, any horses or relay teams without payment of relay fees and without a travel warrant. Families remaining under exemptions in colonies that have already emerged from these exemptions must not be drawn into performing the relay-horse duty until the terms fixed for those exemptions granted particularly to those families have expired.

1850 Oct. 16 (24549).

214. Travelers are forbidden to demand a greater number of horses than is stated in the travel warrant.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 33; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 35; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 33.

215. So that no burden may arise anywhere, special registers must be kept in the colonies, in which are to be entered the names of travelers and by whom the travel warrant was issued, for exactly how many horses, and whether that number was actually given; likewise it must be recorded who did the driving, and whether the travelers paid the prescribed relay fees.

*Ibid.*

216. The assignment of relay horses from colonists in all lawful cases is made by the Head and Schulzes, who in this matter must act with strict fairness and with careful observance of the actual rotation established by themselves, under penalty, for failure to comply, of strict and unremitting exaction.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 12; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 39; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) §38[37]. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________449

217. Entirely exempted from the provision of relay horses are:

1) The Brethren of the Evangelical Community, settled in Sarepta and in the Baltic governorates (a);

2) The Livonian colonists residing in Wenden District (б);

3) The Scottish colonists settled in Stavropol Governorate (в), and

4) Of the St. Petersburg colonists: the Sredniaya Rogatka, Izhora, Novo-Saratov, and Yamburg colonists (г).

(a) 1767 Mar. 27 (12852) para. 7; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 8; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 7. — (б) Conditions concluded with the Livonian colonists, 1766 Nov. 21. — (в) 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) para. 4. — (г) 1805 Jul. 18 (21837); 1823 Jul. 13 (29541).

Section Three.

On the communal duties in kind of the colonists.

218. By the term communal duties in kind of the colonists are meant those the performance of which constitutes an exclusive obligation of the colonist settlements and which do not extend at all to district inhabitants of other departments.

219. Such duties include: 1) housing for the District Offices (a); 2) the assignment of quarters for Overseers (б); 3) the provision of relay horses and quarters for officials sent by the authorities for necessary inspection and examination of the colony, or generally for the performance of official duties (в); 4) the delivery from one settlement to another of packets sent by the authorities (г).

(a) 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 4; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 8; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 8. — (б) 1825 Oct. 10 (30537). — (в) 1797 Jul.[Jun.] 20 (18011) art. 8, cf. also the enactments cited in articles 236–243. — (г) 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 40; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 34; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 32.

220. For the housing of the District Office, one of the inhabitants' cottages is designated annually in rotation in the settlement where the Head resides, or a special building is erected for this purpose by the voluntary agreement of all the settlements subordinate to that District Office, through levy or contract at their expense.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 4; 1801 May 16 (19873) §8; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) §8.

221. For the housing of Overseers in the Saratov colonies, the District Offices are each obliged to allot a suitable lodging for their Overseer in the houses of the colonists, changing it annually so as to equalize this duty among all.

1825 Oct. 10 (30537).

222. In assigning relay horses and quarters to officials sent by the colonist administration, the Heads must in all respects act in accordance with the rules established with regard to the general natural zemstvo duties.

Cf. the enactments cited in articles 236–243.

223. Letters and packets sent by the authorities must be delivered to their destination with the utmost dispatch, from one colonist settlement to another in rotation and without objection, under penalty of punishment.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 40; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 34; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 32.

224. For recording all envelopes received and dispatched, the Heads and Rural Schulzes must keep a special book, in which is to be noted in detail when and from where an envelope was received, and likewise to where and with whom it was sent.

*Ibid.*

##### CHAPTER THREE.

On monetary obligations.

225. The monetary obligations that colonists must pay upon expiration of the exemption years are: 1) general zemstvo obligations, and 2) private zemstvo, or communal, obligations.

Cf. the enactments cited under this chapter.

Section One.

On general zemstvo monetary obligations.

226. Under the name of general zemstvo monetary obligations of colonists are understood those in which they participate equally with all other inhabitants of the taxable estates among whom they are settled.

1800 Sept. 6 (19546) p. 7; 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) p. 3; 1808 Dec. 18 (23408); 1823 Jul. 13 (29541).

227. The objects of general zemstvo obligations and the procedure for compiling, reviewing, approving, and executing the estimate and assessment are defined in the Statute on Zemstvo Obligations.

228. Exempted from payment of general monetary zemstvo obligations are:

1) Members of the Evangelical Brethren Society settled at Sarepta and in the Baltic governorates (a);

2) Livonian colonists settled in Wenden district (b);

3) Scottish colonists settled in Stavropol governorate (c); and

4) Of the number of St. Petersburg colonists: those of Srednyaya Rogatka, Izhora, Novo-Saratovka, and Yamburg (d).

(a) 1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 7; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 8; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 7. — (b) Conditions concluded with the Livonian colonists, 1766 Nov. 21, art. 10. — (c) 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) p. 4. — (d) 1805 Jul. 18 (21837); 1823 Jul. 13 (29541).

Section Two.

On communal monetary obligations of colonists.

229. Communal monetary obligations are assessed solely upon the colonists of the governorate in which they are settled.

230. To such obligations belong: 1) maintenance of the colonial administration; 2) maintenance of the Fathers [Catholic priests] and Pastors and payment to them of travel money for journeys among the colonies (a); 3) maintenance of schoolmasters (b); 4) payment of salary to the Heads, District Assessors, and Schulzes (c); and 5) collection from colonists absent for outside earnings of money for charitable institutions in the colonies (d).

Note 1. The sum fixed by the establishment for the maintenance of the administration of foreign settlers was ordered, from 1 January 1834, to be charged to the settlers themselves, apportioning it upon the total number of census souls of all colonists in Russia, according to what falls to each by assessment, and forwarding this collection to the District Treasuries within the deadlines established DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 451

for payment of taxes. As for the application to this purpose of a portion of the communal revenues received by the colonists from various items and lands, as well as the subsequent apportionment of the aforementioned establishment expenses upon the land held by the colonists, this is left to the further consideration of the Minister of State Domains, the latter matter to be addressed upon completion of the allotment of land to the settlers in the statutory proportion (g).

Note 2. The Livonian colonists, the Chernigov colonists known as those of Belovezh, and those settled in Stavropol governorate, over whom no separate administrations have been established, have been exempted from the collection for the maintenance of such administrations since the second half of 1836 (h). The St. Petersburg, Voronezh, and Transcaucasian colonists, whose administration is entrusted to the local Chambers of State Domains and the Transcaucasian Expedition, have been included in the general assessment together with the state peasants for the maintenance of this administration (i).

(a) 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 2 and 3; 1801 May 16 (19873) §§ 2, 4; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) §§ 2, 4; 1803 Oct. 27 (21014); 1808 Mar. 31 (22935); 1809 Aug. 25 (23807); 1810 Mar. 23 (24166) and Apr. 13 (24198); 1814 Jul. 17 (25622); 1817 Sept. 18 (27056). — (b) 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 2; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 3; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 2. — (c) 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 17; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 12; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 12. — (d) 1819 Feb. 24 (27689). — (g) 1833 Jul. 1 (6298) p. 8; 1837 Dec. 26 (10834). — (h) 1836 Jun. 23 (9337). — (i) 1845 Nov. 1 (19434) p. 2.

231. To the communal monetary obligations of the colonists of the southern region of Russia, in addition to those indicated above (art. 230), belongs also: 1) maintenance at the colonists' expense of deputies to sit on the Guardianship Committee for judicial and litigation matters (a), and 2) maintenance at communal expense of herdsmen (b).

(a) 1818 Mar. 22 (27312) art. III, p. 4. — (b) 1803 Jul. 7 (20841) sec. III, § 10; 1833 Jul. 1 (6298).

232. To the communal monetary obligations of the Saratov colonists, in addition to those enumerated in article 230, belongs also the maintenance in their colonies of schools for the teaching of the Russian language.

Note. In 1833 it was ordered that, for the time being, only two such schools be established, each for twenty-five pupils, at the most convenient locations, on the understanding that the establishment of schools in the other colonies, should this prove necessary, be postponed until the settlers had paid off their debts to the treasury, and that the selection of children for the schools be left to the communities themselves, with the approval of the Pastors, preferably from the more populous colonies and from among orphans; meanwhile, fifty trained colonists, each in his own colony, shall be obliged, over the course of six years, to teach children Russian in the same schools in which the schoolmasters teach German, with the time divided between the two languages in all classes. Subsequently, on this same basis, the best of the pupils may also be appointed as teachers in the other colonies as well.

1833 Nov. 7 (6551).

I. On the maintenance of Fathers, Pastors, and schoolmasters.

233. Colonists, upon the expiration of the exemption years and after payment of their debts to the treasury, are obliged to provide the Fathers and Pastors, at their own expense, with all the support that the latter had previously received from the treasury (a).

Note. Pastors, during the colonists' exemption years, receive from the treasury a salary of one hundred seventy-one rubles sixty kopecks, and Fathers one hundred forty-two rubles ninety kopecks (b). (a) 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 2; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 2; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 2; 1809 Aug. 25 (23807); 1810 Mar. 23 (24166); 1814 Jun. [Jul.] 17 (25622); 1817 Sept. 18 (27056). — (b) 1817 Sept. 18 (27056); 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

234. The sum of money needed for this is levied upon the colonists according to the number of souls composing the parish, and the collection of money is apportioned in the St. Petersburg colonies by household, while in the Saratov, New Russia, and Bessarabia colonies it is apportioned according to the number of workers, counting as such those from sixteen to sixty years of age.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 2; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 2; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 2.

235. Such collection is made three times a year, namely in the months of January, May, and September, and is entrusted to special Church Elders elected annually for that purpose from among the settlers, who, collecting the money fixed for this purpose by the community with common consent, must hand over each third to the District Head and obtain receipts from him. The Schulzes and Vorstehers, for their part, are obliged to render every assistance to such Church Elder so that no arrears whatsoever be allowed to accumulate (a).

Note. To the Pastor attending the Saratov Office of Foreign Settlers on ecclesiastical-economic matters of the foreign settlers, sixty rubles a year are to be disbursed from the Office for visitation travel, this money to be collected from the colonists (b).

(a) 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 2; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 2; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) [§ 2]. — (b) 1838 Nov. 9 (11730); 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

236. For the support of the widows and orphans of Pastors of the Saratov Protestant colonies a special fund has been established. The Minister of Internal Affairs is authorized to permit changes in the original regulation concerning it of 1806.

1806 Oct. 12 (22313); 1854 Dec. 28 (28873).

II. Payment of salary to Heads, Assessors, and Schulzes.

237. Payment of salary to the Heads, District Assessors, and Schulzes is made by the colonists in the amount defined above in article 35.

III. On the collection from colonists absent for outside earnings,

of money for charitable institutions in the colonies.

238. From colonists absent for outside earnings a collection is to be made for the construction, in those colonies, of a home for poor and disabled colonists and for its maintenance.

1819 Feb. 24 (27689).

239. The scale and apportionment of this collection is left to the colonial communities themselves.

*Ibid.*

240. If in the execution of this provision any difficulties should arise, the colonial authorities are obliged, according to local circumstances, to submit their opinions for the consideration of the Minister of State Domains.

*Ibid.; 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).*

IV. On the maintenance in the colonies of the southern region of deputies to attend

the Guardianship Committee for judicial and litigation matters.

241. The determination of the deputies' maintenance depends on the Guardianship Committee, which makes arrangements to that effect and submits them for approval to the Minister of State Domains.

1818 Mar. 22 (27312) art. III, p. 4; 1837 Dec. 26 (10834). DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 453

V. On the maintenance in the colonies of the southern region of special herdsmen.

242. In each settlement there must be special herdsmen for the herding of calves, pigs, and domestic fowl, each kind separately, whom the Rural Board must hire at the community's expense. This is prescribed so that young fruit and mulberry trees, likewise grapevines and other produce, not be damaged or entirely destroyed by livestock.

1803 Jul. 7 (20841) § 10.

##### CHAPTER FOUR.

On the state taxes of colonists.

243. To the state taxes of colonists belong: 1) the levy for the maintenance of government offices; 2) the levy for the maintenance of land and water communications, and 3) the land tax.

244. The established state taxes the colonists are obliged to pay in full for each colony, notwithstanding that a change may sometimes occur in the number of persons (a). <...>

(a) Cf. the enactments cited below <...>

Section One.

On the levy from colonists for the maintenance of government offices.

245. All colonists residing in Russia must, after the expiration of the exemption years, participate in the maintenance of the provincial offices and officials by contribution, from whole settlements collectively, of such amount of money as is due according to the number of census souls residing in each settlement, reckoning five kopecks annually per soul.

1807 Dec. 4 (22706); 1809 Feb. 12 (23480); 1812 Mar. 12 (25031) p. 1; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

246. The apportionment among each settlement of the sum due on account of this tax is left to the colonists themselves, without being limited to a collection of five kopecks per soul, but being guided solely by the particular means of each of them.

1807 Dec. 4 (22706); 1809 Feb. 12 (23480); 1812 Mar. 12 (25031) p. 1; 1818 Aug. 9 (27462); 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

Section Two.

On the levy for the maintenance of land and water communications.

247. For the maintenance of land and water communications the colonists, except for those settled in the Transcaucasian region and Bessarabia, pay annually nine kopecks per each census male soul.

1816 Oct. 25 (26477); 1818 Mar. 22 (27314); 1828 Jan. 18 (1718); 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

Section Three.

On the land tax.

I. Rates of the land tax.

248. Colonists, upon the expiration of the exemption years, must pay the land tax.

1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 12; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) p. 11; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) art. 9; 1802 Dec. 19 (20556); 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) p. 3; 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) p. 4; 1808 Dec. 18 (23408); 1812 Mar. 12 (25031); 1820 Feb. 2 (28124); Apr. 24 (28252); 1825 Mar. 9 (30281); 1826 Jan. 9, Highest-approved decision of the Committee of Ministers.

249. The land tax on colonists is determined according to the amount of land actually in their possession.

This is evident from consideration of the enactments cited below.

250. From the Saratov colonists a land tax is levied equal to the taxes paid by the local state peasants.

1808 Dec. 18 (23408); 1812 Mar. 12 (25031) p. 2; 1815 Dec. 8 (26013).

251. They pay this tax only for arable land; all unsuitable and saline land remains in their possession without payment of money for it.

1802 Dec. 19 (20556).

252. The Sarepta Society is obliged to pay seven and a quarter kopecks per year for each desyatina of arable land.

1767 Mar. 27 (12852) art. 12; 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) p. 11; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

253. Of the St. Petersburg colonists, the following pay per desyatina of arable land:

Srednyaya Rogatka, seventy-one and a half kopecks;

Novo-Saratovka, Strelna, and Peterhof, fifty-seven and a quarter kopecks;

Kronstadt and Kipen, fifty-one and a half kopecks;

Oranienbaum, forty-five and three-quarter kopecks;

Izhora, forty-three kopecks;

Yamburg, thirty-five and a quarter kopecks.

1812 Mar. 12 (25031); 1820 Apr. 24 (28252); 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

254. Such a land levy from the St. Petersburg colonists does not remain constant and unchangeable, but, depending on the improvement of their condition and in proportion to their means, may be increased (a).

Note. The thirty-one families of colonists of the Novo-Saratovka and Izhora colonies settled in the former District No. 2 of arable soldiers, upon the expiration of the ten-year exemption granted to them, are obliged to pay only a single quitrent, designated for entry into the capital of the Military Settlements, of seventeen rubles fifteen kopecks a year per household head (b).

(a) 1820 Feb. 2 (28124). — (b) 1836 May 2 (9129); 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

255. The Tsarskoye Selo colonist-manufacturers are subject to no other taxes, save the discharge of the obligations pertaining to Tsarskoye Selo, to which other inhabitants of taxable status are subject.

1825 Aug. 20 (30459).

256. The Belovezh colony in Chernigov governorate pays twenty-eight and three-quarter kopecks per desyatina of arable land.

1812 Mar. 12 (25031) p. 1; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

257. From the Riebensdorf colony in Voronezh governorate twenty-one and a half kopecks per desyatina are levied.

The same enactments. DOCUMENTS________________________________________________________________________________ 455

258. The Scottish Missionaries settled in Karras, Stavropol governorate, and the Basel Missionaries residing in the town of Shusha, are obliged to pay four and a half kopecks per desyatina.

1806 Dec. 25 (22410) p. 4; 1828 Dec. 15 (2517); 1839 Nov. 9 (12867); 1840 Apr. 10 (13368) §5.

259. German colonists settled in Stavropol governorate near the mineral waters, as well as in the town of Svyatoy Krest, are placed on equal footing in taxes and obligations with the local state peasants.

1817 Sept. 29 (27070); 1828 Dec. 15 (2517).

260. Mennonites pay four and a half kopecks per desyatina of land allotted to them.

1800 Sept. 6 (19546) art. 9; 1801 May 23 (19887); 1825 Mar. 9 (30281) p. 1; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

261. All New Russia and Bessarabia colonists settled on treasury lands, not excluding even those not engaged in grain farming, must, upon the expiration of the exemption years, be placed on equal footing in the payment of taxes with the local state peasants, except only for the Mennonites, as well as the Bulgarians, Rumelians, and other Trans-Danubian settlers in the Bessarabia region (arts. 260 and 262).

1853 Mar. 2 (27068).

<...>

263. From the Livonian colonists settled in Wenden district on the two treasury manors of Hirschenhof and Helfreichshof, a land tax of seventeen rubles fifteen kopecks per family is collected, pending improvement of their condition and a new regulation concerning them.

1826 Jan. 9, Highest-approved decision of the Committee of Ministers; 1839 Nov. 9 (12867).

264. The members of the Evangelical Brethren Society settled in the Baltic governorates, on account of the very small number of its members and the insignificance of their holdings, and equally in consideration of their generally useful labors and occupations, are exempted from all communal taxes, both ordinary and extraordinary.

Note. In the charter granted to this society on 27 October 1817, it is stated, among other things, that if in time the holdings of the Brethren Society in the Baltic governorates should multiply and considerably expand, the government will then take under consideration what moderate taxes their lands might be assessed with, similar to those paid by the Sarepta Society.

1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 7.

265. Such a privilege applies solely to those actual members of the Brethren Society who arrived in Russia from abroad and are properly enrolled, together with their descendants, in the organized Brethren Society, and does not extend to all others who have already joined it within Russia.

1824 Feb. 19 (29798); 1834 May 3 (17089).

266. Heads, Assessors, Clerks, Schulzes, and Tithingmen are not exempted from the payment of treasury taxes.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 17; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 13; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 12.

II. Apportionment, collection, and remittance.

267. The apportionment of taxes among the colonists is of two kinds: a) general, over the whole governorate, and b) internal, within each colony.

1853 Mar. 2 (27068).

268. The general apportionment of taxes throughout each governorate is carried out by converting them to a land basis, on the grounds of the Regulation on the Equalization of Taxes by Land among the state peasants.

*Ibid.*

269. The internal apportionment of taxes within the colonies is left to the community of each colony to make at its own discretion, in proportion to the means and advantages of each householder, not excluding even those colonists who, being occupied in crafts, let out their land allotments for rent.

*Ibid.*

270. Proper and arrears-free collection of the assessed taxes is entrusted, in the colonies of the southern region, to the special care of the Guardianship Committee, and in the Saratov colonies to the local Office, as well as equally to the Heads and Schulzes.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 12; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 39; 1833 Jul. 1 (6298) p. 8.

271. In the St. Petersburg colonies responsibility for this matter is placed upon the Superintendent (a); and in the Scottish colony upon the Board (b).

(a) 1797 Jun. 20 (18006) p. 7 and 8; 1809 Aug. 7 (23773); 1833 Jul. 1 (6298). — (b) 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) p. 7; 1821 Dec. 17, Highest command, communicated by the former Ministry of Spiritual Affairs and National Enlightenment to the Administrator of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

272. Apart from the collections established by law, no Head or Schulz, without reporting to his local administration and without its permission, may institute any new collections whatsoever from the colonists, for any purpose, in any place, or under any pretext. Otherwise, should even the slightest unauthorized collection be discovered anywhere, the Schulzes and Heads shall be subject to trial and to the strictest punishment prescribed by law.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 13; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 24; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 22.

273. Each colony must remit the portion due from it to the District Board, and the latter is then obliged to present the money due, on behalf of the whole district, according to the regulation, to its local administration; in the St. Petersburg colonies, however, the district delivers such money to the Superintendent.

1797 Jun. 20 (18006) p. 7, 8; Jun. 30 (18022) p. 9; 1800 Jul. 26 (19492) art. 7; Sept. 17 (19562) art. 12; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 39; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 37; Jul. 7 (20841) § 13; 1833 Jul. 1 (6298).

274. Local administrations are obliged to remit the collected money directly to the Chambers of State Domains, or to the District Treasuries, so as thereby to eliminate any direct dealings of the settlers with these offices (a); the Superintendent of the St. Petersburg colonies, however, must deliver the money collected from them to the departments to which the lands settled by the colonists belong (b).

Note. Thus the revenues from the two St. Petersburg colonies, Srednyaya Rogatka and Izhora, settled on lands belonging to the Tsarskoye Selo Palace, are remitted to the department of that palace (c). DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 457

(a) 1797 Jun. 30 (18022) p. 9; 1800 Jul. 26 (19492) art. 7. — (b) 1797 Jun. 20 (18006) p. 7, 8; 1811 Sept. 12 (24766) art. 5; 1812 Mar. 12 (25031) p. 5; 1820 Feb. 2 (28124); 1833 Jul. 1 (6298). — (c) 1812 Mar. 12 (25031) p. 5.

275. For the remittance of the colonists' land taxes to the aforesaid offices, two deadlines are fixed, namely: for the first half of the year, by 1 March, and for the second, by 1 January.

1769 May 19 (13300) p. 1; 1797 Jun. 30 (18022) p. 9; 1800 Jul. 26 (19492) art. 7; 1832 Jun. 15 (5436) IV, 6, a.

276. Excepted from this rule are only the Livonian colonists, who, on the basis of the special conditions concluded with them, are obliged to pay the land money assessed on them for the past year from 1 to 15 May of the following year; and they must make this payment nowhere else but in Riga.

Conditions concluded with the Livonian colonists, 1766 Nov. 21, art. 9.

##### CHAPTER FIVE.

On the accounting of duties and taxes of colonists.

277. Heads and Schulzes must annually receive from their local administrations bound and sealed ledgers, for recording therein all monetary collections from the colonists, with a clear and accurate indication of: for what purpose and from whom exactly how much was taken, and for what and when it was spent.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 13; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 40; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 38; and Jul. 7 (20841) § 13.

278. Heads and Schulzes are strictly forbidden to spend monetary collections from the colonists without reporting to their local administrations; otherwise, if unauthorized spending of money is discovered anywhere, the Heads and Schulzes shall be subject to trial and the strictest punishment according to law.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 13; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 24; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 22.

279. At the end of each year, in order to reckon the money collected by the Heads and Schulzes, the colonists must elect from among themselves three trustworthy and knowledgeable householders and entrust them with the verification of the accounts.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 13; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 40; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 38.

280. If they discover a shortfall or deficiency in the money, they must report this to their local administration, and with its authorization recover from the Head or Schulz whatever is owed; the aforesaid ledgers, signed by the Schulzes and the elected communal representatives, are to be submitted annually to the local administration for examination and audit.

*Ibid.*

281. In the colonies of St. Petersburg, the bound ledgers for collections are issued and, at the end of the year, audited by the Overseer of the colonies.

1803 Jun. 16 (20798) §§ 22 and 38; 1809 Aug. 7 (23773); 1827 Jun. 9 (1162); 1833 Jul. 1 (6298).

282. All money collected from the colonists and kept in their local administrations must be verified monthly.

1797 Jun. 30 (18022) item 11; 1800 Jul. 26 (19492) art. 7.

283. The Board of Trustees for Foreign Settlers of the Southern Region and the Saratov Office shall submit monthly statements on all sums in their charge to the Ministry of State Domains.

1833 Jul. 1 (6298); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

284. The Board of Trustees sends the annual account of sums, on the basis of general statutes, to the State Comptroller, and at the same time submits a copy of that account to the Minister of State Domains.

1818 Mar. 22 (27312) art. and [11], item 7; 1836 Dec. 30 (9812); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

##### CHAPTER SIX.

On state expenditures for the settlement of colonists.

285. State expenditures used for the settlement of colonists are of two kinds: 1) non-returnable, 2) returnable.

Cf. the statutes cited in the following articles.

Section One.

On non-returnable state expenditures.

286. Non-returnable expenditures are those used for the purchase of lands, the construction of churches, the salaries of officials, priests and pastors, and other expenses.

1816 [1817] Nov. 19 (27149); 1820 Feb. 2 (28124); 1825 Mar. 9 (30281).

287. Also included among non-returnable expenditures are the subsistence allowances that were paid to colonists from the day of their arrival at the border until their settlement, and which they are obliged to repay only if they wish to leave Russia or change to another status; otherwise, they do not repay them to the treasury.

In addition to those statutes: 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) art. 7, 11; 1808 Dec. 18 (23408).

288. Of such money, three kopecks per day are allotted for an adult soul and one and four-fifths kopecks for a minor soul per day.

1804 Feb. 20 (21163) art. 7; 1840 Aug. 31 (13750).

289. The colonist authorities are obliged to make a calculation of how much of these non-returnable funds will be attributable to each family, so that, in the event of a family leaving colonist status, it will be possible to conveniently demand repayment of the treasury funds from it.

1825 Mar. 9 (30281).

Section Two.

On returnable expenditures.

290. Returnable expenditures include money issued to colonists from the treasury as a loan for the construction of houses, the purchase of livestock, and in general for all household establishment.

1763 Jul. 22 (11880) art. 6, item 4; 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) item 9.

291. Heads, Schulzes and other rural authorities and Elders are obliged to watch over and be answerable that the loan money issued to colonists is used for no other purpose than the establishment of their household; upon each request and receipt of money, they must indicate what they intend to use it for and what they have actually purchased with it, and such expenditures of theirs must be verified by the authorities.

Terms concluded with the Livonian colonists, 1766 Nov. 21, item 6.

292. Likewise the colonists are obliged to present to their authorities accurate inventories of everything with which they have provided themselves using money received from the treasury, and to keep all such items intact, neither damaging nor allowing the loss of any of them, nor selling them, so that all of it may serve as security for the treasury until such time as they have settled accounts with the treasury for the money received and paid it all off.

*Ibid., item 7.*

293. Loans made by the treasury for the settlement of colonists are considered a debt owed not personally by each colonist, but by the entire colony community; therefore, upon the departure of any colonist, the treasury's debt cannot be excluded from the accounts, but must be paid by the community to which the departing member belonged.

1825 Sept. 16 (30428).

294. Colonists who have voluntarily enlisted in military service are likewise not exempted from paying their debt to the treasury.

1804 Feb. 20 (21163) item 4. <...>

<...>

296. In payment of the treasury debt, each colony is obliged to remit annually, after the expiration of the grace years, the sum determined for it.

Note. Although the 1763 manifesto ordered colonists to repay loan money after ten years, in three years in equal installments (a), and subsequently, by a report of the Minister of Internal Affairs confirmed by His Imperial Majesty, it was established as a general rule that colonists should pay off the treasury debt, after the expiration of the grace years, over the following ten years; but it always turned out that upon the expiration of their grace period, they were unable to remit their debts within the appointed time without utter ruin to themselves, and therefore a measure of annual payment corresponding to their condition was established for them by special enactments (b).

(a) 1763 Jul. 22 (11830 [11880]) art. 6, item 4. — (b) 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) item 5.

297. Saratov colonists have been assigned payment of debts by families, which, according to the condition of each of them, are divided into ten categories, such that some families pay off their debts in one year, others in two years, others in three years, and so on up to ten years; and it has been granted to them that the sum due from each family be remitted after the harvesting of grain and tobacco, during the months of November and December.

1833 May 31, Opinion of the State Council, confirmed by His Imperial Majesty.

298. The amount of the collection of the treasury debt in various colonies, and the dates from which this collection is to begin, are determined by special decrees for the Saratov, St. Petersburg, and other colonists.

1793 Aug. 17 (11147 [17147]); 1814, privilege to the Warsaw colonists; 1817 Aug. 28 (27029); Nov. 19 (27149); 1820 Feb. 2 (28124); <...> Apr. 24 (28252); 1823 Jul. 13 (29541); 1825 Mar. 9 (30281); 1840 Aug. 31 (13750); 1843 Jul. 20 (17045).

299. The deadlines for the payment of debt money are set to be the same as those for the payment of the land tax.

1800 Jul. 26 (19492) art. 7.

300. The proper and arrears-free collection from the colonists of debt money is entrusted to the Heads and Schulzes, who in this matter are obliged to act entirely in accordance with the rules prescribed with respect to tax collection, and explained in detail in Chapter IV of this section.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 12; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 30 [39]; 1803 Jun. 17 [16] (20798) § 37.

301. The Minister of State Domains (a) is granted the right to forgive the treasury loan debt recorded against colonist Pastors and priests, in the event that it is impossible, after their death, to recover this debt from the remaining estate (b).

(a) 1837 Dec. 26 (10834). — (b) 1831 May 6 (4539) item 5.

#### SECTION FIVE. ON GOOD ORDER IN THE COLONIES.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

On provisions.

302. To avert a possible shortage of grain arising from crop failure and other extraordinary circumstances, and for the benefit of all settlers themselves, grain storehouses must be established in the colonies.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 29; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 67; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 63 [64]; 1822 Apr. 14 (29000) item 66.

303. To fill them, there shall be collected annually, after the completion of the harvest, from all settlers, per revision soul, a half-chetverik of rye, and, wherever it is grown, a half-garnets of spring grain; and however much grain enters a given storehouse, the Head, after its collection, must send detailed reports to his local administration annually in the month of November.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 29, item 1; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 67, item 1; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 64, item 1.

304. So that these reserves may serve to the greater benefit of the settlers, and, in case of shortage and genuine need, may be issued to them both for subsistence and for sowing, the reserve grain must be collected as whole grain.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 29, item 2; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 67, item 2; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 64, item 2.

305. When anyone needs to take some portion of grain from the storehouse, it is to be issued to him, upon the general communal resolution and with the permission of the authority established over the colonies, with an entry made in the ledger; for which purpose ledgers are to be kept at every storehouse for both income and expenditure.

*Ibid.*

306. In order to keep the reserve grain fit for use and to protect it from spoilage, the grain held in the storehouses must be exchanged annually by the settlers for fresh grain, which is to be carried out only by order of the local colonist authorities. Colonists themselves are forbidden to do this on their own without such permission.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 29, item 3; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 67, item 3; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 64, item 3; 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1121. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 461

307. The keeping of the grain and the maintenance of its income and expenditure records is entrusted to one of the Rural Beisitzers, of whom two are established in each colony, such that the Beisitzer holds the key to the storehouse, while the Schulz holds the seal; and therefore both are to be answerable for its safekeeping.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 29, item 4; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 67, item 4; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 64, item 4.

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On agriculture.

Section One.

General provisions.

308. Heads and Schulzes are obliged to attend to agriculture in general and, according to the nature of the soil and climate, to make observations of what may appear necessary for the common good of the colonists, and to report on this directly to their authorities; and moreover to explain and impress upon the settlers the advantages contained therein.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 28 and 57; 1801 May 16 (19873) §§ 69 and 80; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) §§ 66 and 75.

309. No colonist shall, under any pretext, hand over or sell his household, except in the case where someone, having no children or heirs, is, owing to old age, infirmity, or illness, entirely unable to manage it himself; but even in this case it is not to be handed over except with the permission of his local authority, and not on his own by communal arbitrariness. The one who takes over the household must at the same time assume all the treasury debts recorded against such an elderly or sick person, and moreover must endeavor to provide for his subsistence (a).

<...>

(a) 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 39; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 32; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 30. <...>

Section Two.

On the grain farming of colonists.

310. Heads, Schulzes and Beisitzers are obliged to encourage colonists toward grain farming and toward better cultivation of the land.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 57, item 2; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 80, item 3; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 75, item 3.

311. They must keep unrelenting watch that the householders themselves, who are able to work, without fail engage in agriculture and attend to their household diligently.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 23; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 37; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 35.

312. Colonists are obliged to keep ready plows, wooden ploughs, harrows, carts, and other implements needed for field work, so that, for want of them, the time for cultivating the fields is not missed; and should anyone be found deficient in this not through negligence but owing to some other circumstances or unfortunate accidents, all possible assistance should be rendered to such a person by the combined effort of all the inhabitants.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 51 and 54; 1801 May 16 (19873) §§ 72 and 78; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 68 and Jul. 7 (20841) § 5.

313. Likewise, the Schulzes must see to it and endeavor that, everywhere in the colonies, the lands are divided into three fields, and that trials be made of dividing them into six or seven fields.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 51; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 72; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 68.

314. As soon as the prescribed time for plowing arrives, the Schulzes must give notice so that all inhabitants go out to the field in the earliest morning hours and work with due diligence; Tithingmen are assigned to oversee this.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 52; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 73; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 69.

315. Heads and Schulzes must train everyone to look after his own household, to regard it as necessary to keep a sufficient supply for his own use, and to have on hand double the seed for everything he is accustomed to sow in his fields and gardens, so that at the time of new sowing he does not experience a shortage.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562 [19562]) art. 57, item 5; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 80, item 6; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 75, item 5.

316.
