Persons accused of such offenses are, in the colonies of the southern territory, presented, with reports containing a detailed description of the incident, to the Board of Guardians; in the Saratov colonies, to the Office; and in the St. Petersburg and Transcaucasian colonies, to the Superintendent; from distant colonies, without presenting the offenders themselves, but having detained them under guard, a report is to be sent immediately, describing their offenses, and a decision awaited.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 6; 1801 May 16 (19873) §20; 1803 June 16 (20798) §18; 1833 July 1 (6298); 1841 Jan. 5 (14157).

499. In adjudicating offenses, the utmost prudence and caution are to be exercised; for example: if anyone commits an offense intentionally, and some harm or loss to the settlement or to a neighbor results from it, such person must be punished more severely, or more perceptibly, than one who offends unintentionally and causes no harm to anyone, and who, moreover, has not previously been guilty of any vice; namely, the second offender, as against the first, is to be punished one-third or one-half less, which is left to the discretion of the judges.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 19; 1801 May 16 (19873) §66, note; 1803 July [June] 16 (20798) §62, note.

##### CHAPTER THREE.

Department and conduct of criminal cases.

500. Criminal cases of colonists are handled in the general courts of law.

1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 4; 1800 Jul. 26 (19492) para. 4; Sept. 17 (19562) art. 5; 1801 May 16 (19873) §20; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 18; 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) para. 8; 1819 May 29 (27822).

501. In the event of a criminal offense, it is required to report to the authorities or to the Overseer as soon as possible, and to present the offenders themselves under guard, who are sent by way of the Governorate Board to the District Court.

1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 4; 1800 Jul. 26 (19492) para. 4; Sept. 17 (19562) art. 5; 1801 May 16 (19873) §20; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 18; 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) |para. 8|; 1819 May 29 (27822).

502. When colonies are situated at a distance, the Schulzen are obliged, with a clear and detailed description of the incident, to bring the offender directly to the Zemstvo Court and, at the same time, immediately report to their superior authority.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 5; 1801 May 26 (19373) § 20; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 18; 1837 Jun. 3 (10305).

503. For the judgment and decision of criminal cases relating to colonists, deputies are appointed by the colony authorities to the District and Conscience Courts and to the Criminal Chambers, on the same basis as stated above, in articles 493–496, concerning civil cases.

1827 Jun. 9 (1162); 1833 Jul. 19 (6337).

#### SECTION NINE. ON COLONISTS SETTLED ON THEIR OWN LANDS AND ON THE LANDS OF PRIVATE LANDOWNERS.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

On colonists settled on their own lands.

504. Foreigners are permitted to acquire land in ownership from private persons and to settle on it.

1804 Mar. 1 (21192).

505. Foreigners who have settled on land they have purchased enjoy the following privileges.

506. Foreigners who have settled on land they have purchased are granted the general ten-year exemption from payment of taxes and performance of obligations established for all colonists; upon the expiration of which they are subject to taxation on an equal footing with landlords' peasants, according to the rate specified in the table appended to the Statute on Taxes.

1824 Dec. 23 (30179 [30172]); 1849 Mar. 23, information of the Ministries of Finance and State Domains; cf. Statute on Taxes.

507. Zemstvo obligations, in all respects, they must, from the time of their settlement, bear on an equal footing with the other native inhabitants of the region where they settle.

1804 Mar. 1 (21192) para. 3.

508. In the event that any of such settlers, owning land in ownership, should wish to leave the state entirely, he must, upon his departure, sell the land he has purchased to someone residing in Russia; otherwise it shall pass to the treasury without payment.

*Ibid., para. 4.*

509. This right extends not only to the original acquirers of the lands, but also to their heirs, in case they should wish to leave Russia.

*Ibid.*

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On colonists settled on the lands

of private landowners in general.

510. Colonists may be received for settlement by all persons in general who have the right to acquire and own land, without distinction of rank (a).

Note. The settlement of colonists on the lands of private landowners was first begun in 1765, when both noblemen and merchants residing in St. Petersburg were permitted to induce foreigners arriving in Russia to settle on their lands in Ingermanland, under special agreements concluded between them with the confirmation of the former Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners; this was subsequently extended to the interior governorates as well (b).

(a) 1765 Nov. 1 (12503); 1767 May 19 (12897); 1803 Jul. 11 (20843); 1804 Apr. 12 (21254); 1817 Aug. 25 (27022) para. 1; Oct. 1 (27072) para. 1. — (b) 1765 Nov. 1 (12503); 1767 May 19 (12897).

511. The settlement of colonists on the lands of private landowners is accomplished by mutual agreements between them and the latter.

Cf. the same statutes.

512. Landlords and other landowners wishing to bring in and settle colonists on their property must notify the Minister of State Domains thereof through the Governors, informing him at the same time:

1) On what exact number of desyatinas of free land, in what locations, jointly or separately, and from how many families they intend to establish the settlement.

2) What exactly will constitute the main terms of the conditions on the basis of which it is proposed to settle the colonists, such as, for example: concerning the construction of houses, the establishment of farmsteads, the number of years, and the obligations involved.

3) At whose expense their resettlement and travel costs are to be carried out, whether at the landlord's or at the colonists' own expense; in the former case, the sum which it is proposed to allocate for this purpose must also be indicated.

1817 Oct. 1 (27072); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

513. Based on this information, the Minister of State Domains uses his good offices to induce and bring in such people, in accordance with the amount of land and the means proposed by the landowners.

The same statutes.

514. Agreements concluded with colonists, after being presented and examined at the appropriate government office, must be submitted for confirmation to the Minister of State Domains.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254); 1817 Aug. 25 (27022) para. 2; Oct. 1 (27072); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834). DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 491

515. Such agreements must be concluded each time for a period of no more than twenty years, with a detailed statement of all circumstances, both on the part of the landlords and landowners and on the part of the colonists being settled.

1817 Oct. 1 (27072) para. 3.

516. Colonists are permitted to discharge their obligations on landlords' lands through personal labor, provided that the conditions clearly specify: the types of work, the number of working days, and the like.

1817 Aug. 25 (27022) para. 3.

517. Likewise, mutual payments, such as may be established by voluntary agreement of the contracting parties, upon the expiration of the term of the agreement, in the event of the colonists leaving the land, or in the event that the landlord does not agree for the colonists to remain on his land beyond the term, must be precisely and clearly defined in the agreement.

*Ibid., para. 4.*

518. Disputes arising under the agreements shall be resolved by the proper government offices in accordance with the statutes on contracts.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254) para. 5.

519. If the landlord to whom the land given to the colonists for settlement belongs should die, or should wish to sell or mortgage it, then in such case all the terms of the mutual obligations must remain inviolable, and the heirs or acquirers may not alter the conditions except with the consent of the colonists themselves, notifying the local authorities thereof for submission to the Minister of State Domains.

1817 Aug. 25 (27022) para. 5; 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

520. A landlord who has taken colonists onto his land must immediately present the border-crossing certificates given to them by the border authorities for registration with the Zemstvo Court, which shall report thereon monthly to the Governorate Board; the latter, comparing these reports with the registers furnished by the border authorities, is obliged each time to notify the Treasury Chamber accordingly of the number of these people, the status they have chosen, and the time of their settlement, for the proper action on its part.

1802 May 9 (20259) para. 8; 1824 Dec. 2[3] (30172).

521. A landlord who has not presented the certificate for registration with the Zemstvo Court within three months shall be deemed to be harboring fugitives.

1802 May 9 (20259) para. 9.

522. Colonists, having fulfilled all the obligations made with the landowner, may move from him to another.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254) para. 6.

523. Colonists settled on the lands of private landowners have freedom of religion and are exempt for the entire duration of their residence in Russia from military and civil service.

1765 Nov. 1 (12503); 1767 May 19 (12897); 1803 Jul. 11 (20843); 1804 Apr. 12 (21254) para. 1; 1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

524. They forever retain their personal freedom, and landowners may under no circumstances bind them to themselves as property, even should these settlers themselves request it.

1765 Nov. 1 (12503); 1767 May 19 (12897); 1802 May 9 (20259) para. 7; 1803 Jul. 11 (20843); 1804 Apr. 12 (21254) |para. 4|; 1817 Aug. 25 (27022); 1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

525. The general rule of a ten-year exemption from payment of taxes extends to colonists settled on landlords' lands, provided that such exemption is to be reckoned from the time of their initial settlement with the landlords.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254) para. 2; 1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

526. Colonists who have availed themselves of the ten-year exemption, or who during the period of exemption have moved, or shall move, to other landlords' lands, or from one district to another, or from one governorate to another, are not to be granted the exemption a second time; for which purpose the local authorities must ensure that colonists do not leave their settlements without their knowledge.

1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

527. Upon the expiration of the exemption period, treasury taxes are collected from all colonists settled on landlords' lands on an equal footing with landlords' peasants.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254) para. 2; 1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

528. Colonists must bear zemstvo obligations from the time of their settlement, on an equal footing with the other villagers of the governorate in which they settle.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254) |para. 3|; 1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

529. Colonists settling on lands belonging to landlords or private landowners fall under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of State Domains, but only with regard to ensuring that mutual obligations are not violated.

1818 Mar. 22 (27312) art. 9; 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 115.

This document is not the first attempt to codify the numerous statutes on the colonies of foreigners in the Russian Empire. In a number of earlier acts published in the present edition, earlier codes of the corresponding laws are mentioned under various names. Thus doc. No. 112 refers to the Regulations on the Colonies of Foreigners of 1842.

The Statute of 1857 became the best known — it was the latest and most complete code of laws of this kind. Thereafter it was amended annually in accordance with newly adopted statutes, but no other such statute ever again appeared, and from 1871, when the colonist status was abolished, the need for one disappeared as well.

The present publication omits fragments not relating to the German colonies, as well as Arts. 543—577, devoted to German colonists whom it was planned to settle on landowners' estates in Transcaucasia (this measure produced no notable results), and the appendix to Art. 387, which sets out the content of the document we publish as No. 94.

The German colony in Stavropol governorate near the mineral waters is the German part of the colony of Karras, founded by Scottish missionaries. The German colony near the town of St. Cross (now the town of Budyonnovsk) and the colony of the Basel missionaries near the town of Shusha (Nagorno-Karabakh) are not, strictly speaking, separate colonies: these settlements were located within the territory of the towns named (Art. 2).

The Tsarskoye Selo colonist-manufacturers are the inhabitants of the small colony of Friedental in Tsarskoye Selo district. The colony of Alexandriyskaya (Alexandrovka) belonged to Oranienbaum volost, Peterhof district, and was, by the standards of the St. Petersburg colonies, of medium size — 700 inhabitants in 1897, including 348 Germans (Art. 84).

In 1852 the German colony near Tiflis (Neu-Tiflis) had not yet been definitively incorporated into the city — see doc. No. 122 (Art. 92).

On the presence of Germans in Jewish colonies, see: Feldman, D.Z. The Role of German Colonists in the Formation and Development of Jewish Agricultural Colonies in Southern Russia // The Germans of Russia in the Context of National History: General Problems and Regional Peculiarities. Moscow, 1999. Pp. 120—145 (Art. 108).

## No. 117. DECREE OF ALEXANDER II ON THE TAXES AND OBLIGATIONS OF THE NOVGOROD COLONISTS (1858)

33951. — December 24. Personal decree, announced to the Senate by the Chairman of the Department of Appanages on March 31, 1859. — On the taxes and obligations levied on the colonists of the villages of Gorelovo, Nikolaevskoye, and Aleksandrovskoye, which have passed into appanage administration from the former districts of plowman-soldiers of Novgorod governorate.

Together with the former districts of plowman-soldiers in Novgorod governorate, there also passed into appanage administration the three colonies of foreign settlers located in these districts — the villages of Gorelovo, Nikolaevskoye, and Aleksandrovskoye — in which, according to the tenth census, there are registered six hundred nineteen male souls and four thousand one hundred fifty desyatinas of arable land.

Upon the most humble report of the Minister of the Imperial Court, the Sovereign Emperor, on December 24, 1858, Most highly deigned to command: that the following taxes be levied henceforth on the colonists settled in the aforementioned villages:

1. The general poll tax at eighty-six kopecks and, for the construction of means of communication, at nine kopecks per soul, on an equal footing with all colonists who, residing on state lands, have been equalized with state peasants, namely: the Saratov, the German colonists of Stavropol governorate, the New Russian, and the Bessarabian colonists.

2. General zemstvo monetary obligations — on an equal footing with the other rural inhabitants of Novgorod governorate, since all colonists settled in the Empire participate in the payment of monetary zemstvo obligations, except for members of the Evangelical Brotherhood in Sarepta and in the Baltic governorates, the Livonian colonists of Wenden district, the Scottish colonists of Stavropol, and the Srednyaya Rogatka, Izhora, Novosaratovka, and Yamburg colonists of St. Petersburg governorate.

3. A land tax at the rate established for the Novosaratovka and Strelna colonists, at fifty-seven and a quarter kopecks per desyatina of arable land in their use; the collection of this tax in full is to begin on January 1, 1862, and until then only two-thirds thereof is to be collected, that is, thirty-eight kopecks per desyatina, in order thereby to ease the colonists' transition to their future payments.

Accordingly, payments in the aforementioned colonies will amount, until 1862, to four rubles nine and three-quarter kopecks per soul, including in this figure treasury taxes, zemstvo obligations, and the land tax calculated according to the land due to each soul, and from 1862 this sum will rise to five rubles thirty-eight kopecks.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XXXIII. Part 2. P. 559.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 117.

This concerns the daughter settlements established in 1834—1836 northeast of Novgorod by émigrés from Novosaratovka and other St. Petersburg colonies. The Novgorod settlements belonged to Novo-Nikolayevskaya and Vysokovskaya volosts of Novgorod district. The colony of Gorelovo was small, while Alexandrovskoye and Nikolayevskoye (Novo-Nikolayevka) were rather large by the standards of the St. Petersburg colonies: Alexandrovskoye had 486 inhabitants (1885), and Nikolayevskoye had 966 inhabitants in 1897, including 924 Germans.

## No. 120. DECREE OF ALEXANDER II ON THE ECONOMIC RIGHTS OF FOREIGNERS IN RUSSIA (1860)

35880. — June 7. Imperial decree, given to the Senate, published on 20 June. — On the rights of foreigners residing in Russia.

The Manifesto of 1 January 1807 (22418) established certain restrictions on the trading rights of foreigners permanently or temporarily residing in Russia. At present, with the gradual improvement of means of communication and the rapid development of international trade relations, these restrictions no longer correspond to the needs of the time. On the other hand, in the principal European states Our subjects, like all foreigners in general, are permitted to engage in commercial affairs on equal terms with native inhabitants. Taking into consideration the beneficial influence which affording greater convenience for the use of foreign capital as well, in enterprises of every kind, may have on all branches of the national wealth, and desiring to give a new token of Our particular concern for the prosperity of trade, agriculture, and industry generally in the Empire, as well as to show foreign Powers just reciprocity, We have deemed it right to grant to foreigners residing in Russia the same rights in this respect as are already enjoyed by Our subjects in the principal European states.

In consequence of this, in accordance with the opinion of the State Council, We command:

1. Foreigners are permitted to enter all merchant guilds on an equal footing with native subjects of the Empire, and thereafter to enjoy all trading rights by guild granted to the Russian merchantry (Articles 77–107 of the Trade Statute of the Digest of Laws, ed. 1857, Vol. XI).

<...>

2. The dwellings and stores of foreigners and all lands belonging to them are protected by the general laws. The search of their homes and the examination of their trading books may be undertaken only on the basis of the same rules as are prescribed for Russian subjects of the same estate.

3. Foreigners may acquire, whether by purchase or by inheritance, testament, deed of gift, grant from the treasury, and the like, movable and immovable property of every kind, with the sole exception of those which, under the laws in force, may be owned only by persons belonging to the Russian hereditary nobility and by foreigners who have obtained the rights thereof; — and

4. Foreigners, except Jews, may, by power of attorney from the owners of populated estates, administer such estates in the capacity of stewards. They may also rent and hold in lease, on possessory tenure, and generally, on the basis of any obligations not forbidden by law, immovable populated and unpopulated properties, subject only to those conditions and restrictions established for native subjects of the Empire (Civil Laws, Book IV, Part III, Chapter 2).

The Governing Senate will not fail to make the appropriate arrangements for the execution of the foregoing.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XXXV. P. 706–707.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 120.

The implementation of this act, which conformed to European legislative standards, substantially expanded the commercial activity of foreigners, chiefly Germans, in Russia. Many of the Europeans who came to the country, having joined merchant guilds, acquired real property or taken over its management, settled in Russia for a long time or permanently.

---

## No. 121. RULES FOR THE SETTLEMENT OF PRIVATELY OWNED LANDS IN CRIMEA BY FOREIGN IMMIGRANTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER II

36298. — November 8. Most Highly confirmed Rules on the procedure for settling proprietary lands in Crimea by immigrants from abroad.

Resolution of the Committee of Ministers, Most Highly confirmed on 8 November 1860, announced in a Senate decree of 27 January 1861. — The Governing Senate heard: a report of the Minister of State Domains, of the 4th of this January, that in consequence of a petition of the nobles of the Crimean peninsula concerning the provision of various means for maintaining the order of the proprietary estates there, he, the Minister, submitted to the Committee of Ministers a proposal on measures for the settlement of the peninsula in view of the departure of Tatars abroad, together with a draft of Rules on the settlement of proprietary lands in Crimea by foreign immigrants. By extracts from the journals of the Committee of Ministers, of 25 October and 8 November 1860, he, the Minister, was informed, first, that the Committee, independently of these rules, resolved: to allow Crimean landowners to hire foreign workers on the basis of the general regulations in force in Russia concerning personal hire, permitting the issuance to such foreigners of passports for the entire term of hire, which by law may not extend beyond five years; and second, to grant to those foreigners who wish to settle permanently in Crimea and adopt Russian subjecthood all the rights and privileges provided for this case in the draft Rules drawn up by the Ministry of State Domains. The Sovereign Emperor was Most Highly pleased to confirm the Resolutions of the Committee. He, the Minister of State Domains, in reporting such Most High commands to the Governing Senate, also submits the above-mentioned Rules for the settlement of proprietary lands in Crimea by foreign immigrants, with the request that the Governing Senate be so good as to make the appropriate arrangement for their publication. — Ordered: For the due execution of this Most High command, to instruct by decree the Taurida Provincial Board and Treasury Chamber, which decrees are to inform the Chamber of Criminal and Civil Court there and to notify the Governor-General of New Russia and Bessarabia and the Ministers of State Domains, Internal Affairs, and Finance, with the Rules attached, as submitted with the aforementioned report of the Minister of State Domains.

Rules.

1. The settlement of proprietary lands in Crimea by foreigners, by voluntary agreement with the owners, is carried out on the basis of the right already granted to all landowners under Article 510 of the Statute on Colonies of Foreigners in Russia; but for the purpose of facilitating this matter, the following are established, in addition to and amendment of the existing rules:

2. Landowners are permitted to enter into preliminary agreements with foreigners who present a certificate from the appropriate Russian Imperial Mission that there are no obstacles to their settlement in Russia, with the exclusion thereafter of any mediation of the Government in this matter, which, in particular, will make no solicitations of foreigners whatsoever.

3. The foreign immigrants accepted by landowners must be settled not in whole masses or contiguous districts, but only in villages and hamlets, alongside Russian settlers, or on farms and homesteads, being in every case subject not to separate but to the general local administration and management applicable to other estates.

4. All foreign immigrants who settle permanently on proprietary lands in Crimea and adopt Russian subjecthood shall enjoy freedom of religion, and, together with their sons then living, shall be exempt for life from conscription duty; but if there should be Mennonites among them, then, upon expiry of the twenty-year exemption period, they shall be subject, in place of personal performance of military service, to a permanent monetary levy, called the recruit levy, following the example of the Mennonites settled in Samara Governorate.

5. In the contracts concluded by landowners with foreign immigrants, the following must be set forth with due clarity and definiteness: First, all obligations mutually accepted, on the part of the owner, with regard to the lands, forests, and other lands granted for the use of foreigners, and, on the part of the latter, with regard to the performance by them of various duties in favor of the owner. In this connection it must be precisely indicated at whose expense the resettlement and travel costs will be borne — whether at the landlord's or the colonists' own expense; in the former case, the sum intended to be allotted for that purpose must also be indicated. Second, the mutual settlements between landowners and immigrants in the event that the latter, upon expiry of the term of the agreement, should not wish to renew it.

In this connection the following rules are to be observed:

a) The duties of the immigrants in favor of the owner of the land may be of three kinds:

a) monetary, or land quitrent; b) in kind, or remuneration of the owner with produce of the land; and c) personal, or labor in favor of the owner.

b) The amount of the monetary payment for the use of the land, as well as remuneration in produce of the land, depends on the mutual terms of the contracting parties, and is fixed in the contract itself.

c) If the immigrants undertake to perform personal agricultural labor in favor of the owner of the land, such labor must be precisely specified in the contract.

d) Contracts must be concluded, in conformity with Article 515 of Volume XII, Part 2, for a term of no more than twenty years; they are drawn up on stamped paper of the lowest denomination, under the signatures of the contracting parties and two witnesses as required by law.

e) The said contracts, concluded by landowners with foreign immigrants, must be certified in the District Courts, which, however, are obliged to certify these contracts only upon confirmation, from examination of the documents, of the actual ownership of the lands by the former.

f) The contract remains in force even if the land occupied by the immigrants should pass, for whatever reason, to another owner, and the heirs or acquirers may not alter the terms except with the consent of the settlers themselves; the immigrants, for their part, are permitted to transfer their rights and obligations under the contract to another person, but only with the consent of the owner of the land; — and

g) Disputes concerning the terms are settled by the appropriate government offices, under the general laws. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 501

6. Immigrants who, under the terms concluded with landowners, obtain permanent settlement and enter Russian subjecthood are required to be enrolled in the free taxable estate not enjoying special rights; for their enrollment in the rank of colonists, with the rights and privileges granted to the latter under former statutes, is not permitted.

7. The enrollment of these immigrants is carried out in the generally established manner, by order of the Treasury Chamber, to which the landowner must, immediately upon conclusion of the contracts, report both the number of settlers established on his lands and the time of their settlement, for its appropriate action.

8. Those of the foreign immigrants who wish to enter the free rural estate require no admission resolutions whatsoever, but upon expiry of the exemption years, they are personally liable for the timely payment of taxes and duties, which must without fail be included in the contracts concluded with landowners.

9. For the possible acceleration of the settlement of the depopulated lands of the Crimean peninsula, there is granted to foreigners who, in compliance with these conditions, conclude contracts with landowners, settle permanently on their lands, adopt Russian subjecthood, and choose their estate at that time, — exemption from payment of treasury taxes and monetary duties and from the performance of general duties in kind: to those settling in 1861, 1862, 1863, and 1864, for a period of ten years, and to later settlers, for a period of five years, from the time of the enrollment of these persons in the estate chosen by them.

10. Foreign immigrants are not deprived of the right to enjoy these privileges even if, before the expiry of the exemption period, they should move to another piece of land, or, while remaining Russian subjects, should change the estate originally chosen.

11. Upon expiry of the exemption period, these persons are subject to treasury taxes and monetary duties, and are drawn into the performance of general duties in kind, on equal terms with the estate to which they belong. For their diligence in the performance of duties in kind, as falling upon the land, the owner on whose land they are settled by contract is answerable, concerning which the immigrants enter into mutual agreement with the landowners.

12. The Minister of State Domains is authorized, in communication with the chief administration of the New Russian territory, to permit additions or changes to these rules which, according to circumstances and the indications of experience, shall be recognized as corresponding to the views of the Government and the benefit of the matter itself, with a view to the more successful settlement of Crimea.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XXXV, Part 2. P. 224–226.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 121.

This act shows that the problem of settling foreigners in Crimea, which had already been placed on the agenda at the beginning of the 19th century (see doc. No. 45), remained relevant in connection with the continued emigration of Tatars abroad. The document was aimed not only at temporary but also at permanent attraction of foreigners, and as a result, from the second half of the 19th century, many small German settlements appeared in Crimea, especially in its central and northern parts.

---

## No. 122. DECREE OF ALEXANDER II ON THE INCORPORATION OF THE GERMAN COLONY NEAR TIFLIS INTO THE CITY (1861)

36968. — May 3. Imperial decree, announced to the Senate by the Acting Minister of Justice. — On the conversion of the Tiflis German colony into a part of the city of Tiflis.

In 1852 the late Chairman of the Caucasus Committee, the late Adjutant General Prince Chernyshev, communicated to the Ministry of Justice the Most High command, proposed to the Governing Senate on 11 September 1852 (26578), on the incorporation into the city of Tiflis of the German colony located near it, with the concentration of the internal administration of the colony in a single Office, subordinate to the jurisdiction of the Tiflis city police.

Now the Sovereign Emperor, upon the submission of the Viceroy of the Caucasus and the resolution of the Caucasus Committee, has been Most Highly pleased to command:

1. To convert the Tiflis German colony into a part of the city of Tiflis, and to include the colonists settled therein among the city inhabitants.

2. To transfer the plots of land now held by the colonists to them in full ownership, providing each owner with a title deed.

3. Upon the alienation of a plot of land in the colony, to grant the new owner of that plot the right, proportional to the size of the land acquired, to use the water-supply ditch constituting the communal property of the colony, with the obligation imposed upon him to participate to the same extent in the maintenance of the ditch.

4. To distribute the treasury debt owed by the Tiflis colonists, subject to repayment, in the amount of 6,671 rubles 88 kopecks silver, among the owners of the plots of land, in proportion to the size of these plots; to preserve, for those of them who retain their lands for themselves, the extensions of time granted to the colonists for the repayment of the debt, but those who sell such lands are obliged, at the very time of the sale, to pay in full the portion of the debt attributable to the plot being alienated.

5. To now cancel the irrecoverable treasury debt of the Tiflis colonists, in the amount of 8,042 rubles 30¾ kopecks silver, which would have been subject to collection from them in the event of their departure from the borders of the Russian Empire or voluntary withdrawal from colonist status.

6. To subject the colonists, upon their inclusion among the city inhabitants of the city of Tiflis, to all the levies and duties established for the inhabitants of that city, at the same time abolishing the reductions in the rate of the land tax granted to the colonists on the basis of the Most High decree to the Governing Senate of 16 June 1831.

7. To allow colonists wishing to continue enjoying the personal rights granted to their estate to enter the membership of other colonist communities with the consent of the latter, expressed in a proper resolution. Such colonists are not to be deprived of the right to own immovable property in Tiflis, but on condition that they bear duties under both estates, in accordance with Article 139 of the Statute on Colonies of Foreigners in the Empire, Digest of Laws, Vol. XII, Part II, ed. 1857.

8. To leave the Tiflis colonist church, with the pastor's residence, and the school for the time being in their previous condition, for the use of colonists of various colonies residing in Tiflis, obliging these persons to keep them in proper repair; — and

9. To close the Rural Office of the Tiflis colony, with the abolition of the community of Tiflis colonists.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XXXVI, Part 1. P. 703–704.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 122.

The document completed the incorporation of the predominantly artisanal German colony of Nei-Tiflis (New Tiflis) into the city. This process had begun in 1852 (see doc. No. 115, art. 92, note). The colony of Nei-Tiflis was small — 257 inhabitants in 1843. Subsequently the population on its territory began to grow rapidly (to 2,500 people in 1900), but mainly not through Germans.

---

## No. 123. RESOLUTION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON RAISING LEVIES ON THE GERMAN COLONISTS OF NEW RUSSIA AND BESSARABIA, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER II (1861)

37062. — May 30. Most Highly confirmed resolution of the Committee of Ministers, announced to the Senate by the Minister of State Domains. — On increasing the levy on the German colonists of the New Russian governorates and the Bessarabian region.

The Sovereign Emperor, upon the submission of the Minister of State Domains and the resolution of the Committee of Ministers, on the 30th day of May of this year, was Most Highly pleased to command: that the colonists of the three New Russian governorates and the Bessarabian region, beginning with this year 1861, be assessed, in place of the levy now paid, a levy for the repayment of the treasury debt for settlement, in the following amounts:

1. German colonists of the Bessarabian region, 10 rubles per family.

2. German colonists of Yekaterinoslav Governorate: those of Josephstal and Rybalskoye, 2 rubles 85 kopecks, except two families of the latter, now paying 4 rubles 28 kopecks, who shall pay 5 rubles, and the colonists of Yamburg, 2 rubles 30 kopecks per family.

3. German colonists of Kherson Governorate: a) of the Liebental and Berezan districts, 15 rubles per family; b) of the Kuchurgan and Glückstal districts and the separate colony of Hoffnungstal, 10 rubles; and c) of the Swedish district, 3 rubles.

4. German colonists of Taurida Governorate: a) of the Neusatz and Zürichtal districts, 3 rubles, except the colony of Hertsenberg, which for the time being remains at the former rate of 1 ruble 42¾ kopecks per family, and b) 382 families of colonists of the Molochna district, from 10 to 20 rubles per family.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XXXVI, Part 1. P. 800.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 123.

The increase in dues under this document was intended to speed up the completion of the repayment of the treasury debt by the colonists of southern Russia.

Hoffnungstal (Tsebrikovo) — a colony of Hoffnungstal volost, Tiraspol district, located northeast of Tiraspol, founded in 1819, 1,145 inhabitants (1859).

Herzenberg (Kizilnik) — a colony of Zürichtal district (later Salyn volost, Feodosia district), located north of Feodosia, founded in 1804, 39 inhabitants (1858).

## No. 124. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON SANCTIONS AGAINST COLONISTS WHO RESETTLED WITHOUT PERMISSION FROM ONE GOVERNORATE TO ANOTHER, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER II (1865)

41919. — March 14. Most Highly confirmed opinion of the State Council, published on 26 April. — On depriving colonists who resettled without permission from one governorate to another of the rights granted to colonist status.

The State Council, in the Department of State Economy and in General Session, having examined the submission of the Minister of State Domains on supplementing Article 435 of the Statute on Colonies, resolved: to confirm the present submission and, in consequence thereof, to supplement Article 435 of the Statute on Colonies (Digest of Laws, Vol. XII, Part 11, ed. 1857) with a note of the following content: "Colonists who resettle without authorization and without the permission of the Minister of State Domains from one governorate to another are excluded by the chief local administration from colonist status and, forever losing the rights and privileges granted to that status, are enrolled among other taxable estates on general grounds."

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was Most Highly pleased to confirm the opinion rendered in the General Session of the State Council on supplementing Article 435 of the Statute on Colonies, and commanded its execution.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XL, Part 1. P. 315.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 124.

By introducing strict sanctions, the authorities sought to curb the unauthorized resettlement of colonists from one governorate to another. Amid an increasingly acute shortage of land, especially in the Volga region, with its rapidly growing colonist population and archaic system of per-capita land use, this process had taken on wide proportions. The document had no appreciable effect: only a few years later, in 1871, colonist status was abolished (see doc. No. 129), and with it disappeared the main obstacle to the widespread resettlement of former colonists across the territory of Russia.

---

## No. 126. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A LUTHERAN AUXILIARY FUND IN THE BESSARABIAN COLONY OF TARUTINO, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER II (1866)

43642. — September 16. Most Highly confirmed resolution of the Committee of Ministers. — On the establishment, in the colony of Tarutino, Bessarabian region, of a District Committee of the auxiliary fund of the Evangelical Lutheran parishes.

A memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs, of 20 August, was heard, on the establishment in the colony of Tarutino, Bessarabian region, of a District Committee of the auxiliary fund of the Evangelical Lutheran parishes. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 505

The Committee resolved: to request the Most High consent of His Imperial Majesty to the implementation of the conclusion of the Minister of Internal Affairs.

The Sovereign Emperor, on the 16th day of September 1866, was Most Highly pleased to consent to this.

Memorandum. — On the basis of § 12 of the Most Highly confirmed Statute, of 8 August 1858 (33454), of the auxiliary fund of the Evangelical Lutheran parishes in Russia (appendix to Article 603, Vol. XI, Part I, of the Digest of Laws, per the 1863 Continuation), District Committees are established, to assist the Central Committee of the said fund, in consistorial districts, in cities where Evangelical Lutheran Consistories are located, and in other more significant places.

The Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory, reporting that five Lutheran colonial parishes in the Bessarabian region and their preachers desire the establishment of a special District Committee in the colony of Tarutino, as the largest of all the said colonies, explained that, as the population in these colonies, which already number 28,000 inhabitants, increases, new settlements are being founded and there arises a need for the establishment of new parishes. For the construction of churches and schools in these parishes, given the insufficiency of the means of the inhabitants of the new settlements, assistance from the original parishes is necessary; but the readiness to make contributions in these parishes would be strengthened by the assurance that the sums collected would be applied to the needs of their own district, in particular to providing the new settlements with churches and schools. Meanwhile, at present all contributions of the colonists of the Bessarabian region go to the Odessa District Committee, which is located across the Dniester River, at a very great distance from the Bessarabian colonies, and which could confine its activity to the colonies of Kherson Governorate. Therefore the General Consistory requests authorization for the establishment of a District Committee of the auxiliary fund in the colony of Tarutino.

Concerning this petition of the General Consistory, the Minister of Internal Affairs communicated it for the opinion of the Minister of State Domains, who, having considered all the local circumstances, replied that he not only saw no obstacle, but for his part found it very useful to open, in the Bessarabian colony of Tarutino, a District Committee of the auxiliary fund of the Evangelical Lutheran parishes in Russia.

Although, on the basis of the above-cited § 12 of the Most Highly confirmed Statute, of 8 August 1858, of the auxiliary fund of the Evangelical Lutheran parishes in Russia, District Committees of this fund are established only in cities, yet since the establishment, in accordance with the petition of the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory, in the colony of Tarutino, Bessarabian region, of a District Committee of the auxiliary fund of the Evangelical Lutheran parishes in Russia, is recognized as very useful by the Minister of State Domains, the Minister of Internal Affairs deemed it proper to request Most High consent to this, which he has the honor to submit for the consideration of the Committee of Ministers.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XLI, Part 2. P. 25–26.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 126.

The auxiliary fund of Evangelical Lutheran parishes, established in 1859, provided substantial support to the Lutheran churches of Russia and their clergy. In particular, the fund's resources significantly accelerated the establishment of new parishes. This can be seen in the example of Bessarabia, where after 1858 the parishes of Benkendorf, Eigenheim, Nei-Sarata, and Alboto were formed. Tarutino was not only the largest German colony in Bessarabia (1,938 inhabitants in 1859) but also the center of the oldest Bessarabian Evangelical Lutheran parish, founded in 1815.

Over the first 50 years of its activity, the fund provided significant assistance in the construction or repair of 206 churches, 318 schools and prayer houses, and 100 parsonages; it supported 200 parishes and 500 schools, and financed the training of 100 pastors and 350 kusters (sextons). See: Luther's Legacy in Russia. Moscow, 2003. P. 19.

---

## No. 127. DECISION ON SUBORDINATING THE COLONIES OF A NUMBER OF GOVERNORATES TO THE GENERAL INSTITUTIONS FOR PEASANT AFFAIRS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER II (1866)

44000. — December 17. Highest-confirmed resolution of the Main Committee on the organization of the rural estate, communicated to the Senate by the Minister of State Domains. — On the transfer of the colonies of foreign settlers to the jurisdiction of the general institutions for peasant affairs.

The Sovereign Emperor, upon the report of the Minister of State Domains and the finding of the Main Committee on the organization of the rural estate, on 17 December 1866, was Highest pleased to command:

1. The colonies of foreign settlers, which are under the jurisdiction of the Chambers of State Domains in the governorates of Voronezh, Novgorod, Samara, St. Petersburg, and Chernigov, shall henceforth be transferred to the jurisdiction of the general provincial and district institutions, as well as the local institutions for peasant affairs.

2. Until such time as the question of the organization of public administration in the colonies, as well as of the courts, is resolved in the established manner, the currently existing rules on the internal public administration of the colonies (Code of Laws, Vol. XII, Part II, Statute on Colonies) shall remain in force, while the authority belonging to the Chambers of State Domains, with respect to colonies passing out of their jurisdiction, for the adjudication of litigation among colonists (Arts. 6, 38 clause 7, 485 and 488 of the Statute on Colonies) shall be transferred to the local Provincial Presences for Peasant Affairs.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XLI. Sec. 2. P. 408.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 127.

This act began the process of transferring the colonies to the jurisdiction of the general administrative bodies, completed in 1871 (see doc. No. 129). In Samara governorate it affected the colonists who had settled in Samara district since the late 1850s (see doc. No. 118). Now only the remaining colonies of the Volga region, the colonies of southern Russia, Transcaucasia, and Livonia remained under the jurisdiction of special administrative bodies.

## No. 128. DECREE OF ALEXANDER II ON THE PROCEDURE FOR ISSUING PASSPORTS TO FOREIGN SETTLERS (1868)

45922. — May 29. By Imperial Name, communicated to the Senate by the Minister of State Domains on the 31st of that same May, published on 4 July. — On the procedure for issuing passports to foreign settlers.

The Governing Senate heard the report of the Minister of State Domains of 31 May 1868, of the following content: upon his, the Minister of State Domain's, most humble report concerning measures to remove the difficulty encountered by foreign settlers, under the temporary rules currently in force, in obtaining passports in a timely manner, the Sovereign Emperor, on the 29th day of May of this year, was Highest pleased to command: until the confirmation of a new statute on the colonies of foreign settlers, it is to be established, as an amendment to the temporary rules set forth in the note to Article 424, Vol. XII, of the Statute on Colonies, that — "The issuance of passports to foreign settlers shall be carried out by the District and Village Boards, provided that the blank forms for passports and the stamped paper for tickets, as needed, shall be obtained by the District Boards directly from the District Treasuries, for cash." Of this Highest command DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 507

he, the Minister of State Domains, reports to the Governing Senate, requesting that it be pleased to make the appropriate arrangements for its execution. It was ordered: (To send decrees where required).

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XLII. P. 685.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 128.

By removing the intermediate authorities (the Saratov Office, the Guardianship Committee, and the overseers of the colonies of southern Russia) from issuing passports to foreign settlers for travel from the colonies to other colonies or other settlements in the country, the authorities helped simplify this procedure. Along with administrative countermeasures against the increasingly intense migration of colonists (see doc. No. 124), this was another measure intended to bring order to this process.
