## No. 129. RULES FOR THE ORGANIZATION OF SETTLER-PROPRIETORS (FORMER COLONISTS), CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER II (1871)

49705. — June 4/16. Highest-confirmed Rules on the organization of settler-proprietors (former colonists) settled on state lands in the governorates of St. Petersburg, Novgorod, Samara, Saratov, Voronezh, Chernigov, Poltava, Yekaterinoslav, Kherson, and Tavrida, and in the Bessarabian oblast.

Opinion of the State Council, Highest confirmed on 31 May 1871, published on 5 July. — The State Council, in General Assembly, having examined the finding of the Main Committee on the organization of the rural estate concerning the draft rules submitted by the Acting Minister of State Domains on the organization of foreign rural settlers (colonists) settled on state lands, opined:

I. The draft Rules on the organization of settler-proprietors (former colonists) settled on state lands in the governorates of St. Petersburg, Novgorod, Samara, Saratov, Voronezh, Chernigov, Poltava, Yekaterinoslav, Kherson, and Tavrida, and in the Bessarabian oblast, as corrected in accordance with the comments of the Main Committee and the State Council, shall be submitted for the Highest confirmation of His Imperial Majesty.

II. Upon the Highest confirmation of these rules following:

1) The Minister of State Domains shall be authorized to take the appropriate measures for their implementation and to draw up the necessary instructions and rules for this purpose, in agreement, where required, with the relevant Ministers, and, on matters exceeding the limits of their authority, to seek resolution through the Main Committee on the organization of the rural estate.

2) The Minister of State Domains shall be authorized, in agreement with the Chief Administrator of the Second Section of His Imperial Majesty's Own Chancellery and the Minister of Internal Affairs, to undertake a review of the Statute on Colonies of Foreigners (Code of Laws, Vol. XII) and, should there be found in this Statute such rules as would retain their force even under the operation of the new rules concerning the former colonists, to consider the possibility of transferring these rules to the relevant parts of the Code of Laws, with the subsequent repeal of the separate Statute on Colonies.

3) The Ministers of State Domains, of Internal Affairs, and of Public Education shall be authorized, by mutual agreement, in the established manner, to submit a proposal for the transfer, as appropriate, of the duties assigned to the Saratov Office and the Guardianship Committee of Foreign Settlers with respect to the chief ecclesiastical guardianship and the manner of filling vacant parishes, as well as concerning the organization of the school system in the villages of the settlers (colonists).

4) The Minister of State Domains shall be authorized to make all such changes in the composition of the Saratov Office and the Guardianship Committee, as well as of the institutions subordinate to them, as experience shall show to be necessary for the speediest completion of the matters remaining within the duties of these institutions, so that, upon the completion of such matters, all existing special institutions for the administration of foreign settlers shall be abolished.

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was Highest pleased to confirm and ordered to be executed the opinion rendered in the General Assembly of the State Council, upon the draft Rules on the organization of foreign settler-proprietors (former colonists) settled on state lands in the governorates of St. Petersburg, Novgorod, Samara, Saratov, Voronezh, Chernigov, Poltava, Yekaterinoslav, Kherson, and Tavrida, and in the Bessarabian oblast.

Rules.

I. On the public organization and administration of settler-proprietors

(former colonists) and on their transfer to the jurisdiction of the general provincial and district,

as well as local institutions for peasant affairs.

1. Settler-proprietors (former colonists), whether under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of State Domains or removed from its jurisdiction on the basis of the Highest-confirmed resolution of the Main Committee on the organization of the rural estate of 17 December 1866 (44000), shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the general provincial and district, as well as local institutions for peasant affairs, on the grounds and in the manner indicated in the following articles.

Note. The present rules do not extend to the colonies of Jewish agriculturalists of the Kherson and Yekaterinoslav governorates, or to the colony of the Evangelical Brethren of Sarepta, Saratov governorate, concerning which special rules will be issued.

2. The said settlers shall be included among the rural inhabitants and, being assigned to the category of peasant-proprietors, shall retain, on the grounds indicated below, the personal privileges which they have hitherto enjoyed.

3. Rural societies and volosts (townships) of settlers shall be organized on the grounds set forth in Articles 40–45 of the General Statute on Peasants of 19 February 1861 (36657), and in the supplementary enactments thereto, subject to the following rules:

a) The colonist districts now existing shall each form a separate volost, with the exceptions indicated below in points b and c.

b) Villages (colonies) forming part of a district situated in several counties shall form separate volosts by county, which may nonetheless continue to preserve the existing connection among themselves in matters of economy.

c) A village which, owing to the distance involved, cannot be included in a volost formed by other villages, shall constitute a separate volost if it contains about three hundred or more revision souls, or else it shall be attached to the nearest peasant volost.

d) A change in the composition of volosts formed on the basis of the present rules shall be permitted, with the authorization of the provincial authorities, upon petition of the societies and in compliance with the rules of the General Statute on Peasants, as well as with what is established in point b of the present article. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 509

4. The public rural and volost administration, as well as the volost court of the settlers, shall be organized on the basis of Articles 46–129 of the General Statute on Peasants and the supplementary enactments thereto, subject to the following rules:

a) The Village Assembly shall be composed of the settler-householders belonging to the rural society, possessing a homestead, with or without field allotments, and of all persons elected to village offices. In villages where household land tenure exists, settlers possessing neither a homestead nor a field allotment (landless) shall send to the Assembly one elected representative for every ten adult workers.

Note. Settlers assigned to the society who, without participating in the use of communal lands, acquire plots in ownership outside the boundaries of the communal allotment, as well as elected representatives of landless settlers (point a), shall have a voice at the Assembly in all matters concerning them, such as: the apportionment of state taxes and of zemstvo and public obligations, deliberations on communal needs and benefits, the election of officials, and the disposition of communal quitrent items and land holdings generally used by the whole society; but they shall not take part in matters concerning the lands of the communal allotment held by individual householders.

b) Each category of settlers among those indicated in point a and the note thereto — namely, settler-householders, settlers possessing only homesteads, settlers who, without participating in the use of communal lands, acquire plots in ownership outside the communal allotment, and finally the elected representatives of landless settlers — shall be permitted, under the chairmanship of the village elder or his deputy, to convene separately in private meetings, independently of the general Village Assembly, to discuss matters concerning exclusively themselves and not the whole society.

c) If any rural society, owing to the size of its population and its commercial and industrial activity, deems the convening of an Assembly of all householders to be difficult, such a society may entrust the resolution of certain matters within the jurisdiction of the Village Assembly to a small Village Assembly. The small Village Assembly shall be composed of the officials required to attend the Village Assembly, and of elected representatives — one for every ten households. These representatives shall be appointed for a term of one year. The matters indicated in points 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, and 17 of Article 51 of the General Statute on Peasants may not be entrusted to the small Assembly. Landless settlers shall send to the small Assembly one elected representative for every hundred adult workers, or, if their number is smaller, not less than one representative.

d) In addition to the matters indicated in Article 51 of the General Statute on Peasants, the Village Assembly shall have jurisdiction over: 1) authorizing the transfer of household plots from one householder to another; 2) the disposition of communal quitrent items; and 3) the administration of common forests and plantations.

e) Among the matters requiring the consent of not less than two-thirds of all settlers entitled to vote at the Village Assembly, in addition to those indicated in Article 54 of the General Statute on Peasants and in points a and b of Article 19 of the present rules, are: 1) the establishment of a small Village Assembly, and 2) authorization to lease out communal lands and income-producing items.

f) In villages where household land tenure exists, the landless settlers of each rural society shall send to the Volost Assembly one elected representative for every twenty adult workers. But the number of such representatives shall in no case exceed the number of representatives from householders.

g) In a volost consisting of several villages, and having a population of more than 2,000 souls, the establishment of a small Volost Assembly shall be permitted, by resolution of the Volost Assembly adopted by not less than two-thirds of all settlers entitled to vote at the Assembly. This Assembly shall be composed of the officials required to attend the Volost Assembly under Article 71 of the General Statute on Peasants, and of elected representatives: one for every twenty-five households, and one for every fifty adult workers among the landless settlers. If, however, the societies find that the small Assembly, even at such a size, would be too numerous, then, upon their resolutions, the Provincial Presence for Peasant Affairs shall authorize the appointment of representatives to the small Assembly from a greater number of households and, where there are landless settlers, from a greater number of adult workers, provided that each village and settlement has one representative at the Assembly, and that the landless do not exceed the householders in the composition of the Assembly. Representatives to the small Volost Assembly shall be replaced each year by a new election. The small Assembly may, by decision of the general Volost Assembly, be entrusted with all matters within the latter's jurisdiction, except for the election of volost officials and judges of the Volost Court.

h) Rural societies within a volost that have joint land use, or that constitute a separate parish, etc., may, in matters concerning such land tenure, parish, etc., convene, under the chairmanship of the Volost Elder or one of his assistants, private Assemblies, independently of the general Volost Assemblies. Representatives for such private Assemblies shall be appointed one for every ten households or, at the discretion of the societies concerned, in a smaller number.

i) In addition to the matters indicated in Article 89 of the General Statute on Peasants, matters within the jurisdiction of the Volost Board shall include: 1) arrangements, on the basis of resolutions of the Volost Assembly, concerning communal lands and quitrent items belonging to the whole volost or jointly to several rural societies within the volost; 2) arrangements concerning insurance against fire, hail, and the like, and the payment of compensation for damage caused; and 3) arrangements concerning the operations of savings and loan funds and the recoveries arising from these operations.

Resolutions of Village and Volost Assemblies, as well as of Volost Courts, shall be drawn up, and all record-keeping in the public administration shall be conducted, in the Russian language.

j) In volosts where the hearing of cases by the Volost Court at the seat of the Volost Board may encounter difficulty, the Volost Assembly shall be authorized either to designate in advance those villages within the volost to which the court is obliged to travel at fixed intervals for the hearing of cases, or to permit the court itself to send special divisions of the court, consisting of not less than 3 judges, with the powers of a volost court, to those villages of the volost where, owing to the accumulation of cases or the convenience of summoning the persons required for the hearing, the need for this shall arise.

k) The current officials of the present District Administrations, with the exception of those occupying positions to be abolished as a result of the reorganization of these administrations, shall remain in their positions, until the expiration of their terms of service, and shall retain the compensation they receive even if the said positions are given a different title (as, for instance, Volost Elder instead of District Head or District Elder); but the election of judges to the Volost Courts must be undertaken immediately.

l) In cases where volosts are formed consisting of settlers (former colonists) and other rural inhabitants, as well as in the case of the division of the present districts into smaller volosts, new elections of all volost administration officials must be held.

5. The payment by settlers of taxes and monetary levies, as well as the performance by them of obligations, shall be carried out on the following grounds:

a) Settlers are obliged to pay, on the existing grounds, the state taxes and, until the issuance of title deeds, the quitrent or land tax for the lands in their use, and also to perform, on general grounds, without further exemptions in this respect, the zemstvo and other monetary and labor obligations. In addition, they shall be assessed a levy for the maintenance of the local institutions for peasant affairs, on the general basis established for this levy. Likewise, until special arrangements are made, those special levies which exist in some colonies, in the form of a public levy for the maintenance of special colonist administrations, central Russian schools, clergy, etc., shall not be abolished.

Note. Exemption from the obligation of billeting troops shall be retained for the settlers, from the date of issuance of the present rules, for a further 10 years. With respect to the conscription obligation, the statutes currently in force with regard to colonists shall retain their force until the issuance of a general law on military service.

b) The calculation of the said levies and the drawing up of assessment sheets for them shall be carried out in the manner now existing, until special arrangements are made on this subject.

c) Insurance levies for the compensation of fire victims shall be made on the basis of the special statutes in force among the settlers (former colonists).

d) With respect to the communal obligations of the settlers, the provisions set forth in Articles 177–186 of the Highest-confirmed General Statute on Peasants of 19 February 1861, and the supplements thereto, shall apply.

e) The proper fulfillment by the settlers of the taxes and levies due from them, as well as of the zemstvo and communal obligations, shall be ensured in the manner indicated in Articles 187–191 of the Highest-confirmed General Statute on Peasants of 19 February 1861, and the supplementary enactments thereto.

6. Grain reserves belonging to the societies, remaining under the jurisdiction of these societies, shall, as regards the manner of their disposition, be subject to those rules established for peasant-proprietors.

7. Communal capital shall be placed at the disposal of the societies concerned on the grounds established for peasant-proprietors. Accordingly, capital belonging to individual rural societies shall be transferred directly to the communal funds of each society, as appropriate; while capital constituting the joint property of several societies shall be deposited, as contributions from the latter, in local (volost) credit institutions, on the basis of resolutions of the Volost Assemblies concerned (general or private, depending on the ownership of the capital), retaining the special purposes assigned to this capital.

8. The volost funds existing among the settlers, on various grounds and under various names (orphans' funds, savings and loan funds, etc.), shall continue their operations under the rules currently in force for them.

9. The discharge of settlers from rural societies and volosts, as well as their enrollment therein, their assessment for taxation, their removal from the tax rolls, and their transfer from one tax assessment to another, shall be carried out in the manner established in Articles 130, 132–140, 142, 146, and 147 of the General Statute on Peasants of 19 February 1861 and the supplements thereto, subject to the following rules:

a) Only persons enjoying, personally and by status, the same rights as are assigned to the members of the society into which they are being enrolled may be assigned to societies of settlers.

b) Within 10 years from the date of issuance of the present rules, settlers may: 1) enroll in other estates, remaining, if they wish, in their former estate; in this case, acquiring all rights and privileges under both estates, they shall discharge all obligations and assessed levies under both estates; 2) renounce Russian subjecthood and leave Russia, without payment into the treasury of any part of the capital they have acquired; upon the expiration of the 10-year term, however, they shall become subject to the general laws of the Empire regarding the renunciation of Russian subjecthood.

10. The reorganization and establishment, on the grounds set forth above, of the rural and volost administrations of the settlers shall be carried out, under the immediate supervision of the Governors and the Provincial Presences for Peasant Affairs, by special Commissions composed of the local Peace Mediator, an official of the Ministry of State Domains, and an official appointed by the Governor, applying the procedure indicated in Articles 10 and 11 of the Imperial Decree by Name given to the Governing Senate on 19 February 1861 on the promulgation and implementation of the Statutes on Peasants. This reorganization shall be completed within three months from the time of the distribution of the settlers' volosts among the mediation districts, and, in those mediation districts established specifically for these settlers, within three months from the appointment of the Peace Mediators.

11. As the volost and rural administration in the societies of settlers (former colonists) is reorganized, on the grounds set forth in the preceding articles, these settlers shall pass into the jurisdiction of the general provincial and district administrations, as well as the local institutions for peasant affairs, on the basis of the Highest-confirmed Statute on these institutions of 19 February 1861.

12. The distribution of the settlers' villages among the mediation districts, and the formation, where necessary, of new districts, shall be entrusted to the Provincial Presences for Peasant Affairs. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 513

13. The transfer, on the grounds set forth, of the settlers (former colonists) currently under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of State Domains to the jurisdiction of the general provincial and local institutions for peasant affairs, shall be carried out, by mutual agreement of the Ministers of Internal Affairs and of State Domains, within six months from the date of the promulgation of the present rules.

14. All contested judicial matters of the settlers, arising prior to the issuance of the present rules in the Provincial Presences for Peasant Affairs, in the Saratov Office, and in the Guardianship Committee of Foreign Settlers, and not yet concluded by proceedings, shall either be terminated on the basis of Articles 21 and 22 of the Highest-confirmed opinion of the State Council of 10 March 1869 (46840) on the procedure for the conduct of cases of former judicial establishments, or shall be transferred for resolution, as appropriate, to the newly formed public administrations of the settlers, or to the judicial establishments, with notice thereof given to the parties involved in the case.

15. The present rules, with the exception of those concerning land organization, shall also extend to settlers (former colonists) who, while remaining registered by revision in their original societies, settled, prior to the issuance of these rules, in separate villages and settlements on their own lands, or on lands acquired at the expense of the original societies, or on the lands of private owners, under term contracts with the owners. The land relations of such settlers shall be determined by the contracts concluded by them with the original societies — the owners, or the landowners; in the event that such settlers acquire the lands occupied under contract in full ownership, the manner of land use shall be established by communal resolutions, applying the present rules.

II. On the land organization of settlers (former colonists)

settled on state lands.

16. Rural societies of settlers shall retain all lands and tracts allotted to them and remaining in their permanent use. In this connection, settler societies in whose holdings there is found land in excess of the established normal allotment shall be obliged, within 10 years from the date of confirmation of the present rules, to admit into their midst, without special admission resolutions, such number of migrants from land-poor original settlements as can be provided with the normal allotment out of the surplus lands available to each society.

Note 1. The migrants mentioned in this article who wish to settle in those societies which have surplus lands shall apply with a request to that effect to the local Provincial Presence for Peasant Affairs, which shall make the appropriate arrangement in response to such requests.

Note 2. Lands set aside for settlement by migrants from the original settler (colonist) settlements, but not yet settled by them to this day, shall be deemed free state lands and shall be assigned preferentially for the allotment of settlers (former colonists) of those villages whose societies, in accordance with Article 33 of the Highest-confirmed Rules of 31 March 1867 (44418) for the drawing up and issuance of title deeds to state peasants, shall receive permission for the resettlement of part of their members onto state lands.

17. For ownership of the lands and tracts allotted to each society, a special document called a title deed shall be issued to it.

18. The settlers, holding the lands and tracts granted to them under the deeds mentioned in Article 17, shall be obliged to pay into the treasury an annual payment fixed by law, called the state quitrent tax. The amount of this tax shall be determined in the manner established in Article 25 of the present rules.

19. Settlers shall have the right to use and dispose of, at their discretion, the lands granted to them in ownership under the deeds, subject to the following rules:

a) With the consent of two-thirds of the members of the society entitled to vote at the Assembly, the society may divide the lands belonging to it into household plots; whereupon the sum of the state quitrent tax charged on the whole society shall be divided among the householders according to the size and quality of their household plots.

b) The allotment of plots to individual householders from land held in communal ownership shall likewise be permitted by resolution of two-thirds of the members of the society entitled to vote at the Assembly; whereupon the amount of quitrent tax attributable, by calculation, to the allotted plots shall also be determined.

c) Resolutions of the society concerning allotment, as well as resolutions concerning the division of land into household plots, must, before being put into effect, be certified by the Peace Mediator, who shall submit a copy of the resolution to the Provincial Presence for Peasant Affairs for information and for confirmation of the distribution of the quitrent tax among the householders made by the society.

d) Within three years from the time of receiving the title deeds, societies, in the case of communal tenure, and householders, in the case of household tenure, may not alienate their lands to persons not belonging to the same society.

e) After the expiration of three years from the issuance of the title deeds, both societies and owners of household plots may alienate the lands of their allotment, by means permitted by law, not only to fellow villagers but also to outside persons, subject to the following conditions: 1) deeds of conveyance for the acquisition of these lands shall be executed in the general manner established for the execution of such deeds; 2) a society may sell plots of land held in communal ownership only pursuant to a resolution of two-thirds of the members of the society entitled to vote at the Assembly, certified by the Peace Mediator; 3) upon the alienation of household plots held in the personal possession of their owners, the obligation to pay the state quitrent tax due on the plot shall pass to the new acquirer.

f) In the division, allotment, and alienation of land, the rules established by the Highest-confirmed opinion of the State Council of 23 November 1870 (48946) for ensuring the payment of the state quitrent tax upon the sale and division of the lands of former state peasants shall be observed.

g) Settlers shall be permitted to be guided by their local customs in matters of inheritance of land.

20. Lands allotted not to a single society but to several societies (districts or volosts) for forest plantations, farmsteads, and other economic and industrial establishments, the societies are obliged to maintain in the future as well, without changing the purpose assigned to these lands and without departing, in their disposition of them, from the DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 515

established procedure except with the special authorization of the Provincial Presence for Peasant Affairs.

21. Subject to compliance with the restrictions indicated above (Articles 19 and 20), settlers shall enjoy, in respect of the possession of the lands of their allotment, all rights granted to peasant-proprietors from among former state peasants.

22. Title deeds shall be drawn up by officials of the Ministry of State Domains and presented to the settlers, in the presence of the Peace Mediators, in the manner established by the Highest-confirmed Rules of 31 March 1867 for drawing up title deeds for state peasants.

23. The extent (number of desyatinas) of the existing allotment of the settlers, granted to them in ownership under the deeds, shall be determined according to plans of economic survey.

24. Title deeds must be drawn up and issued to the settlers within three years, counting from the date of issuance of the present rules, except in the governorates of Chernigov and Poltava, where title deeds must be issued to the settlers simultaneously with the issuance of such deeds to former state peasants.

25. The amount of the state quitrent tax due from each settler society for the lands and tracts of its allotment shall be calculated and entered into the title deed: a) in villages where valuations of those lands have already been made — in the amount determined by such valuations; and b) in the remaining villages, where valuations have not yet been made, — in the amount corresponding to the multiplication of the total quantity of usable land in those villages by the average, apportioned, quitrent tax per desyatina of usable land in the adjacent or nearest villages of state peasants, whose lands, by degree of profitability and local conditions, most closely approximate the lands of the settler (former colonist) society concerned.

Note. The Mennonites of the volosts of Khortitsa and Mariupol, Yekaterinoslav governorate, Molochna, Tavrida governorate, and Malyshinsk, Samara governorate, shall be assessed the state quitrent tax at the rate of fifteen kopecks per usable desyatina of the allotment according to the plans of economic survey, with the exception, however, of the lands of the salt-transport route additionally allotted to the Molochna Mennonites in 1869, which they accepted with the obligation of paying quitrent tax on the general basis.

26. The amount of the quitrent tax determined in the title deed, on the grounds set forth in Article 25, shall remain unchanged until the expiration of 20 years from the date of issuance of the present rules. Subsequent changes in the assessments of this tax may be made only by legislative procedure.

27. Societies and owners of household plots of land subject to the state quitrent tax shall be permitted to obtain exemption from payment of all or part of this tax, by depositing with the provincial or district treasury, in state interest-bearing securities, such capital as would yield interest equal to the amount of quitrent tax from which the society or the owner of the plot wishes to free its lands. The capital deposited in interest-bearing securities must amount to not less than one hundred rubles at the nominal value of the securities.

28. Lands which, by means of a deposit with the treasury of the corresponding capital, on the basis of the preceding Article 27, shall be freed from the whole of the state quitrent tax charged upon them, as well as plots of land sold by rural societies with the conversion into the treasury of the sum due for them on the basis of the rules indicated in point e of Article 19, shall, constituting the full property of their owners, be excluded from the number of lands subject to payment of the state quitrent tax.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XLVI. P. 813-819.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 129.

This document is among the most important state acts concerning Russian Germans. It determined the future fate of hundreds of thousands of former German colonists for decades to come. The Regulations of 1871 belong to a series of reform laws of the reign of Alexander II intended to modernize the entire system of agrarian relations, a process begun by the Peasant Reform of 1861.

Except for Sarepta, which is covered by a proviso in art. 1 of the Regulations, the document also did not apply to the Transcaucasian and Livonian colonies, although they had been established on state lands. Special acts were subsequently adopted for all these groups of colonists (see docs. No. 136, 161, 162).

The document was drafted over a number of years by a representative commission that included such an expert on colonist affairs as A.A. Klaus, a high-ranking official of the Ministry of State Domains and himself descended from the colonists of southern Russia, author of the book *Our Colonies: Experiments and Materials on the History and Statistics of Foreign Colonization in Russia* (St. Petersburg, 1869). After the commission presented the results of its work to this ministry, the Regulations were discussed and revised for several more years in the higher state bodies. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. Pp. 281–284.

As often happens, such a lengthy process of preparation and coordination did not benefit the document. It is marked by neither clarity nor consistency. Even the new concept it introduces, "peasant-proprietors (former colonists)," is quite ambiguous, which had significant consequences later on (see doc. No. 149). Proceeding from the well-meaning intention to bring colonists as close as possible in legal status to Russian peasants of other estates, while at the same time preserving, as far as possible, the tried-and-tested system of organization and self-government of the colonies (insofar as it is even appropriate to speak of self-government under the extremely strict regulation prescribed by the Colony Statute of 1857), the authorities ultimately arrived at a number of highly questionable decisions.

Thus, the Regulations provide that all record-keeping at village and volost assemblies of the former colonies and in the corresponding volost courts be conducted only in Russian (art. 4, para. i), a language which at that time the overwhelming majority of German colonists did not know (in large part through the fault of the authorities themselves). The document states that the existing norms for performing recruit duty (from which all colonists settled on state lands, except for the Volga Mennonites, had been exempted) would be preserved only "until the issuance of a general law on military service" (art. 5, para. a, note), making it clear that with the adoption of this law a number of the most important conditions, guaranteed "in perpetuity," on which the colonists had at one time agreed to settle in Russia, would be abolished. The Regulations state that the transformation and organization of the village and volost administrations of the settlers would be handled by various officials, without any participation whatsoever by the former colonists themselves (art. 10). The document requires communities of settlers who have surplus land compared to the "established normal allotment" to admit into their midst those with insufficient land (art. 16), even though, for example, in the Volga colonies with their system of per-capita land use, the concept of a "normal allotment" had long since lost any real meaning. And to top it all off, while declaring the preservation of the former colonists' existing personal privileges (art. 2), the Regulations at the same time unambiguously show them the door, offering anyone who wishes to do so the right, within 10 years, to renounce Russian citizenship and leave Russia on favorable terms — without paying into the treasury a portion of the capital they had accumulated, as had previously been required of colonists (art. 9, para. b).

The German colonists themselves could not fail to notice such provisions, although, of course, few of them studied and absorbed from beginning to end this voluminous document, written in dry bureaucratic language. It is not surprising that in the very same Volga colonies the Regulations were met with considerable wariness. The matter evidently lay not only in a whole series of points in the document that provoked at the very least bewilderment, but also in the fact that unerring popular instinct told the colonists: it was not merely certain rules of their life that were changing, but that fundamental changes were coming in the very attitude of the authorities toward Russian Germans, or even toward Germans as such. In principle this conclusion was obvious, especially since the issuance of the Regulations practically coincided in time with the unification of Germany and the proclamation of the German Empire — events that were received in Russia, to put it mildly, without enthusiasm.

In accordance with this document (art. 3), the existing German colonist districts were reorganized into the following volosts. Saratov governorate: Yagodno-Polyansky — Yagodno-Polyanskaya (Saratov district), Ilovlinsky — Ilovlinskaya (Kamyshin district), Sosnovsky — Sosnovskaya, Oleshinskaya (both Kamyshin district), Kamensky — Kamenskaya (Kamyshin district), Ust-Kulalinsky — Ust-Kulalinskaya (Kamyshin district), Norsky — Norskaya, Linevo-Ozerskaya, Oleshinskaya (all Kamyshin district), Medveditsko-Krestovo-Buerakskaya (Atkarsk district); Samara governorate: Paninsky — Paninskaya (Nikolaevsk district), Ekaterinstadtsky — Ekaterinstadtskaya (Nikolaevsk district), Krasnoyarsky — Krasnoyarskaya (Novouzensk district), Tonkoshurovsky — Tonkoshurovskaya (Novouzensk district), Tarlytsky — Tarlytskaya, Stepnovskaya, Rovninskaya (all Novouzensk district), Eruslansky — Verkhne-Eruslanskaya, Nizhne-Eruslanskaya, Bizyukskaya (all Novouzensk district), Malyshinsky — Malyshinskaya (Novouzensk district), Torgunsky — Torgunskaya (Novouzensk district), Nizhne-Karamansky — Nizhne-Karamanskaya (Novouzensk district), Verkhne-Karamansky — Verkhne-Karamanskaya (Novouzensk district), Konstantinovsky — Konstantinovskaya (Samara district), Mennonitsky — Aleksandrtalskaya (Samara district); Chernigov governorate: Belovezhsky — Kalchinovskaya (Borzna district); Bessarabia oblast: Saratsky — Saratskaya (Akkerman district), Maloyaroslavetsky — Maloyaroslavetskaya, Kulmskaya, Tarutinskaya, Krasnyanskaya, Teplitskaya (all Bendery district), Klyastitsky — Klyastitskaya, Parizhskaya, Artsizskaya (all Bendery district); Kherson governorate: Libentalsky — Gross-Libentalskaya, Freidentalskaya, Gildendorfskaya (all Odessa district), Kuchurgansky — Zeltsskaya, Badenskaya, Mannheimskaya (all Odessa district), Berezansky — Landauskaya, Rohrbachskaya, Neifreidentalskaya (all Odessa district), Rashtatskaya (Ananyev district), Glikstalsky — Glikstalskaya, Kasselskaya (both Tiraspol district), Shvedsky — Staroshvedskaya (Kherson district); Ekaterinoslav governorate: Khortitsky — Khortitskaya (Ekaterinoslav district), Iozefstalskaya (Novomoskovsk district), Petrovskaya (Aleksandrovsk district), Mariupolsky Mennonitsky — Petropavlovskaya (Aleksandrovsk district), Mariupolsky Kolonistsky — Aleksandro-Nevskaya, Romanovskaya (both Aleksandrovsk district); Tavrida governorate: Berdyansky — Neihoffnungskaya (Berdyansk district), Molochansky Mennonitsky — Halbstadtskaya, Gnadenfeldskaya (both Berdyansk district), Iogannesruskaya (Melitopol district), Molochansky Kolonistsky — Prishibskaya, Eigenfeldskaya (both Melitopol district), Neizatsky — Neizatskaya, Bulganakskaya (both Simferopol district), Zürichtalsky — Zürichtalskaya, Taraktashskaya, Salynskaya (all Feodosia district).

## No. 130. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE PROCEDURE FOR FOREIGNERS TO RENOUNCE RUSSIAN SUBJECTHOOD, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER II (1874)

53255. — March 15. Imperially confirmed statute of the Committee of Ministers. — On the procedure for the release of foreigners from Russian subjecthood.

The memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs, of February 12, 1874, together with the register for the September third of 1873 concerning the release of 162 persons from Russian subjecthood, was heard.

The Committee resolved:

1) To request His Imperial Majesty's Supreme consent to the release from Russian subjecthood of the persons named in the register, on condition that, with regard to Otton Fiebiger, Baron von Firks, Baron Simolin-Batory, Otton Löwenstein, and Nikolai, son of the Kurland nobleman Count Nikolai Lamsdorff (Nos. 116, 122, 123, 146, and 141 in the registers), of whom the first four are shown as 21 years of age and the last as 14 years of age, Articles 3 and 11 of the Imperially confirmed Statute on Military Conscription of January 1, 1874, be strictly observed; and

2) To authorize the Minister of Internal Affairs henceforth, when submitting reports to the Committee of Ministers on release from Russian subjecthood, to attach a certification that no obstacles exist to the requested release under the Statute on Military Conscription.

The Sovereign Emperor, on the 15th day of March, 1874, was Graciously pleased to consent to this.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XLIX. Pt. 1. P. 368.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 130.

After the Regulations of 1871 (doc. No. 129), the "general law on military service" promised in them (art. 5, para. a, note) was not long in coming — the Statute on Military Service of January 1, 1874. The Regulations themselves may be regarded as a rather clumsy embodiment of fairly sound ideas. The Statute, in all likelihood, deserves a more critical assessment. The point is not that the German colonists in principle rejected performing military service on an equal footing with other Russian subjects. Only the Mennonites (for religious reasons) were its categorical opponents, and even then not all of them. However, Alexander II and his government had no right to forget that previous Russian emperors, beginning with Catherine II, had solemnly promised all colonists entering Russia, as well as their descendants, exemption from military service for all time. The Statute of 1874 struck down these highest assurances at a single stroke, and no intelligible explanations, let alone apologies, followed from the authorities.

This high-handed action profoundly undermined the trust of Russian Germans in the supreme authority, which over the eight decades since Catherine II had never once deceived them and which they had therefore long been accustomed to trust unconditionally. This distrust naturally extended not only to the issue of military service. If the government had carelessly violated the laws that existed with respect to colonists in this sphere, then who could guarantee that it would not do the same in any other matter? The result, which could easily have been foreseen had anyone wished to, was a sharp rise in emigration sentiment — above all among the Mennonites, but partly also among other groups of Russian Germans, including not only colonists.

This phenomenon is reflected in the present act, which appeared almost immediately after the adoption of the Statute of 1874. Judging by the surnames listed in the act, the persons in question are not colonists but Baltic German nobles. They had wished to renounce Russian citizenship as early as 1873, that is, under the influence not of the Statute on Military Service itself but, evidently, already of the announcement of its forthcoming adoption, contained in the Regulations of 1871. The authorities, as the document shows, used the Statute to counteract the emigration sentiment that it itself had provoked, but this could not, of course, reverse the general trend that had emerged.

---

## No. 131. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON THE PROCEDURE FOR FORMER COLONISTS TO DEPART ABROAD, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER II (1874)

53521. — May 14. Imperially confirmed opinion of the State Council, published June 10. — On clarifying the procedure by which former colonists may be released from Russian subjecthood and emigrate from Russia prior to fulfilling their military service obligation.

The State Council, in the Special Presence on Military Conscription, having examined the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs on clarifying the procedure by which former colonists may be released from Russian subjecthood and emigrate from Russia prior to fulfilling their military service obligation, resolved to clarify: 1) that settlers-proprietors (former colonists) established on state lands who, by age, are subject to military conscription must be entered, on the general basis, in the conscription lists; 2) that those of them who wish to exercise the right granted to them by the Imperially confirmed Statute on the Organization of Their Life of July [June] 4, 1871, to leave Russia, must declare such intention before September 1 of the year in which they are subject to conscription; and 3) that those former colonists of conscription age who, having declared within the specified period their intention to emigrate from Russia, fail to carry this out by the day their peers draw lots, and fail to notify the competent Presence on Military Conscription thereof, shall be compelled to perform this obligation, as persons evading it, without the drawing of lots; whereas those who have duly declared that they will not leave Russia shall be permitted to participate in the drawing of lots on the general basis.

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was Graciously pleased to confirm the opinion rendered in the Special Presence on Military Conscription, established under the State Council, on clarifying the procedure by which former colonists may be released from Russian subjecthood and emigrate from Russia prior to fulfilling their military service obligation, and commanded that it be carried out.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XLIX. P. 772.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 131.

This act, by introducing sanctions against peasant-proprietors (former colonists) of conscription age who had declared their intention to leave Russia but had not done so in time (para. 3), in fact only fanned the emigration fever caused by the Statute on Military Service of 1874.

The Statute of June 4, 1871 — doc. No. 129.

## No. 134. DECISION ON THE REDEMPTION OF LAND BY THE IZHORA COLONY NEAR ST. PETERSBURG, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER II (1877)

56910. — February 1. Imperially confirmed statute of the Main Committee on the Organization of the Rural Estate, announced to the Senate, on behalf of the Minister of Justice, by the Deputy Minister of Justice on the 28th of the same February. — On the redemption by the colonists of the Izhora colony of the land in their use.

By the sense of the Imperially confirmed enactment of the Main Committee on the Organization of the Rural Estate of November 2, 1863 (40183), incorporated into the note to Article 159 of the Digest of Laws, 1857 edition, Vol. XII, Part II, Statute on Colonies of Foreigners in the Empire, per the 1868 Continuation, the law set forth in the said enactment concerning the redemption of land by colonists settled on palace lands must apply to all colonists to whose use palace lands were allotted. Meanwhile, this law names the colonies of Strelna, Znamenka, Oranienbaum, Alexandria, Srednyaya Rogatka, and Kipen, but does not mention the Izhora colony, settled on the lands of the Sovereign's Tsarskoye Selo estate, St. Petersburg governorate. Therefore, deeming it necessary to extend the force of the above-mentioned law to the Izhora colony, the Minister of the Imperial Court and Crown Lands applied to the Main Committee on the Organization of the Rural Estate with a submission to permit the redemption of the palace land in the use of the colonists of the Izhora colony, by agreement of these colonists with the Crown Lands Department and with the confirmation of the Minister of the Imperial Court and Crown Lands, in the same manner as was granted to the colonists of the Srednyaya Rogatka and Kipen colonies by the Imperially confirmed journal of the Main Committee of November 2, 1863.

The Administrator of the Affairs of the Main Committee on the Organization of the Rural Estate, State Secretary Zhukovsky, has now communicated to the Minister of the Imperial Court and Crown Lands, for due execution, an extract from the Imperially confirmed journal of the Main Committee of February 1, 1877, whereby the Main Committee resolved: to confirm the said submission of the Minister of the Imperial Court and Crown Lands.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. LII. Pt. 1. P. 99.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 134.

The decision on the redemption by the St. Petersburg colonists of the crown lands on which they had been settled was made in accordance with the provisions of the Peasant Reform of 1861.

The small colony of Znamenskaya, founded in 1843 and part of Konstantinovskaya (Strelinskaya) volost, Peterhof district, has not previously been mentioned in the documents published in this edition.

## No. 135. DECREE OF ALEXANDER II ON THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE LIPPERT SCHOLARSHIPS (1877)

57046. — March 11. Personal decree, announced to the Senate by the Minister of Internal Affairs on April 22. — On assigning to the scholarships established from the interest on the capital donated by the colonist Lippert the designation "Lippert Scholarships."

Peter Lippert, a former colonist of Ekaterinenstadt, Samara governorate, by his testament of January 24, 1861, donated 5,000 rubles for the establishment, from the interest on this capital, of scholarships for the purpose of teaching various trades to poor children of settlers-proprietors of the Samara and Saratov governorates.

The Saratov Governor communicated to the Ministry of Internal Affairs a petition of the Congress of Delegates from the society of settlers-proprietors (former colonists) of the said governorates requesting permission to assign to these scholarships the designation "Lippert Scholarships," in memory of the deceased benefactor, as their original founder.

Upon the most loyal report on this matter, His Imperial Majesty, on the 11th day of March of this year, was Graciously pleased to grant the said petition.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. LII. Pt. 1. P. 187.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 135.

Lippert, Pyotr Ivanovich (?–1861) — grain merchant, owner of a farmstead in Verkhne-Kushumskaya volost, Novouzensk district, Samara governorate; in 1830 he initiated the writing of memoirs by a number of the first Volga colonists (published in the Volga Protestant journal *Friedensbote* in 1900–1901); in 1857 he was decorated for making donations toward the construction of the monument to Catherine II in Ekaterinstadt. From 1877, using donations from Lippert and certain other funds, the education and upbringing of colonist boys aged 12–16 was organized in private or trade schools for 5–8 years, after which they were required to work for at least 6 years in the area of the colonies in the trade they had learned. See: Dietz Ya.E. Op. cit. Pp. 11–12, 370.

## No. 137. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON THE ORGANIZATION OF LUTHERAN PARISHES IN THE SETTLEMENTS OF FORMER COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER II

76. — December 27, 1877. — Imperially confirmed opinion of the State Council, submitted to the Governing Senate by the Minister of State Domains on January 11, 1878. — On the administration of the properties of Evangelical-Lutheran churches in the settlements of settlers-proprietors (former colonists) and on the procedure for appointing preachers to them.

HIS IMPERIAL MAJESTY was Graciously pleased to confirm the opinion rendered in the General Assembly of the State Council on the administration of the properties of Evangelical-Lutheran churches in the settlements of settlers-proprietors (former colonists) and on the procedure for appointing preachers to them, and commanded that it be carried out.

Signed: Chairman of the State Council CONSTANTINE.

OPINION OF THE STATE COUNCIL. December 27, 1877.

Extracted from the journals of: the Joint Departments of Laws and State Economy of October 7, and the General Assembly of December 5, 1877.

The State Council, in the Joint Departments of Laws and State Economy and in General Assembly, having examined the submission of the Minister of State Domains on the administration of the properties of Evangelical-Lutheran churches in the settlements of settlers-proprietors (former colonists) and on the procedure for appointing preachers to them, and concurring in substance with the Minister's conclusion, resolved:

I. In amendment and supplement of the relevant statutes, to enact:

1) The administration of the properties of Evangelical-Lutheran churches in the settlements of settlers-proprietors (former colonies of foreign settlers) in the governorates of Samara, Saratov, Ekaterinoslav, Tavrida, Kherson, Bessarabia, and Voronezh (the settlement of Rybensdorf) shall be entrusted to church councils established in each parish, attached to the parish church, with the same rights granted to them and the same duties imposed upon them as are defined in the statutes in force for church councils in cities.

2) The said church councils must consist of no fewer than four members, namely: the parish preacher and three lay persons elected by the parishioners of the parish church; furthermore, the parishioners of filial churches shall be granted the right to elect one member to the church council from each filial church. The chairmanship of these councils shall, until further order, be entrusted to the parish preacher.

3) At filial churches, special church councils may be established, by resolution of the parishioners and with the permission of the General Evangelical-Lutheran Consistory, on the same bases as at parish churches. In such case the parishioners of the filial church shall not elect a member to the council of the parish church.

4) To parishes in the settlements of settlers-proprietors (former colonies of foreign settlers) shall be extended the effect of Article 294 of the Statutes on the Spiritual Affairs of Foreign Confessions (Digest of Laws, Vol. XI), granting parishioners the right to call and appoint preachers.

II. To disburse, at the disposal of the Minister of Internal Affairs, for augmenting the resources of the Evangelical-Lutheran General Consistory, from January 1, 1878, the sum of two thousand seven hundred ninety-two rubles and eighty-seven kopecks per year, charging this expenditure to the account of the public levy entered in the estimates of the Ministry of State Domains, collected from settlers-proprietors (former colonists) for the maintenance of the colonial administration.

III. The implementation of the enactments set forth in Article I shall be entrusted to the Minister of Internal Affairs. Arrangements for the review and transfer, as appropriate, of matters previously conducted within the Ministry of State Domains regarding the chief ecclesiastical trusteeship in the former colonies of foreign settlers, and regarding the filling of vacant parishes therein, shall be left to the mutual agreement of the Ministers of State Domains and Internal Affairs.

The original opinion is signed in the journals by the Chairmen and Members.

*SURP. 1878. 1st half-year. No. 20. Pp. 148-149.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 137.

In 1877, in accordance with art. II, para. 4 of the preamble to the Regulations of 1871 (doc. No. 129), the Saratov Office of Foreign Settlers and the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers of the Southern Territory ceased their activity. Prior to that, in accordance with the Statute on the Spiritual Affairs of Foreign Confessions (doc. No. 114), the administration of the property of churches in the Evangelical Lutheran colonies had been under the oversight of these bodies (art. 623), and the same bodies had served as intermediaries between the relevant Evangelical Lutheran consistory and the lay assembly of parishioners in the process of calling and appointing priests (art. 292). This act abolished these two special norms established for the colonist parishes.

It is notable in the document that the funds for the maintenance of the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory, which were contributed by the former colonists, were administered by the Ministry of Internal Affairs (art. II). This circumstance, together with similar provisions of the Statute on Spiritual Affairs, vividly illustrates the degree to which church life in the Russian Empire had been brought under state control.

## No. 138. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON THE SCHOOL AT THE MOSCOW LUTHERAN CHURCH OF SS. PETER AND PAUL, APPROVED BY ALEXANDER II (1878)

59059. — November 28. Opinion of the State Council, Highest confirmed. — On the reorganization of the school attached to the Evangelical-Lutheran Church of SS. Peter and Paul in Moscow.

The State Council, in the Joint Departments of Laws and of State Economy and in General Assembly, having examined the submission of the Minister of National Enlightenment on the reorganization of the school attached to the Evangelical-Lutheran Church of SS. Peter and Paul in Moscow, and agreeing in substance with the Minister's conclusion, resolved as its opinion:

I. To authorize the Church Council of the Evangelical-Lutheran Church of SS. Peter and Paul in Moscow, beginning with the 1878/79 academic year, to reorganize the school maintained at the expense of the said church on the following bases:

1. The said school, while under the general administration of the Church Council of the Church of SS. Peter and Paul, is subject to the authority of the Trustee of the Moscow educational district. It is divided into three sections: a) an elementary school, b) a Realschule with a commercial department, and c) a Gymnasium. As regards the organization of instruction and upbringing, the school is governed by the Statutes of Gymnasiums and Progymnasiums and of Realschulen, Highest confirmed on 30 July 1871 and 15 May 1872 (49860 and 50834), with the rules prescribed for Gymnasiums and Progymnasiums observed in respect of the elementary school and the gymnasium section, and the rules of the Statute on Realschulen observed in respect of the Realschule section, subject to the following exceptions:

2. The elementary school of the institution, corresponding to the preparatory class of government Gymnasiums and Progymnasiums, is divided into three annual courses and consists of two sections: one for children speaking Russian, and the other for those speaking German. Children who cannot yet read or write are admitted to the first course. In addition to the subjects taught in the preparatory class of Gymnasiums, German is added in the elementary school.

3. In the Realschule section, the teaching of general history and geography, arithmetic, correspondence and bookkeeping, and German may be conducted in German, and in the Gymnasium, the teaching of ancient languages and German, of general history and geography in all classes, and of arithmetic in the 1st and 2nd classes, may likewise be conducted in German.

4. Immediate administration of the school belongs to the School Council, composed of: the President of the Church Council, the senior pastor, the second preacher, two members of the Church Council chosen by it, one member elected by the general assembly of the church's parishioners for a term of three years, and the Director and Inspector of the school.

5. The School Council reviews the resolutions of the Pedagogical Council, receives and verifies the reports on the academic and educational condition of the school submitted by the Director, elects, upon the Director's proposals, teachers, tutors, and other persons employed at the school, grants employees leave within the limits of authority granted to Directors of government Gymnasiums and Realschulen, submits recommendations for the dismissal of employees, exempts needy and deserving pupils from tuition fees, and awards stipends.

6. The Director and Inspector of the school are elected upon the proposal of the School Council at a joint session of the Church Council and the School Council. The Church Council submits, through the Trustee of the Moscow educational district, the confirmation of the Director of the school in office to the Minister of National Enlightenment. The Inspector and other officials of the school, in a number not exceeding that established by the Statutes and staff tables of Gymnasiums, Progymnasiums, and Realschulen, are confirmed in office by the Trustee of the district.

II. To grant the employees of the School of SS. Peter and Paul all the service rights bestowed by the Statutes of 30 July 1871 and 15 May 1872, Highest confirmed, upon employees of government Gymnasiums, Progymnasiums, and Realschulen, except for the right to receive from the treasury a third of a term's salary not counted toward pay upon appointment to service, as well as the right to lump-sum benefits and pensions for service at the school, applying in this regard the provisions of the Statute on Gymnasiums and Progymnasiums to employees of the elementary school and gymnasium section of the school, and the provisions of the Statute on Realschulen to employees of the Realschule section.

III. To extend to pupils studying in the Realschule and gymnasium sections of the School of SS. Peter and Paul the rights enjoyed by pupils of the corresponding government educational institutions of the Department of the Ministry of National Enlightenment.

IV. To authorize the Minister of National Enlightenment to confirm, on these bases, the Statute of the School of SS. Peter and Paul in Moscow.

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was pleased to confirm, Highest, the opinion rendered in the General Assembly of the State Council on the reorganization of the school attached to the Evangelical-Lutheran Church of SS. Peter and Paul in Moscow, and commanded that it be carried out.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. LIII. Pt. 2. Pp. 256-257.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 138.

The school at the Moscow Evangelical Lutheran Church of Sts. Peter and Paul was founded as early as 1626, at the same time as the parish itself. Already in the second half of the 19th century the church maintained 5 educational institutions: boys' and girls' gymnasiums, a real school for boys, and primary schools for boys and girls; by 1910 they had about 1,400 pupils. See: Kovrigina V., Petrov Yu. Moscow // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. P. 567.

## No. 139. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON EXEMPTIONS FROM MILITARY SERVICE FOR FOREIGN SETTLERS, APPROVED BY ALEXANDER II (1878)

59120. — December 12. Opinion of the State Council, Highest confirmed, published 3 January 1879. — On granting exemption from military conscription to foreign settlers who settled in Russia on the same terms as the persons named in point 1 of note 1 to Article 62 of the Statute on Military Conscription (1876 edition).

The State Council, in the Special Presence on Military Conscription and in General Assembly, having examined the submission of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs on granting exemption from military conscription to peasant-proprietors, former Austrian subjects of Czech nationality, who settled in 1860–1870 in Perekop county, Tavrida governorate, resolved as its opinion to decree: "The exemption from military conscription specified in point 1 of note 1 to Article 62 of the Statute on Military Conscription, 1876 edition, shall be enjoyed, in addition to the persons named in that point, also by all other foreign settlers who settled in Russia on the same terms as those persons. Should any doubts arise in applying this rule, the Ministers of Internal Affairs and of War shall submit reports to the Special Presence on Military Conscription."

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was pleased to confirm, Highest, the opinion rendered in the General Assembly of the State Council on granting exemption from military conscription to foreign settlers who settled in Russia on the same terms as the persons named in point 1 of note 1 to Article 62 of the Statute on Military Conscription (1876 edition), and commanded that it be carried out.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. LIII. Pt. 2. P. 301.*

**Compiler's endnote (Примечание):**

### No. 139.

Under the Military Service Statute of 1874, sons of foreign colonists who had settled on private lands on the basis of the decree of 18 December 1861 and had accepted Russian citizenship, and who had been born before their arrival in Russia, were exempted for life from military service. Among the German colonists, this privilege applied chiefly to peasants who had moved to the southwestern governorates from Poland during the Polish uprising of 1863–1864. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. S. 310.

Czechs who settled in Perekop uezd founded 4 colonies in 1863–1864: Tabor (Tabor-Kirei) — Dzhurchinskaia (Ishunskaia) volost, Bogemka (Dzhadra) — Bogemskaia (Burlaktaminskaia) volost, Tsarekvich (Kurman-Kemelchi) — Aleksandrovskaia volost, and Aleksandrovka 3rd (Kemelchi) — Aleksandrovskaia (Aibarskaia) volost. In time, Germans came to make up a significant part of their population (in the last two, the majority).
